# OpenTAP Architecture Brainstorm 03 (async replication, SVM-first, single-node-first): full record

Produced 2026-10-12 by a workflow of four specialist personas (round 1), cross-examination (round 2), independent web fact-checks of the load-bearing claims, revised positions (round 3), and four critics (completeness, ONTAP veteran, homelab operator, Rust/kernel implementer). The charter is docs/04-project-brief-async-svm.md. The lead architect's synthesis, trait contracts and Phase C plan are in 05-architecture-brainstorm-03.md. Headings inside each agent's text are demoted three levels.

Provenance note: the workflow ran 57 agents between 19:22 and 22:36 on 2026-10-12. The homelab-operator critic finished its document but its return to the workflow failed on the account's usage limit, so the workflow recorded an empty result for it. The document it had written to its working file (review.md, 24,571 bytes, saved 22:36:16, complete with eight sections and a closing list) is included below unchanged. Everything else is the workflow's own output.

## Round 1: brainstorms

### Opus-Storage

#### Opus-Storage, Session 03: the single-node engine, the async delta shipper and nvfail

##### 1. Executive take

The pivot removes the partner from the acknowledgement path, and that changes what every engine structure is for. In round 2 the arena was half of a mirrored log, the CP was a drain, and the partner's inbound ring was the durability device. Now the arena is the only copy of an acknowledged write until the CP commits; the CP is the unit of durability, replication, snapshots and rollback; and the partner is a consumer that runs behind the CP. Three things follow. First, the acknowledgement is a local insert: the engine's share is 2.5 to 5 us on a busy-polled reactor (table in 2.7) and nothing on the data path waits for a network. Second, "one CP window of acknowledged writes" is the loss figure for every unplanned event, on a single node and after a takeover alike, so the arena is sized by exposure (about 10 s of ingest), not by link arithmetic, and nvfail stops being a dual-power-loss special case and becomes the engine's standard answer to any boot or promotion that is not at the acknowledged state. Third, the sync-era machinery (`MirrorLink`, `MirrorInbound`, `BatchPage`, `Placed`, `Credit`, the `GrantUnmirrored` hysteresis, the tmpfs inbound ring and `otap-ringd`) has no job left; its 8 GiB goes to a read cache and the CP staging pool, and the replication engine is built on the CP's own output. Phase C's real novelty is portability: the flusher must find full stripes on a PERC virtual drive, an LSI IR volume, an mdadm RAID6 and a lone NVMe, and must know which of them hides its write cache.

Top five positions:

1. The CP's write set is the delta: steady-state replication ships the CP's staged stripe images (a self-describing summary page plus data) straight from the hugetlbfs staging pool with `IORING_OP_SEND_ZC`, so the on-disk stripe format, the CP log and the wire chunk are one format, and the map walk over `birth > base` (pruned by a per-page `max_birth`) serves only catch-up and resync.
2. Replication direction and state are per volume, the transport is per aggregate pair, and the receiver applies each sender CP atomically through per-volume shadow roots switched at one receiver CP, so a replica is always at a sender CP boundary and multi-volume consistency groups cost nothing.
3. nvfail is decided by on-disk evidence only: a `run_state` field and a per-volume `write_active` set in the superblock, kept exact by one FUA intent write per idle-to-active transition, evaluated at boot after a dirty shutdown and at promotion of a lagging replica, on by default for LUN and datastore classes and alert-only for file and object classes (owner decision).
4. Geometry is read from md sysfs when the backstore is md and otherwise found by a mandatory write-amplification probe at pool creation; hardware-RAID write-back is accepted only with an attested cache protection; discard defaults to `Never`; and the commit protocol tolerates one torn CP because a segment freed by CP N is never reused before CP N+1 commits.
5. Cut `otap-ringd` and the inbound ring: in Phase C the arena is a systemd-created hugetlbfs file the engine re-attaches to, the CP is triggered by a timer (10 s HDD, 5 s flash), the arena half-full mark, a snapshot or a ship deadline, and back-pressure exists only when CP N+1's half fills while CP N is still draining, capped at 2 s per request and then Transitioning, exactly as R7 says.

##### 2. Design

###### 2.1 Focus 1: the single-node allocator: dirty index, CP assembly, full-stripe flush

**What stays from round 2.** Thread-per-core reactors on `io-uring` 0.7.15 [verified: https://crates.io/crates/io-uring] with `IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER` and `IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN`, both in the 6.12 uapi header [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h]; one ublk device per LUN with `libublk` 0.4.8 (0.4.7 and 0.4.3 are yanked; pin exactly and vendor) [verified: https://crates.io/crates/libublk]; the hugetlbfs arena with 2 MiB pages reserved at boot; CRC32C through `crc-fast` 1.10.0 [verified: https://crates.io/crates/crc-fast]; `zerocopy` 0.8.62 for every `repr(C)` page [verified: https://crates.io/crates/zerocopy]; `rustix` 1.1.5 and `memmap2` 0.9.11 for mmap, `fallocate` and the block ioctls [verified: https://crates.io/crates/rustix and https://crates.io/crates/memmap2]; never-overwrite segments, four superblock slots, `MediaProfile` as the only media knob.

**The write path.** A ublk WRITE arrives as a CQE on the reactor that owns the LUN's queues. The reactor reserves a slot run in the arena (a per-reactor bump allocator with a lap counter; a run is 1 to 256 slots of 4 KiB), issues `IORING_OP_READ_FIXED` on `/dev/ublkcN` at the user-copy position (`UBLKSRV_IO_BUF_OFFSET` 0x80000000 plus the queue and tag fields; `UBLK_F_USER_COPY` is documented as "Copy between request and user buffer by pread()/pwrite()" and is "Not available for UBLK_F_UNPRIVILEGED_DEV" [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/uapi/linux/ublk_cmd.h]), so the one kernel copy lands directly in the slot. On completion it computes CRC32C per 4 KiB, takes the next aggregate-wide `seq`, inserts into the volume's dirty index and issues `UBLK_IO_COMMIT_AND_FETCH_REQ`. That commit is the acknowledgement. Nothing else is on the path; the partner is not consulted.

**The dirty index: how random writes queue.** One `BTreeMap<u64, DirtyExtent>` per volume per generation, keyed by LBA in 4 KiB units, value `{len, slot: RingRef, seq, mask}`. An insert splits or trims any older overlapping entry, so a generation holds the newest bytes for every LBA and nothing else: a block overwritten five times in one interval occupies one entry and ships once. Memory is about 80 B per entry including node overhead; an 8 GiB arena is at most 2 M slots, so a generation is at most 160 MiB and the two generations (active, frozen) are the 0.3 GiB line in the budget. The sorted key order is what turns random writes into sequential ones: the CP walks each volume in LBA order and the physical write is sequential by construction (log-structured), while logically adjacent blocks written minutes apart land adjacent on disk, which helps later sequential reads modestly and makes the shipping order deterministic (a resumable cursor is a `(vol, lba)` pair). Read-your-writes resolves active, then frozen, then the in-memory map overlay (2.1, "map"), then the map; patch records for the `Esxi512e` class keep a sector mask and are merged at CP time against the old block, which was pinned into the read cache at ingest (round 2 rule, unchanged).

**The cut.** The epoch-flip cut stands: the CP engine swaps the active generation, then waits until no reactor is inside an insert of the old epoch (`crossbeam` 0.8.5 epoch pins per insert, about 20 to 50 ns each; the wait is under 50 us) [verified: https://crates.io/crates/crossbeam]. A seq-prefix is then exactly an image a power cut could have produced, because a guest can only make W2 depend on W1 by waiting for W1's commit, which happens after W1's insert.

**CP assembly: the staging pool.** The frozen generation is drained volume by volume in LBA order; adjacent dirty extents coalesce into runs; runs are packed into stripe images in a hugetlbfs staging pool. A stripe image is `[summary pages][data blocks]`: the summary carries a 64 B header (`agg, cp_seq, seg, stripe_idx, nblocks, crc`) and 16 B per data block (`vol: u32, lba: u64 (4 KiB units), birth: u32 = cp_seq` folded with `crc32c: u32`), rounded up to 4 KiB, so a 2.5 MiB HDD stripe spends 12 KiB (0.5%) and a 256 KiB flash stripe 4 KiB (1.6%). The last stripe of a CP is padded and the pad is accounted free. Why stage rather than gather from slots: 6.12 has `IORING_OP_WRITE_FIXED` but no `IORING_OP_WRITEV_FIXED` (absent from the 6.12 header; the crate exposes `WritevFixed`, which 6.12 rejects) [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h and https://docs.rs/io-uring/0.7.15/io_uring/opcode/index.html], so a gather from registered buffers would be a plain `WRITEV` with up to 640 iovecs pinned per call; staging gives one SQE with two huge-page bvecs per stripe, merges patches in place, decouples slot layout from disk layout (compression later), and hands the shipper one contiguous buffer per stripe. Cost: every byte is copied once more, 0.12 core at 1.2 GB/s and 0.4 core at 4 GB/s, assuming 10 GB/s single-core hugetlbfs-to-hugetlbfs memcpy. Slots are freed as soon as their bytes are staged; the staging buffer, also in hugetlbfs, is the recovery source for a daemon crash mid-CP (a power cut loses both, by design).

**Flush and commit.** Data stripes go out as `WRITE_FIXED` with O_DIRECT, 32 stripes in flight per HDD array (80 MiB, 67 ms of queue at 1.2 GB/s) and 64 per flash array. Then the metadata stream, on the flash metadata class when one exists and on the pool otherwise: the CP log record (the CP's extent list, 16 B per block, so a 4 GiB CP of 4 KiB random writes logs 16 MiB), the segment-table delta, the snapshot table delta, and changed map pages when a map checkpoint is due. Then one flush: `IORING_OP_FSYNC` with `IORING_FSYNC_DATASYNC` on the block device fd, which md raid456 serves through `md_flush_request` when no journal device is present [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/md/raid5.c]. Then the superblock stripe, written with `RWF_DSYNC`, which the block layer turns into REQ_FUA where `queue/fua` is 1 and into write-plus-flush otherwise [believed]; raid456 propagates REQ_FUA to the member bios, parity devices included, through `R5_WantFUA` [verified: raid5.c, `ops_run_biodrain`, `ops_complete_reconstruct`, `ops_run_io`]. Slots and staging buffers of the CP are released after the superblock completion (staging only once the shipper has released them, 2.2).

**The torn-CP rule.** Readers take the superblock with the highest `(epoch, cp_seq)` whose map roots verify (R19). For a fall-back to CP N-1 to be safe when CP N is torn by a controller that lost its cache, nothing CP N-1 references may have been overwritten: therefore a segment freed by CP N enters the free list only when CP N+1 commits. It costs one CP's worth of freed space in flight (under 4 GiB) and makes the four-slot superblock ring a real rewind, not decoration.

**The map in Phase C.** Per-volume two-level radix map: a page index (8 B per 4 MiB of LBA, 20 MB for 10 TB) kept in memory, and 16 KiB pages of 1024 entries (`pba: u64` as `seg:28 | off:20 | plen:16`, `birth: u32`, `crc32c: u32`), so 0.4% of volume size on disk, and every read verifies the block's CRC against its map entry, which also catches misdirected writes. The map is not rewritten per CP: a random 4 KiB write would dirty a 16 KiB page (4x amplification). Instead the CP log is the map's journal, an in-memory overlay (up to 1.4 GB in the pathological 250 K-IOPS case, about 100 MB normally) answers lookups for entries since the last checkpoint, and a map checkpoint (dirty pages rewritten copy-on-write in page order) runs when the CP log exceeds 1 GiB or 10 minutes, whichever first, so boot replay stays under 5 s at 200 MB/s. Each page-index entry carries `max_birth` of its page; that is what makes the `diff` walk cheap (2.4). Hole extents are first-class entries (`pba = HOLE`, with a birth) for the reason in 2.2. The extent B+tree of round 2 moves to Phase 3 with compression.

**md versus hardware RAID in the flusher.** On md the geometry is exact: raid456 sets `io_min = chunk_sectors << 9` and `io_opt = io_min * (raid_disks - max_degraded)` [verified: raid5.c `raid5_set_limits`], so `/sys/block/mdN/queue/optimal_io_size` is the full data stripe; `stripe_cache_size` 32768 and `group_thread_cnt` as in round 2; the write-intent bitmap stays (a 128 MiB bitmap chunk costs one 4 KiB update per region transition and is what saves a 20-hour resync after a crash); discard needs `devices_handle_discard_safely` and whole stripes (Appendix A) and is off on HDD anyway. A hardware-RAID virtual drive is a plain SCSI disk to the kernel: geometry comes from VPD B0 or from the probe (2.6); its write cache is usually invisible (2.6); discard is usually absent; and `max_sectors_kb` may split a 2.5 MiB stripe into 256 KiB commands, which matters on write-through controllers (2.6). A lone NVMe reports `io_opt` 0: the profile uses 1 MiB write units, 64 MiB segments and whole-segment `BLKDISCARD` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/uapi/linux/fs.h] after RZAT verification.

```rust
pub struct Geometry { pub stripe_data_bytes: u32, pub chunk_bytes: u32, pub data_disks: u16,
    pub alignment_offset: u32, pub max_sectors_bytes: u32, pub discard: DiscardCaps,
    pub write_cache: WriteCacheView /* KernelWriteBack | KernelWriteThrough */,
    pub source: GeomSource /* MdSysfs | VpdB0 | Probe { knee_bytes, ratio } | Manual */ }
pub struct MediaProfile { pub geom: Geometry, pub segment_bytes: u64 /* whole stripes; 80 MiB HDD, 8 MiB flash, 64 MiB NVMe */,
    pub cp_timer: Duration /* 10 s HDD, 5 s flash */, pub arena_bytes: u64, pub staging_bytes: u64,
    pub inflight_stripes: u16 /* 32 HDD, 64 flash */, pub metadata_class: Option<DevPath>,
    pub cache_protection: CacheProtection /* Bbu | FlashBacked | None | Unknown */,
    pub reserves: (f32, f32, f32) /* 0.70, 0.80, 0.90 */ }
pub trait Backstore {                       // Md | HwRaidVd | SingleNvme
    fn profile(&self) -> &MediaProfile;
    fn write_stripe(&mut self, seg: SegId, idx: u32, staged: StagedStripe, tag: u64) -> Result<(), Busy>; // WRITE_FIXED, O_DIRECT
    fn write_meta(&mut self, pba: Pba, pages: &[MetaPage], tag: u64) -> Result<(), Busy>;
    fn flush(&mut self, tag: u64) -> Result<(), Busy>;                                   // FSYNC datasync on the bdev
    fn commit(&mut self, sb: &Superblock, slot: SbSlot, tag: u64) -> Result<(), Busy>;    // RWF_DSYNC stripe
    fn read(&mut self, pba: Pba, len: u32, dst: &mut [u8], tag: u64) -> Result<(), Busy>; // CRC checked by the caller against the map
    fn discard_segment(&mut self, seg: SegId) -> Result<(), Busy>;                        // no-op under Discard::Never
    fn poll(&mut self, out: &mut Vec<Done>) -> usize;
}
pub trait Allocator {                        // the D-Blade allocator the synthesis asked for
    fn reserve(&mut self, lun: LunId, nslots: u32) -> Result<RingRef, Full>;              // bump + lap; never blocks past the throttle
    fn insert(&mut self, vol: VolId, lba: u64, ext: DirtyExtent) -> Seq;                  // split/trim; epoch-pinned
    fn cut(&mut self) -> Generation;                                                      // epoch flip + grace
    fn stage(&mut self, gen: &Generation, out: &mut StagingPool) -> CpProgram;            // LBA-ordered packing, patch merge
    fn release(&mut self, cp: CpSeq);                                                     // slots and staging after commit
}
```

###### 2.2 Focus 2: the async snapshot and delta shipper

**How dirty extent boundaries are tracked.** The boundary between CPs is the cut. Every extent packed by CP N is stamped `birth = N` in its summary entry, in the CP log and in the map. Holes are tracked the same way: a discard, a WRITE SAME of zeroes or a volume shrink writes a hole extent with `birth = N`, because a stream that only ships "blocks with birth greater than base" silently misses blocks that became zero, which is precisely the OpenZFS hole-birth defect class, where holes with a zero birth were left out of incremental sends and the destination silently diverged [verified: https://openzfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Project%20and%20Community/FAQ%20hole%20birth.html]. Hole entries older than the oldest pinned snapshot are elided at map checkpoint time. The invariant the property tests encode: every logical change, including a free, carries a birth, and `diff(base)` over the map equals the union of CP write sets for `cp > base` with later writes winning.

**Serialization.** The stream is a sequence of records framed by Fabrics; the content is mine:

```rust
pub enum StreamRec<'a> {
    CpBegin { agg: AggId, cp: CpSeq, vols: &'a [VolDelta] /* create/delete/resize/rename */, snaps: &'a [SnapEvent],
              write_active: VolBitSet, acked_bytes: &'a [(VolId, u64)], mode: Mode /* Steady | CatchUp { from: SnapUuid, to: SnapUuid } */ },
    Chunk  { cp: CpSeq, idx: u32, image: &'a [u8] /* one staged stripe image: summary pages + data, verbatim */ },
    CpEnd  { cp: CpSeq, nchunks: u32, bytes: u64, digest: [u8; 32] /* blake3 over chunk summaries in idx order */,
             sb: SuperblockDigest /* the sender's map roots per volume, for the weekly full compare */ },
    Heartbeat { cp_committed: CpSeq, acked_seq: u64, write_active: VolBitSet, lag_hint_bytes: u64 },
}
pub trait DeltaSource {                      // sender side, one per aggregate pair; direction per volume
    fn next(&mut self, budget: usize, out: &mut Vec<StreamRec<'_>>) -> Progress;        // Steady: staging buffers; CatchUp: disk reads
    fn ack(&mut self, applied: CpSeq, cursor: Cursor);                                   // releases staging holds, advances base
    fn detach_to_disk(&mut self, cp: CpSeq);                                             // called when the hold budget is exceeded
    fn direction(&self, vol: VolId) -> Direction;
}
pub trait DeltaSink {                        // receiver side, inside dbladed
    fn begin(&mut self, b: &CpBegin) -> Result<(), Reject /* base mismatch, direction epoch */>;
    fn apply_chunk(&mut self, c: &Chunk) -> Result<Cursor, Corrupt>;                     // stage into own segments, shadow roots
    fn end(&mut self, e: &CpEnd) -> Result<Applied, Corrupt>;                            // verified; switched at the next own CP
    fn resume_point(&self) -> Option<(CpSeq, Cursor)>;                                   // survives receiver restart and reboot
}
```

Records are self-describing because the chunk is the stripe image: the receiver parses the summary, verifies each 4 KiB CRC (`crc-fast` 1.10.0, about 20 GB/s per core [believed]), and treats the chunk as a container of `(vol, lba, data)` records, never as a stripe. That is what makes the stream geometry-independent: a 2.5 MiB chunk from an mdadm sender is repacked into 256 KiB stripes on a flash receiver by the receiver's own CP assembler. `blake3` 1.8.7 [verified: https://crates.io/crates/blake3] digests the summaries per CP; `postcard` 1.1.3 encodes the non-chunk records [verified: https://crates.io/crates/postcard]; `lz4_flex` 0.14.0 or `zstd` 0.14.2 are available to Fabrics for optional compression of chunks [verified: https://crates.io/crates/lz4_flex and https://crates.io/crates/zstd]. The arena-era `Patch` op does not exist on the wire: patches are merged at staging, so every shipped block is a full 4 KiB.

**Steady state: ship from the staging pool as the CP flushes.** The shipper is a consumer of the CP program. As each stripe image is staged, it is queued to the shipper and to the flusher at once; the shipper sends it with `IORING_OP_SEND_ZC` using `IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF` from the registered staging pool [verified: io_uring.h, 6.12 has both and `IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS`], and the buffer is released when the disk write and the send notification have both completed. The hold budget is 2 GiB of staging (budget table in 2.8): at 10GbE (1.1 GB/s) against 1.2 GB/s of ingest the hold grows at 0.1 GB/s and lasts 20 s; against 2 GB/s of flash ingest it lasts 2 s. When exceeded, the shipper detaches from CP N, releases its holds, marks the volume `Lagging`, and the CP engine takes a transfer snapshot at the next cut. Steady-state lag is therefore one CP interval plus ship time: on HDD at 10 s CPs and 1 GB/s ingest a CP is 10 GB and ships in 9 s on 10GbE, so a replica is 10 to 19 s behind; on 25GbE 10 to 13 s; a 5 s flash CP at 2 GB/s is 10 GB and needs 25GbE to keep steady state at all.

**Catch-up and resync: ship from disk by map walk.** In `CatchUp`, the sender pins a transfer snapshot T (the latest CP), walks each volume's page index for pages with `max_birth > base`, reads only those pages, emits entries with `birth > base` (later births win by construction, so overwritten blocks ship once) and holes, reads the data from disk in PBA order per volume, and packs it into chunks with freshly built summaries. The read pattern is the CP's own fresh segments, so it is largely sequential; the shipper is capped at 30% of the pool's read bandwidth so it never starves clients. When the walk ends, T becomes the new base, and if the next round is a single CP, the volume returns to `Steady`. Each round shrinks; this is SnapMirror's convergence loop. Resync is the same walk after a rollback (2.5).

**The sender relationship state machine (per volume).**

| State | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Idle | relationship created, no common snapshot | full copy = CatchUp with base = none | CatchUp |
| Steady | CP N cut | queue CP N chunks from staging | Steady |
| Steady | hold budget exceeded or link down > 10 s | detach; release holds; alert if lag > 60 s | Lagging |
| Lagging | link up and receiver cursor known | pin transfer snapshot T; start walk from base | CatchUp |
| CatchUp | walk complete and receiver applied T | base = T; drop old base pin | Steady if one CP behind, else CatchUp |
| any | receiver reports base mismatch (divergence) | compute newest common snapshot; receiver rolls back | Resync |
| Resync | receiver rolled back to common C | walk from C | CatchUp |
| any | pool crosses `break_at` because of the base pin, or no common snapshot survives | drop pins; CRIT alert | Broken |
| Broken | operator `resync` or a common scheduled snapshot exists on both sides | pick newest common | Resync |
| any | operator `pause` | keep pins; stop sending | Paused |

**The receiver: always at a CP boundary.** The receiver stages CP N's records into its own fresh segments through its own CP assembler, updates a per-volume shadow root (a writable child root in the CoW sense; for the radix map it is a copy of the page index with CoW pages), and at `CpEnd` verifies the digest. The shadow roots become the visible roots at the receiver's next own CP, all volumes of sender CP N together, so a replica never exposes half a CP and consistency groups are free. If the stream breaks mid-CP, the partial data stays in segments that no visible root references, the receiver's own periodic CP persists `(cp, cursor, partial segments)` in its superblock, and the sender resumes from the cursor; a receiver reboot loses nothing. Apply cost equals a local CP: sequential full-stripe writes plus the CP log, so a receiver on the same media as the sender keeps up exactly when the sender's pool would.

| Receiver state | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Idle | `CpBegin` with base == my applied CP for every volume | open shadow roots | Receiving(N) |
| Idle | `CpBegin` with base mismatch | reply Reject{my snapshots} | Idle |
| Receiving(N) | `Chunk` | CRC each block, stage, advance cursor | Receiving(N) |
| Receiving(N) | link lost | persist cursor at my next CP | Partial(N) |
| Partial(N) | sender resumes at cursor | continue | Receiving(N) |
| Receiving(N) | `CpEnd` verifies | mark N complete | Committing(N) |
| Committing(N) | my CP commits | switch roots; record `promote_hint` from `CpBegin`; ack N | Idle |
| Receiving(N) | digest or CRC failure | discard N; request resend from cursor 0 | Idle |

**Transport.** Fabrics owns framing, flow control, TLS, compression and link selection; the contract I need is an ordered byte stream per connection, resumability at `(cp, chunk idx, byte offset)`, up to 4 connections with out-of-order chunks allowed inside a CP (the receiver counts completions), and zero-copy sends from the registered staging pool. FC as a bulk transport is priced in Fabrics' section; from my side it is a `DeltaSink` whose chunks arrive by a kernel target writing into a tmpfs file, which the receiver scans, and I recommend not building it before Phase B is proven on TCP.

###### 2.3 Focus 3: nvfail: state machine and on-disk flags

**On-disk evidence.** The superblock carries everything nvfail needs; nothing in `/var` or in Raft is load-bearing for it (invariant 9).

```rust
#[repr(C)] pub struct Superblock {           // v2; four slots A0 A1 B0 B1; max (epoch, cp_seq) whose roots verify
    pub ver: u16, pub agg: AggId, pub epoch: u64, pub cp_seq: CpSeq, pub cut_seq: u64,
    pub run_state: u8,            // Running | CleanShutdown
    pub write_active: VolBitSet,  // volumes that may have acknowledged writes not covered by this CP
    pub acked_bytes: [u64; MAX_VOLS],   // bytes acknowledged since the previous CP, for the alert's estimate
    pub nvfail: VolBitSet,        // volumes currently offline in nvfail; persists across reboots until cleared
    pub nvfail_cause: [NvCause; MAX_VOLS],  // DirtyBoot{cp_seq, wall_ns, window_ms} | Promote{rel, lag_cps, lag_bytes}
    pub freed_pending: SegListPba, // segments freed by this CP, reusable only after the next commit
    pub map_roots: Pba, pub seg_table: Pba, pub cp_log_head: Pba, pub snap_table: Pba,
    pub promote_hint: [PromoteHint; MAX_RELS],  // last CpBegin/Heartbeat write_active + acked_bytes per inbound relationship
    pub opened_stamp: u64, pub wall_ns: u64, pub crc: u32,
}
```

**Precision: the intent write.** `write_active` must be set on disk before the first acknowledgement it covers, otherwise a dirty boot cannot tell an idle volume from one that lost 9 s of writes. Rule: a volume is "active" from its first write after an idle period until it has been idle for two consecutive CPs. The idle-to-active transition writes a superblock (one FUA stripe: 5 to 15 ms on HDD, 0.1 to 0.5 ms on flash) with the bit set before the write is acknowledged; the active-to-idle transition clears the bit at an ordinary CP. A steady workload pays nothing, a bursty one pays one FUA stripe per burst, and the list in the alert is exact. `nvfail_intent = conservative` skips the intent write and treats every writable online volume as active; it is for operators who would rather have a longer list than a 10 ms first-write latency.

**Evaluation at boot (dirty shutdown).** Max-select the superblock; if `run_state == Running`, this is a dirty boot: for every volume in `write_active` with `nvfail = on` for its class, set `nvfail[vol]` with `DirtyBoot{cp_seq, wall_ns, window}` where the window is now minus `wall_ns` of the CP, bounded by the arena's interval; write that superblock (FUA) before any device is exported, so the state survives a second reboot; then raise the CRIT alert with the volume list, the CP sequence, the window and the per-volume `acked_bytes` estimate, and the clear command. Clean shutdown writes a final CP with `run_state = CleanShutdown` and an empty `write_active`, so it never trips.

**Evaluation at promotion (stale replica).** When a replica is promoted with lag, the receiver's `promote_hint` for the relationship (the sender's last `write_active` and `acked_bytes`, refreshed by every `CpBegin` and every 1 s heartbeat) names the volumes that had acknowledged writes beyond the applied CP. Those with `nvfail = on` go to nvfail with `Promote{rel, lag_cps, lag_bytes}`; idle volumes come online directly. Consensus' `max_auto_takeover_lag` gate and the fence evidence precede this; I only consume the decision.

**The state machine (per volume).**

| State | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Online(idle) | first write after idle | intent superblock with `write_active[v]=1`, then ack | Online(active) |
| Online(active) | two CPs with no write | clear bit at CP | Online(idle) |
| Online(active) | clean shutdown | final CP, `run_state = CleanShutdown` | Offline(clean) |
| Offline(clean) | boot | export | Online(idle) |
| Online(active) | power loss or crash with no final CP | nothing (volatile) | Offline(dirty) |
| Offline(dirty) | boot, class policy `on` | set `nvfail[v]`, FUA superblock, alert, LUN Unavailable and exports withdrawn via `nbladed` | NvFailed |
| Offline(dirty) | boot, class policy `alert` | alert only, export | Online(idle) |
| Replica(applied K) | promoted, `promote_hint.write_active[v]` set, policy `on` | set `nvfail[v]` with `Promote` | NvFailed |
| Replica(applied K) | promoted, bit clear or policy `alert` | export | Online(idle) |
| NvFailed | `otapctl volume nvfail-clear <vol>` | clear bit, superblock, re-export | Online(idle) |
| NvFailed | `nvfail-clear --restore <snap>` | roll the root back to the snapshot first | Online(idle) |
| NvFailed | any I/O | fail with EIO at the engine (defence in depth; the client-visible state is `nbladed`'s) | NvFailed |

**Class defaults (owner decision; this is the prepared table).**

| Volume class | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Block LUN (iSCSI, FC, NVMe-oF) | `on` | the hypervisor's journals and caches are ahead of the disk; silent corruption otherwise |
| NAS datastore (NFSv3 for ESXi and Proxmox) | `on` | VM disks on NFS have the same exposure as LUNs |
| NAS file (NFSv4.1, SMB home and project shares) | `alert` | XFS replays cleanly at the CP boundary; clients see lost recent saves, not corrupt metadata; an outage costs more than a notice |
| Object (versitygw buckets) | `alert` | PUTs are idempotent and clients retry; multipart parts in flight are re-uploaded |
| SVM root volume | `on` | tenant state (`secrets.tdb`, `nfsdcld`) must not silently rewind |

Auto-clear after a configurable delay (R5's single-UPS option) stays an install-time opt-in; it is dangerous for LUN classes and the installer says so.

###### 2.4 Is the CP's own write set the delta, or a map walk? What does the receiver need?

The CP's write set is exactly the set of map entries with `birth == N`, so the two are the same data; the difference is where it is read from and whether later writes have compacted it. Steady state ships the write set from the staging pool: zero disk reads, zero extra serialization CPU, and the stream is at most one CP behind. Catch-up and resync use the map walk: it reads from disk, but it is compacted (a block overwritten in 50 CPs ships once) and it needs no record of which CPs were missed, only the base. The crossover is the hold budget: once the shipper falls more than 2 GiB behind the flusher, reading later from disk is cheaper than holding staging memory, and the walk's compaction pays for the reads. The receiver needs, per CP: every record (chunks) with per-block CRCs; the volume-table and snapshot events of that CP; the hole records; a completion marker with a count and a digest; the sender's `write_active` and `acked_bytes` for nvfail; and its own shadow roots so that visibility changes only at its own CP commit. It does not need the sender's physical addresses, segment numbers or geometry, and it never needs the sender's superblock to be at the same `cp_seq` numbering as its own: common snapshots are pairs `(SnapUuid, sender cp_seq, receiver cp_seq)` in both snapshot tables, and each side's `birth` values are local.

###### 2.5 Base snapshot pins, space, the partner away for a day, spill and break

**What is pinned.** On both sides the relationship pins the newest common snapshot (the base) and, during a transfer, the transfer snapshot; the previous base is dropped only when the new base is acknowledged by the receiver. Every scheduled snapshot that exists on both sides is also a candidate base, which is what makes `Broken` recoverable without a full copy: with a daily schedule retained on both sides, breaking the base pin costs at most one day of resync.

**Resync in both directions after a takeover.** Node A owned volume V, acknowledged through CP M, had shipped through CP K; B was promoted at K and has written K'1..K'j. When A returns (fenced by Consensus, never acknowledging), the newest common snapshot is K, which both sides still pin. A rolls V back to K: its page index is reset to the pinned K root, and a `diff(K)` walk over the abandoned root yields the PBAs to free (data of M-K CPs). By default A first pins the abandoned root as snapshot `divergent-<timestamp>` (`keep_divergent_days = 7`, autodeleted at space pressure) so an operator can clone it and recover a file a guest wrote in the last seconds before the crash. A then becomes the receiver with base K and B walks `birth > K` in its own numbering. The direction flip is a Raft fact (a per-volume direction epoch); my `DeltaSink::begin` rejects any `CpBegin` whose direction epoch is older than the one Raft gave me, which is how an un-fenced late sender is refused at the data layer.

**Space when the partner is away.** The base pin holds every block that has been overwritten or freed since the base, not new allocations. For a day away:

| Unique overwrite rate | Held after 24 h | On a 100 TB pool at 60% used | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 MB/s (typical homelab VMs) | 0.86 TB | 60.9% | nothing |
| 50 MB/s (busy lab) | 4.3 TB | 64.3% | nothing |
| 200 MB/s (sustained churn) | 17 TB | 77% | GC runs at `gc_start` 70%, drain curve falls to about 0.4 GB/s |
| 1 GB/s (synthetic) | 86 TB | over the pool | break within hours |

**Spill policy.** The relationship has `on_space_pressure = break | hold`. `break` (default): when the pool crosses `gc_urgent` (80%) and the base pin accounts for more than half of the space above `gc_start`, the pin is dropped, the relationship goes `Broken`, a CRIT alert names the next common snapshot (if any) and the resync cost. `hold`: keep the pin until `write_stop` (90%), then break; this is for people who would rather hit the write-stop throttle than lose the base. No policy ever throttles the sender to the partner's speed (pivot 4). The break threshold and the pin accounting are reported per volume as `replication_hold_bytes`.

###### 2.6 Geometry discovery on arbitrary devices; write-back, write-through and no discard

**Sources, in order of trust.**

1. md sysfs: `/sys/block/mdN/md/level`, `raid_disks`, `chunk_size` (bytes), `layout`, `degraded`, `stripe_cache_size` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/Documentation/admin-guide/md.rst], plus `queue/minimum_io_size` and `queue/optimal_io_size`, which raid456 computes from the chunk and the data-disk count [verified: raid5.c]. Exact; no probe needed, but the probe runs anyway as a check.
2. Block-queue sysfs for any device: `queue/minimum_io_size` ("for RAID arrays it is often the stripe chunk size"), `queue/optimal_io_size` ("for RAID arrays it is usually the stripe width... If no optimal I/O size is reported this file contains 0"), `/sys/block/<disk>/alignment_offset`, `queue/physical_block_size`, `queue/logical_block_size`, `queue/discard_max_bytes` and `discard_granularity` (0 means no discard), `queue/write_zeroes_max_bytes`, `queue/fua`, `queue/write_cache`, `queue/max_sectors_kb` and `max_hw_sectors_kb` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/Documentation/ABI/stable/sysfs-block]. The same values are available through `BLKIOMIN`, `BLKIOOPT`, `BLKALIGNOFF`, `BLKPBSZGET`, `BLKSSZGET` [verified: fs.h].
3. SCSI VPD page B0 for a hardware-RAID virtual drive: the kernel parses OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH GRANULARITY into `min_xfer_blocks` and OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH into `opt_xfer_blocks`, validates them (a multiple of the physical block size, at least a page, not above the device maximum) and only then sets `io_min` and `io_opt` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/sd.c `sd_read_block_limits`, `sd_validate_opt_xfer_size`]; the raw page is readable at `/sys/class/scsi_device/*/device/vpd_pgb0` together with `vpd_pg83`, `vpd_pgb1`, `vpd_pgb2` and `vpd_pgb7` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c]. Whether a given MegaRAID or PERC firmware fills B0 with the stripe width is firmware-dependent and must not be assumed [believed]; `storcli` and `perccli` are vendor downloads, not Debian packages, so the installer cannot rely on them.
4. Admin override in TOML (below), required when the probe is inconclusive.
5. The write-amplification probe, mandatory at pool creation for every non-md backstore and run as a check on md: for each candidate full-stripe size S in {256 KiB, 512 KiB, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 MiB}, write 16 GiB of S-aligned, S-sized O_DIRECT writes at queue depth 8 and measure steady-state throughput; 16 GiB is at least four times any controller cache up to 4 GB, so a write-back cache cannot mask the result. The full stripe is the smallest S whose throughput is within 10% of the best; a knee at `max_sectors_kb` rather than at the configured stripe means the controller does not coalesce split commands (next paragraph). Cost: about 7 x 16 GiB at 1 GB/s, two minutes, and `GeomSource::Probe { knee_bytes, ratio }` is recorded in the pool for support.

```toml
[aggregate.agg0]
backstore = "/dev/sdb"             # PERC virtual drive; "/dev/md0" for mdadm; "/dev/nvme0n1" for a lone NVMe
media = "hdd"                      # hdd | flash
geometry = { source = "probe" }    # md | vpd | probe | manual
#### geometry = { source = "manual", stripe_data_bytes = 2097152, chunk_bytes = 262144, data_disks = 8 }
cache_protection = "bbu"           # bbu | flash_backed | none | unknown   (non-md backstores only; attested by the operator)
discard = "never"                  # never | whole_segment (requires RZAT verified at creation)
metadata_class = "/dev/nvme1n1p1"  # optional flash device for map pages, CP log and superblocks
cp_timer_s = 10
arena_gib = 8
staging_gib = 2.5
reserves = { gc_start = 0.70, gc_urgent = 0.80, write_stop = 0.90 }
nvfail_intent = "precise"          # precise | conservative
```

**Write-back (BBU or flash-backed) controller.** The kernel's view comes from the caching mode page: `sd_set_flush_flag` sets `BLK_FEAT_WRITE_CACHE` only when the device reports WCE=1 and `BLK_FEAT_FUA` only with DPOFUA [verified: sd.c]. MegaRAID and PERC virtual drives report WCE=0 in both write-back and write-through policy, so `queue/write_cache` reads "write through" and the kernel issues neither flushes nor FUA to them [believed; the design reads the file and does not assume]. The consequence: our commit ordering (data, flush, FUA superblock) is enforced only by the controller's cache protection. Hence the attestation: `cache_protection = bbu | flash_backed` is required for a non-md backstore whose `write_cache` reads "write through"; `unknown` is refused at pool creation; `none` is accepted only with the operator's explicit acknowledgement that a power loss can tear a CP, and then the torn-CP rule is what saves the previous CP. Writing "write back" into `queue/write_cache` changes only the kernel's view ("it doesn't alter the device state") [verified: sysfs-block], which would make the kernel send SYNCHRONIZE CACHE to a controller that ignores it in write-back policy; writing to the sd `cache_type` attribute sends a real MODE SELECT [verified: sd.c `cache_type_store`], which controller firmware generally rejects [believed]. Neither is a substitute for the attestation. With write-back the flusher behaves as on md: full-stripe writes complete at cache speed until the cache fills (a 2 GB cache at 1.2 GB/s fills in under 2 s) and then at the drive drain; alignment errors show up as read-modify-write only in the probe, never in `iostat`, which is why the probe is mandatory here.

**Write-through controller (or BBU failed and the policy fell back to write-through).** Every write completes when the disks have it; full-stripe writes still avoid read-modify-write, but only if the controller sees the full stripe in one command. The kernel splits a 2.5 MiB stripe into `max_sectors_kb` pieces (often 256 KiB on MegaRAID virtual drives [believed]); whether the firmware coalesces consecutive pieces is firmware-specific, and the probe exposes it as a knee at `max_sectors_kb`. The rule the installer prints: on a write-through controller, create the virtual drive so that strip times data disks is at most `max_hw_sectors_kb` (for example 8 data drives at 32 KiB strips = 256 KiB), or raise `max_sectors_kb` to `max_hw_sectors_kb`, and let the probe confirm. The superblock write is then a plain write, which is safe.

**Discard unsupported** (`discard_max_bytes = 0`, the normal case for hardware RAID and for md raid456 without the module parameter): `Discard::Never`; the allocator reuses free segments by overwriting them with full stripes, which costs nothing on HDD. On flash behind such a controller the SSDs' FTLs never learn of frees, so their internal write amplification rises with pool fullness; the mitigation is only `write_stop` at 90% and a warning at creation that over-provisioning must come from the drives themselves. `write_zeroes_max_bytes` of 0 similarly turns zeroing into map holes rather than device commands.

###### 2.7 The 6.12 ublk data path: user copy versus legacy copy, cost per 4 KiB, where the 5 to 10 us go

Both modes copy exactly once. In legacy mode the driver copies WRITE data into the daemon's pre-registered per-tag buffer at dispatch time (`ublk_map_io` through `ublk_copy_user_pages`, "we delay copy WRITE request data into ublksrv") and copies READ data back at commit; in user-copy mode the daemon reads or writes the request's pages through `/dev/ublkcN` at an offset that encodes queue, tag and buffer offset (`ublk_check_and_get_req`, `ublk_ch_read_iter`), with the same `ublk_copy_user_pages` doing the move [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/block/ublk_drv.c]. The difference is who chooses the destination and when: user copy lets the reactor pick an arena slot after seeing the LBA and length, so the arena is the only copy; legacy mode forces per-tag buffers (queues times depth times the maximum I/O size, 1 GiB for 8 queues at depth 128 and 1 MiB) and a second memcpy into the arena. `ublks_max` defaults to 64 and is a runtime module parameter up to `UBLK_MINORS` [verified: ublk_drv.c], so the platform profile sets `options ublk_drv ublks_max=1024` for LUNs plus snapshot mounts.

| Step, 4 KiB WRITE, busy-polled reactor | Cost | Assumption |
|---|---|---|
| FETCH completion delivered as a CQE | 0.5 to 1.5 us | reactor polling; 5 to 10 us if it must be woken |
| `READ_FIXED` on `/dev/ublkcN` into the slot (pin one huge page, one 4 KiB memcpy) | 1.0 to 2.0 us | 10 GB/s memcpy plus op dispatch |
| CRC32C of 4 KiB | 0.2 to 0.3 us | `crc-fast` at about 20 GB/s [believed] |
| seq, BTreeMap insert with split or trim | 0.5 to 1.0 us | 2 M entries, cache-warm |
| `COMMIT_AND_FETCH_REQ` SQE, batched submit | 0.3 to 0.5 us | amortized over the batch |
| Engine total | 2.5 to 5.3 us | 8 to 13 us with wakeups |

The owner's 5 to 10 us is the engine's share, and it holds only on busy-polled reactors (R16's isolation profile). The client sees more: LIO, iblock and blk-mq above ublk add 15 to 30 us, an iSCSI round trip on 10GbE 50 to 80 us, and the completion path 10 to 20 us, which is the 100 to 200 us QD1 figure of round 2 with the mirror removed. Legacy copy would save the READ SQE (about 0.5 us) and cost a second memcpy (0.4 us) plus the pinned per-tag memory; user copy stays. Reads run the opposite way (`WRITE_FIXED` into the request from the read cache or from a slot) and reads that hit the arena or the DRAM read cache complete in the same 3 to 5 us engine budget.

###### 2.8 Memory model for a 64 GB node; CP triggers; back-pressure

| Consumer | Phase C | Phase B | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arena (hugetlbfs, 2 MiB pages, boot-reserved) | 8 GiB | 8 GiB | 10 s of ingest at 0.8 GB/s; this is the loss window |
| CP staging pool (hugetlbfs) | 0.5 GiB | 2.5 GiB | 0.5 GiB disk-side (200 stripes in flight) plus a 2 GiB shipper hold |
| Dirty indexes, two generations | 0.3 GiB | 0.3 GiB | 2 M entries at 80 B |
| Map: page index, page cache, CP-log overlay | 6 GiB | 6 GiB | covers about 1.5 TB of 4 KiB-granular hot data; cold lookups cost a page read |
| DRAM read cache (HDD pools) | 8 GiB | 8 GiB | reduced to 2 GiB when an NVMe read cache exists |
| NVMe read-cache index | 0.6 GiB per TB | same | 32 KiB lines, 20 B each |
| md stripe cache | 1.5 GiB per array | same | software RAID only |
| Receiver staging | 0 | 2 GiB | inbound chunks before their CP |
| `otap-ctl`, `nbladed`, metrics | 0.5 GiB | 0.5 GiB | |
| Kernel and OS | 2 GiB | 2 GiB | |
| Per-SVM slices (XFS page cache, smbd, nfsd, versitygw) | about 32 GiB | about 28 GiB | 59.6 GiB minus the above |

A 32 GB single-node box halves the arena, the read cache and the map cache and keeps everything else. A 128 GB node doubles the arena only if the operator accepts a 20 s loss window; by default it doubles the read cache and the map cache instead.

**CP triggers**, in priority order: `Shutdown` and `UpsOnBattery` (immediate, then `CleanShutdown`); `Snapshot(id)` (immediate unless a CP is in flight, then at the next one, so snapshot latency is at most one CP duration, under 4 s on HDD); `ArenaHalfFull` (the active half at 50%, 4 GiB: 4 s at 1 GB/s); `Timer` (10 s HDD, 5 s flash); `BackToBack` (the previous CP committed and the active half is above 25%); `ShipDeadline` (Phase B: a relationship's configured interval). The effective interval under load is min(timer, half-arena divided by ingest).

**Back-pressure when CP N+1 fills while CP N is still flushing.** The arena is double-buffered; while CP N drains half A, writes fill half B. If B reaches 60%, the ZFS-shaped delay applies: `delay = k * occ / (1 - occ)` with k recomputed from the last three CPs' drain rates, capped at 2 s per request; past 2 s the owner's ports go Transitioning (R7's contract, unchanged). Numbers: an HDD pool at 80% full drains 0.3 to 0.5 GB/s, so a 4 GiB half takes 8 to 13 s to flush; sustained ingest above the drain hits the throttle within 10 to 20 s, and a 4 GiB burst at 2 GB/s is absorbed in 2 s and drained over 3 to 10 s with no throttle. The owner's "no throttling" (pivot 4) is about the partner, and this design honours it absolutely: no replication state ever delays a request. Local disk speed is still physics; the arena buys bursts, not sustained excess.

###### 2.9 Snapshots as user-visible objects

**The object.** `Snapshot { vol, name, uuid: SnapUuid, cp_seq, created_wall, kind: Scheduled(policy, tier) | User | Transfer | Divergent, pins: [User | Schedule | Replication(rel) | Clone(vol)] }`, stored in the snapshot table referenced by the superblock; a snapshot is a pinned root plus a deadlist of the blocks freed while it was the newest snapshot.

```toml
[snapshot_policy.default]
hourly = { keep = 24, at = "*:05" }
daily  = { keep = 7,  at = "00:10" }
weekly = { keep = 4,  on = "sun", at = "00:15" }
autodelete = "scheduled_only"        # scheduled_only | all | never
nas_consistency = "fsfreeze"         # fsfreeze | crash
freeze_timeout_ms = 3000             # thaw and take a crash-consistent snapshot if the sync takes longer
[volume.vm_datastore]
snapshot_policy = "default"
nvfail = "on"
```

**Schedules and retention.** The scheduler is in `dbladed` (it must work on a single node with no control plane), driven by the policy in Raft and mirrored into the aggregate so a node booting alone keeps its schedule. Retention is by count per tier; deletion merges the snapshot's deadlist into the next-older one (O(deadlist)). Autodelete runs when the pool crosses `gc_urgent`: oldest unpinned scheduled snapshot first, user snapshots only under `autodelete = all`, never a replication base or a clone parent.

**Space accounting with a replica.** Per volume: `used`, `snapshot_used` (bytes referenced only by snapshots, from the deadlists), `replication_hold_bytes` (the base pin's share), `unique(snap)` (what deleting that snapshot frees). Snapshot reserves per volume are dropped: thin LUNs and NAS volumes alike account at the aggregate (R18's thick reservation for file volumes stays), and the replica side shows the same numbers for its copy, which differ only by the receiver's own pins.

**Taking one.** Block LUNs: crash-consistent at the next cut, 0 ms of client-visible pause. NAS volumes: `FIFREEZE` on the XFS inside the SVM's mount namespace ("all dirty data, metadata, and log information are written to disk"; writers block until thaw) [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/fsfreeze.8.html and `FIFREEZE`/`FITHAW` in fs.h], then the cut, then thaw immediately, not after the flush: the freeze window is the page-cache sync (at most `dirty_expire` 2 s of ingest, so about 2 GB at 1 GB/s, 2 to 3 s worst case) plus a sub-millisecond flip. The frozen XFS has a clean log, so the snapshot mounts without recovery.

**Exposing a snapshot of an XFS-on-LUN volume to NAS clients.** The volume's data is a LUN to the engine and a filesystem to the SVM, so a snapshot becomes a NAS object by becoming a device: `dbladed` creates a read-only ublk device over the pinned root (reads resolve through the snapshot's page index; writes are refused) and `nbladed` mounts it inside the SVM's mount namespace at `/vol/<svm>/<vol>/.snapshot/@GMT-YYYY.MM.DD-hh.mm.ss` with `-o ro,nouuid,norecovery` ("nouuid... often used in combination with norecovery for mounting read-only snapshots"; "Filesystems mounted norecovery must be mounted read-only") [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/xfs.5.html]. Mounts are on demand through systemd automount units with a 300 s idle timeout and a cap of 8 mounted snapshots per SVM, because each costs a ublk device and a mount. NFS clients reach them through the parent export with `crossmnt` ("it will be implicitly exported with the same export options as the parent, except for fsid=") [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/exports.5.html]; SMB clients get Previous Versions through `vfs_shadow_copy2` with `shadow:snapdir = .snapshot` and the default `shadow:format = @GMT-%Y.%m.%d-%H.%M.%S` [verified: https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/vfs_shadow_copy2.8.html], which is why the mount directories carry that name. A writable clone is a child root exposed as a new LUN or, for NAS, a new volume whose XFS gets `xfs_admin -U generate` before its first mount [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/xfs_admin.8.html]. Block LUN snapshots are never mounted by us; they are exposed as clone LUNs on request.

##### 3. Bottlenecks and edge cases

1. **Link versus media in steady state.** 10GbE moves 1.1 GB/s; an empty 12-drive RAID6 absorbs 1.2 to 2 GB/s and an 80%-full one 0.3 to 0.5 GB/s under uniform overwrite (Appendix A). Replication is link-bound on an empty pool and drain-bound on an aged one; a 2 GB/s flash pool needs 25GbE for steady state or it lives in `CatchUp` permanently (assumption: ingest at line rate for minutes; homelab bursts are shorter).
2. **The shipper hold budget.** 2 GiB of staging at a 0.1 GB/s deficit lasts 20 s; at a 0.9 GB/s deficit (flash to 10GbE) 2.3 s. Below the budget there are no disk reads for replication; above it, catch-up reads cost HDD pools 30 to 40% of drain because reads and writes interleave at 2.5 MiB granularity (assumption: 10 ms per seek, 2.5 MiB transfers at 250 MB/s). Flash pays nothing measurable.
3. **Map traffic under random writes.** 1 M random 4 KiB writes per CP (250 K IOPS at a 4 s CP) dirty up to 1 M map pages; without the CP log that is 16 GiB of map writes per CP. With it, the CP log is 16 MiB per CP and the 10-minute checkpoint rewrites at most 2.5 M pages (40 GB) for a 10 TB volume, 67 MB/s amortized, which an HDD pool cannot afford alongside 1 GB/s of ingest; the flash metadata class (round 2's hybrid) is mandatory above about 20 K sustained random IOPS on HDD and recommended above 15 TB. At realistic homelab rates (5 to 20 K IOPS) the amortized cost is 1 to 5 MB/s.
4. **Cold map lookups on HDD.** 6 GiB of map cache covers about 1.5 TB of 4 KiB-granular data; a random read outside it costs a 16 KiB map page read (10 ms seek) before the data seek, halving random-read IOPS on cold data. Same remedy: the metadata class.
5. **Hardware-RAID write-through and `max_sectors_kb`.** A 2.5 MiB stripe arriving as ten 256 KiB commands on a write-through controller that does not coalesce costs a read-modify-write per command: 2 to 4x write amplification and a drain of 150 to 300 MB/s instead of 1.2 GB/s (assumption: parity RMW needs two reads and two writes per strip). The probe finds it; the 256 KiB-stripe VD rule fixes it.
6. **The controller cache that hides itself.** A write-back controller whose BBU died and whose policy is "write back regardless" loses up to its cache (1 to 8 GB) on power loss with no flush ever requested by the kernel. The attestation and the torn-CP rule are the only defences; the installer refuses `unknown`.
7. **Hole-birth class bugs.** Any path that changes logical content without a birth (an optimization that drops a hole, a resize that truncates the page index) diverges replicas silently. The property test `diff(base) == model(base)` over 10 K random snapshot pairs and a weekly full-map digest compare (the `SuperblockDigest` in `CpEnd`) are the detectors; the OpenZFS history says this bug class ships if it is not tested [verified: the OpenZFS FAQ above].
8. **Snapshots during continuous high ingest.** The cut is exact (epoch grace under 50 us), but a snapshot requested while a CP is in flight waits for the next cut: up to one CP duration, 4 s on HDD at 1 GB/s. The NAS freeze adds the page-cache sync, 2 to 3 s worst case under `dirty_expire` 2 s; `freeze_timeout_ms` falls back to a crash-consistent snapshot rather than stalling NFS past the budget Protocols sets.
9. **Many volumes.** 1,000 volumes mean 1,000 shadow-root switches per receiver CP and 1,000 page-index headers per CP log record: about 100 KiB and under 10 ms. The idle-to-active intent write is the only per-volume latency cost: 1,000 bursty volumes could in theory each pay 10 ms once per burst; the two-CP hysteresis keeps it to one FUA stripe per volume per quiet-then-busy episode.
10. **Patch writes on `Esxi512e`.** A 512 B write occupies a 4 KiB slot, so a pathological all-512 B workload inflates the arena 8x; the CP-time merge needs the old block, pinned in the read cache at ingest; an alarm fires above 5% patch rate (ESXi guests write 4 KiB-aligned almost always; VMFS metadata is the minority path).
11. **Receiver reboot mid-CP.** Partial chunks are in unreferenced segments and the cursor is persisted only at the receiver's own CP (10 s), so a reboot can lose up to 10 s of received chunks, which are re-sent; no correctness issue, 10 GB of extra traffic worst case.
12. **Divergent-write preservation.** The `divergent-<ts>` snapshot pins up to M-K CPs of data (bounded by one arena, 8 GiB, plus whatever the shipper had not sent: at a 60 s lag and 1 GB/s, 60 GB). Space pressure autodeletes it; the alert says so.
13. **Boot time after a crash.** Four superblock reads, the segment table (80 MiB for 100 TB at 80 MiB segments), the page indexes (20 MB per 10 TB), and the CP-log replay (at most 1 GiB at 200 MB/s = 5 s): under 10 s to serving at 50 TB, with nvfail evaluated before any export.

##### 4. What I would cut or defer, and why

- **Cut: `MirrorLink`, `MirrorInbound`, `BatchPage`, `Placed`, `Credit`, `GrantUnmirrored` and its hysteresis, `Cut` as a Placed-gated object, the tmpfs inbound ring, and `otap-ringd`.** None has a role once no acknowledgement waits for a partner. The arena and the state pages are hugetlbfs and tmpfs files created by systemd units (R4's mechanism), `dbladed` re-attaches to them, and the request-age page the watchdog petter reads is a shared mapping; no holder process is needed. In Phase B the receiver lives inside `dbladed` because a 2 to 5 s receiver outage only adds lag.
- **Cut: plex-by-reference and the `CpManifest`.** The async stream subsumes it; the owner's "plex delta shipping" is this design.
- **Defer to Phase C+1: `LocalNvmeRing`** as an opt-in durable single-node mode (per-record FUA to a PLP NVMe, Placed being the FUA completion, 10 to 20 us added to each acknowledgement on Optane). It contradicts "acknowledge at DRAM speed" and the owner has priced the window; the hook (`CpTrigger::UnmirroredFlush`, the slot-state page) stays so it can land without a format change.
- **Defer to Phase 3: the extent B+tree map and CP-time compression.** The radix map with the CP log is simpler, O(1) on lookup, and already carries `plen`.
- **Defer to Phase B+: volume-level relationships to a third destination and to S3.** Phase B is one partner per aggregate pair with per-volume direction; a second destination is the same `DeltaSource` in map-walk mode and nothing else, so it is a scheduling feature, not an engine one.
- **Defer: FC as a replication transport.** Fabrics prices it; from the engine's side it is one more `DeltaSink` and I would not build it before TCP replication has survived the Phase B exit tests.
- **Defer: snapshot reserves per volume and the Phase-2 autogrow.** Aggregate-level accounting with autodelete covers the homelab case; per-volume reserves return with quotas.
- **Not building: a takeover-triggered CP, replay-all-valid and the four-barrier data steps that depended on an inbound ring.** With no mirror there is nothing to replay; takeover is "promote at K, evaluate nvfail", and the barriers are Consensus' to simplify.

##### 5. Phase C work items, then what Phases B and A add

Phase C (single-node v0.1), in order, each with its exit test:

1. **`otap-format` v2 frozen**: superblock (four slots), stripe summary, CP log record, map page and page index, segment table, snapshot table, stream records; property tests with `proptest` 1.12.0 [verified: https://crates.io/crates/proptest]. Exit: 1 M round-trip cases per structure, N/N-1 read compatibility test, fuzz corpus for the scanner.
2. **`otap-arena`**: hugetlbfs arena and staging pool from systemd mount and setup units, slot-state page, re-attach after `kill -9`. Exit: 100 kills at 1 GB/s re-attach in under 2 s p99 with zero acknowledged writes lost (the checker).
3. **`otap-index`**: per-volume BTreeMap, split and trim, aggregate seq, epoch-flip cut, patch masks, read-your-writes. Exit: linearizability versus a model under `proptest`; flips under 1 M inserts/s with grace under 50 us.
4. **`otap-geom`**: sysfs and md discovery, VPD B0 parsing from `vpd_pgb0`, the probe, the attestation and refusals. Exit: on mdadm RAID6 10+2 (256 KiB chunk) and on a PERC VD the probe reports the configured stripe within one candidate; `unknown` protection refused; the write-through `max_sectors_kb` knee reproduced on a VD deliberately built with a 2 MiB stripe.
5. **`otap-cp`**: staging, `WRITE_FIXED` flusher, metadata stream, flush and `RWF_DSYNC` superblock, CP log and map checkpoints, deferred-reuse rule, triggers and the throttle. Exit: D1's drain curve (at least 1.2 GB/s empty with zero member reads during a CP, measured from `/sys/block/sdX/stat`); `dm-log-writes` replay at 1,000 cut points yields an image equal to a CP prefix and XFS mounts clean at every point; a torn superblock stripe injected with `dm-flakey` falls back to CP N-1 with intact data.
6. **`otap-map`**: radix map, per-entry CRC, `max_birth`, hole entries, pins, deadlists, `diff`. Exit: `diff(base)` equals the model over 10 K random snapshot pairs including discards and resizes; every read verifies its CRC; a bit flip and a misdirected write injected under the map are caught.
7. **nvfail**: `run_state`, `write_active` with intent writes, boot evaluation, `otapctl volume nvfail-clear`, the alert. Exit: 1,000 simulated and 50 real power cuts engage nvfail on every dirty boot with a volume list that equals the checker's set of volumes with unflushed acknowledged writes; clean shutdowns never trip; a volume idle for two CPs never appears; intent-write latency p99 under 20 ms on HDD.
8. **GC, reserves, scrub**: cost-benefit victim selection, 70/80/90, summary-driven scrub. Exit: the aged-pool curve at 70% and 80% published; scrub finds 100% of injected CRC and placement faults.
9. **Snapshots as objects**: scheduler, retention, autodelete, `fsfreeze` snapshots, `.snapshot` mounts over read-only ublk devices, clone LUNs and clone volumes. Exit: Windows 11 Previous Versions shows 24 hourlies through Samba 4.22; the freeze window p99 under 3 s at 1 GB/s NFS ingest; 64 snapshots per volume created, mounted, unmounted and deleted in a loop with stable RSS.
10. **The ublk front door in `dbladed`**: `UBLK_F_USER_COPY` with `READ_FIXED` and `WRITE_FIXED`, `USER_RECOVERY` with `REISSUE` and the `ReqId` dedupe, `Esxi512e` and `Native4k`, `ublks_max` in the profile. Exit: 50 K 4 KiB IOPS on at most 4 cores; engine-side acknowledgement p50 under 5 us and p99 under 15 us at QD1 busy-polled; zero duplicate applies over 100 kills.
11. **Replication groundwork without a partner**: `DeltaSource` in both modes, `otapctl volume dump --since <snap>` to a file and `restore` into a second aggregate on the same node. Exit: dump, restore and a full-map digest compare equal for 1,000 random snapshot pairs; this doubles as the backup-to-file feature and is the bridge to Phase B.

**Phase B adds** (two nodes, internal drives, async replication): the TCP `DeltaSink` inside `dbladed` with shadow roots and persisted cursors; the per-volume relationship state machine, lag metrics (CPs, bytes, seconds) on the 1 s replication heartbeat; `promote_hint` and nvfail-on-promote; resync in both directions with rollback to the common base and the divergent snapshot; the direction epoch check; `on_space_pressure`; the 2 GiB shipper hold and receiver staging in the budget; and my inputs to Consensus' Phase B timer table: CP interval 10 s HDD and 5 s flash, lag warn 60 s and crit 600 s, `max_auto_takeover_lag` proposed at two CP intervals plus 30 s, hold budget 2 GiB, catch-up read share 30%, base-pin break at `gc_urgent`.

**Phase A adds** (shared SAS shelf, PR, ALUA): aggregate import and export on shared disks (md assembled only by the lease holder, PR keys registered before `mdadm --add`), the epoch page check at submission, CP submit, superblock write and completion against the shelf's owner epoch, the four-slot max-select as defence against a stale writer, and a priced option, `ShelfSsdRing`: two SAS SSDs in the shelf as a RAID1 per-record FUA log (R11's device, reachable by both nodes), which is the only way Phase A takeover of unflushed acknowledged writes exists; without it, an unplanned takeover on the shelf has exactly the single-node loss window and the same nvfail evaluation, with a shorter rollback bound (one CP interval, no ship time).

##### 6. Questions for the other personas

**Opus-Protocols.**
1. For nvfail on a LUN, which client-visible state do you want `nbladed` to apply: ALUA Unavailable on the LUN's target port group, a LUN unmap (PDL for ESXi), or NOT READY with ASC 04h/02h? The engine can only fail I/O with EIO, which becomes a medium error through LIO, so the honest state must come from configfs; I need to know what to signal and when.
2. What is the NFS and SMB stall budget for the `fsfreeze` window? I budget 2 to 3 s worst case at 1 GB/s under `dirty_expire` 2 s and fall back to crash-consistent past `freeze_timeout_ms`; is 3 s acceptable for ESXi NFSv3 datastores and for SMB clients?
3. For `.snapshot` exposure, does the SVM's mount namespace plus `crossmnt` on the parent export cover NFSv3 and v4.1 clients, or do you need explicit exports with pinned `fsid` per snapshot mount? And for `vfs_shadow_copy2`, is `shadow:snapdir = .snapshot` with `shadow:basedir` at the volume root enough when each snapshot is its own mount?
4. Is the SVM root volume part of a consistency group with the SVM's data volumes for replication purposes, that is, must `secrets.tdb` and the `nfsdcld` database be at the same sender CP as the data on promotion, or can the root volume lag independently?
5. After nvfail on a NAS volume, you want an export `fsid` bump to force ESTALE; does knfsd honour a changed `fsid` for an export that is re-added without a remount, or do you need the engine to present the volume as a new device?

**Opus-Fabrics.**
1. `IORING_OP_SEND_ZC` with `IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF` from a registered hugetlbfs staging pool: can you send one 2.5 MiB chunk as one SQE, and what is the per-chunk cost of the two CQEs (completion and notification) at 1 GB/s?
2. Resumability: my cursor is `(cp, chunk idx, byte offset)` and chunks within a CP may complete out of order across up to 4 connections; is a byte-level resume acceptable or do you need chunk-aligned resume only?
3. Flow control: I release staging holds on your acknowledgement of the receiver's apply, not on TCP send completion; the hold budget is 2 GiB. Does your window size need to be smaller than that, and what do you report to me when the link is up but the receiver's apply stalls?
4. If FC is ever a transport, the receiver side is a kernel target writing into a tmpfs file that my `DeltaSink` scans; what is the per-2.5 MiB write cost on 8GFC and 16GFC, and does it beat 10GbE TCP by enough to justify a second code path?
5. Optional compression of chunks (`lz4_flex` 0.14.0 or `zstd` 0.14.2): do you compress per chunk on the mirror core, and what CPU do you budget at 1 GB/s? I can hand you chunks whose summaries say which blocks are zero so they are never sent.

**Opus-Consensus.**
1. I will report per-volume lag as `(cps_behind, bytes_behind, seconds_behind)` on a 1 s replication heartbeat; I propose `max_auto_takeover_lag` defaults to two CP intervals plus 30 s, automatic takeover below it and manual above it. Do you want the lag on your 100 ms control heartbeat instead?
2. On promotion, the volumes that enter nvfail are those in the sender's last known `write_active`, which I persist in the receiver's superblock as `promote_hint`; I propose Raft holds only the relationship direction and its epoch, never the per-volume write sets. Agreed, and does your `NvFail` cluster op then become a mirror of my superblock rather than the source of truth?
3. A returning old owner must be fenced before my rollback to the common base, and my `DeltaSink` refuses `CpBegin` records carrying an older direction epoch. Does Raft give me a monotonically increasing per-volume direction epoch at every flip, including flips during a no-quorum freeze?
4. Phase C has one voter. I propose the superblock is authoritative for nvfail state and the operator's clear, so a single node works with no control plane at all, and `otap-ctl` only reflects it; is that compatible with your "same control plane with one voter" posture?
5. For the no-quorum posture in Phase B, what does the engine need to do on "freeze ownership": keep serving and keep shipping, or keep serving and stop shipping? Shipping during a partition is harmless to me (the receiver cannot promote without quorum), but you may want the link quiet for your own fence evidence.


### Opus-Protocols

#### 1. Executive take

The pivot changes four things for SVMs and protocols. First, with no synchronous mirror on the write path, every protocol's acknowledgement latency collapses to the engine's local DRAM figure: the round-2 budgets lose their 25 to 35 us mirror term (iSCSI 4 KiB QD1 goes from 100 to 150 us to 70 to 100 us; NFSv3 FILE_SYNC from 300 to 450 us to 200 to 300 us), and FLUSH and COMMIT stay ordering barriers, so nothing in the protocol stack waits for a partner any more. Second, the SVM stops being "the migration mechanism" of R8 and becomes the unit of everything: of namespaces, of configuration, of identity, of replication consistency (the root volume ships with its data volumes), and of mobility. Third, single-node-first means that SVM create, start, stop and LIF move must be perfect on one node before any cross-node move exists; a Phase B move is then "stop here, ship, start there" with the same ladder, and a Phase B unplanned takeover is that ladder plus a rollback, which turns nvfail into a per-volume, protocol-visible state for NAS as well as for LUNs. Fourth, kernel 6.12 lets block protocols live inside the SVM network namespace, so iSCSI and NVMe/TCP become SVM protocols with SVM LIFs, exactly as in ONTAP, and the round-2 "block stays at node level" assumption is retired; only Fibre Channel stays at node level.

Top five positions:

1. An SVM is exactly three Linux namespaces, network, UTS and mount, pinned as files under `/run/opentap/svm/<id>/ns/`, entered by `nsenter` from transient systemd units in a per-SVM slice; no PID, user, IPC or cgroup namespace.
2. The SVM's mount namespace is a `pivot_root`ed tmpfs view in which the junction tree sits at `/`, so NFSv3, NFSv4.1, SMB and S3 all see ONTAP paths (`svm:/vm/iso`) while the host sees `/vol/<svm>_root/vm/iso`.
3. The root volume holds only state that a daemon mutates by itself (`secrets.tdb`, the keytab, `winbindd_idmap.tdb`, statd's `sm` directory and state number, nfsdcld's SQLite); everything an operator declares lives in Raft and is regenerated into tmpfs at every start, so there is never a stale copy to reconcile.
4. iSCSI portals and NVMe/TCP ports bind in the network namespace of the process that writes configfs on 6.12, so block LIFs are SVM LIFs; because the iSCSI portal list is global and keyed by address only, block LIF addresses must be unique cluster-wide even across IPspaces.
5. Slices govern userspace (smbd, winbindd, versitygw, the NFS helper daemons) and nothing else; the engine's per-volume token bucket at the ublk queue is the only I/O governor, cgroup I/O controllers are not used, and nvfail is surfaced per protocol as PDL for LUNs, an export `fsid` generation bump for NFS and share-offline for SMB.

#### 2. Design

##### 2.1 The namespace set and how systemd units enter it

**Network namespace.** It is the IPspace: LIFs, routes, the port space (2049, 445, 111, 3260 per SVM), the nftables ruleset and the iSCSI and NVMe/TCP listeners all live in it. The node's management and cluster traffic stays in `init_net`.

**UTS namespace.** Its nodename is the SVM name. knfsd copies the caller's nodename into the per-namespace NFSv4 server scope and major id on every `nfsd_svc()` (Appendix A, verified in round 2), Samba's `netbios name` defaults to the host's DNS name [verified: https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smb.conf.5.html], statd and versitygw's metrics name default to the hostname, so one `sethostname()` gives all four protocols the same identity on whichever node runs the SVM.

**Mount namespace: required.** Four independent reasons. (a) nfs-utils 2.8.3 hard-codes `/etc/nfs.conf`, `/etc/exports`, `/var/lib/nfs` and `/run/rpcbind.sock`, and the `nfsd` filesystem is a per-network-namespace instance that must be mounted at `/proc/fs/nfsd` by a process inside that netns: `nfsd_fs_get_tree()` calls `get_tree_keyed(fc, nfsd_fill_super, get_net(fc->net_ns))` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfsctl.c]. Two SVMs cannot both own the host's `/proc/fs/nfsd`. (b) Samba's client libraries do not honour `winbindd socket directory`; they need `WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR` [verified: smb.conf(5) above], and `ncalrpc dir`, pid files and the privileged winbind pipe all default under `/run/samba` and `/var/lib/samba`; a private `/run` per SVM solves all of them at once. (c) Per-tenant `/etc/resolv.conf`, `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/krb5.conf`, `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/group` and `/etc/nsswitch.conf`: the SVM netns cannot reach systemd-resolved's 127.0.0.53 in `init_net`, and local SMB users need Unix accounts that differ per SVM. (d) The junction tree at `/` (2.3). Not PID (systemd and journald must see the daemons as ordinary processes; a PID namespace needs an init and hides them from `systemctl kill`), not user (nfsd, mount and raw sockets need real root), not IPC (Samba's inter-process state is tdb files and unix sockets under the private `/run`), not cgroup (slices do that), not time.

**Creation.** `nbladed` is the sole writer. It forks a single-threaded helper (`otap-nsinit`, part of `otap-blade`) that calls `unshare(CLONE_NEWNET | CLONE_NEWUTS | CLONE_NEWNS)`, `sethostname(<svm>)`, makes `/` recursively slave, builds the view of 2.3, brings `lo` up, then pins `/proc/self/ns/{net,uts,mnt}` by bind-mounting them onto `/run/opentap/svm/<id>/ns/{net,uts,mnt}`. `/run/opentap` is a tmpfs with private propagation because a namespace pin "must be located on a mount whose propagation type is not shared" [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/unshare.1.html]. Pins hold the namespaces alive with no holder process, the `ip netns` convention. `nbladed`'s own threads enter an SVM on demand: the network namespace with `setns` on any thread; the mount namespace only after that thread has done `unshare(CLONE_FS)`, because `setns(CLONE_NEWNS)` refuses a caller "sharing filesystem-related attributes with another process" [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/setns.2.html]. rustix 1.1.5 provides `move_into_link_name_space`, `unshare_unsafe`, `mount_bind_recursive`, `mount_change`, `open_tree` and `move_mount` [verified: https://docs.rs/rustix/latest/rustix/thread/index.html and https://docs.rs/rustix/latest/rustix/mount/index.html]; `pivot_root` and `sethostname` come from nix 0.31.3 [believed]. Building the three namespaces and the view costs about 3 ms (25 mounts at about 100 us each).

**Units.** systemd 257.13-1~deb13u1 has `NetworkNamespacePath=` but no directive that joins an existing mount or UTS namespace by path [verified: https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/systemd/systemd.exec.5.en.html and https://packages.debian.org/trixie/systemd], so the `ExecStart` wrapper is `nsenter --net=<pin> --uts=<pin> --mount=<pin> -- <daemon>` from util-linux 2.41.5-0+deb13u1 [verified: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/nsenter.1.html, https://packages.debian.org/trixie/util-linux]. `nsenter` execs in place, so the unit's main PID is the daemon. Units are transient, created with `StartTransientUnit` over D-Bus (zbus 5.19.0 [verified: https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/zbus]) under `svm-<id>.slice`, itself under `svm.slice`; no unit files on disk, no `daemon-reload`, nothing in `/etc` or `/var` load-bearing (invariant 9). Properties: `Slice`, `ExecStart`, `Environment` (`WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR`, `KRB5_CONFIG`, `GOMEMLIMIT`), `KillMode=mixed`, `TimeoutStopSec=10`, `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=1`, `OOMPolicy=continue` for smbd so one child's OOM kill does not stop the service, `TasksMax=4096`, `Type=exec`; readiness is probed by `nbladed` from inside the netns (TCP connect to 2049 or 445, `rpcinfo -p` for rpcbind). Logs go to journald per unit; Samba uses `logging = systemd@1` [believed].

| Protocol | Units, in start order | Binary and package |
|---|---|---|
| NFS core | `otap-svm-rpcbind@`, `-statd@`, `-mountd@`, `-nfsd@` (oneshot, `RemainAfterExit`) | rpcbind 1.2.7-1, nfs-kernel-server 1:2.8.3 [verified: https://packages.debian.org/trixie/rpcbind, round-2 Appendix A] |
| NFSv4.1 | plus `-nfsdcld@` before nfsd, `-idmapd@` | nfs-common 2.8.3 |
| NFS krb5 (deferred) | plus `-gssd@` | nfs-common |
| SMB | `-smbd@`; `-winbindd@` when `identity = ad` | samba 2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1 [verified: https://packages.debian.org/trixie/samba] |
| S3 | `-versitygw@` | versitygw v1.8.0 static binary, see 2.7 |
| iSCSI, NVMe/TCP | none; configfs written by `nbladed` from inside the netns (2.8) | kernel |

##### 2.2 SVM lifecycle: create, start, stop, move, delete

| State | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Absent | `svm create` committed in Raft | engine creates the root volume (1 GiB thin `Native4k` LUN), `mkfs.xfs`, mount once, write the `.otap` skeleton, unmount | Stopped |
| Stopped | `svm start`, placement = this node | S1 namespaces and pins; S2 mount root volume at `/vol/<svm>_root`; S3 create LIF devices without addresses; S4 mount junction volumes by depth, in parallel per depth; S5 generate overlays into `/run/opentap/svm/<id>/etc`; S6 start units in table order; S7 add LIF addresses, send GARP; S8 `sm-notify -f` (NFSv3 SVMs); S9 commit `Running` | Starting, then Running |
| Starting | any step fails or exceeds 15 s | run the stop ladder, CRIT alert with the step | Failed |
| Running | `svm stop` | T1 remove LIF addresses (clients see link loss, not errors); T2 stop units in reverse order, `rpc.nfsd 0` last; T3 remove iSCSI portals and nvmet ports; T4 delete LIF devices; T5 unmount junctions deepest first, then the root volume; T6 unmount pins | Stopping, then Stopped |
| Stopping | a step exceeds 10 s | `systemctl kill -s KILL svm-<id>.slice`, lazy unmount, retry once; if a mount is still busy (D state on a hung volume) raise `Stuck`, mark the node unclean for giveback, hand to `otap-ctl` | Stuck |
| Running | unit exits | systemd restarts after 1 s; three restarts in 60 s raise a WARN alert | Running (Degraded) |
| Running | home port down | re-parent the LIF to another port of the same broadcast domain on this node, same MAC, GARP; pause under 1 s; else alert | Running |
| Running | protocol toggled in Raft | start or stop only that protocol's units; no namespace change | Running |
| Stopped | `svm move` (Phase B) | stop on A, final CP and ship of the SVM's consistency group, start on B | Running on B |
| Stopped | `svm delete` | if AD-joined, a last short start to run `net ads leave`; release the junction volumes; delete the root volume; remove the Raft entry | Absent |
| Running | nvfail on volume V | per 2.11: unexport V, share offline, LUN unmapped; alert | Running (V nvfailed) |

Timing on a single node, standalone identity, root plus four volumes with clean logs: namespaces 3 ms, LIF devices 10 ms, five mounts in parallel about 60 ms, overlays 5 ms, rpcbind to nfsd about 400 ms, address and GARP 5 ms, so `svm start` is about 0.5 s; smbd adds 150 ms; winbindd adds 0.5 to 3 s of DC discovery off the critical path; versitygw adds 100 ms. `svm stop` is 3 to 6 s typical: smbd 1 to 2 s, versitygw up to 5 s of in-flight PUTs, nfsd threads to zero under 100 ms unless a WRITE is held, XFS unmount flushes at most `dirty_expire` of data (2 s at 1 GB/s is 2 GiB, written at engine DRAM speed in 1 to 2 s). The 10 s step budget comes from the round-2 hard hold bound.

```rust
pub struct SvmId(pub u128);
pub enum SvmState { Absent, Stopped, Starting { step: u8 }, Running { degraded: bool, nvfailed: Vec<VolId> },
    Stopping { step: u8 }, Stuck { busy: Vec<PathBuf> }, Failed { step: u8, err: String } }
pub enum Presence { Full, BlockStandby }           // Phase A: block target present on the partner, NAS absent
```
