### [C16] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: A bind-mount pin of /proc/self/ns/mnt created by the process that executed unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) is visible only inside the new mount namespace unless the target directory (/run/opentap) has private propagation, which is why util-linux 2.41's unshare --mount=FILE forks a helper that stays in the original mount namespace (bind_ns_files_from_child) to create the pin; a pin made from inside the new namespace is absent on the host and nsenter --mount=<pin> fails.
- Raised by: Opus-Consensus, Opus-Protocols
- Why it matters: The otap-nsinit helper as described (unshare, build the view, pivot_root, then pin /proc/self/ns/{net,uts,mnt} onto /run/opentap) cannot produce host-visible mount pins, so every transient unit using nsenter would fail to start until the helper is restructured.
- Summary: The conclusion stands: a helper that has already called unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) cannot produce a host-visible pin of its own mount namespace, util-linux's unshare --mount=FILE really does fork a child (bind_ns_files_from_child) that stays in the original mount namespace for exactly this reason, and without a host-side pin nsenter --mount=<pin> fails. The stated mechanism is wrong on two points, though: (1) the kernel does not create an in-namespace-only pin — bind-mounting your own /proc/self/ns/mnt is refused outright with EINVAL by mnt_ns_loop() in fs/namespace.c (v6.12), because the caller's namespace seq is >= the target's; (2) the propagation condition is inverted — private propagation is what confines a mount to the new namespace, and for mount-namespace files a *shared* target with peers or slaves makes even the parent-side pin fail (unshare(1): "file must be located on a mount whose propagation type is not shared (or an error results)"). No empirical test was run (execution not permitted); the verdict rests on the 6.12 kernel source, util-linux 2.41 source/commits and the man pages.
- Evidence: KERNEL v6.12 (fs/namespace.c, fs/pnode.c, fs/pnode.h at tag v6.12; Elixir pages returned only site navigation, so the torvalds/linux GitHub mirror of the same tag was read):
- mnt_ns_loop(): "/* Could bind mounting the mount namespace inode cause a mount namespace loop? */ ... mnt_ns = to_mnt_ns(get_proc_ns(dentry->d_inode)); return current->nsproxy->mnt_ns->seq >= mnt_ns->seq;". seq is monotonic: alloc_mnt_ns() "new_ns->seq = atomic64_add_return(1, &mnt_ns_seq);". do_loopback(): "err = -EINVAL; if (mnt_ns_loop(old_path.dentry)) goto out;". Hence a process binding its own ns/mnt (seq == seq) gets EINVAL, nothing is mounted anywhere; a process in the older parent namespace (smaller seq) binding /proc/<child>/ns/mnt passes the check.
- copy_tree(): "if (!(flag & CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE) && is_mnt_ns_file(dentry)) return ERR_PTR(-EINVAL);". __do_loopback() passes CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE for the explicit bind, but attach_recursive_mnt() does "if (IS_MNT_SHARED(dest_mnt)) { ... err = propagate_mnt(dest_mnt, dest_mp, source_mnt, &tree_list); }" and fs/pnode.c propagate_one() calls "child = copy_tree(last_source, last_source->mnt.mnt_root, type); if (IS_ERR(child)) return PTR_ERR(child);" with type only CL_MAKE_SHARED / CL_SLAVE (pnode.h: CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE 0x40) — so a mnt-ns-file bind onto a shared mount that has any peer or slave where the mountpoint is visible fails with EINVAL. Origin: commit 4ce5d2b1a8fd (Eric W. Biederman, 2013) "vfs: Don't copy mount bind mounts of /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt between namespaces": "These files hold references to a mount namespace and copying them between namespaces could result in a reference counting loop. The current mnt_ns_loop test prevents loops on the assumption that mounts don't cross between namespaces."
- copy_mnt_ns(): "copy_flags = CL_COPY_UNBINDABLE | CL_EXPIRE;" (no CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE), and copy_tree's child loop: "if (!(flag & CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE) && is_mnt_ns_file(src_mnt->mnt.mnt_root)) { src_mnt = skip_mnt_tree(src_mnt); continue; }" — an existing mnt pin is silently omitted from every mount namespace created afterwards.
- mntns_install(): "/* Find the root */ err = vfs_path_lookup(mnt_ns->root->mnt.mnt_root, &mnt_ns->root->mnt, "/", LOOKUP_DOWN, &root); ... set_fs_pwd(fs, &root); set_fs_root(fs, &root);" — entering a pinned mount namespace lands at its current (post-pivot_root) root.

UTIL-LINUX 2.41 sys-utils/unshare.c (Debian trixie ships util-linux 2.41.5-0+deb13u1; sources.debian.org shows bind_ns_files_from_child at about lines 309-322 and its call at about line 1087):
- "#define UNSHARE_PROPAGATION_DEFAULT (MS_REC | MS_PRIVATE)".
- main(): "if (npersists && (unshare_flags & CLONE_NEWNS)) pid_bind = bind_ns_files_from_child(&fd_bind);" comes BEFORE "if (-1 == unshare(unshare_flags))"; afterwards "if (pid_bind && (unshare_flags & CLONE_NEWNS)) sync_with_child(pid_bind, fd_bind); else /* simple way, just bind */ bind_ns_files(getpid());" and only then "if ((unshare_flags & CLONE_NEWNS) && propagation) set_propagation(propagation);".
- bind_ns_files_from_child(): "ino_t ino = get_mnt_ino(ppid); child = fork_and_wait(fd); if (child) return child; if (get_mnt_ino(ppid) == ino) exit(EXIT_FAILURE); bind_ns_files(ppid); exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);" — bind_ns_files() loops over ALL requested persistent files: "snprintf(src, sizeof(src), "/proc/%u/%s", (unsigned) pid, ns->name); if (mount(src, ns->target, NULL, MS_BIND, NULL) != 0) err(EXIT_FAILURE, _("mount %s on %s failed"), ...)". So the child, still in the parent's mount namespace, pins mnt, net, uts, etc. for the parent after the parent's ns/mnt inode has changed.
- Commit c84f259 "unshare: allow persisting mount namespaces" (Karel Zak, 2015-04-09, released in v2.27 per the v2.27 release notes): "We can create a reference (bind mount) to the new namespace after unshare(2), but it does not make sense to do it within unshared namespace. (And if I read kernel fs/namespace.c: do_loopback() correctly than copy mount bind mounts of /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt between namespaces is unsupported.) This patch bypass this problem by fork() where parent continue as usually (call unshare(2), ...), but child waits for /proc/[ppid]/ns/mnt inode number change ... and then it bind mounts the new namespaces and exit." Parent commit 0490a6c: "Note that the problem is mount namespace, because create bind mount to ns/mount file within unshared namespace does not make sense."
- unshare(1), upstream v2.41 adoc and manpages.debian.org/trixie (util-linux 2.41.5-0+deb13u1): "-m, --mount[=file] Create a new mount namespace. If file is specified, then the namespace is made persistent by creating a bind mount at file. Note that file must be located on a mount whose propagation type is not shared (or an error results). Use the command findmnt -o+PROPAGATION when not sure about the current setting." "--propagation ... The default is to set the propagation to private." EXAMPLES: "# mount --bind /root/namespaces /root/namespaces" / "# mount --make-private /root/namespaces" / "# touch /root/namespaces/mnt" / "# unshare --mount=/root/namespaces/mnt".
- nsenter.c: "*fd = open(path, O_RDONLY); if (*fd < 0) err(EXIT_FAILURE, _("cannot open %s"), path);" and do_setns(): "err(EXIT_FAILURE, _("reassociate to namespace '%s' failed"), name)". setns(2): EINVAL when "fd refers to a namespace whose type does not match that specified in nstype"; joining a mount namespace "requires that the caller possess both CAP_SYS_CHROOT and CAP_SYS_ADMIN capabilities".

MAN PAGES on propagation: mount_namespaces(7): "the mount list of the new namespace is a copy of the mount list in the caller's previous mount namespace"; a shared mount "replicated during the creation of a new mount namespace ... joins the peer group of which the existing mount is a member"; "systemd(1) automatically remounts all mounts as MS_SHARED on system startup"; unshare(1) "reverses the step performed by systemd(1), by making all mounts private in the new namespace"; "the new mount created under the private mount /mntP did not propagate". pivot_root(2) ERRORS: EINVAL if "Either the mount point at new_root, or the parent mount of that mount point, has propagation type MS_SHARED" and if "put_old is a mount point and has the propagation type MS_SHARED" — so a helper that pivot_roots has necessarily made its tree non-shared, and its net/uts pins cannot propagate back to the host either.

NOT DONE: the suggested empirical test on Debian 13 (no execution allowed); git.kernel.org and kernel.googlesource.com returned HTTP 403, so GitHub mirrors of the same commits/tags were used.
- Corrected claim: A process cannot pin its own mount namespace: in Linux 6.12, do_loopback() returns EINVAL when mnt_ns_loop() finds the caller's mount-namespace sequence number >= that of the namespace file being bound, so a helper that has already executed unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) cannot bind-mount /proc/self/ns/mnt anywhere — the mount is refused, not merely confined to the new namespace. Pins of its net and uts namespace files made from inside the new mount namespace do succeed, but land in that namespace's own (private, pivoted) mount tree and are not visible on the host; they would only reach the host if the target were still a shared peer of the host mount, which unshare's default --propagation private (and the non-shared propagation that pivot_root(2) requires) rules out. The pin must therefore be created by a process that remains in the original, older mount namespace: util-linux 2.41 (Debian 13: 2.41.5-0+deb13u1) unshare --mount=FILE forks bind_ns_files_from_child() before calling unshare(); the child stays in the parent's mount namespace, waits until /proc/<ppid>/ns/mnt's inode changes, then bind-mounts /proc/<ppid>/ns/{mnt,net,uts,...} onto the requested files (commit c84f259, 2015: "it does not make sense to do it within unshared namespace ... copy mount bind mounts of /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt between namespaces is unsupported"). The target must additionally sit on a non-shared mount (unshare(1): "file must be located on a mount whose propagation type is not shared (or an error results)"; the documented recipe is mount --bind DIR DIR; mount --make-private DIR), because propagate_one() copies without CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE and the whole bind fails with EINVAL if the ns-file mount would have to propagate to any peer or slave. A mnt pin is also omitted from the mount tree of every mount namespace created afterwards (copy_mnt_ns copies without CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE). Without a host-visible pin, nsenter --mount=/run/opentap/<unit>/mnt fails with "cannot open ...: No such file or directory" (or "reassociate to namespace 'ns/mnt' failed: Invalid argument" if only a placeholder file exists).
- Design impact: The otap-nsinit sequence as written (unshare -> build view -> pivot_root -> pin /proc/self/ns/{net,uts,mnt} onto /run/opentap) cannot work: the mnt pin is refused by the kernel (EINVAL) and the net/uts pins stay inside the private, pivoted tree, so every transient unit using nsenter --mount=... would fail at start. Required changes: (1) Split the helper into two processes mirroring util-linux: a pinner that never leaves the host mount namespace, and a builder that unshares, builds the view and pivot_roots. The builder signals readiness (pipe/eventfd); the pinner verifies /proc/<builder>/ns/mnt's inode differs from its own (as bind_ns_files_from_child does, to avoid racing and pinning the host namespace), then bind-mounts /proc/<builder>/ns/{mnt,net,uts} onto /run/opentap/<unit>/{mnt,net,uts}. The mnt pin may be taken right after unshare(); mntns_install() resolves the namespace root with LOOKUP_DOWN at setns time, so a later pivot_root is honored. Alternatively exec `unshare --mount=F1 --net=F2 --uts=F3 --propagation private --fork -- builder` and let util-linux do it. (2) Make the pin directory a private mount on the host before any pin is created (mount --bind /run/opentap /run/opentap; mount --make-private /run/opentap, e.g. a systemd mount unit or a daemon start-up step verified with findmnt -o+PROPAGATION); on a systemd host /run is MS_SHARED and the mnt pin would otherwise fail with EINVAL whenever the mount point is visible in a peer or slave namespace. (3) The transient units that call nsenter must not be given their own mount namespace by systemd sandboxing options (PrivateTmp=, ProtectSystem=, etc.), because a freshly copied mount namespace silently omits mnt-ns-file mounts; they also need CAP_SYS_CHROOT and CAP_SYS_ADMIN. If sandboxing is wanted, pass the namespaces by process instead of by file: keep a holder process alive in the namespaces and use nsenter --target <pid> --mount --net --uts (or a pidfd), which needs no bind mounts or propagation prerequisites. (4) Document teardown as umount of each pin, and note that the pins are not inherited by other mount namespaces, so only the host namespace (or a pidfd/--target path) can be used to re-enter the view.
- Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/namespace.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/pnode.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/pnode.h ; https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/4ce5d2b1a8fd ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/util-linux/util-linux/v2.41/sys-utils/unshare.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/util-linux/util-linux/v2.41/sys-utils/unshare.1.adoc ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/util-linux/util-linux/v2.41/sys-utils/nsenter.c ; https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commit/c84f259.patch ; https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commit/c84f259 ; https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commit/0490a6c ; https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commits/v2.27/sys-utils/unshare.c ; https://mirrors.edge.kernel.org/pub/linux/utils/util-linux/v2.27/v2.27-ReleaseNotes ; https://sources.debian.org/src/util-linux/2.41.5-0+deb13u1/sys-utils/unshare.c/ ; https://packages.debian.org/trixie/util-linux ; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/util-linux/unshare.1.en.html ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/unshare.1.html ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/mount_namespaces.7.html ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pivot_root.2.html ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/setns.2.html

### [C17] CONFIRMED
- Claim: multipath-tools 0.11.1 (Debian 13 trixie 0.11.1-2, as used by Proxmox VE 9.x) has a built-in hardware-table entry for vendor regex (LIO-ORG|SUSE), product .*, with pgpolicy GROUP_BY_PRIO, prio alua, checker directio, no_path_retry 12, immediate failback and detect_checker off, so with the default polling_interval of 5 s it queues I/O for 60 s after all paths fail and then fails it, which contradicts the round-2 Appendix B recipe of no_path_retry queue.
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Storage, Opus-Protocols, Opus-Consensus
- Why it matters: Keeping vendor 'LIO-ORG' so Proxmox 8/9 hosts multipath correctly with an empty multipath.conf, and the choice between 'fail after 60 s' versus 'queue forever and silently resume' under nvfail and under the no-quorum stop posture, depend on this; one shipped multipath.conf must be ruled.
- Summary: Every element of the claim checks out against primary sources: Debian trixie ships multipath-tools 0.11.1-2 with no Debian patch touching hwtable.c or the defaults, Proxmox VE 9.0 is "Based on Debian Trixie (13)" and its own package repository ships no multipath-tools at all, and the upstream 0.11.1 hwtable.c entry is exactly vendor "(LIO-ORG|SUSE)", product ".*", GROUP_BY_PRIO, -FAILBACK_IMMEDIATE, no_path_retry 12, PRIO_ALUA, DIRECTIO, DETECT_CHECKER_OFF. The timing is confirmed in code: enter_recovery_mode() sets retry_tick = no_path_retry * checkint + 1 (= 61 with the default polling_interval 5 and no WatchdogSec in Debian's multipathd.service), the checkerloop decrements it once per sleep(1) pass and then calls dm_queue_if_no_path(mpp, 0), after which the kernel's multipath_clone_and_map() returns DM_MAPIO_KILL (EIO). Two precision notes only: detect_prio stays on, so the effective prioritizer on a TPGS-capable LIO LUN is "sysfs" (ALUA state read from the kernel) rather than "alua", and the 60 s countdown starts when multipathd sees the last path fail, i.e. after transport/checker detection time; the directio checker was chosen upstream (commit 71448bb, issue #54) precisely because "LIO always responds with GOOD status to TUR", which also contradicts Appendix B's `path_checker tur`.
- Evidence: 1. hwtable entry (upstream tag 0.11.1, libmultipath/hwtable.c, identical in sources.debian.org multipath-tools 0.11.1-2): "/* Linux-IO (LIO) Target */ .vendor = \"(LIO-ORG|SUSE)\", .product = \".*\", .pgpolicy = GROUP_BY_PRIO, .pgfailback = -FAILBACK_IMMEDIATE, .no_path_retry = 12, .prio_name = PRIO_ALUA, .checker_name = DIRECTIO, .detect_checker = DETECT_CHECKER_OFF". No .hwhandler field in 0.11.1 (the 0.9.4 entry additionally had .hwhandler = "1 alua" and lacked the two checker fields).
2. Debian: packages.debian.org/trixie heading "Package: multipath-tools (0.11.1-2)"; debian/patches/series contains only 0001-Update-build-flags, 0003-kpartx-rules-use-Debian-specific-partx-path, 0004-Debian-specific-priority-of-udev-rules; debian/ ships no multipath.conf and no multipathd.service override; upstream multipathd.service.in has "no WatchdogSec line". Bookworm (Proxmox 8 base) ships "multipath-tools (0.9.4-3+deb12u2)".
3. Proxmox: Roadmap "Proxmox VE 9.0 ... Based on Debian Trixie (13) ... Released 05. August 2025 ... Latest 6.14.8-2 Kernel"; 9.1 "Based on Debian Trixie (13.2)"; 8.4 "Based on Debian Bookworm (12.10)". The PVE 9 pve-no-subscription trixie Packages index (2012 packages, downloaded) contains zero occurrences of "multipath", so PVE 9 uses Debian's 0.11.1-2 unchanged. Proxmox wiki "Multipath": "If your SAN vendor does not provide recommendations, you should start with an empty /etc/multipath.conf" and it links to upstream hwtable.c for device defaults.
4. multipath.conf(5) for trixie 0.11.1-2: polling_interval "Interval between two path checks in seconds ... The default is: 5" and "will be overridden by the WatchdogSec setting in the multipathd.service definition if systemd is used"; max_polling_interval "The default is: 4 * polling_interval" (applies to "properly functioning paths" only); no_path_retry numeric "Number of retries until disable I/O queueing", "fail: For immediate failure (no I/O queueing)", "queue: For never stop I/O queueing ... See KNOWN ISSUES", "The default is: fail"; dev_loss_tmo: multipathd "will make sure that the value of dev_loss_tmo is larger than no_path_retry * polling_interval"; detect_checker "The default is: yes" (switches to tur on ALUA devices); detect_prio "The default is: yes" ("sysfs prioritizer if the required sysfs attributes access_state and preferred_path are supported, or the alua prioritizer if not"); failback default manual; path_grouping_policy default failover; path_checker default tur; "the built-in hardware table has the lowest precedence"; "If there are multiple matches for a given device, the attributes of all matching entries are applied to it"; KNOWN ISSUES: queue_if_no_path "can lead to D state processes being hung and not killable", recommends no_path_retry, and warns of "a deadlock if the dev_loss_tmo setting results in a device being removed while I/O is still queued"; "Currently used multipathd configuration can be displayed with the multipath -t or multipathd show config command."
5. Timing in code (0.11.1): libmultipath/defaults.h "#define DEFAULT_CHECKINT 5", "#define DEFAULT_NO_PATH_RETRY NO_PATH_RETRY_UNDEF"; libmultipath/config.c: "if (conf->checkint == CHECKINT_UNDEF) conf->checkint = DEFAULT_CHECKINT; conf->max_checkint = ... conf->checkint * 4"; libmultipath/structs_vec.c enter_recovery_mode(): "mpp->retry_tick = mpp->no_path_retry * checkint + 1; condlog(1, \"%s: Entering recovery mode: max_retries=%d\" ...)", entered from update_queue_mode_del_path() "if (active == 0) enter_recovery_mode(mpp)"; leave_recovery_mode() re-enables queueing ("queue_if_no_path enabled ... Recovered to normal mode") when a path returns; multipathd/main.c retry_count_tick(): "if(--mpp->retry_tick == 0) { mpp->stat_map_failures++; dm_queue_if_no_path(mpp, 0); condlog(2, \"%s: Disable queueing\" ...)", called once per checkerloop pass which ends with "sleep(1)". So 12 * 5 + 1 = 61 one-second ticks. Kernel v6.12 drivers/md/dm-mpath.c: multipath_clone_and_map() "if (!pgpath) { if (must_push_back_rq(m)) return DM_MAPIO_DELAY_REQUEUE; dm_report_EIO(m); return DM_MAPIO_KILL;" where must_push_back_rq tests MPATHF_QUEUE_IF_NO_PATH; the "fail_if_no_path" message calls queue_if_no_path(m, false, ...) which runs process_queued_io_list(m).
6. Selection order (libmultipath/propsel.c): select_prio() consults detect_prio autodetection first ("(setting: storage device autodetected)"), then multipaths, overrides, hwtable, defaults; select_checker() likewise autodetects first unless detect_checker is off, then overrides, hwtable, defaults; select_no_path_retry(): multipaths, overrides, hwtable, defaults, no internal default (undef = fail behaviour in the kernel map).
7. Why directio: commit 71448bb37424 (Martin Wilck, 2023-03-23, in 0.9.5+): "LIO always responds with GOOD status to TUR. Thus TUR is not useful as path checker for LIO targets. Fixes #54 ... v2: fixed up with .detect_checker setting." Issue #54 ("IO process is D+ when path_checker is tur and there some problem in backstores"): "the path will be down->up->down->up and no_path_retry doesn't work because the tur check is OK but IO is fail"; mwilck: "LIO always reports GOOD status to TUR. You can't use the TUR checker with LIO."
8. Local design text (E:/Coding/OpenTAP/docs/03-architecture-brainstorm-02.md line 832, Appendix B): "Linux. multipath.conf: ALUA priority, path_checker tur, no_path_retry queue, fast_io_fail_tmo 5, dev_loss_tmo 30, both portals; node.session.timeo.replacement_timeout 15."
- Corrected claim: multipath-tools 0.11.1 (Debian 13 trixie package 0.11.1-2, unpatched in this respect, and the package Proxmox VE 9.x uses since PVE 9.0 is based on Debian 13 and the PVE repository ships no multipath-tools of its own) carries a built-in hardware-table entry for vendor "(LIO-ORG|SUSE)", product ".*": path_grouping_policy group_by_prio, failback immediate, no_path_retry 12, prio alua, path_checker directio, detect_checker no (detect_prio stays at its default yes, so on a TPGS-capable LIO LUN the effective prioritizer is "sysfs", which reads the same ALUA state from the kernel). With the default polling_interval of 5 s (Debian's multipathd.service sets no WatchdogSec), multipathd enters recovery mode when it sees the last path fail, sets retry_tick = 12 x 5 + 1 and counts it down once per second, then disables queue_if_no_path, so I/O that was held is failed with EIO about 60 s after the last path is marked failed (plus transport or checker detection time, e.g. fast_io_fail_tmo 5 s); queueing is re-enabled automatically when a path returns. Proxmox VE 8.x (Debian 12, multipath-tools 0.9.4-3+deb12u2) has the same entry minus the checker fields (tur via detect_checker, plus hwhandler "1 alua"), so the 60 s behaviour is the same there but backstore failures are not detected because LIO answers TUR with GOOD. The built-in entry therefore contradicts the round-2 Appendix B recipe on two points: no_path_retry (12, i.e. fail after about 60 s, versus queue) and path_checker (directio, chosen upstream in commit 71448bb for issue #54, versus tur).
- Design impact: (1) Keep the LIO INQUIRY vendor "LIO-ORG": it is what makes a Proxmox 8/9 or Debian host with an empty /etc/multipath.conf get group_by_prio, ALUA priority, immediate failback and a 60 s no-path grace. Changing vendor_id would drop hosts to the internal defaults (failover grouping, no_path_retry fail = immediate EIO, failback manual, tur checker) unless OpenTAP ships a matching device block. (2) Rule one shipped multipath.conf and make Appendix B consistent with it. The built-in default means "fail after about 60 s with no path"; Appendix B's "queue" means "hold forever and silently resume". Under nvfail/ROLLBACK or the no-quorum stop posture the design must pick one: if the intent is that a stalled or rolled-back LUN surfaces an error to the guest rather than resuming against lost acknowledged writes, the 60 s built-in default already does that and the shipped file should either omit no_path_retry or set an explicit number (and the takeover budget of 10 s p99 / 15 s hard fits inside 60 s); if the intent is ESXi-like indefinite hold, the file must contain devices { device { vendor "LIO-ORG" product ".*" no_path_retry queue } } (the entry is merged with the built-in one; only listed attributes change), accepting the man page's KNOWN ISSUES warnings about unkillable D-state processes and the dev_loss_tmo interaction (Appendix B's dev_loss_tmo 30 with no_path_retry queue falls under that warning and multipathd will adjust dev_loss_tmo; re-derive those two numbers together). (3) Drop "path_checker tur" from Appendix B or justify it: upstream switched LIO to directio because LIO returns GOOD to TUR even when the backstore cannot do I/O, so tur would hide exactly the backend failures OpenTAP cares about; keep directio (and detect_checker no) in the shipped recipe. (4) State the timing precisely in the document: Linux hosts with the built-in entry get EIO roughly 60 s plus detection time after the last path fails, not at 15 s and not "fail" immediately; the earlier round-1 statement that dm-multipath fails at about 15 s with no_path_retry=fail applies only to targets that do not match the LIO-ORG entry. (5) Add a verification step to Host Utilities: "multipath -t | grep -A12 LIO-ORG" on a Proxmox 8/9 host to show the effective built-in values, and note that Proxmox's own guidance is to start from an empty multipath.conf, so the shipped file should be a small devices-section override rather than a full defaults rewrite.

### [C18] CONFIRMED
- Claim: Linux 6.12 LIO (drivers/target/target_core_configfs.c, target_core_fabric_configfs.c, target_core_alua.h) exposes per target-port-group attributes alua_access_state, alua_access_type, alua_support_{transitioning,offline,lba_dependent,unavailable,standby,active_nonoptimized,active_optimized}, implicit_trans_secs (max 255), preferred and tg_pt_gp_id, plus lun_N/alua_tg_pt_gp per LUN; the alua_access_state store handler calls core_alua_do_port_transition and returns -EINVAL when TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA is disabled or the group has no valid tg_pt_gp_id; wwn/vendor_id (8 bytes), product_id (16) and revision (4) are writable only while no exports exist; and dbroot defaults to /var/target with /etc/target preferred.
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Consensus
- Why it matters: The implicit-only ALUA design with a Standby partner group, the planned-cutover primitive (Transitioning on the old owner, Active/Optimized on the new, Standby on the old) as configfs writes, the day-one vendor/product decision, and the PR APTPL persistence location depend on these attributes and their write rules.
- Summary: Every element of C18 is present in the Linux v6.12 target code, and Debian trixie's packaged kernel source (linux 6.12.111-1, the current stable-security/proposed-updates version; stable is 6.12.94-1) shows the same constants. The tg_pt_gp attribute set, the 255-second cap, the store handler's -EINVAL paths for no valid tg_pt_gp_id and for TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA disabled, the 8/16/4-byte vendor/product/revision limits gated on dev->export_count, the lun_N/alua_tg_pt_gp attribute, and the /var/target default with /etc/target preferred are all verbatim in the source. The claim omits a few conditions the design should carry: the handler also returns -ENODEV for an unconfigured device and -EINVAL for LBA_DEPENDENT when explicit ALUA is enabled; alua_support_* bits are writable only after tg_pt_gp_id is set (write-once); the default alua_access_type is 3 (implicit+explicit), so implicit-only must be written explicitly; implicit_trans_secs is advisory (only reported in RTPG); and the kernel creates metadata files but never their directories.
- Evidence: Verification note: git.kernel.org/plain returned HTTP 403 and elixir.bootlin.com pages came back as version navigation only, so kernel code was read from the GitHub mirror of the v6.12 tag (torvalds/linux) and cross-checked against Debian's packaged source on sources.debian.org at 6.12.111-1.

1. Target port group attributes (drivers/target/target_core_configfs.c, v6.12): "CONFIGFS_ATTR(target_tg_pt_gp_, alua_access_state);" ... "alua_access_status" ... "alua_access_type" ... "alua_support_transitioning" ... "alua_support_offline" ... "alua_support_lba_dependent" ... "alua_support_unavailable" ... "alua_support_standby" ... "alua_support_active_optimized" ... "alua_support_active_nonoptimized" ... "alua_write_metadata" ... "nonop_delay_msecs" ... "trans_delay_msecs" ... "implicit_trans_secs" ... "preferred" ... "tg_pt_gp_id"; "CONFIGFS_ATTR_RO(target_tg_pt_gp_, members);" all listed in "static struct configfs_attribute *target_core_alua_tg_pt_gp_attrs[]". The alua/ directory is created per backstore device in target_core_make_subdev: 'config_group_init_type_name(&dev->t10_alua.alua_tg_pt_gps_group, "alua", &tb->tb_dev_alua_tg_pt_gps_cit);' and mkdir there calls "core_alua_allocate_tg_pt_gp(alua->t10_dev, name, 0)". The default group is 'core_alua_allocate_tg_pt_gp(dev, "default_tg_pt_gp", 1)' and with def_group the code sets "tg_pt_gp->tg_pt_gp_valid_id = 1;".

2. implicit_trans_secs max (drivers/target/target_core_alua.h): "#define ALUA_MAX_IMPLICIT_TRANS_SECS 255", "#define ALUA_DEFAULT_IMPLICIT_TRANS_SECS 0"; store handler core_alua_store_implicit_trans_secs: "if (tmp > ALUA_MAX_IMPLICIT_TRANS_SECS) {" ... "return -EINVAL;". Its only consumer is the RTPG extended header: "buf[4] = 0x10;" "buf[5] = tg_pt_gp->tg_pt_gp_implicit_trans_secs;" — core_alua_state_transition does not reference it. Same values on Debian: sources.debian.org linux 6.12.111-1 target_core_alua.h shows "#define ALUA_MAX_IMPLICIT_TRANS_SECS 255", "TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA 0x10", "TPGS_EXPLICIT_ALUA 0x20", states 0x0 AO, 0x1 ANO, 0x2 Standby, 0x3 Unavailable, 0x4 LBA dependent, 0xe Offline, 0xf Transition.

3. alua_access_state store handler (target_tg_pt_gp_alua_access_state_store): no valid ID -> 'pr_err("Unable to do implicit ALUA on invalid tg_pt_gp ID\n"); return -EINVAL;'; device not configured -> "return -ENODEV;"; kstrtoul failure -> returns its error; implicit disabled -> "Unable to process implicit configfs ALUA transition while TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA is disabled" and "return -EINVAL"; explicit enabled and new_state == ALUA_ACCESS_STATE_LBA_DEPENDENT -> -EINVAL; then "ret = core_alua_do_port_transition(tg_pt_gp, dev, NULL, NULL, new_state, 0);" and "return (!ret) ? count : -EINVAL;". core_alua_do_port_transition itself (target_core_alua.c) returns -ENODEV for TRANSPORT_FLAG_PASSTHROUGH_ALUA backends, computes "valid_states = l_tg_pt_gp->tg_pt_gp_alua_supported_states;" and returns -EINVAL if core_alua_check_transition fails; in that check "case ALUA_ACCESS_STATE_TRANSITION: if (!(valid & ALUA_T_SUP) || explicit) goto not_supported;" (comment: "Transitioning is set internally and by tcmu daemon, and cannot be selected through a STPG"), so a configfs write of 15 is accepted when alua_support_transitioning=1. core_alua_do_transition_tg_pt sets "tg_pt_gp_alua_access_state = ALUA_ACCESS_STATE_TRANSITION", queues a UA (ASC 0x2A, ASCQ_2AH_ASYMMETRIC_ACCESS_STATE_CHANGED), and "if (new_state == ALUA_ACCESS_STATE_TRANSITION) { ... return 0; }"; otherwise it optionally sleeps "msleep_interruptible(tg_pt_gp->tg_pt_gp_trans_delay_msecs)" then sets the new state and, if alua_write_metadata, writes metadata. While in Transition, core_alua_state_transition services only INQUIRY, REPORT_LUNS, MAINTENANCE_IN/MI_REPORT_TARGET_PGS, REQUEST_SENSE, READ_BUFFER, WRITE_BUFFER; everything else gets "return TCM_ALUA_STATE_TRANSITION;". Defaults in core_alua_allocate_tg_pt_gp: supported states "ALUA_T_SUP | ALUA_O_SUP | ALUA_U_SUP | ALUA_S_SUP | ALUA_AN_SUP | ALUA_AO_SUP", state ACTIVE_OPTIMIZED, access type "TPGS_EXPLICIT_ALUA | TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA". core_alua_store_access_type accepts only 0..3 (1 = TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA only). The ALUA_SUPPORTED_STATE_ATTR store macro begins with "if (!t->tg_pt_gp_valid_id)" -> 'pr_err("Unable to set " #_name " ALUA state on invalid tg_pt_gp ID\n"); return -EINVAL;'. tg_pt_gp_id store: "> 0x0000ffff" -> -EINVAL; core_alua_set_tg_pt_gp_id: "if (tg_pt_gp->tg_pt_gp_valid_id) { pr_warn("ALUA TG PT Group already has a valid ID, ignoring request\n"); return -EINVAL; }" and "tg_pt_gp_id_tmp = (tg_pt_gp_id != 0) ? tg_pt_gp_id : dev->t10_alua.alua_tg_pt_gps_counter++;". preferred store accepts only 0 or 1.

4. Per-LUN attribute (drivers/target/target_core_fabric_configfs.c): "CONFIGFS_ATTR(target_fabric_port_, alua_tg_pt_gp);" plus alua_tg_pt_offline, alua_tg_pt_status, alua_tg_pt_write_md in "target_fabric_port_attrs[]"; the LUN directory name is user supplied and checked with 'if (strstr(name, "lun_") != name)' then "kstrtoull(name + 4, 0, &unpacked_lun)". The store delegates to core_alua_store_tg_pt_gp_info, which rejects passthrough-ALUA devices (-ENODEV), limits the name to TG_PT_GROUP_NAME_BUF, treats "NULL" as revert to default_tg_pt_gp, and core_alua_get_tg_pt_gp_by_name skips groups with "!tg_pt_gp->tg_pt_gp_valid_id". core_tpg_add_lun attaches new LUNs to "dev->t10_alua.default_tg_pt_gp".

5. INQUIRY identity (include/target/target_core_base.h): "#define INQUIRY_VENDOR_LEN 8", "#define INQUIRY_MODEL_LEN 16", "#define INQUIRY_REVISION_LEN 4". target_core_configfs.c: "CONFIGFS_ATTR(target_wwn_, vendor_id);" "product_id" "revision" "company_id" "vpd_unit_serial" (plus RO vpd_protocol_identifier and vpd_assoc_*). target_wwn_vendor_id_store: "if (len < 0 || len > INQUIRY_VENDOR_LEN) {" ... "return -EINVAL;"; product_id/revision use INQUIRY_MODEL_LEN / INQUIRY_REVISION_LEN with the same -EOVERFLOW / -EINVAL pattern and a printable-ASCII check (target_check_inquiry_data). target_core_tpg.c: core_tpg_add_lun does "dev->export_count++;" under se_port_lock; core_tpg_remove_lun does "dev->export_count--;". target_core_device.c defaults: 'strscpy(dev->t10_wwn.vendor, "LIO-ORG", ...)', model from "dev->transport->inquiry_prod", revision from "dev->transport->inquiry_rev".

6. dbroot: target_core_internal.h (v6.12 and Debian 6.12.111-1): "#define DB_ROOT_LEN 4096", '#define DB_ROOT_DEFAULT "/var/target"', '#define DB_ROOT_PREFERRED "/etc/target"', "extern char db_root[];". target_core_configfs.c: "char db_root[DB_ROOT_LEN] = DB_ROOT_DEFAULT;"; target_init_dbroot() (called from target_core_init_configfs under kernel creds) does "snprintf(db_root_stage, DB_ROOT_LEN, DB_ROOT_PREFERRED); fp = filp_open(db_root_stage, O_RDONLY, 0);", requires "S_ISDIR(file_inode(fp)->i_mode)", then "strncpy(db_root, db_root_stage, DB_ROOT_LEN);". "CONFIGFS_ATTR(target_core_item_, dbroot);" in target_core_fabric_item_attrs; the store refuses with 'pr_err("db_root: cannot be changed because it's in use\n")' when target_devices is non-zero and requires an existing directory. Consumers: target_core_pr.c 'path = kasprintf(GFP_KERNEL, "%s/pr/aptpl_%s", db_root, &wwn->unit_serial[0]);' opened "O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC" 0600; target_core_alua.c primary metadata '"%s/alua/tpgs_%s/%s", db_root', secondary '"%s/alua/%s/%s/lun_%llu"' (or "%s+%hu" with a TPG tag); core_alua_write_tpg_metadata uses "filp_open(path, O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0600)" and never creates directories.

7. Platform: tracker.debian.org/pkg/linux lists "6.12.94-1 stable (trixie)" and "6.12.111-1 stable-security (trixie) and stable-proposed-updates"; sources.debian.org at 6.12.111-1 shows identical ALUA and DB_ROOT constants.
- Corrected claim: Linux 6.12 LIO (Debian trixie ships linux 6.12.94-1 / 6.12.111-1 with identical code) exposes, under each backstore's alua/<group>/ directory (default_tg_pt_gp is created automatically with a valid ID; mkdir creates more), the attributes alua_access_state, alua_access_status, alua_access_type, alua_support_{transitioning,offline,lba_dependent,unavailable,standby,active_nonoptimized,active_optimized}, alua_write_metadata, nonop_delay_msecs (max 10000), trans_delay_msecs (max 30000), implicit_trans_secs (0..255, default 0; advisory only: it is reported in the RTPG extended header and does not time anything in the target), preferred (0/1), tg_pt_gp_id (1..65535, 0 = auto-assign; write-once, a second write returns -EINVAL) and read-only members. Each fabric LUN directory lun_N (name supplied at mkdir, must start with "lun_") has alua_tg_pt_gp (write a group name with a valid ID, or "NULL" to revert to default_tg_pt_gp), alua_tg_pt_offline, alua_tg_pt_status and alua_tg_pt_write_md. The alua_access_state store handler returns -EINVAL if the group has no valid tg_pt_gp_id, -ENODEV if the backstore is not configured, -EINVAL if TPGS_IMPLICIT_ALUA is not set in alua_access_type, -EINVAL for state 4 (LBA dependent) while explicit ALUA is enabled, and otherwise calls core_alua_do_port_transition(..., explicit=0) and returns -EINVAL if that fails (state not in the alua_support_* mask, or a passthrough-ALUA backend). The alua_support_* bits can only be written after tg_pt_gp_id is valid; alua_access_type defaults to 3 (implicit+explicit) and must be written as 1 for implicit-only. State values are 0 Active/Optimized, 1 Active/Non-optimized, 2 Standby, 3 Unavailable, 4 LBA dependent, 14 Offline, 15 Transitioning; 15 is accepted from configfs (never from an initiator STPG) when alua_support_transitioning=1, takes effect immediately, queues a 2Ah/06h unit attention, and while it lasts only INQUIRY, REPORT LUNS, RTPG, REQUEST SENSE, READ BUFFER and WRITE BUFFER are serviced (everything else returns NOT READY / ALUA state transition); any other target state passes through Transitioning internally, sleeping trans_delay_msecs if non-zero. wwn/vendor_id (max 8 bytes, default "LIO-ORG"), wwn/product_id (max 16, default the backend's inquiry_prod) and wwn/revision (max 4, default the backend's inquiry_rev) must be printable ASCII (longer values return -EOVERFLOW) and are writable only while dev->export_count is 0, i.e. before the backstore is linked into any TPG LUN (-EINVAL afterwards). db_root is initialised to "/var/target" and switched to "/etc/target" at target_core_mod load if that directory exists; /sys/kernel/config/target/dbroot can be rewritten only while no backstore devices exist and must name an existing directory. The kernel writes PR APTPL state to <dbroot>/pr/aptpl_<vpd_unit_serial> and ALUA metadata to <dbroot>/alua/tpgs_<group>/... and <dbroot>/alua/<fabric>/<tpg>/lun_N with O_CREAT on the file only; it never creates the directories.
- Design impact: No change to the architecture: implicit-only ALUA with a Standby partner group, the planned-cutover primitive as configfs writes, the day-one vendor/product decision and the APTPL location all rest on attributes and rules that exist exactly as assumed in 6.12. The design document should add these operational rules so the implementation does not trip over them: (1) group setup order per backstore is mkdir alua/<name>, write tg_pt_gp_id (write-once; choose stable IDs that are identical on both nodes), then alua_support_* bits (they return -EINVAL before the ID is valid), then alua_access_type=1 (the default 3 would also accept initiator STPGs), preferred, implicit_trans_secs, and only then alua_access_state and lun_N/alua_tg_pt_gp assignment; (2) the cutover sequence (write 15 to the old owner's group, 0 to the new owner's group, 2 to the old owner's group) is valid, but note that the write of 15 returns immediately and blocks all data commands on that port until the follow-up write, that the write to 2 is a no-op if the state is already 2, that trans_delay_msecs is an optional pause in the Transitioning window, and that implicit_trans_secs only tells initiators how long to tolerate Transitioning; pick a value matching the worst-case cutover time (ESXi uses it as its transition timeout base); (3) vendor_id/product_id/revision must be written in the device-creation path before the first LUN link, which also means changing them later requires unlinking every LUN (an export-visible event), so the day-one values are effectively permanent; (4) the install step must create /etc/target before target_core_mod loads (or write dbroot before creating any backstore) and must create /etc/target/pr and /etc/target/alua/tpgs_<group> directories, since the kernel only creates files; the APTPL file name is keyed on wwn/vpd_unit_serial, so the unit serial must be set before any LUN link and be identical on both nodes for the replicated PR state to map to the same file after failover.
- Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_configfs.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_alua.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_alua.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_fabric_configfs.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_internal.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/target/target_core_base.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_pr.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_device.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/target/target_core_tpg.c ; https://sources.debian.org/src/linux/6.12.111-1/drivers/target/target_core_alua.h/ ; https://sources.debian.org/src/linux/6.12.111-1/drivers/target/target_core_internal.h/ ; https://tracker.debian.org/pkg/linux

### [C19] CONFIRMED
- Claim: When an export has no fsid= option, knfsd and rpc.mountd (nfs-utils 2.8.3) identify the exported filesystem by its filesystem UUID, so two XFS snapshot mounts of the same image mounted with nouuid under a crossmnt parent receive identical fsids and identical NFS file handles for the same inode and lookups can resolve to either mount; XFS accepts the mount options nouuid (skip duplicate-UUID check) and norecovery (read-only, no log replay), and xfs_admin -U generate assigns a new UUID to an unmounted filesystem; exports(5) crossmnt implicitly exports child mounts with the parent's options except fsid; Samba's vfs_shadow_copy2 exposes snapshot directories named by shadow:format (default @GMT-%Y.%m.%d-%H.%M.%S) under shadow:snapdir as Previous Versions.
- Raised by: Opus-Protocols, Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: The NAS exposure of LUN snapshots as read-only ublk devices mounted at .snapshot/@GMT-... and auto-exported via crossmnt either works or silently serves the wrong snapshot's data, in which case every snapshot mount needs an explicit export with a unique fsid (or a fresh UUID), and writable clones need xfs_admin -U.
- Summary: Every sub-claim checks out against nfs-utils 1:2.8.3-1 (the trixie version), Linux 6.12 fs/nfsd and fs/xfs, xfsprogs 6.13.0-2+deb13u1 and the Samba 4.22.0 man page, and the real mechanism is worse than "either mount": rpc.mountd derives an export's UUID with libblkid from the block device under the path, knfsd resolves file handles only by (client, fsid type, fsid), and mountd answers a UUID lookup with the first matching path (the crossmnt export's own path first, then its sub-mounts in /etc/mtab order) and logs nothing for duplicates inside one crossmnt export, so all handles carrying the duplicated UUID land on one mount for the life of the cache entry, and if the crossmnt parent is the live volume the snapshots were taken from, it shares the UUID and captures every snapshot handle (a parent fsid=N does not prevent this). Conditions the design must carry: norecovery mounts must be read-only and can never be remounted rw; xfs_admin -U generate needs an unmounted, writable device with a clean log (xfs_db refuses on a dirty log), so it cannot be applied to read-only or crash-consistent snapshot devices; Samba's default shadow:snapdir is .snapshots, so a .snapshot directory must be configured explicitly.
- Evidence: Versions: tracker.debian.org/pkg/nfs-utils lists "stable: 1:2.8.3-1"; packages.debian.org/trixie/nfs-kernel-server shows "Package: nfs-kernel-server (1:2.8.3-1)"; trixie samba is 2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1; trixie xfsprogs is 6.13.0-2+deb13u1; trixie linux is 6.12.x (6.12.107-1 current). Elixir pages returned no code body through the fetch tool and git.kernel.org "plain" URLs answered 403, so kernel files were read from the torvalds/linux mirror at tag v6.12 and nfs-utils/xfsprogs from sources.debian.org.

(1) mountd identifies filesystems by blkid UUID. nfs-utils 2.8.3 support/export/cache.c get_uuid_blkdev(): "devname = blkid_devno_to_devname(stb.st_dev); ... dev = blkid_get_dev(cache, devname, BLKID_DEV_NORMAL); ... if (strcmp(type, "UUID") == 0) uuid = val;". uuid_by_path(): "blkid must be preferred" over the statfs f_fsid; XFS is not in nonblkid_filesystems[] (ZFS, BTRFS, CIFS, DEVFS, CODA, NCP, NFS, PROC, SYSFS, SMB, TMPFS only), so for XFS the export UUID is the superblock UUID read from the backing block device, identical for every block-level copy. dump_to_cache() hands it to the kernel: "if (exp->e_uuid == NULL || different_fs) { ... uuid_by_path(path, 0, 16, u)) { qword_add(&bp, &blen, "uuid"); qword_addhex(&bp, &blen, u, 16);".

(2) crossmnt children: same options except fsid. exports(5) from nfs-utils 2.8.3: "If a child of a crossmnt file is not explicitly exported, then it will be implicitly exported with the same export options as the parent, except for fsid=." and under fsid=: "Normally it will use a UUID for the filesystem (if the filesystem has such a thing) or the device number of the device holding the filesystem". Code: dump_to_cache(): "int different_fs = strcmp(path, exp->e_path) != 0; int flag_mask = different_fs ? ~NFSEXP_FSID : ~0;" and the child gets its own blkid uuid (quoted above). lookup_export(): "If one is a CROSSMOUNT, then prefer the longest path" -> an explicit export of the child overrides the implicit one.

(3) knfsd puts the UUID in the handle and resolves handles only by fsid. fs/nfsd/nfsfh.c set_version_and_fsid_type(): "} else if (exp->ex_flags & NFSEXP_FSID) { fsid_type = FSID_NUM; } else if (exp->ex_uuid) { if (fhp->fh_maxsize >= 64) { if (is_root_export(exp)) fsid_type = FSID_UUID16; else fsid_type = FSID_UUID16_INUM;"; is_root_export(): "return exp->ex_path.dentry == exp->ex_path.dentry->d_sb->s_root;" (a snapshot mounted and exported at its root gets FSID_UUID16). fh_compose(): "mk_fsid(fhp->fh_handle.fh_fsid_type, fhp->fh_handle.fh_fsid, ex_dev, d_inode(exp->ex_path.dentry)->i_ino, exp->ex_fsid, exp->ex_uuid);" and nfsfh.h: "case FSID_UUID16: memcpy(fsidv, uuid, 16);". nfsd_set_fh_dentry(): "exp = rqst_exp_find(..., fh->fh_fsid_type, fh->fh_fsid);" then "dentry = exportfs_decode_fh_raw(exp->ex_path.mnt, fid, data_left, fileid_type, 0, nfsd_acceptable, exp);". export.c exp_find_key(): "key.ek_client = clp; key.ek_fsidtype = fsid_type; memcpy(key.ek_fsid, fsidv, key_len(fsid_type));" and exp_find(): "exp = exp_get_by_name(cd, clp, &ek->ek_path, reqp);"; expkey_parse() comment: "client fsidtype fsid expiry [path]" with "err = kern_path(buf, 0, &key.ek_path);" i.e. the fsid->path mapping is whatever mountd answers, cached until expiry. fs/nfsd/vfs.c nfsd_cross_mnt() crosses by path ("exp2 = rqst_exp_get_by_name(rqstp, &path);"), so directory traversal enters the right mount; only handle-based operations collapse. The NFS fsid attribute is identical too: nfs4xdr.c "case FSIDSOURCE_UUID: xdr_encode_opaque_fixed(p, args->exp->ex_uuid, EX_UUID_LEN);", nfs3xdr.c "fsid = ((u64 *)fhp->fh_export->ex_uuid)[0]; fsid ^= ((u64 *)fhp->fh_export->ex_uuid)[1];".

(4) Same inode -> same handle, decoded silently on the wrong mount. fs/xfs/xfs_export.c xfs_fs_encode_fh(): "fid->i32.ino = XFS_I(inode)->i_ino; fid->i32.gen = inode->i_generation;" (64-bit variant likewise); xfs_nfs_get_inode(): "error = xfs_iget(mp, NULL, ino, XFS_IGET_UNTRUSTED, 0, &ip);" and "if (VFS_I(ip)->i_generation != generation || IS_PRIVATE(VFS_I(ip))) { ... return ERR_PTR(-ESTALE);" -> an inode with the same number and generation (any inode unchanged between the snapshots) decodes successfully on whichever mount the fsid resolved to.

(5) mountd picks the first match, silently, for crossmnt sub-mounts. cache.c nfsd_fh() (comment: "interpret fsid, find export point and options"): for an export with NFSEXP_CROSSMOUNT it first tests "path = exp->m_export.e_path;" then "path = next_mnt(&mnt, exp->m_export.e_path);" where next_mnt() does "f = setmntent("/etc/mtab", "r");" and returns mounts "at or below a given path" in table order. match_fsid() for FSID_UUID8/FSID_UUID16: "if (!is_mountpoint(path)) ... goto nomatch;" then "for (type = 0; uuid_by_path(path, type, parsed->uuidlen, u); type++) if (memcmp(u, parsed->fhuuid, parsed->uuidlen) == 0) goto match;" (used whenever exp->m_export.e_uuid is NULL, i.e. regardless of a numeric fsid= on the parent). Selection: "if (!found || subexport(&exp->m_export, found)) { found = &exp->m_export; ... found_path = strdup(path);" else "if (strcmp(found->e_path, exp->m_export.e_path) != 0 && !subexport(found, &exp->m_export)) { xlog(L_WARNING, "%s and %s have same filehandle for %s, using first", ..." — a second matching sub-mount of the same crossmnt export has the same e_path, and subexport() ("True iff e1 is a child of e2 (or descendant) and e2 has crossmnt set") is false for an entry against itself, so neither branch fires: the first match stays and no warning is logged. Because the export's own path is tested before its sub-mounts, a live parent filesystem with the same UUID wins over every snapshot.

(6) XFS mount options. fs/xfs/xfs_super.c: "fsparam_flag("nouuid", Opt_nouuid)", "fsparam_flag("norecovery", Opt_norecovery)"; xfs_fs_validate_params(): "if (xfs_has_norecovery(mp) && !xfs_is_readonly(mp)) { xfs_warn(mp, "no-recovery mounts must be read-only."); return -EINVAL;"; xfs_remount_rw(): "ro->rw transition prohibited on norecovery mount". fs/xfs/xfs_mount.c xfs_uuid_mount(): "if (xfs_has_nouuid(mp)) return 0;" ... "xfs_warn(mp, "Filesystem has duplicate UUID %pU - can't mount"); return -EINVAL;". xfs(5): nouuid "Don't check for double mounted file systems using the file system uuid. This is useful to mount LVM snapshot volumes, and often used in combination with "norecovery" for mounting read-only snapshots."; norecovery "Filesystems mounted "norecovery" must be mounted read-only or the mount will fail." and "Some files or directories may not be accessible because of this."

(7) xfs_admin -U generate. xfs_admin(8) (xfsprogs 6.13.0): "Devices that are mounted cannot be modified. Administrators must unmount filesystems before xfs_admin or xfs_db(8) can convert parameters."; "-U uuid ... may also be generate, which will generate a new UUID for the filesystem. Note that on CRC-enabled filesystems, this will set an incompatible flag such that older kernels will not be able to mount the filesystem. To remove this incompatible flag, use restore". db/xfs_admin.sh: "U) DB_OPTS=$DB_OPTS" -c 'uuid "$OPTARG"'" require_offline=1", "if mntpt="$(findmnt -t xfs -f -n -o TARGET "$1" ...)"; then if [ -n "$require_offline" ]; then echo "$1: filesystem is mounted." exit 2", "eval xfs_db -x -p xfs_admin ...". db/sb.c uuid_f(): "if ((x.flags & LIBXFS_ISREADONLY) || !expert_mode) { dbprintf(_("%s: not in expert mode, writing disabled\n")" (device must be writable); "/* clear the log (setting uuid) if it's not dirty */ if (!sb_logzero(&uu)) return 0;" and sb_logcheck(): "ERROR: The filesystem has valuable metadata changes in a log which needs to be replayed. Mount the filesystem to replay the log, and unmount it before re-running %s. If you are unable to mount the filesystem, then use the xfs_repair -L option to destroy the log"; do_uuid() on V5: "mp->m_sb.sb_features_incompat |= XFS_SB_FEAT_INCOMPAT_META_UUID; ... memcpy(&tsb.sb_meta_uuid, &tsb.sb_uuid, sizeof(uuid_t));" (meta UUID keeps the old value; the user-visible sb_uuid, which blkid and the duplicate check use, changes).

(8) Samba vfs_shadow_copy2(8), "This man page is part of version 4.22.0 of the Samba suite": "allows Microsoft Shadow Copy clients to browse through file system snapshots as "shadow copies" on Samba shares"; "Filesystem snapshots must be available under specially named directories in order to be recognized by vfs_shadow_copy2"; "shadow:snapdir = .snapshots" (default); "shadow:format = "@GMT-%Y.%m.%d-%H.%M.%S"" (default); shadow:localtime "If it is disabled then UTC/GMT is expected"; "shadow:fixinodes = no" and "shadow:sort = desc" defaults. The page uses the term "shadow copies"; "Previous Versions" is the Windows Explorer label for the same feature.
- Corrected claim: With no fsid= option, rpc.mountd (nfs-utils 2.8.3, Debian 1:2.8.3-1) identifies an exported filesystem by the libblkid UUID of the block device under the export path (for XFS, the superblock UUID; mountd prefers blkid over the statfs f_fsid) and passes it to knfsd as uuid=; knfsd 6.12 embeds that UUID as the fsid of every file handle (FSID_UUID16 for an export at a filesystem root) and in the NFSv3/NFSv4 fsid attribute, and resolves incoming handles solely by (client, fsid type, fsid) through the nfsd.fh cache, which mountd answers with the first path whose filesystem UUID matches: the crossmnt export's own path first, then its sub-mounts in /etc/mtab order; a second match inside the same crossmnt export is ignored without any log message. Two XFS snapshot mounts of the same image (mounted with nouuid) under a crossmnt parent therefore receive identical fsids and byte-identical file handles for every inode that has the same inode number and generation, and all such handles are decoded (by inode number and generation, via exportfs) on the first-matching mount for the lifetime of the cache entry; if the crossmnt parent is the live filesystem the snapshots were taken from, it shares the UUID and captures all snapshot handles, and a numeric fsid= on the parent does not prevent this because match_fsid() compares the parent's blkid UUID whenever the export has no fsid=<uuid>. XFS 6.12 accepts nouuid (skips the duplicate-UUID table check) and norecovery (no log replay; the mount must be read-only, may leave files inaccessible, and can never be remounted rw). xfs_admin -U generate assigns a new UUID only to an unmounted, writable filesystem with a clean log (xfs_admin exits 2 if findmnt shows the device mounted; xfs_db refuses with "valuable metadata changes in a log which needs to be replayed", so a dirty log must first be replayed by a mount+unmount or destroyed with xfs_repair -L); on V5 filesystems it sets the META_UUID incompatible feature flag, which Linux 6.12 supports. exports(5): a child of a crossmnt export that is not explicitly exported is implicitly exported with the parent's options except fsid=, and an explicit export of the child takes precedence over the implicit one. Samba 4.22 vfs_shadow_copy2 presents the subdirectories of shadow:snapdir (default .snapshots) whose names match shadow:format (default "@GMT-%Y.%m.%d-%H.%M.%S", interpreted as UTC unless shadow:localtime = yes) to Windows clients as shadow copies ("Previous Versions").
- Design impact: 1) Auto-exporting .snapshot/@GMT-* mounts through a crossmnt parent with no per-snapshot fsid is unsafe for NFS and must be dropped: because each snapshot is a block copy of the live volume, the live volume, every read-only snapshot mount and every writable clone all carry the same XFS UUID, so mountd resolves any snapshot file handle to the first UUID match, normally the live parent volume itself; NFS clients would silently read live (or another snapshot's) data under snapshot paths, see one fsid for all of them, and Linux clients would alias the inodes since the handles are byte-identical. Nothing is logged, so this cannot be caught by monitoring. 2) Required remedy: every snapshot mount gets its own explicit export line with a unique fsid= (a small integer, or a 32-hex-digit UUID string), generated deterministically per snapshot (e.g. from the snapshot ID) and kept stable across reloads and reboots so client handles do not go ESTALE; explicit child exports override the crossmnt implicit export, the parent keeps crossmnt (NFSv4 traversal needs crossmnt or nohide on the parent), and exportfs -r (or exportfs -o ... path / -u) must run on every snapshot mount and unmount. FSID_NUM handles are matched only against the export carrying that number, which closes the hole. mountd finds sub-mounts via /etc/mtab, so keep Debian's default /etc/mtab -> /proc/self/mounts symlink. 3) The "fresh UUID" alternative only applies to writable clones: xfs_admin -U generate cannot run on a read-only ublk snapshot device and refuses a dirty log. For a writable clone the sequence is: mount rw with nouuid once to replay the log (or quiesce the source with xfs_freeze before snapshotting so the log is clean), unmount, xfs_admin -U generate, then mount normally without nouuid; after that the clone gets a distinct blkid UUID and may be exported without fsid=. Read-only snapshots must use -o ro,nouuid,norecovery and the explicit fsid= export; note that an unreplayed log may leave some files inaccessible in the norecovery view, so crash-consistent snapshots should be taken while the source is frozen if a consistent NFS/SMB view is required. 4) Samba side needs no fsid work (shadow_copy2 resolves by path) but the config must set shadow:snapdir = .snapshot explicitly, since the default is .snapshots, and keep the GMT naming with shadow:localtime = no; shadow:fixinodes is unnecessary because each snapshot is a separate block device (distinct st_dev), and shadow:sort = desc is the default. 5) The design text should replace "lookups can resolve to either mount" with the deterministic first-match behaviour described in the corrected claim and should state that the live parent is also captured.
- Sources: https://sources.debian.org/data/main/n/nfs-utils/1:2.8.3-1/support/export/cache.c ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/n/nfs-utils/1:2.8.3-1/utils/exportfs/exports.man ; https://tracker.debian.org/pkg/nfs-utils ; https://packages.debian.org/trixie/nfs-kernel-server ; https://packages.debian.org/trixie/samba ; https://sources.debian.org/api/src/xfsprogs/ ; https://sources.debian.org/api/src/linux/ ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfsfh.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfsfh.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/export.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/vfs.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfs4xdr.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfs3xdr.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/xfs/xfs_mount.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/xfs/xfs_super.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/xfs/xfs_export.c ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/xfs.5.html ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/xfs_admin.8.html ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/x/xfsprogs/6.13.0-2+deb13u1/db/sb.c ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/x/xfsprogs/6.13.0-2+deb13u1/db/xfs_admin.sh ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/x/xfsprogs/6.13.0-2+deb13u1/man/man5/xfs.5 ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/x/xfsprogs/6.13.0-2+deb13u1/man/man8/xfs_admin.8 ; https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/4.22/man-html/vfs_shadow_copy2.8.html ; https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/vfs_shadow_copy2.8.html

### [C20] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: The ESXi 8 NFSv3 client issues every datastore WRITE with stable_how = FILE_SYNC (so a knfsd sync export performs an XFS log force per WRITE and an async export would not change what the client requests), and after receiving NFS3ERR_STALE for its cached root filehandle it does not automatically re-issue the MOUNT protocol for a fresh root handle; the datastore stays inaccessible until unmounted and remounted by the administrator.
- Raised by: Opus-Storage, Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Protocols
- Why it matters: The 200 to 300 us FILE_SYNC latency budget, the dirty-page arithmetic and the engine's 'FLUSH is an ordering barrier' rule depend on every ESXi write carrying a log force; the NFS nvfail forcing function (re-export with the next fsid generation) only works if ESXi stays stuck rather than remounting by path and resuming against a rolled-back image.
- Summary: The "stuck after a stale root handle" half is supported by Broadcom's own KBs for ESXi 7.x/8.x (heartbeat = GETATTR on the cached root filehandle; a mounted volume "never needs to be remounted"; when the backend changes under the same IP the volume goes inaccessible/APD "because the ESXi host is unaware of the changes made to the backend storage" and a reboot or esxcli remove/add is needed), with one correction: a host reboot also ends the stuck state because ESXi re-mounts NFSv3 datastores by stored server+path at boot. The "every WRITE is FILE_SYNC" half has no VMware/Broadcom primary source; the best protocol-level evidence is the FreeBSD NFS maintainer's packet-trace observation (2018, ESXi NFS 4.1 datastore: "this client does all write FILESYNC") plus consistent community reports for NFSv3, so it must be confirmed by capture on ESXi 8 NFSv3 before the latency budget relies on it. The knfsd/XFS corollary is confirmed from the v6.12 source with a precision: per stable WRITE knfsd sets RWF_SYNC, which on XFS yields a log force when the inode is pinned or otherwise a data-device cache flush, and an async export leaves the client's request unchanged while the server silently downgrades to UNSTABLE yet still replies committed=FILE_SYNC.
- Evidence: A. ESXi write stability (not documented by VMware; strong secondary evidence only)
- Broadcom KB 312130 (legacy 1012143, "Maintaining write-ordering and write-through integrity using NFS") is the only VMware statement on NFS write integrity: "Currently this FUA bit is NOT honored by the SCSI emulation layer, hence Write-Through is NOT guaranteed on NFS datastores." It says nothing about stable_how/FILE_SYNC. KB 370665 (NFS support in vSphere 8), KB 323325 (advanced NFS options), the vSphere 8 NFS guidelines and the VMware "Best Practices for Running NFS with VMware vSphere" PDF (text extracted locally) contain no statement about write stability.
- FreeBSD NFS maintainer Rick Macklem, freebsd-stable, 8 Mar 2018 (thread "NFS 4.1 RECLAIM_COMPLETE FS failed error in combination with ESXi client"): "I took a quick look at your packet trace and it appears that this client does all write FILESYNC." "As such, setting vfs.nfsd.async=1 won't have any affect." "If you apply the attached patch, it should change the FILESYNC->UNSTABLE so that vfs.nfsd.async=1 will make a difference." Tester (NAGY Andreas, 9 Mar 2018): "Yes, ESXi writes everything sync." This is an NFS 4.1 datastore; ESXi version not stated (2018 era).
- Community corroboration for NFSv3 (no captures published): TrueNAS resource by jgreco (2017): "VMware writes nearly everything to the datastore as a sync write"; "NFS by default will implement sync writes as requested by the ESXi client." Frank Leonhardt (2017) inferred from FreeBSD nfsd code and tests that ESXi forces sync on every write. No published ESXi 8 NFSv3 capture showing nfs.write.stable was found.

B. knfsd 6.12 and XFS behaviour (confirmed from source, Linux v6.12 tag)
- fs/nfsd/vfs.c nfsd_vfs_write: "if (!EX_ISSYNC(exp)) stable = NFS_UNSTABLE;" then "if (stable && !fhp->fh_use_wgather) flags |= RWF_SYNC;" then "host_err = vfs_iter_write(file, &iter, &pos, flags);". Write gathering is NFSv2-only: comment "Note: we do this only in the NFSv2 case, since v3 and higher have a better tool (separate unstable writes and commits)"; fs/nfsd/nfsfh.c sets "fhp->fh_use_wgather = true;" only under "if (EX_WGATHER(exp))" in the NFS_FHSIZE (v2 handle) branch of nfsd_set_fh_dentry.
- fs/nfsd/nfs3proc.c nfsd3_proc_write: "resp->committed = argp->stable;" and nfsd_write(..., resp->committed, resp->verf) — so with an async export the reply still reports the client's requested FILE_SYNC although nfsd_vfs_write downgraded its local stable to NFS_UNSTABLE. exports(5): async "allows the NFS server to violate the NFS protocol and reply to requests before any changes made by that request have been committed to stable storage"; sync: "Reply to requests only after the changes have been committed to stable storage"; sync is the default since nfs-utils 1.0.0.
- include/linux/fs.h: "#define IOCB_SYNC (__force int) RWF_SYNC"; generic_write_sync calls vfs_fsync_range with datasync = 0 when IOCB_SYNC is set. fs/xfs/xfs_file.c: xfs_file_buffered_write ends with "ret = generic_write_sync(iocb, ret);"; xfs_file_fsync does file_write_and_wait_range, then "Any inode that has dirty modifications in the log is pinned." → xfs_fsync_flush_log (xfs_log_force_seq), and "If we only have a single device, and the log force about was a no-op we might have to flush the data device cache here" → blkdev_issue_flush. So each FILE_SYNC WRITE costs data writeback plus either a log force (inode pinned, e.g. mtime/ctime or extent changes) or a device cache flush; never nothing.

C. ESXi behaviour after the cached root handle stops resolving (Broadcom primary sources, ESXi 7.x/8.x)
- KB 323325: "NFS heartbeats are actually GETATTR requests on the root file handle of the NFS Volume." "The volume is marked unavailable if it loses connectivity to the NFS server but it still remains mounted." "The NFS heartbeat world always issues heartbeats for NFS volumes which are marked unavailable." NFS.VolumeRemountFrequency "determines how often an NFS volume attempts to mount when it is initially unable to mount. After a volume is mounted it never needs to be remounted." Defaults 7.x/8.x: HeartbeatFrequency 12, HeartbeatTimeout 5, HeartbeatDelta 5, HeartbeatMaxFailures 10. The older VMware white paper says the same: "Once a volume is mounted, it never needs to be remounted."
- VMware "Best Practices for Running NFS with VMware vSphere": "If ESXi gives up on 10 consecutive heartbeats, it treats the NFS datastore as unreachable. This is 125 seconds in total"; "ESXi hosts continue to make heartbeat requests in the hope that the datastore does become available once again."
- KB 323107 "Troubleshooting NFS datastore connectivity issues", Scenario 2: "The new NFS server uses the same IP address as the old one." "If the same IP address is used, the volume will be marked as inaccessible, and APD (All Paths Down) errors will appear in the logs." "This happens because the ESXi host is unaware of the changes made to the backend storage." "A reboot of the host is required to restore access to the NFS server."
- KB 344470: inaccessible states "often persist if the NFS server share is disconnected, modified, or removed"; remedy is esxcli storage nfs remove -v / esxcli storage nfs add -H -s -v. KB 381569: failed GETATTR heartbeats are counted in the datastore's vsish opsStats "getAttrFailed" and cause APD.
- Contrast for plain connectivity loss, KB 339587: "Once connectivity to the NFS server is restored, the volume automatically reconnects." (same root handle, no remount needed).
- Reboot caveat: KB 416172: a datastore "mounted using NFS v3 ... remains connected and persists across reboots"; "NFS v3 includes a retry mechanism during boot." KB 377606 treats NFSv3 datastores not being "automatically mounted as expected" after reboot as a bug. So a rebooted host re-issues MOUNT by stored server+path without administrator action.
- None of the Broadcom sources names NFS3ERR_STALE on the root handle explicitly; the Scenario 2 case (backend replaced, same IP) is the same mechanism. The nfs-ganesha HA thread (NFS 4.1, Dec 2020) shows the ESXi client logging "Remount data store to access" rather than remounting itself — corroborative, but v4.1.

D. NetApp NVFAIL (for the "forcing function" analogy): ONTAP MetroCluster NVFAIL doc (GitHub source of the docs.netapp.com page): "ONTAP returns a stale file handle (ESTALE) error to NFS clients trying to access the database"; "For NFS clients, files remain inaccessible until you reset the in-nvfailed-state option on the affected volume." NetApp KB shows the client symptom "touch: cannot touch `filetest': Stale file handle".
- Corrected claim: ESXi NFSv3 datastore WRITEs are expected to carry stable_how = FILE_SYNC, but VMware/Broadcom publish no statement of the value; the only protocol-level evidence is an NFS implementer's packet-trace observation of an ESXi NFS 4.1 datastore (2018: "this client does all write FILESYNC") plus consistent community reports for NFSv3. Treat FILE_SYNC-on-every-WRITE as an assumption to be confirmed by capture on ESXi 8 NFSv3 (pktcap-uw/Wireshark field nfs.write.stable on WRITE calls under VM load, and a near-zero COMMIT count in nfsstat -s on the server). On knfsd 6.12 with a sync export, every WRITE whose stable_how is not UNSTABLE is issued to the filesystem with RWF_SYNC; on XFS this is data writeback plus a log force when the inode has unlogged changes (which includes the mtime/ctime update most writes cause) or otherwise a data-device cache flush, i.e. at least one flush/FUA to the device per WRITE. An async export does not change what the client sends: knfsd downgrades the write to UNSTABLE internally but still replies committed = the client's requested stable_how (resp->committed = argp->stable), so the client believes the data is stable when it is not; async is therefore not a legitimate option for VM datastores. ESXi mounts an NFSv3 datastore once (MOUNT protocol at mount time and again at every host boot, with retries for NFSv3) and "never needs to be remounted"; its heartbeat is a GETATTR on the cached root filehandle. If the backend changes so that the cached handles no longer resolve (e.g. a new fsid under the same server IP, or NFS3ERR_STALE on the root handle), the volume is marked inaccessible/APD after NFS.HeartbeatMaxFailures (about 125 s at defaults), ESXi keeps heartbeating with the same handle and does not re-run MOUNT by itself, and access returns only when an administrator unmounts and remounts the datastore (esxcli storage nfs remove/add or the vSphere client) or the host is rebooted, at which point ESXi remounts by stored server+path and resumes.
- Design impact: 1. Keep the per-WRITE flush cost in the FILE_SYNC latency budget, but describe it precisely: on XFS each stable WRITE ends in xfs_file_fsync, which is a log force when the inode is pinned and otherwise a blkdev_issue_flush; the 200-300 us budget therefore requires a log/data device whose flush/FUA latency fits it (PLP NVMe), and the dirty-page arithmetic may assume no server-side accumulation only once the ESXi 8 NFSv3 capture confirms FILE_SYNC on every WRITE. Add that capture (Windows and Linux guests, vmdk creation/zeroing, .lck lock-file updates) as a lab verification item; until then mark the budget "pending capture".
2. State explicitly that the async export option is forbidden for datastores because knfsd replies committed=FILE_SYNC without stable storage (resp->committed = argp->stable); it does not reduce what ESXi requests, it only removes the guarantee.
3. Weaken the nvfail forcing function: the fsid-generation re-export reliably puts ESXi NFSv3 hosts into APD and they will not re-MOUNT on their own, but any host reboot (crash, HA remediation, operator reboot per Broadcom KB 323107) remounts by stored server+path and resumes against the rolled-back image without acknowledgement. The fence must therefore be server-side: after a rollback do not expose the datastore path at all (refuse MOUNT/export for that path, or publish it under a new path) until the operator acknowledges; the fsid bump alone is a notification mechanism, not a gate. Document the ESXi timeline: GETATTR heartbeat failures → unavailable after ~125 s → APD; Misc.APDTimeout and VMCP may then act, and all hosts are affected identically because they share the stale root handle.
4. Scope the statement to NFSv3. ESXi NFS 4.1 datastores have no MOUNT protocol, use a different client (it logs "Remount data store to access" and needs esxcli storage nfs41 remove/add), and their behaviour on stale handles must be verified separately if the design supports them.
5. Recovery runbook should list both paths: administrator unmount/remount, and host reboot (which re-mounts automatically), and note that remounting requires VMs on the datastore to be unregistered or powered off (Broadcom KB 344470).
- Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/vfs.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfs3proc.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/fs/nfsd/nfsfh.c ;
