### [C21] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: md's Partial Parity Log (mdadm --consistency-policy=ppl) is available for RAID5 only on mdadm 4.x with kernel 6.12; a RAID6 array without a --write-journal device has an open write hole, so a power loss during a read-modify-write of a sub-stripe write leaves the whole stripe's parity inconsistent and a later member failure reconstructs garbage for previously committed blocks sharing that stripe.
- Raised by: Opus-Consensus, Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: The torn-CP rule ('nothing CP N-1 references is overwritten') assumes a torn write damages only its own blocks; on RAID6 HDD pools with the metadata stream on the pool, either metadata must be full-stripe, the flash metadata class must be mandatory, or a journal device is required.
- Summary: The substance is confirmed by kernel 6.12 source, the kernel's md documentation and the Debian trixie mdadm 4.4-11 man pages and source: PPL is hard-restricted to RAID5 in both the kernel (ppl_init_log returns -EINVAL for any other level) and mdadm 4.4, the only md mechanism that closes the RAID6 write hole is a --write-journal device, and the kernel documents exactly the failure the claim describes ("data calculated from parity for array blocks that have not been touched by a write request during the unclean shutdown can be incorrect"). Two precisions are needed: the inconsistency is confined to the parity (P and Q) of the 4 KiB stripe rows the torn write touched (md's stripe_head unit), not the whole chunk-wide stripe, and the garbage reconstruction requires the member to be missing before md's post-crash resync has recomputed those rows — md refuses by default to start an array that is both dirty and degraded, so that path needs mdadm --force / start_dirty_degraded, or a member loss during the resync window.
- Evidence: A. PPL is RAID5-only (kernel 6.12 and mdadm 4.4). drivers/md/raid5-ppl.c at tag v6.12 (torvalds mirror) and in Debian trixie's linux 6.12.107-1 (sources.debian.org), ppl_init_log(): "if (mddev->level != 5) { pr_warn("md/raid:%s PPL is not compatible with raid level %d\n", mdname(mddev), mddev->level);" then "return -EINVAL". The same function also rejects "PPL is not compatible with bitmap", "PPL is not compatible with journal" and "PPL doesn't support over %d disks in the array" (64). drivers/md/raid5.c v6.12 raid5_change_consistency_policy() only enables PPL under "if (!raid5_has_ppl(conf) && conf->level == 5)". raid5_run(): "using journal device and PPL not allowed - disabling PPL". Documentation/driver-api/md/raid5-ppl.rst (v6.12): "Partial Parity Log (PPL) is a feature available for RAID5 arrays." ... "PPL is available for md version-1 metadata and external (specifically IMSM) metadata arrays. It can be enabled using mdadm option --consistency-policy=ppl." ... "using write-intent bitmap and PPL together is not supported." ... "Unlike raid5-cache, the other solution in md for closing the write hole, PPL is not a true journal. It does not protect from losing in-flight data, only from silent data corruption. If a dirty disk of a stripe is lost, no PPL recovery is performed for this stripe (parity is not updated)." mdadm 4.4-11 (trixie) mdadm.c: for CONSISTENCY_POLICY_PPL with s.level != 5 -> "PPL consistency policy is only supported for RAID level 5."; --write-journal with level outside 4..6 -> "--write-journal is only supported for RAID level 4/5/6." mdadm(8) trixie: "ppl: For RAID5 only, Partial Parity Log is used to close the write hole and eliminate resync. PPL is stored in the metadata region of RAID member drives, no additional journal drive is needed." md(4) trixie: "From Linux 4.12 md supports Partial Parity Log (PPL) for RAID5 arrays only." packages.debian.org: trixie ships mdadm 4.4-11.

B. RAID6: only the journal closes the hole. md(4) "RAID WRITE HOLE": "Due to non-atomicity nature of RAID write operations, interruption of write operations (system crash, etc.) can lead to inconsistent parity and data loss (so called RAID-5 write hole). To plug the write hole md supports two mechanisms described below." — "DIRTY STRIPE JOURNAL: From Linux 4.4, md supports write ahead journal for RAID456. Before writing to the data disks, md persists data AND parity of the stripe to the journal device. After crashes, md searches the journal device for incomplete write operations, and replay them to the data disks." "When the journal device fails, the RAID array is forced to run in read-only mode." mdadm(8): "journal: For RAID levels 4/5/6, the journal device is used to log transactions and replay after an unclean shutdown." "--write-journal: Specify journal device for the RAID-4/5/6 array. The journal device should be an SSD with a reasonable lifetime." raid5-cache.rst (v6.12): "Raid 4/5/6 could include an extra disk for data cache besides normal RAID disks. The cache can be in write-through (supported since 4.4) or write-back mode (supported since 4.10)." "This mode mainly fixes the 'write hole' issue." Write-back: "If a write crosses all RAID disks of a stripe, we call it full-stripe write. For non-full-stripe writes, MD must read old data before the new parity can be calculated." "Write-back cache will aggregate the data and flush the data to RAID disks only after the data becomes a full stripe write." raid5-cache.c v6.12 r5l_init_log(): no level check at all (only PAGE_SIZE == 4096 and "write journal/cache doesn't work for array with %d disks"); raid5-cache.c also logs "Disabling writeback cache for degraded array." raid5.c raid5_run(): "array cannot have both journal and bitmap" (-EINVAL); "don't support reshape with journal - aborting."; "journal disk is missing, force array readonly" with mddev->ro = 1 and set_disk_ro(). admin-guide/md.rst: journal_mode "The mode can be 'write-throuth' and 'write-back'. The default is 'write-through'."

C. Mechanism and the member-loss consequence. raid5-cache.rst: "For RAID 4/5/6 array, an unclean shutdown can cause data in some stripes to not be in consistent state, eg, data and parity don't match. The reason is that a stripe write involves several RAID disks and it's possible the writes don't hit all RAID disks yet before the unclean shutdown." "MD tries to resync the array to bring it back to normal state. But before the resync completes, any system crash will expose the chance of real data corruption in the RAID array. This problem is called 'write hole'." raid5-ppl.rst: "The issue addressed by PPL is that after a dirty shutdown, parity of a particular stripe may become inconsistent with data on other member disks. If the array is also in degraded state, there is no way to recalculate parity, because one of the disks is missing. This can lead to silent data corruption when rebuilding the array or using it is as degraded - data calculated from parity for array blocks that have not been touched by a write request during the unclean shutdown can be incorrect. Such condition is known as the RAID5 Write Hole. Because of this, md by default does not allow starting a dirty degraded array." md(4) UNCLEAN SHUTDOWN: "If a RAID4, RAID5 or RAID6 array is degraded ... when it is restarted after an unclean shutdown, it cannot recalculate parity, and so it is possible that data might be undetectably corrupted." admin-guide/md.rst "Boot time assembly of degraded/dirty arrays": "If a raid5 or raid6 array is both dirty and degraded, it could have undetectable data corruption." "the fact that it is dirty means that the parity cannot be trusted" ... "degraded means that some datablocks are missing and cannot reliably be reconstructed" ... "md will normally refuse to start such an array." (override: "mdadm --assemble --force" or "md-mod.start_dirty_degraded=1"). raid5.c v6.12 raid5_run(): "if (mddev->degraded > dirty_parity_disks && mddev->recovery_cp != MaxSector)" -> with MD_HAS_PPL "starting dirty degraded array with PPL."; with ok_start_degraded "starting dirty degraded array - data corruption possible."; otherwise "cannot start dirty degraded array." and abort. md.c v6.12: "module_param(start_dirty_degraded, int, S_IRUGO|S_IWUSR);". mdadm(8) --force (assemble): "For external metadata it allows one to start dirty degraded RAID 4, 5, 6. An array which requires --force to be started may contain data corruption. Use it carefully."

D. Granularity and RMW. drivers/md/raid5.h v6.12: "#define DEFAULT_STRIPE_SIZE 4096"; "#if PAGE_SIZE == DEFAULT_STRIPE_SIZE / #define STRIPE_SIZE PAGE_SIZE"; struct stripe_head "sector_t sector; /* sector of this row */" — md's unit of parity computation is a 4 KiB row across all members (fixed at PAGE_SIZE on x86-64), so a torn partial write leaves P/Q inconsistent only for the rows it touched; the blocks at risk are the other members' 4 KiB blocks in those rows (which may belong to unrelated, already committed objects). raid5.h enum "PARITY_DISABLE_RMW = 0, PARITY_ENABLE_RMW, PARITY_PREFER_RMW"; raid5.c setup_conf() for level 6: "conf->max_degraded = 2;" and "if (raid6_call.xor_syndrome) conf->rmw_level = PARITY_ENABLE_RMW; else conf->rmw_level = PARITY_DISABLE_RMW;" — RAID6 does read-modify-write for partial writes by default when the selected raid6 algorithm provides xor_syndrome; the hole exists for reconstruct-write partial updates as well (the docs describe it as any stripe write that "involves several RAID disks").

Note on sources: elixir.bootlin.com pages returned only their version-list navigation and git.kernel.org's plain endpoint returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool, so the v6.12 source was read from the torvalds GitHub mirror at tag v6.12 and from Debian's linux 6.12.107-1 source (sources.debian.org); the two agree on ppl_init_log.
- Corrected claim: On Debian 13 (linux 6.12.x, mdadm 4.4) md's Partial Parity Log (--consistency-policy=ppl) is accepted only for RAID5: ppl_init_log() returns -EINVAL for any other level ("PPL is not compatible with raid level %d"), raid5_change_consistency_policy() enables it only when conf->level == 5, and mdadm 4.4 rejects it at create time ("PPL consistency policy is only supported for RAID level 5"). PPL is also incompatible with a write-intent bitmap and with a journal, is capped at 64 members, and is not a true journal (it protects untouched blocks from silent corruption but not in-flight data in the written chunks). For RAID6 the only md mechanism that closes the write hole is a --write-journal device (raid5-cache, write-through by default or write-back). A RAID6 array without one has an open write hole: md writes a stripe row's data and P/Q chunks non-atomically, so a crash during a partial-row update (read-modify-write, which RAID6 uses by default, or reconstruct-write) leaves P and Q of the touched 4 KiB stripe rows (md's stripe_head unit, DEFAULT_STRIPE_SIZE 4096 = PAGE_SIZE) inconsistent with the data on the other members — not the whole chunk-wide stripe, but every other member's block in those rows, including already-committed blocks untouched by the interrupted write. If a member is missing when the array restarts, or is lost before md's post-crash resync (bitmap-assisted or full) has recomputed those rows, the missing member's blocks in those rows are reconstructed from stale parity and come back as garbage; the kernel documents this exactly ("data calculated from parity for array blocks that have not been touched by a write request during the unclean shutdown can be incorrect"). md refuses by default to start an array that is both dirty and degraded ("cannot start dirty degraded array"); starting it needs mdadm --assemble --force or md-mod.start_dirty_degraded=1, which md labels "data corruption possible". A write-intent bitmap only narrows the resync window; it does not close the hole. The journal device in turn is a single point of failure for writes (journal loss forces the array read-only), cannot coexist with a write-intent bitmap, and blocks reshape while attached.
- Design impact: The torn-CP rule's assumption ("a torn write damages only its own blocks") does not hold on a journal-less md RAID6 (or RAID5 without PPL/journal), and the hazard is per 4 KiB stripe row and applies to data blocks exactly as much as to metadata blocks: any committed block (CP N-1 or a retained snapshot) that shares a stripe row with a block being written can be destroyed by crash + member loss before resync. Consequences: (1) "Metadata must be full-stripe" is insufficient on its own; what closes the exposure without a journal is stripe-granular allocation and free for everything written to the RAID6 pool — stripe-aligned, stripe-sized allocation units and never writing into a stripe that still holds live blocks on any member — so that a torn write can only damage uncommitted blocks (md then performs full-stripe writes with no RMW, and its post-crash resync repairs that stripe before it is reused). (2) Making the flash metadata class mandatory protects the CP chain but not user data on the HDD pool; the design's data checksums turn the garbage into a detected, unrepairable read error, because the parity itself is what is stale. (3) Requiring --write-journal on RAID6 HDD pools closes the hole inside md (write-through default; write-back additionally aggregates partial writes into full-stripe writes), at the cost of: an SSD journal that is a write-path single point of failure (journal loss → array read-only; the sizing/mirroring of the journal device is a configuration choice not verified here), no write-intent bitmap, no reshape while the journal is attached, and write-back being disabled while the array is degraded. (4) Operational policy must be explicit: after a crash with a member also missing, md will not assemble a journal-less parity array unless forced, so the OS must choose between an outage and a forced start with possible silent corruption of the torn rows; with a journal this dilemma does not arise. (5) Do not plan on PPL for RAID6 pools; even on RAID5 it excludes bitmaps, caps at 64 members and leaves in-flight data unprotected. The design should adopt one of: journal mandatory on parity pools that hold any committed state; strict full-stripe allocation with stripe-granular free for all pool writes (data and metadata); or no md parity levels for pools holding the metadata stream (mirror/flash classes only).
- Sources: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.12/driver-api/md/raid5-ppl.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/Documentation/driver-api/md/raid5-ppl.rst ; https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.12/driver-api/md/raid5-cache.html ; https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.12/admin-guide/md.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/md/raid5-ppl.c ; https://sources.debian.org/src/linux/trixie/drivers/md/raid5-ppl.c/ ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/md/raid5.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/md/raid5-cache.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/md/raid5.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/md/md.c ; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/mdadm/mdadm.8.en.html ; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/mdadm/md.4.en.html ; https://sources.debian.org/src/mdadm/trixie/mdadm.c/ ; https://packages.debian.org/trixie/mdadm

### [C22] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: In Linux 6.12 drivers/md/raid5.c, raid5_set_limits sets lim.io_min = mddev->chunk_sectors << 9 and lim.io_opt = lim.io_min * (conf->raid_disks - conf->max_degraded), so /sys/block/mdN/queue/optimal_io_size on raid456 equals chunk size times data disks; an incoming bio's REQ_FUA is recorded as R5_WantFUA in ops_run_biodrain, OR-ed across the stripe in ops_complete_reconstruct and applied to every written member including P and Q parity devices; and REQ_PREFLUSH is served by md_flush_request when no raid journal is present.
- Raised by: Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: The flusher trusts md sysfs for the full-stripe size and skips the write-amplification probe on mdadm backstores, and the commit protocol relies on FUA and flush reaching every member, parity included, on RAID5 and RAID6.
- Summary: Every code statement in the claim is true in the v6.12 tag (and unchanged in linux-6.12.y, which Debian trixie ships as 6.12.111): raid5_set_limits sets io_min = chunk bytes and io_opt = io_min * (raid_disks - max_degraded); REQ_FUA becomes R5_WantFUA in ops_run_biodrain, is OR-ed across the stripe_head and applied to every written device plus pd_idx and qd_idx in ops_complete_reconstruct, and ops_run_io issues REQ_FUA on those member writes; a REQ_PREFLUSH bio goes to md_flush_request when log_handle_flush_request returns -ENODEV. Three conditions are missing: the sysfs optimal_io_size is the stacked value (LCM with member io_opt, zeroed on physical-block misalignment, and only io_opt is refreshed after a reshape), the md_flush_request path is taken only when there is neither a journal nor PPL (PPL acknowledges upper-layer flushes immediately without flushing members), and the 6.12 md_flush_request neither waits for member flushes before dispatching the data part of a data-carrying PREFLUSH bio nor propagates member flush errors to the caller.
- Evidence: 1. raid5_set_limits (drivers/md/raid5.c v6.12, lines 7716-7775; identical in linux-6.12.y): "lim.io_min = mddev->chunk_sectors << 9;" / "lim.io_opt = lim.io_min * (conf->raid_disks - conf->max_degraded);" followed by "mddev_stack_rdev_limits(mddev, &lim, 0); rdev_for_each(rdev, mddev) queue_limits_stack_bdev(&lim, rdev->bdev, ...)". max_degraded is 2 for level 6, else 1 (raid5.c 7612/7618). raid5_run calls it only "if (!mddev_is_dm(mddev))" (line 8036).

2. Stacking changes the exported value (block/blk-settings.c v6.12, blk_stack_limits): "t->io_min = max(t->io_min, b->io_min);" / "t->io_opt = lcm_not_zero(t->io_opt, b->io_opt);" and "/* Optimal I/O a multiple of the physical block size? */ if (t->io_opt & (t->physical_block_size - 1)) { t->io_opt = 0; t->flags |= BLK_FLAG_MISALIGNED; ...}". lib/math/lcm.c: lcm_not_zero returns the LCM when both are non-zero, otherwise the non-zero one. block/blk-sysfs.c: "QUEUE_RO_ENTRY(queue_io_opt, "optimal_io_size");" so the sysfs file shows the stacked io_opt. After a reshape, end_reshape calls "mddev_update_io_opt(conf->mddev, conf->raid_disks - conf->max_degraded)" and md.c mddev_update_io_opt does "lim.io_opt = lim.io_min * nr_stripes;" — io_min is never recomputed outside raid5_set_limits (the only io_min assignment in raid5.c/md.c), so a chunk-size reshape leaves minimum_io_size/optimal_io_size at the old chunk until re-assembly. md's own sysfs: md.c has __ATTR(chunk_size,...), __ATTR(raid_disks,...), __ATTR(level,...); chunk_size_show prints "%d (%d)" (new, old) while a chunk-size reshape is pending.

3. FUA recording (raid5.c ops_run_biodrain, lines 1955-1956): "if (wbi->bi_opf & REQ_FUA) set_bit(R5_WantFUA, &dev->flags);" — done per device, and repeated for every stripe in a batch ("if (head_sh->batch_head) { sh = list_first_entry(&sh->batch_list, ...); ... goto again; }"). Stripes with different bi_opf are never batched (line 954: "if (head->dev[dd_idx].towrite->bi_opf != sh->dev[dd_idx].towrite->bi_opf || ...) goto unlock_out;").

4. OR-ing and parity (ops_complete_reconstruct, lines 1996-2041): "for (i = disks; i--; ) { fua |= test_bit(R5_WantFUA, &sh->dev[i].flags); ... }" then "if (dev->written || i == pd_idx || i == qd_idx) { ... if (fua) set_bit(R5_WantFUA, &dev->flags); ...}". handle_stripe (line ~5055-5062): "if (test_bit(R5_LOCKED, &dev->flags) && (i == sh->pd_idx || i == sh->qd_idx || dev->written || ...)) { pr_debug("Writing block %d\n", i); set_bit(R5_Wantwrite, &dev->flags);".

5. Applying FUA (ops_run_io, lines 1163-1166 and 1251/1308): "if (test_and_clear_bit(R5_Wantwrite, &sh->dev[i].flags)) { op = REQ_OP_WRITE; if (test_and_clear_bit(R5_WantFUA, &sh->dev[i].flags)) op_flags = REQ_FUA;" ... "bio_init(bi, rdev->bdev, &dev->vec, 1, op | op_flags);" and for a replacement device "bio_init(rbi, rrdev->bdev, &dev->rvec, 1, op | op_flags);". Faulty members are skipped ("if (rdev && test_bit(Faulty, &rdev->flags)) rdev = NULL;"). With PPL the first ops_run_io pass returns early ("if (log_stripe(sh, s) == 0) return;") without consuming the flags; ppl_write_stripe returns -EAGAIN once sh->ppl_io is set, so the second pass still issues REQ_FUA.

6. Flush dispatch (raid5_make_request, lines 6081-6095): "if (unlikely(bi->bi_opf & REQ_PREFLUSH)) { int ret = log_handle_flush_request(conf, bi); if (ret == 0) return true; if (ret == -ENODEV) { if (md_flush_request(mddev, bi)) return true; } /* ret == -EAGAIN, fallback */ ... ctx.do_flush = bi->bi_opf & REQ_PREFLUSH; }". raid5-log.h: "int ret = -ENODEV; if (conf->log) ret = r5l_handle_flush_request(conf->log, bio); else if (raid5_has_ppl(conf)) ret = ppl_handle_flush_request(bio);" — so md_flush_request is reached only with neither journal nor PPL. raid5-ppl.c ppl_handle_flush_request: "if (bio->bi_iter.bi_size == 0) { bio_endio(bio); return 0; } bio->bi_opf &= ~REQ_PREFLUSH; return -EAGAIN;". PPL flushes write-back-cached members itself (ppl_do_flush, bios "REQ_OP_WRITE | REQ_PREFLUSH" for disks in disk_flush_bitmap, wb_cache_on = bdev_write_cache(rdev->bdev)) from ppl_stripe_write_finished, which handle_stripe_clean_event calls (line 57 of the function) only after it has already run "md_write_end(conf->mddev); bio_endio(wbi);" for the data bios. The PPL commit (1532d9e87e8b, Tomasz Majchrzak) states the intent: "As PPL assures all data is flushed to disk at request completion, just acknowledge flush request when PPL is enabled."

7. md_flush_request (drivers/md/md.c v6.12 lines 553-602; byte-identical in linux-6.12.y and in master as of today): "rdev_for_each(rdev, mddev) { if (rdev->raid_disk < 0 || test_bit(Faulty, &rdev->flags)) continue; new = bio_alloc_bioset(rdev->bdev, 0, REQ_OP_WRITE | REQ_PREFLUSH, GFP_NOIO, &mddev->bio_set); new->bi_private = bio; new->bi_end_io = md_end_flush; bio_inc_remaining(bio); submit_bio(new); } if (bio_sectors(bio) == 0) { bio_endio(bio); return true; } bio->bi_opf &= ~REQ_PREFLUSH; return false;". So every active non-faulty member (parity included; spares and faulty excluded) gets a flush, the original bio completes only after all children, but a data-carrying bio continues into raid5 immediately. md_end_flush: "if (bio->bi_status) pr_err("md: %pg flush io error %d\n", ...); bio_put(bio); bio_endio(parent);" — the child's status is not copied to the parent. This implementation comes from commit b75197e86e6d ("md: Remove flush handling", Yu Kuai, 2024-08-27: "This patch removes the flush handling in md, and converts to use general block layer flush handling in underlying disks") plus Li Nan's follow-up that replaced bio_chain with bi_private/bio_inc_remaining, whose message concedes: "in the event of a power failure, if a flush IO on a member disk fails, the upper layers may not be informed."

8. Block layer plumbing: md_init_stacking_limits sets "lim->features = BLK_FEAT_WRITE_CACHE | BLK_FEAT_FUA | BLK_FEAT_IO_STAT | BLK_FEAT_NOWAIT;", and block/blk-core.c only strips flags when "!bdev_write_cache(bdev)", so PREFLUSH/FUA reach raid5_make_request; Documentation/block/writeback_cache_control.rst: "For remapping drivers the REQ_FUA bits need to be propagated to underlying devices, and a global flush needs to be implemented for bios with the REQ_PREFLUSH bit set." At member level a device without a volatile cache has the bits stripped (harmless) and a blk-mq device without FUA gets a post-flush emulation.

9. Platform: packages.debian.org lists trixie linux-image-amd64 6.12.111-1 (linux-image-6.12.111+deb13-amd64); the functions above are identical between v6.12 and linux-6.12.y.
- Corrected claim: In Linux 6.12 (including Debian trixie's 6.12.y), drivers/md/raid5.c raid5_set_limits sets lim.io_min = mddev->chunk_sectors << 9 and lim.io_opt = lim.io_min * (conf->raid_disks - conf->max_degraded) (max_degraded = 1 for RAID4/5, 2 for RAID6) and then stacks the member devices' limits, so /sys/block/mdN/queue/optimal_io_size equals chunk size times data disks only when every member reports io_opt = 0 or a divisor of that value (otherwise it is the LCM, or 0 if misaligned to the physical block size); after a reshape only io_opt is recomputed from the existing io_min, so the authoritative full-stripe size is chunk_size × data disks taken from /sys/block/mdN/md/{level,chunk_size,raid_disks}. An incoming bio's REQ_FUA is recorded per device as R5_WantFUA in ops_run_biodrain, OR-ed across the stripe_head in ops_complete_reconstruct and set on every written device plus the P (pd_idx) and Q (qd_idx) devices, and ops_run_io issues those member writes (including writes to a replacement device) with REQ_FUA; faulty/missing members are skipped. A bio with REQ_PREFLUSH is handled by md_flush_request only when the array has neither a write journal nor PPL: md_flush_request sends an empty REQ_PREFLUSH bio to every member with raid_disk >= 0 that is not Faulty (parity included, spares excluded), completes the original bio only after all member flushes complete, but strips REQ_PREFLUSH from a data-carrying bio and lets its data proceed without waiting for the member flushes, and a member flush error is only logged ("md: ... flush io error"), never reported to the caller. With PPL, md acknowledges an empty flush immediately and strips REQ_PREFLUSH from data bios (PPL flushes write-back-cached members itself after each io_unit, after the data bios have already been completed); with a journal the log device, not md_flush_request, handles the flush.
- Design impact: 1) Full-stripe size: do not read it from queue/optimal_io_size. Compute chunk_size × data_disks from /sys/block/mdN/md/level, md/chunk_size and md/raid_disks (data_disks = raid_disks − 1 for raid4/raid5, − 2 for raid6), parse the "new (old)" form of chunk_size during a reshape, and re-read after reshape completes. If the flusher keeps optimal_io_size as a cross-check, treat a value that is not exactly chunk_size × data_disks (member io_opt LCM, 0 from misalignment, stale io_min after a chunk-size reshape) as "unknown" and fall back to the write-amplification probe rather than trusting it. 2) Commit protocol on plain mdadm RAID5/6 (no journal, no PPL): FUA on the data and parity members is honored as claimed, and an empty flush (fdatasync / blkdev_issue_flush) reaches every active member, so "all writes completed before the flush are durable when the flush completes" holds. Do not rely on a single data-carrying PREFLUSH(|FUA) bio to order the flush before its own payload: md 6.12 dispatches the payload concurrently with the member flushes, so a FUA commit record can become durable before earlier writes are flushed. Issue an explicit empty flush, wait for it, then write the commit record with FUA. 3) Error handling: md completes a flush successfully even if a member flush failed (only a dmesg "md: <dev> flush io error" line). The commit protocol cannot detect a lost flush from the I/O status; monitor kernel log/rdev state and treat member errors as fatal for the commit, or keep FUA on every write that must be durable so the error surfaces on the write. 4) Consistency policy: if any backstore is created with mdadm --consistency-policy=ppl, upper-layer flushes are not forwarded to members at all; a FUA-only commit protocol still works, a flush-based one does not. Decide explicitly between plain RAID5/6 (flush semantics intact, write hole open), PPL (write hole closed for parity, no flush forwarding) and a write-through journal (flush handled by the log device). 5) Note that FUA/flush do not close the RAID5/6 write hole; a crash mid-stripe while degraded can corrupt unrelated data in the same stripe, which is a separate design decision.
- Sources: https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/raid5.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/md.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/raid5.h?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/raid5-log.h?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/raid5-ppl.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/raid5-cache.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/block/blk-settings.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/block/blk-sysfs.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/block/blk-core.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/lib/math/lcm.c?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/Documentation/block/writeback_cache_control.rst?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/Documentation/driver-api/md/raid5-ppl.rst?h=v6.12 ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/md.c?h=linux-6.12.y ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/raid5.c?h=linux-6.12.y ; https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/plain/drivers/md/md.c?h=master ; https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/b75197e86e6d.patch ; https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/1532d9e87e8b2377f12929f9e40724d5fbe6ecc5 ; https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/1532d9e87e8b2377f12929f9e40724d5fbe6ecc5.diff ; https://lkml.rescloud.iu.edu/2408.3/03286.html ; https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/2409.2/03337.html ; https://packages.debian.org/trixie/linux-image-amd64

### [C23] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: The Linux 6.12 megaraid_sas driver limits max_hw_sectors_kb for PERC H730/H740/H750 (SAS3108/SAS3516) virtual drives to 256 KiB (firmware max_sectors_per_req) according to one persona, or to 128 KiB (MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS_IEEE = 256 sectors on firmware reporting IEEE SGLs) according to another, with the max_sectors module parameter only able to lower the value except on the two GEN2 PCI IDs; a 2.5 MiB O_DIRECT write is therefore split into 10 or 20 commands before reaching the controller.
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Consensus, Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: The write-through RMW analysis, the '256 KiB-stripe VD rule', the S7/S8 drain numbers, and whether the write-amplification probe (smallest candidate 256 KiB) can see the knee at all depend on which value is real; if newer firmware reports 1 MiB or more, the installer's VD guidance changes.
- Summary: In Linux 6.12 (and Debian's 6.12.107-1 copy) the megaraid_sas limit for a Fusion-class controller (H730/SAS3108, H740P, H750 are INVADER/VENTURA/AERO series, not MFI) is driver-computed from the firmware-advertised chain-frame size: 64 IEEE SGEs x 4 KiB = 512 sectors = 256 KiB with the legacy 1 KiB chain frame, or 256 SGEs = 1 MiB when the firmware advertises the 4 KiB "1 MB I/O" chain frame (commit bd5f9484262a, 2015); the ctrl_info limits only cap it lower if smaller and the max_sectors module parameter can only lower it except on the two GEN2 PCI IDs. The 128 KiB MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS_IEEE clamp applies only to MFI-series adapters (fw_support_ieee is set solely in megasas_init_adapter_mfi), so the second persona is wrong for these controllers. The 256 KiB figure is the H730 default (Dell says 1 MB IO "must be enabled" with perccli /cx set largeIOsupport=on), but PERC 10/11 document 1 MB I/O as a controller feature, so on H740P/H750 (or an H730 with largeIOsupport on) max_hw_sectors_kb is 1024 and a 2.5 MiB write is 3 commands, not 10; no first-hand sysfs reading on these cards was found, so the value must be measured.
- Evidence: KERNEL 6.12 SOURCE (raw v6.12 tree; Debian 6.12.107-1 copy of megaraid_sas_base.c has the identical lines). megaraid_sas.h: "#define MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS (2*1024)" (2048 sectors = 1 MiB), "#define MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS_IEEE (2*128)" (256 sectors = 128 KiB), "#define SGE_BUFFER_SIZE 4096". megaraid_sas_base.c: "static unsigned int max_sectors; module_param_named(max_sectors, max_sectors, int, 0444); MODULE_PARM_DESC(max_sectors, "Maximum number of sectors per IO command")". megasas_init_fw: comment "Compute the max allowed sectors per IO: The controller info has two limits on max sectors. Driver should use the minimum of these two"; "max_sectors_1 = (1 << ctrl_info->stripe_sz_ops.min) * le16_to_cpu(ctrl_info->max_strips_per_io); max_sectors_2 = le32_to_cpu(ctrl_info->max_request_size); tmp_sectors = min_t(u32, max_sectors_1, max_sectors_2);" then "instance->max_sectors_per_req = instance->max_num_sge * SGE_BUFFER_SIZE / 512; if (tmp_sectors && (instance->max_sectors_per_req > tmp_sectors)) instance->max_sectors_per_req = tmp_sectors;". megasas_io_attach: "if (instance->fw_support_ieee) instance->max_sectors_per_req = MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS_IEEE; /* Check if the module parameter value for max_sectors can be used */ if (max_sectors && max_sectors < instance->max_sectors_per_req) instance->max_sectors_per_req = max_sectors; else { if (max_sectors) { if (((instance->pdev->device == PCI_DEVICE_ID_LSI_SAS1078GEN2) || (instance->pdev->device == PCI_DEVICE_ID_LSI_SAS0079GEN2)) && (max_sectors <= MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS)) { instance->max_sectors_per_req = max_sectors; } else { dev_info(..."max_sectors should be > 0 and <= %d (or < 1MB for GEN2 controller)\n"...) } } } host->max_sectors = instance->max_sectors_per_req;". fw_support_ieee is assigned only in megasas_init_adapter_mfi ("instance->fw_support_ieee = (instance->instancet->read_fw_status_reg(instance) & 0x04000000)"); the xscale/ppc/skinny/gen2 templates have ".init_adapter = megasas_init_adapter_mfi", the Fusion template ".init_adapter = megasas_init_adapter_fusion" (fusion.c never references fw_support_ieee, only "instance->flag_ieee = 1"); megasas_set_adapter_type maps PCI_DEVICE_ID_LSI_INVADER (0x005d, SAS3108/H730) and FURY to INVADER_SERIES, VENTURA/HARPOON/etc. to VENTURA_SERIES, AERO_10E1/10E2/10E5/10E6 to AERO_SERIES, only "default:" to MFI_SERIES; scsi_host_alloc does "shost = kzalloc(sizeof(struct Scsi_Host) + privsize, GFP_KERNEL)" so fw_support_ieee stays 0 on these cards. megaraid_sas_fusion.c megasas_init_adapter_fusion: reads scratch_pad_1; comment "If scratch_pad_1 & MEGASAS_MAX_CHAIN_SIZE_UNITS_MASK is set, Firmware support extended IO chain frame which is 4 times more than legacy Firmware. Legacy Firmware - Frame size is (8 * 128) = 1K; 1M IO Firmware - Frame size is (8 * 128 * 4) = 4K"; "fusion->max_sge_in_main_msg = (MEGA_MPI2_RAID_DEFAULT_IO_FRAME_SIZE - offsetof(struct MPI2_RAID_SCSI_IO_REQUEST, SGL))/16" (= (256-0x80)/16 = 8); "fusion->max_sge_in_chain = instance->max_chain_frame_sz / sizeof(union MPI2_SGE_IO_UNION)"; "instance->max_num_sge = rounddown_pow_of_two(fusion->max_sge_in_main_msg + fusion->max_sge_in_chain - 2)" -> 64 (legacy) or 256 (4 KiB chain); fusion.h: "#define MEGASAS_256K_IO 128", "#define MEGASAS_1MB_IO (MEGASAS_256K_IO * 4)", "#define MEGASAS_CHAIN_FRAME_SZ_MIN 1024", "#define MEGA_MPI2_RAID_DEFAULT_IO_FRAME_SIZE 256". Result: 64*4096/512 = 512 sectors = 256 KiB, or 256*4096/512 = 2048 sectors = 1 MiB. NVMe override only: megasas_set_static_target_properties "max_io_size_kb will be set to non zero for nvme based vd and syspd"; "if (instance->nvme_page_size && max_io_size_kb) megasas_set_nvme_device_properties(...)" which sets "lim->max_hw_sectors = max_io_size / 512". scsi_lib.c scsi_init_limits: "lim->max_hw_sectors = shost->max_sectors"; "lim->max_segments = min_t(unsigned short, shost->sg_tablesize, SG_MAX_SEGMENTS)" (SG_MAX_SEGMENTS = 2048). blk-settings.c blk_validate_limits: "max_hw_sectors = min_not_zero(lim->max_hw_sectors, lim->max_dev_sectors)" and default "lim->max_sectors = min(max_hw_sectors, BLK_DEF_MAX_SECTORS_CAP)" with "#define BLK_DEF_MAX_SECTORS_CAP 2560u" (1280 KiB), so max_sectors_kb equals max_hw_sectors_kb in both cases (256 or 1024). COMMIT HISTORY: GitHub blame of fusion.h attributes MEGASAS_1MB_IO/MEGASAS_MAX_CHAIN_SIZE_UNITS_MASK to commit bd5f9484262a "megaraid_sas: Support for max_io_size 1MB" (Sumit Saxena, 2015-08-31, merged 2015-10-29): "Driver will expose max sge = 256 (earlier it was 64) if firmware supports extended IO size (1M)." Documentation/scsi/ChangeLog.megaraid_sas: 00.00.04.31-rc1 "Add the input parameter max_sectors to 1MB support to our GEN2 controller"; 00.00.05.34-rc1 "Fix max_sectors setting for IEEE SGL's". FIRMWARE FEATURE: Dell PERC 9 User's Guide (H330/H730/H830) Features: "1 MB IO support for H730, H730P, H730P MX, and H830 controllers." "The 1 MB IO feature must be enabled by using PERC CLI command perccli /cx set largeIOsupport=on." "If the capacity of IO frame is greater than 1 MB, the IO frame is broken into smaller chunks." Dell PERC 11 User's Guide, "1 MB I/O": "PERC 11 controllers support a 1 MB I/O feature; if the capacity of I/O frame is greater than 1 MB, the I/O frame is broken into smaller chunks." (no enable step given). Dell PERC 10 guide lists "1 MB IO" under Controller features (HTML topic body empty on dell.com; mirrored PDF text: "PERC 10 controllers support 1 MB IO feature..."). Broadcom StorCLI Tri-Mode docs: "storcli /cx show largeiosupport — Displays whether largeiosupport is enabled or disabled on the controller"; "set largeiosupport =[on|off]". Supermicro FAQ 33521 for the SAS3108-based AOC-S3108L-H8IR: "The firmware supports large-size I/Os, that is I/Os up to 1 MB are supported. The controller property enableLargeIOSupport is added to either enable or disable this feature." HISTORICAL CORROBORATION of the 256 KiB formula: Red Hat bug 806405 (RHEL 6, non-GEN2 Fusion card, 2013): "max_hw_sectors_kb was 280" and dmesg "max_sectors should be > 0and <= 560 (or < 1MB for GEN2 controller)" — 560 sectors = 70 SGEs x 8 (the same 1 KiB chain-frame math before rounddown_pow_of_two reduced 70 to 64, giving today's 512 sectors = 256 KiB). Thomas-Krenn wiki (kernel 3.2, old MegaRAID, driver 00.00.06.12): default max_hw_sectors_kb 128 raised to 256/512 via max_sectors=512/1024 — the IEEE-128 KiB default plus the GEN2 raise exception, i.e. the MFI/GEN2 path that does not apply to H730/H740/H750. DEBIAN: sources.debian.org lists linux 6.12.107-1 in trixie (6.12.111-1 in trixie-proposed-updates); its megaraid_sas_base.c has the same megasas_io_attach and megasas_init_fw lines. NOT FOUND: any first-hand /sys/block/sdX/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb reading on an H730/H740P/H750 under any kernel; whether PERC 10/11 ship with large IO enabled; whether PERC VDs report a Block Limits VPD MAXIMUM TRANSFER LENGTH (which would enter via max_dev_sectors); the H740P silicon (a secondary source says SAS3508, not the claim's SAS3516).
- Corrected claim: On Linux 6.12 (Debian 13's 6.12.x kernel), megaraid_sas sets max_hw_sectors for every SAS/SATA virtual drive of a Fusion-class PERC (H730/H730P = SAS3108 "Invader" series; H740P = Ventura series; H750/H755 = Aero series) to instance->max_sectors_per_req = max_num_sge x 4 KiB, where max_num_sge is derived at probe time from the chain-frame size the firmware advertises in scratch pad 1: 64 SGEs = 512 sectors = 256 KiB with the legacy 1 KiB chain frame, or 256 SGEs = 2048 sectors = 1 MiB when the firmware advertises the 4 KiB "1 MB I/O" chain frame (commit bd5f9484262a, 2015). The firmware ctrl_info limits (min(2^stripe_sz_ops.min x max_strips_per_io, max_request_size)) only apply if smaller. The 128 KiB MEGASAS_MAX_SECTORS_IEEE clamp exists only on MFI-series (pre-Fusion) adapters and never applies to these controllers. The max_sectors module parameter can only lower the value, except on PCI IDs 0x0078/0x0079 (SAS1078GEN2/SAS0079GEN2) where it may raise it up to 2048 sectors. Dell documents the 1 MB I/O firmware feature for H730/H730P/H830 as off until enabled with "perccli /cx set largeIOsupport=on", and as a supported feature of PERC 10 (H740P/H840) and PERC 11 (H750/H755) without stating the default; therefore max_hw_sectors_kb is 256 on an H730 at defaults and 1024 wherever large-IO firmware is active, and the block layer's default max_sectors_kb (min(max_hw, 1280 KiB) in 6.12) equals it in both cases. A 2.5 MiB O_DIRECT write is split into 10 commands at 256 KiB or 3 commands (1 + 1 + 0.5 MiB) at 1 MiB; the 20-command/128 KiB case does not occur. The actual value on a given card/firmware must be read from /sys/block/sdX/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb and "perccli64 /c0 show largeiosupport"; NVMe-backed VDs/syspds on tri-mode PERC 11 use a different, per-target MDTS-based limit.
- Design impact: 1) Replace the single hard-coded 256 KiB assumption with a measured, firmware-dependent parameter: the installer/probe must read max_hw_sectors_kb, max_sectors_kb and max_segments per VD and query "perccli64 /c0 show largeiosupport"; expect 256 KiB (H730 default) or 1024 KiB (large-IO firmware: H730 with largeIOsupport=on, likely H740P/H750 - unverified default, measure). Drop the 128 KiB/IEEE branch entirely for these controllers. 2) The write-through RMW analysis, the "256 KiB-stripe VD rule" and the S7/S8 drain numbers must be expressed per measured limit: 10 commands per 2.5 MiB at 256 KiB, 3 at 1 MiB; a VD-stripe rule tuned to 256 KiB is wrong on large-IO firmware where the natural knee moves to 1 MiB. 3) The write-amplification probe cannot see the knee if its smallest candidate equals the limit; on 256 KiB firmware it needs candidates below 256 KiB (e.g. 64/128 KiB) and on 1 MiB firmware candidates spanning 256 KiB-2 MiB; the probe should also assert that the VD's strip size times (N-1 data drives) is <= max_sectors_kb or document the split. 4) Do not plan on the max_sectors module parameter to raise the limit (it only lowers it on these PCI IDs); the only lever is the firmware property largeIOsupport, which the driver reads at adapter init, so a change requires a driver re-probe/reboot and should be a documented installer step with a post-check of sysfs. 5) Treat NVMe-backed VDs/syspds (H755N, future tri-mode) as a separate rule (per-target max_io_size_kb/MDTS, plus a pending 2026 stable cap to the PRP chain frame). 6) Residual risks to verify on hardware: a Block Limits VPD MAXIMUM TRANSFER LENGTH from the VD could lower the limit further via max_dev_sectors; PERC 10/11 default state of large IO; H740P silicon naming (SAS3508 per secondary sources, not SAS3516).

### [C24] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: Linux 6.12 include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h defines IORING_OP_SEND_ZC and IORING_OP_SENDMSG_ZC with the IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF flag, posts a second CQE flagged IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF when the buffer may be reused, reports IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED in that CQE's res when IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE is set and the data was copied, defines IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS (30), IORING_OP_READ_FIXED and IORING_OP_WRITE_FIXED, but no IORING_OP_READV_FIXED/WRITEV_FIXED (added in 6.14); the io-uring crate 0.7.15 (published 2026-09-07) exposes opcode::SendZc::new(fd, buf, len) with buf_index(Option<u16>) and zc_flags(u16) builders, and also exposes ReadvFixed/WritevFixed opcodes that 6.12 cannot execute.
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: The zero-copy send from the hugetlbfs arena, releasing arena slots on the NOTIF CQE, the copied-usage fallback, cloning the arena registration into per-connection rings, and staging each stripe in one contiguous buffer written with a single WRITE_FIXED (because vectored fixed I/O is unavailable) all depend on these definitions.
- Summary: The 6.12 definitions, the two-CQE NOTIF model, the ZC_COPIED reporting, CLONE_BUFFERS = 30, READ/WRITE_FIXED, the absence of READV/WRITEV_FIXED, and the io-uring 0.7.15 API (published 2026-09-07) are all confirmed from the kernel sources, man pages, crates.io and docs.rs. Two statements are wrong: IORING_OP_READV_FIXED/WRITEV_FIXED were added in Linux 6.15, not 6.14 (the v6.14 header still ends at IORING_OP_LISTEN), and in 6.12 IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF is accepted only by IORING_OP_SEND_ZC, while IORING_OP_SENDMSG_ZC rejects it with -EINVAL (SENDMSG_ZC gained registered-buffer support in 6.15). Two conditions also apply: the ZC_COPIED bit is set when any fragment was copied or when zero-copy was never confirmed, and 6.12's CLONE_BUFFERS is all-or-nothing into a ring with no registered buffers (the src_off/dst_off/nr/DST_REPLACE form arrived in 6.13).
- Evidence: git.kernel.org's plain-file URLs returned HTTP 403, so the kernel files were read from GitHub's mirror of Linus's tree at the release tags (v6.12, v6.13, v6.14, v6.15), which carry the same content as the kernel.org tags.

- Corrected claim: Linux 6.12 include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h defines IORING_OP_SEND_ZC (47) and IORING_OP_SENDMSG_ZC (48), IORING_OP_READ_FIXED (4) and IORING_OP_WRITE_FIXED (5), the sqe->ioprio flags IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF (1U << 2) and IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE (1U << 3), the CQE flag IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF (1U << 3), IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED (1U << 31), and IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS = 30. It does not define IORING_OP_READV_FIXED or IORING_OP_WRITEV_FIXED: those (values 60 and 61) were added in Linux 6.15, not 6.14, and 6.12's io_init_req rejects any opcode >= IORING_OP_LAST (58) with -EINVAL. In 6.12, IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF is honoured only by IORING_OP_SEND_ZC (a single contiguous range inside registered buffer sqe->buf_index); IORING_OP_SENDMSG_ZC with that flag returns -EINVAL until 6.15, which added vectored registered-buffer support for SENDMSG_ZC. A zero-copy send completes with a first CQE whose flags carry IORING_CQE_F_MORE (set even when the send failed) and, if F_MORE is set, a second CQE with the same user_data flagged IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF, after which the buffer may be reused; the notification says nothing about delivery. The notification's res is 0, except that with IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE it has IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED OR-ed in when any part of the data was copied or no fragment was confirmed as zero-copy (io_notif_tw_complete: zc_copied || !zc_used). IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS in 6.12 copies the source ring's entire registered-buffer table (struct io_uring_clone_buffers has only src_fd, flags = IORING_REGISTER_SRC_REGISTERED, pad[6]) into a destination ring that has no registered buffers, else -EBUSY; src_off/dst_off/nr and IORING_REGISTER_DST_REPLACE exist only from 6.13. The io-uring crate 0.7.15 (crates.io, published 2026-09-07) exposes opcode::SendZc::new(fd, buf: *const u8, len: u32) with builders buf_index(Option<u16>) (which also ORs IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF into ioprio), zc_flags(u16) (written to sqe->ioprio), flags(i32), dest_addr and dest_addr_len; its opcode::ReadvFixed/WritevFixed (sys::IORING_OP_READV_FIXED = 60 / IORING_OP_WRITEV_FIXED = 61, not cfg-gated) build SQEs that a 6.12 kernel fails with -EINVAL.
- Design impact: (1) The conclusion that vectored fixed I/O is unavailable stands, but cite 6.15 (not 6.14) as the first kernel with READV_FIXED/WRITEV_FIXED; staging each stripe contiguously and issuing one WRITE_FIXED per stripe remains the correct 6.12 design. Because the crate happily builds ReadvFixed/WritevFixed SQEs, forbid them in the io_uring abstraction layer and verify opcode support at startup (fail with -EINVAL from 6.12 is the symptom). (2) Zero-copy sends from the hugetlbfs arena must use IORING_OP_SEND_ZC only: SENDMSG_ZC with FIXED_BUF is -EINVAL on 6.12, so there is no scatter-gather zero-copy send; a protocol header plus payload must either be placed contiguously in the arena slot ahead of the data or sent as separate SQEs (or header via a copying send), with the per-message ordering handled by the sender. Use the crate's SendMsgZc only for copying/non-fixed paths. (3) Slot release logic: free the arena slot when the IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF CQE arrives, keyed by user_data; the first CQE's IORING_CQE_F_MORE must be checked, and if it is absent no notification will follow and the slot can be released immediately. Treat the NOTIF as a buffer-lifetime event only, never as a delivery acknowledgement. (4) The copied-usage fallback must interpret IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED as "zero-copy was not (fully) effective", which includes the case where nothing was confirmed zero-copy, not strictly "data was copied"; its presence as bit 31 of res is the only information, so a heuristic (e.g. consecutive copied notifications per connection) should drive the switch to copying sends. (5) Cloning the arena registration into per-connection rings works on 6.12 only as a whole-table copy into a ring with no registered buffers; the clone must be the first and only buffer registration on each per-connection ring, partial or offset clones are impossible, and growing or re-registering the arena in the primary ring does not propagate to existing clones, so size the registered arena table once at startup (or plan ring re-creation on resize). The 6.13+ offset/DST_REPLACE form must not be relied on.
- Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.13/include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.14/include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.15/include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/io_uring/net.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.15/io_uring/net.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/io_uring/notif.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/io_uring/rsrc.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/io_uring/io_uring.c ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/io_uring_enter.2.html ; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/io_uring_prep_send_zc.3.html ; https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/io-uring/versions ; https://docs.rs/crate/io-uring/0.7.15/source/src/opcode.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/io-uring/0.7.15/source/src/sys/sys_x86_64.rs ; https://docs.rs/io-uring/0.7.15/io_uring/opcode/struct.SendZc.html ; https://docs.rs/io-uring/0.7.15/io_uring/opcode/struct.ReadvFixed.html ; https://docs.rs/io-uring/0.7.15/io_uring/opcode/struct.WritevFixed.html

### [C25] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: On Linux 6.12, registered buffers cloned into a second ring with IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS, including hugetlbfs-backed buffers coalesced by io_try_coalesce_buffer (1 GiB per-entry limit), can be used by IORING_OP_SEND_ZC with IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF to send one 2.5 MiB chunk as a single SQE, and the IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF completion arrives only after the TCP stack frees the skbs, i.e. after the peer's TCP acknowledgement, including when the path crosses a macvlan or bridge device (where IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED may be reported).
- Raised by: Opus-Consensus, Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: The sender's hold budgets, arena slot-reuse rules and the 0.5-core-at-10GbE sender figure assume exactly this combination; if cloned buffers cannot be used with SEND_ZC or the notification semantics differ, those figures are wrong.
- Summary: The mechanics are confirmed in the v6.12 source: IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS (opcode 30) makes the destination ring share the very same refcounted io_mapped_ubuf objects (coalesced hugetlb bvecs included), IORING_OP_SEND_ZC with IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF imports any sub-range of a registered entry (1 GiB cap) through io_import_fixed on the submitting ring's table, and the IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF CQE is posted only when the last skb reference to the notification is dropped, which for data that really went out zero-copy is when the ACK frees the retransmit-queue skb and the NIC has released its transmit clone. The claim is wrong in two places and silent on three conditions: the notification is a "pages released" signal, not an ACK signal (on a deferred copy it can arrive before transmission; the kernel docs say so explicitly); crossing a macvlan or bridge does not itself cause a copy, local looping does (sibling macvlan, bridge local delivery, tun/tap ports as used by VMs, packet taps, or a no-SG egress device); a single 2.5 MiB SQE can complete short without MSG_WAITALL; 6.12 cloning is whole-table into an empty table and (in linux-6.12.y, hence Debian) requires both rings to share user and mm_account; and code reading shows io_sg_from_iter's truesize accounting (PAGE_ALIGN(bv_len + bv_offset)) inflates with coalesced large folios, which under the TCP send-buffer gate would throttle sends from deep inside a hugepage; that is unfixed in 6.12.y and mainline and must be measured before the hold-budget and 10GbE figures are trusted.
- Evidence: 1. Cloning exists in 6.12 and shares the same objects. include/uapi/linux/io_uring.h@v6.12: "/* clone registered buffers from source ring to current ring */ IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS = 30" and "struct io_uring_clone_buffers { __u32 src_fd; __u32 flags; __u32 pad[6]; }" (no src_off/dst_off/nr in 6.12), "IORING_REGISTER_SRC_REGISTERED = 1". io_uring/rsrc.c@v6.12 io_register_clone_buffers: "if (ctx->user_bufs || ctx->nr_user_bufs) return -EBUSY;", "if (buf.flags & ~IORING_REGISTER_SRC_REGISTERED) return -EINVAL;", "if (memchr_inv(buf.pad, 0, sizeof(buf.pad))) return -EINVAL;". io_clone_buffers: "ret = -ENXIO; nbufs = src_ctx->nr_user_bufs; if (!nbufs) goto out_unlock;" then "if (src != &dummy_ubuf) refcount_inc(&src->refs); user_bufs[i] = src;" i.e. the destination table points at the source's io_mapped_ubuf structs, so bvecs, folio_shift and coalescing are inherited unchanged; io_buffer_unmap only frees on "if (!refcount_dec_and_test(&imu->refs)) return;". liburing io_uring_register(2): "Kernel 6.12 added support for full range cloning, where src_off, dst_off, and nr must all be set to 0 ... Kernel 6.13 added support for specifying the offsets ... 6.12 would fail that operation with -EBUSY". linux-6.12.y head adds (stable commit 2025-02-01 "io_uring/rsrc: require cloned buffers to share accounting contexts", upstream 19d340a2988d): "if (ctx->user != src_ctx->user || ctx->mm_account != src_ctx->mm_account) return -EINVAL;".

2. Hugepage coalescing and the 1 GiB limit are in 6.12. rsrc.c@v6.12 io_sqe_buffer_register: "/* If it's huge page(s), try to coalesce them into fewer bvec entries */ coalesced = io_try_coalesce_buffer(&pages, &nr_pages, &data);" ... "if (coalesced) imu->folio_shift = data.folio_shift;" and one bvec per folio: "vec_len = min_t(size_t, size, (1UL << imu->folio_shift) - off); bvec_set_page(&imu->bvec[i], pages[i], vec_len, off);". io_buffer_validate: "/* arbitrary limit, but we need something */ if (iov->iov_len > SZ_1G) return -EFAULT;" (man page: "there is a size limit of 1GiB per buffer"). Stable history (gregkh/linux mirror of linux-6.12.y): "io_uring/rsrc: enable multi-hugepage buffer coalescing" (2024-08-25, merged for 6.12); 6.12.y later received "io_uring/rsrc: don't rely on user vaddr alignment" (upstream 3a3c6d61577d), "io_uring/rsrc: fix folio unpinning" (5afb4bf9fc62) and "io_uring: fix potential page leak in io_sqe_buffer_register()" (e1c75831f682), all committed to stable 2025-07-06; the 6.12.y diff shows "off = (unsigned long)iov->iov_base & ~PAGE_MASK; if (coalesced) off += data.first_folio_page_idx << PAGE_SHIFT;" and "unpin_user_folio(folio, 1)". Debian trixie ships 6.12.111-1 (packages.debian.org: linux-image-amd64 6.12.111-1 depends on linux-image-6.12.111+deb13-amd64; tracker.debian.org: stable 6.12.94-1, stable-security/p-u 6.12.111-1), i.e. a 6.12.y later than all of these.

3. SEND_ZC uses the fixed buffer from the submitting ring's table, cloned or not. io_uring/net.c@v6.12 io_send_zc_prep: "if (zc->flags & IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF) { unsigned idx = READ_ONCE(sqe->buf_index); if (unlikely(idx >= ctx->nr_user_bufs)) return -EFAULT; ... req->imu = READ_ONCE(ctx->user_bufs[idx]); io_req_set_rsrc_node(notif, ctx, 0); }" and "zc->msg_flags = READ_ONCE(sqe->msg_flags) | MSG_NOSIGNAL | MSG_ZEROCOPY;". io_send_zc_import: "ret = io_import_fixed(ITER_SOURCE, &kmsg->msg.msg_iter, req->imu, (u64)(uintptr_t)sr->buf, sr->len); ... kmsg->msg.sg_from_iter = io_sg_from_iter;". rsrc.c io_import_fixed accepts any sub-range: "/* not inside the mapped region */ if (unlikely(buf_addr < imu->ubuf || buf_end > (imu->ubuf + imu->len))) return -EFAULT;" and skips whole folio-sized bvecs in O(1) ("seg_skip = 1 + (offset >> imu->folio_shift)"). So a 2.5 MiB chunk anywhere inside a registered entry is one SQE. Completion can be short: io_send_zc "if (msg_flags & MSG_WAITALL) min_ret = iov_iter_count(&kmsg->msg.msg_iter);" ... "if (ret > 0 && io_net_retry(sock, kmsg->msg.msg_flags)) { zc->len -= ret; zc->buf += ret; zc->done_io += ret; ... return -EAGAIN; }" with io_net_retry "if (!(flags & MSG_WAITALL)) return false;". net/ipv4/tcp.c@v6.12: "if (msg->msg_ubuf) { uarg = msg->msg_ubuf; if (sk->sk_route_caps & NETIF_F_SG) zc = MSG_ZEROCOPY; }" (no SG on the route's device: data is copied in sendmsg, no skb ever references the notification). io-uring 0.7.15 (docs.rs source): SendZc::build "sqe.ioprio = zc_flags; if let Some(buf_index) = buf_index { sqe.__bindgen_anon_4.buf_index = buf_index; sqe.ioprio |= sys::IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF as u16; }"; Submitter::register_buffers_clone(src_fd) = "register_buffers_clone_offset(src_fd, 0, 0, 0, CloneBuffersFlags::empty())" via IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS with nr_args 1 (all-zero offsets, valid on 6.12; non-zero src_off/dst_off/nr land in 6.12's pad and give -EINVAL).

4. When the NOTIF CQE fires. io_uring/notif.c@v6.12 io_tx_ubuf_complete: "if (nd->zc_report) { if (success && !nd->zc_used && skb) WRITE_ONCE(nd->zc_used, true); else if (!success && !nd->zc_copied) WRITE_ONCE(nd->zc_copied, true); } if (!refcount_dec_and_test(&uarg->refcnt)) return; ... notif->io_task_work.func = io_notif_tw_complete; __io_req_task_work_add(notif, tw_flags);"; io_notif_tw_complete: "if (unlikely(nd->zc_report) && (nd->zc_copied || !nd->zc_used)) notif->cqe.res |= IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED;". io_send_zc drops io_uring's own reference right after sendmsg ("io_notif_flush(zc->notif)" = io_tx_ubuf_complete(NULL, &nd->uarg, true)) and completes the first CQE with IORING_CQE_F_MORE; each skb takes a reference in io_link_skb ("net_zcopy_get(&nd->uarg); skb_zcopy_init(skb, &nd->uarg)"). net/core/skbuff.c skb_release_data: "if (!skb_data_unref(skb, shinfo)) goto exit; if (skb_zcopy(skb)) { ... skb_zcopy_clear(skb, true);" and skbuff.h skb_data_unref: "if (!skb->cloned) return true; ... else if (atomic_sub_return(bias, &shinfo->dataref)) return false;" so the reference drops only when the last clone sharing the data is freed. tcp_output.c __tcp_transmit_skb: "if (clone_it) { ... skb = skb_clone(oskb, gfp_mask);" (the retransmit-queue original keeps the data until ACK; the NIC frees the clone on TX completion). tcp_input.c tcp_clean_rtx_queue (line 3340) calls "tcp_rtx_queue_unlink_and_free(skb, sk)" (line 3436) which per include/net/tcp.h ends in "__kfree_skb(skb)". Hence for genuinely zero-copied TCP data the NOTIF is posted after the ACK and after all transmit clones are released; it is posted immediately (before any transmission) if no skb used the pages (no-SG path, zero-length, or error). Deferred copy releases early: skb_copy_ubufs ends with "skb_zcopy_clear(skb, false);". Documentation/networking/msg_zerocopy.rst@v6.12: "In all these cases, the kernel returns a completion notification when it releases its hold on the shared pages. That notification may arrive before the (copied) data is fully transmitted. A zerocopy completion notification is not a transmit completion notification, therefore." liburing io_uring_enter(2): "the kernel may hold on to buffers for a long time, e.g. waiting for a TCP ACK ... notifications are only responsible for controlling the lifetime of the buffers, and as such don't mean anything about whether the data has atually been sent out or received by the other end."

5. macvlan and bridge: where copies actually happen. io_uring/notif.h: "#define IO_NOTIF_UBUF_FLAGS (SKBFL_ZEROCOPY_FRAG | SKBFL_DONT_ORPHAN)". include/linux/skbuff.h@v6.12 skb_orphan_frags: "if (skb_shinfo(skb)->flags & SKBFL_DONT_ORPHAN) return 0;" (so plain forwarding, ____dev_forward_skb/pskb_expand_head, does not copy io_uring buffers) versus skb_orphan_frags_rx: "/* Frags must be orphaned, even if refcounted, if skb might loop to rx path */ ... return skb_copy_ubufs(skb, gfp_mask);". Callers of skb_orphan_frags_rx in v6.12: net/core/dev.c deliver_skb (l.2236) and __netif_receive_skb_core (l.5635, local protocol delivery), dev_queue_xmit_nit (l.2346, packet taps such as tcpdump on the egress device), drivers/net/tun.c tun_net_xmit (l.1114, tap ports used by VMs). drivers/net/macvlan.c macvlan_queue_xmit: bridge-mode unicast to a sibling macvlan does "dev_forward_skb(vlan->lowerdev, skb)" (local RX, hence a copy); otherwise "xmit_world: skb->dev = vlan->lowerdev; return dev_queue_xmit_accel(...)" (no copy); multicast goes through macvlan_broadcast/skb_clone/netif_rx (copy on local delivery). net/bridge/br_forward.c, br_device.c, br_input.c, br_netfilter_hooks.c contain no skb_orphan_frags/skb_copy_ubufs call (only skb_clone/pskb_copy for flooding and a plain skb_orphan in br_netfilter_hooks.c:493), so host-originated traffic through a bridge to a physical port stays zero-copy; it is copied when the bridge delivers locally or to a tun/tap port. msg_zerocopy.rst: "all packets generated with MSG_ZEROCOPY that are looped to a local socket will incur a deferred copy. This includes looping onto packet sockets (e.g., tcpdump) and tun devices." The ZC_COPIED flag requires IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE in sqe->ioprio (uapi comment: "cqe.res for IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF if IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE was requested"); io_uring_prep_send_zc(3): "If the value is IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED, then data was copied."

6. Unverified-by-test risk found while reading: truesize inflation with coalesced large folios. net.c@v6.12 io_sg_from_iter (identical in current mainline net.c): "struct bio_vec v = mp_bvec_iter_bvec(from->bvec, bi); copied += v.bv_len; truesize += PAGE_ALIGN(v.bv_len + v.bv_offset);" where include/linux/bvec.h defines "mp_bvec_iter_offset(bvec, iter) (__bvec_iter_bvec((bvec), (iter))->bv_offset + (iter).bi_bvec_done)" and io_import_fixed sets "iter->iov_offset = offset" (the chunk's byte offset inside a folio-sized bvec, up to 1 GiB for a 1 GiB hugetlb folio, up to 2 MiB for 2 MiB hugetlb/THP). net/core/datagram.c __zerocopy_sg_from_iter: "truesize = skb->truesize - orig_size; if (sk && sk->sk_type == SOCK_STREAM) { sk_wmem_queued_add(sk, truesize);". include/net/sock.h __sk_stream_memory_free: "if (READ_ONCE(sk->sk_wmem_queued) >= READ_ONCE(sk->sk_sndbuf)) return false;" and tcp.c tcp_sendmsg_locked "new_segment: if (!sk_stream_memory_free(sk)) goto wait_for_space;"; ip-sysctl.rst tcp_wmem max "Default: between 64K and 4MB, depending on RAM size." By this reading each ~64 KiB TSO skb built from a chunk sitting N bytes into a hugepage folio is charged roughly N bytes of send-buffer, so chunks more than a few MiB into a 1 GiB folio would leave at most one skb in flight per ACK round trip. The linux-6.12.y net.c history (16 commits, e.g. "io_uring/net: fix sendzc double notif flush" 2025-03-28) and mainline contain no change to this line. With 4 KiB-page (non-huge, non-THP) buffers bv_offset < 4 KiB and the accounting is sane. This must be confirmed by the planned empirical test; it was not run here.

7. Other 6.12.y fixes relevant to this path present in Debian's kernel: "io_uring: fix incorrect io_kiocb reference in io_link_skb" (2025-09-25; v6.12 compared the wrong notif in "prev_notif = cmd_to_io_kiocb(nd)"), "io_uring/zctx: check chained notif contexts" (2025-11-13), "io_uring/net: fix sendzc double notif flush" (2025-03-28), "io_uring/rsrc: ignore dummy_ubuf for buffer cloning" (2024-10-16, already in v6.12).
- Corrected claim: On Linux 6.12 (Debian 13 ships 6.12.111-1), IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS clones a source ring's entire registered-buffer table into a destination ring that has no buffers registered (6.12 returns -EBUSY otherwise; offsets, nr and IORING_REGISTER_DST_REPLACE are 6.13 features and give -EINVAL on 6.12), and in linux-6.12.y both rings must belong to the same user and mm (same process credentials), or -EINVAL. The clone shares the same refcounted io_mapped_ubuf objects, so hugetlbfs-backed entries that io_try_coalesce_buffer collapsed to one bvec per folio (each registered iovec at most 1 GiB) are usable from the destination ring exactly as from the source. IORING_OP_SEND_ZC with IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF (ioprio) and buf_index imports any sub-range of such an entry through io_import_fixed, so a 2.5 MiB chunk is one SQE; its first CQE (IORING_CQE_F_MORE) reports bytes queued and may be short unless MSG_WAITALL is set, in which case io_uring retries until the whole chunk is queued. The IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF CQE is posted on the submitting ring when the kernel has dropped every reference to the pages; it is a buffer-lifetime signal, not a delivery or ACK signal. For data that was actually transmitted zero-copy over TCP this happens after the peer's ACK frees the retransmit-queue skb and after the NIC has released its transmit clone(s); when the stack makes a deferred copy (packet looped to a local receiver: sibling macvlan in bridge mode, bridge local delivery, a tun/tap port such as a VM on the same host, a packet tap like tcpdump; or an egress device without NETIF_F_SG, where tcp_sendmsg copies up front) the notification can arrive as soon as the copy is made, before transmission and before any ACK. Merely crossing a macvlan or a bridge toward a physical NIC does not cause a copy. With IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE set, the notification's cqe.res carries IORING_NOTIF_USAGE_ZC_COPIED whenever any part was copied or nothing was sent zero-copy. Caveat requiring measurement: io_sg_from_iter charges skb->truesize as PAGE_ALIGN(bv_len + bv_offset), and with coalesced large folios bv_offset is the chunk's offset inside the folio (up to 1 GiB), so by code reading TCP's sk_wmem_queued/sk_sndbuf gate can limit sends from deep inside a hugepage folio to about one skb per round trip; this is unchanged in linux-6.12.y and mainline, and does not affect 4 KiB-page (non-huge, non-THP) registered buffers.
- Design impact: 1. Reframe the notification semantics: hold budgets and arena slot-reuse must be driven by the NOTIF CQE as a "pages released" event, never as an ACK or flow-control signal; the document must drop "arrives only after the peer's TCP acknowledgement" and say "after ACK plus NIC TX completion when the send really was zero-copy; possibly immediately on a deferred copy". Any latency or in-flight accounting derived from NOTIF timing must handle the early-copy case. 2. Correct the macvlan/bridge statement: copies (and ZC_COPIED) come from local looping, tun/tap ports, packet taps, or a no-SG egress device, not from the macvlan/bridge hop itself. Consequence for the fleet: ESXi/Windows/Debian clients behind a physical NIC get true zero-copy; Proxmox VMs on the same host reached through a tap port on the bridge always get a deferred copy, so for those peers the sender pays a copy plus notification overhead and the 0.5-core figure does not apply; enable IORING_SEND_ZC_REPORT_USAGE, count ZC_COPIED per peer and fall back to plain SEND for peers that consistently copy. Note that running tcpdump on the egress device also forces copies. 3. Set MSG_WAITALL on the 2.5 MiB SEND_ZC SQEs (or handle short completions and resubmit the remainder), otherwise one-SQE-per-chunk accounting breaks when the socket send buffer fills. 4. Cloning rules on Debian's 6.12.y: clone the whole table into a still-empty ring using io-uring 0.7.15 Submitter::register_buffers_clone (register_buffers_clone_offset with non-zero fields fails with -EINVAL on 6.12); clone before submitting any FIXED_BUF SQE on that ring; all rings sharing the arena must be created in the same process/credentials (user and mm_account check); per-ring sparse/partial tables and DST_REPLACE need 6.13+. 5. Before committing to a hugetlbfs arena, run the planned empirical test specifically with chunks located near the end of a 1 GiB (and 2 MiB) folio and watch sk_wmem_queued / throughput; if the truesize inflation reproduces, back the send arena with 4 KiB pages (madvise MADV_NOHUGEPAGE so THP cannot coalesce it either), accept 640 bvecs per 2.5 MiB chunk (io_import_fixed skips in O(1), skbs carry up to MAX_SKB_FRAGS 4 KiB frags which matches the 64 KiB GSO size), or carry a kernel patch; otherwise the 10GbE/0.5-core sender figure and the hold budgets are unsupported for hugepage-backed buffers. 6. Keep the arena pinned-page accounting in mind: registered buffers count against RLIMIT_MEMLOCK of the registering user and are shared by clones; unregistering on one ring does not free the pages while another ring or an in-flight notification (io_req_set_rsrc_node on the notif) still references them.
