https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vsphere/vsphere/8-0/release-notes/esxi-update-and-patch-release-notes/vsphere-esxi-801-release-notes.html ; https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vsphere/vsphere/8-0/release-notes/esxi-update-and-patch-release-notes/vsphere-esxi-802-release-notes.html ; https://support.hpe.com/docs/display/public/synergy-sw-release/ESXi_V80_U1_May.html ; https://vmware.lenovo.com/content/2023_06/Lenovo_Custom_ISO/8.0u1/readme.html

### [C31] CONFIRMED
- Claim: Proxmox VE 9.0 was released on 5 August 2025 on Debian 13 with kernel 6.14.8 and added, as a technology preview, VM snapshots as qcow2 volume chains on thick-provisioned LVM storage (for LUNs over iSCSI or Fibre Channel); Proxmox VE 9.1 was released on 19 November 2025 on Debian 13.2 with kernel 6.17.2.
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics
- Why it matters: The claim that FC/iSCSI LUNs under Proxmox 9 support VM snapshots, and the Phase C Proxmox exit test, depend on it.
- Summary: Every element of the claim checks out against Proxmox's own Roadmap page, forum announcements, press release and admin guide: PVE 9.0 was released 5 August 2025 on Debian 13 "Trixie" with kernel 6.14.8-2 as stable default and introduced, as a technology preview, VM snapshots on thick-provisioned LVM storages implemented as qcow2-layered volume chains, explicitly aimed at shared LUNs over iSCSI/Fibre Channel; PVE 9.1 was released 19 November 2025 on Debian 13.2 with kernel 6.17.2-1. Two precision points for the design: the feature is still labelled a technology preview in the current admin guide (9.1 improved it rather than promoting it), and PVE 9.0 actually shipped four days before Debian 13.0 itself (released 9 August 2025).
- Evidence: Proxmox VE Roadmap (pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Roadmap), 9.0 section: "Released 05. August 2025"; "Based on Debian Trixie (13)"; "Latest 6.14.8-2 Kernel as new stable default". Highlights: "VM snapshots on thick-provisioned LVM storages with snapshots as volume chains (technology preview)." Storage: "A new property on thick-provisioned LVM storages enables support for snapshots as volume chains." ... "This enables VM snapshots on shared thick-provisioned LVM storages, as they are often used on LUNs provided by a storage box via iSCSI/Fibre Channel." ... "Logical volumes for snapshots are currently thick-provisioned, but an underlying storage box may implement thin provisioning." ... "The setting only affects newly created VM disks." ... "VMs currently cannot be migrated if they have snapshots with disks on a local storage that allows snapshots as volume chains."

Roadmap, 9.1 section: "Released 19. November 2025"; "Based on Debian Trixie (13.2)"; "Latest 6.17.2-1 Kernel as new stable default". Highlights: "Storages with "snapshots as volume chains" (technology preview) enabled now support taking offline snapshots". Storage: "Improvements to snapshots as volume chains (technology preview):" ... "Disallow disabling volume-chain snapshots if a qcow2 image exists, as this can have unintended consequences." ... "Fix cluster-locking behavior when performing snapshot operations on a shared LVM storage." ... "As "snapshot as volume chains" requires machine version 10 or higher".

Forum announcement "Proxmox Virtual Environment 9.0 released" (first post dated August 5, 2025): "The new version is based on the great Debian 13 "Trixie"" ... "we're using a newer Linux kernel 6.14.8-2 as stable default in Proxmox VE." ... "Snapshots as volume chains provide vendor-agnostic support for snapshots on any storage system that supports block storage." ... "This includes iSCSI and Fibre Channel-attached SANs." ... "Debian 13 is scheduled for its stable release this Saturday, August 9."

Press release (proxmox.com): dateline "VIENNA, Austria – August 05, 2025"; "a modernized core built upon Debian 13 "Trixie""; "Proxmox VE is using a newer Linux kernel 6.14.8-2 as stable default"; "Virtual Machines (VMs) utilizing thick-provisioned LVM shared storages, such as those backed by iSCSI or FC-based SANs" ... "implementing snapshots as volume chains, where a volume based on a snapshot only records differences".

Forum announcement "Proxmox Virtual Environment 9.1 available" (first post dated Nov 19, 2025): "This release is based on Debian 13.2 "Trixie" but we're using the newer Linux kernel 6.17.2 as new stable default."

Admin guide chapter "Proxmox VE Storage" (chapter-pvesm.html) and wiki Storage: LVM, option snapshot-as-volume-chain: "Set this flag to enable snapshot support for virtual machines on LVM with a volume backing chain." ... "This feature manages the snapshot volume through the storage plugin and uses qcow2 to layer separate volumes as a backing chain." ... "Note that, although this feature relies on qcow2, it only uses qcow2's ability to layer multiple volumes in a backing chain, not qcow2's snapshot functionality" ... "Snapshot volumes are currently thick-provisioned LVM logical volumes." ... "Enabling or disabling this flag only affects newly created virtual disk volumes." ... "For efficient support of snapshot-as-volume-chain, the backing storage must support thin-provisioning and discard." ... "Snapshots as volume chains are currently a technology preview in Proxmox VE." Storage-types table marks iSCSI and FC/SAS snapshots "yes" with footnote 4: "Since Proxmox VE 9, snapshots as a volume chain have been available for VMs. These snapshots use separate volumes for the snapshot data and layer them." LVM feature table lists image formats "raw, qcow2" and Snapshots "yes" with footnote 1: "Since Proxmox VE 9, snapshots as a volume chain have been available for VMs".

Debian news (debian.org/News/2025/20250809): "Debian 13 trixie released", dated August 9th, 2025, shipping "Linux kernel 6.12 LTS series" — i.e. PVE 9.0 (5 August) preceded Debian 13.0 by four days and ships its own 6.14/6.17 kernels rather than Debian's 6.12.
- Corrected claim: Proxmox VE 9.0 was released on 5 August 2025, based on Debian 13 "Trixie" (four days before Debian 13.0's own release on 9 August 2025) with Proxmox's kernel 6.14.8-2 as the stable default. It added, as a technology preview, VM snapshots on thick-provisioned LVM storages ("snapshots as volume chains", storage.cfg flag snapshot-as-volume-chain): the storage plugin lays out each snapshot as a separate thick-provisioned logical volume and uses qcow2 only to layer those volumes as a backing chain, which gives vendor-agnostic snapshots on shared LVM over iSCSI or Fibre Channel LUNs; the flag affects only disks created after it is enabled, and Proxmox states that efficient operation requires the backing storage to support thin provisioning and discard. Proxmox VE 9.1 was released on 19 November 2025, based on Debian 13.2 with kernel 6.17.2-1 as the stable default; it kept the feature in technology preview but added offline snapshots, fixed cluster locking for snapshot operations on shared LVM, and requires QEMU machine version 10 or higher for volume-chain snapshots.
- Design impact: The dependency holds: FC/iSCSI LUNs from OpenTAP can carry Proxmox VM snapshots under PVE 9.x with no SAN-side snapshot API, since the feature is implemented entirely on the hypervisor as a qcow2-layered LVM volume chain. The design should state the feature's status precisely and shape the Phase C Proxmox exit test accordingly: (1) label it "technology preview (still preview in 9.1)" and target PVE 9.1 or later for the exit test, because 9.1 carries the cluster-locking fix for snapshot operations on shared LVM and adds offline snapshots; (2) the test procedure must create the LVM storage with snapshot-as-volume-chain enabled before creating VM disks (the flag does not apply to existing volumes) and use VMs with QEMU machine version 10 or higher; (3) OpenTAP's LIO backstore for these LUNs must advertise thin provisioning and honour discard/UNMAP (LIO emulate_tpu/emulate_tpws and the thin-provisioning VPD bits), since Proxmox says efficient volume-chain support "must support thin-provisioning and discard" and 9.1 wipes removed volumes with blkdiscard; the exit test should verify that deleting a snapshot returns space on the OpenTAP side; (4) do not claim snapshot support for Proxmox LXC containers or for pre-9.0 Proxmox on these LUNs, and note that the Debian 13 base of Proxmox runs Proxmox's 6.14/6.17 kernels, not Debian's 6.12 LTS, so any kernel-version assumptions about the Proxmox initiator (qla2xxx, open-iscsi, multipath) should reference 6.14.8-2 (9.0) and 6.17.2-1 (9.1).
- Sources: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Roadmap ; https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/proxmox-virtual-environment-9-0-released.169258/ ; https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/proxmox-virtual-environment-9.1-available.176254/ ; https://www.proxmox.com/en/about/company-details/press-releases/proxmox-virtual-environment-9-0 ; https://pve.proxmox.com/pve-docs/chapter-pvesm.html ; https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Storage:_LVM ; https://www.debian.org/News/2025/20250809

### [C32] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: openraft 0.9.25 is the newest stable release on crates.io (published 2026-07-28, not yanked; 0.10 exists only as 0.10.0-alpha.37 of 2026-10-10); in 0.9.25 RaftLogStorage::save_vote must persist the vote before returning and append signals durability through a LogFlushed callback, so a witness that fsyncs only on votes and appended entries, never on heartbeats, conforms to the trait contract; and redb 4.3.0 (crates.io 2026-09-15) provides Durability::Immediate (persistent when WriteTransaction::commit returns) and Durability::None (not persisted until a later Immediate commit).
- Raised by: Opus-Consensus
- Why it matters: The Raspberry Pi-on-microSD witness with under 100 fsyncs per day, keeping lag and CP progress out of the Raft log, and the 'one fsync per configuration change' cost figure all rest on these contracts.
- Summary: Every factual statement in C32 checks out against crates.io and docs.rs: openraft 0.9.25 (2026-07-28, not yanked) is the newest stable, 0.10 exists only as pre-releases (latest 0.10.0-alpha.37, 2026-10-10), save_vote "must be persisted on disk before returning", append takes a LogFlushed callback that must fire only once entries "are persisted on disk", and redb 4.3.0 (2026-09-15) defines exactly Durability::None and Durability::Immediate with the semantics claimed. The 0.9.25 engine source also confirms that a steady-state heartbeat (empty AppendEntries, unchanged vote, unchanged commit index) reaches no RaftLogStorage write at all. Two corrections: "0.10 exists only as alpha.37" should read "only as an alpha series, latest alpha.37", and the heartbeat conclusion holds for the RaftLogStorage trait only; the separate RaftStateMachine contract requires either persisting state before apply() returns or persistent snapshots, and a heartbeat that advances leader_commit does invoke save_committed (documented optional) and apply, which the "one fsync per configuration change" figure must account for.
- Evidence: VERSIONS (crates.io API, https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/openraft): max_stable_version 0.9.25, default_version 0.9.25, created 2026-07-28, yanked: false. max_version = newest_version = 0.10.0-alpha.37, created 2026-10-10, not yanked. The 0.10 line is a series of alphas (alpha.14 2026-02-28 ... alpha.36 2026-09-29, alpha.37 2026-10-10); no 0.10.0 stable, beta or rc exists. No 0.9.26. (0.9.24 was 2026-04-21.)

redb (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/redb): max_version = max_stable_version = 4.3.0, created 2026-09-15 03:46:14 UTC, yanked: false. Note newest_version is 2.6.4 (published 2026-10-02), a 2.x maintenance release; 4.3.0 remains the highest stable. Other 4.x: 4.2.0 (2026-08-17), 4.1.0 (2026-04-19), 4.0.0 (2026-04-02).

OPENRAFT 0.9.25 TRAIT CONTRACT (docs.rs source src/storage/v2.rs, trait RaftLogStorage):
- save_vote: "### To ensure correctness: The vote must be persisted on disk before returning." Signature: fn save_vote(&mut self, vote: &Vote<C::NodeId>) -> Result<(), StorageError<C::NodeId>>.
- append: "async fn append<I>(&mut self, entries: I, callback: LogFlushed<C>) -> Result<(), StorageError<C::NodeId>>". Docs: "Append log entries and call the `callback` once logs are persisted on disk." "It should returns immediately after saving the input log entries in memory, and calls the `callback` when the entries are persisted on disk, i.e., avoid blocking." "### To ensure correctness: - When this method returns, the entries must be readable, i.e., a `LogReader` can read these entries. - When the `callback` is called, the entries must be persisted on disk. NOTE that: the `callback` can be called either before or after this method returns. - There must not be a **hole** in logs."
- LogFlushed (src/storage/callback.rs): "A oneshot callback for completion of log io operation." pub fn log_io_completed(self, result: Result<(), io::Error>) — "Report log io completion event. It will be called when the log is successfully appended to the storage or an error occurs." On Ok sends Ok(log_io_id) over a oneshot; on Err logs "LogFlush error" and sends Err.
- RaftCore (src/core/raft_core.rs): Command::SaveVote -> "self.log_store.save_vote(&vote).await?"; Command::AppendInputEntries -> append_to_log builds "let callback = LogFlushed::new(log_io_id, tx);" then "self.log_store.append(entries, callback).await?" and then awaits the oneshot ("rx.await"), mapping errors to StorageIOError::write_logs. Command::Commit -> "self.log_store.save_committed(Some(upto.clone())).await?" then apply_to_state_machine. Command::DeleteConflictLog -> log_store.truncate; Command::PurgeLog -> log_store.purge.
- save_committed docs: "Saves the last committed log id to storage. # Optional feature. If the state machine flushes state to disk before returning from `apply()`, then the application does not need to implement this method. Otherwise, this method is also optional(but not recommended), but your application has to deal with state reversion of state machine carefully upon restart." Default impl: "By default `committed` log id is not saved".
- truncate / purge docs state only "It must not leave a **hole** in logs." — no "before returning" persistence wording.
- RaftStateMachine::apply docs: "An implementation may choose to persist either the state machine or the snapshot: - An implementation with persistent state machine: persists the state on disk before returning from `apply()`. So that a snapshot does not need to be persistent. - An implementation with persistent snapshot: `apply()` does not have to persist state on disk. But every snapshot has to be persistent. And when starting up the application, the state machine should be rebuilt from the last snapshot." applied_state: "upon startup, the last membership will be loaded by scanning logs from the `last-applied-log-id`."

HEARTBEATS NEVER REACH THE LOG STORE (0.9.25 source):
- Leader (src/replication/mod.rs): Data::Heartbeat -> send_log_entries with start == end: "// Heartbeat RPC, no logs to send, last log id is the same as prev_log_id ... (vec![], r)"; the request is AppendEntriesRequest { vote, prev_log_id: matching, leader_commit, entries: vec![] }. Replicate::Committed also sends such an empty AppendEntries carrying the new leader_commit.
- Follower, RaftCore handle_append_entries_request: "let is_ok = self.engine.handle_append_entries(&req.vote, req.prev_log_id, req.entries, Some(tx));" then, only if ok, "self.engine.handle_commit_entries(req.leader_commit);".
- Engine append_entries (src/engine/engine_impl.rs): "self.vote_handler().update_vote(vote)?;" then "fh.ensure_log_consecutive(prev_log_id.clone())?;" then "fh.append_entries(prev_log_id, entries);". No other Command is pushed.
- VoteHandler::update_vote (src/engine/handler/vote_handler/mod.rs): Command::SaveVote is pushed only under "if vote > self.state.vote_ref() {"; an equal vote hits the else branch "self.state.vote.touch(C::now());" — no storage write.
- FollowingHandler::append_entries -> "let since = self.state.first_conflicting_index(&entries);" ; first_conflicting_index (src/raft_state/mod.rs) loops over entries and returns l (= entries.len()) if none conflict, so for an empty slice it returns 0; do_append_entries then early-returns at "if since == l { return; }" before "self.output.push_command(Command::AppendInputEntries {". ensure_log_consecutive pushes DeleteConflictLog only when prev_log_id is not found locally (conflict case, not steady state).
- FollowingHandler::commit_entries pushes Command::Commit only inside "if let Some(prev_committed) = self.state.update_committed(&committed) {"; RaftState::update_committed: "Update field `committed` if the input is greater. If updated, it returns the previous value in a `Some()`." guard "if committed.as_ref() > self.committed() {" — so a heartbeat triggers save_committed + apply only when the commit index actually advances (once per newly committed entry), never in steady state.

OPENRAFT 0.10 ALPHA (docs.rs 0.10.0-alpha.37): append is "fn append<I>(&mut self, entries: I, callback: IOFlushed<C>)" (LogFlushed renamed to IOFlushed); save_vote takes &VoteOf<C>, no callback, still "The vote must be persisted on disk before returning." Same persistence semantics, different type names — pin openraft 0.9.

REDB 4.3.0 (docs.rs enum.Durability, src/transactions.rs): enum is #[non_exhaustive] with exactly two variants. None: "Commits with this durability level will not be persisted to disk unless followed by a commit with [`Durability::Immediate`]." Immediate: "Commits with this durability level are guaranteed to be persistent as soon as [`WriteTransaction::commit`] returns." No Eventual/Paranoid variants in 4.x (CHANGELOG: Paranoid appears only at 2.3.0/3.0.0). set_durability: "Set the desired durability level for writes made in this transaction. Defaults to [`Durability::Immediate`]"; signature "pub fn set_durability(&mut self, durability: Durability) -> Result<(), SetDurabilityError>" (errors with PersistentSavepointModified if a persistent savepoint was created/deleted and durability < Immediate). WriteTransaction::new sets "durability: InternalDurability::Immediate". commit doc: "All writes performed in this transaction will be visible to future transactions, and are durable as consistent with the [`Durability`] level set by [`Self::set_durability`]". Dispatch in commit_inner_helper: "InternalDurability::None => { self.non_durable_commit(...)" vs "InternalDurability::Immediate => self.durable_commit(" -> "self.mem.commit(". design.md: "redb supports "non-durable" commits, meaning that there is no guarantee of durability." "Non-durable commits are implemented with an in-memory flag that directs readers to read from the secondary page" ... "In the event of a crash, the database will simply rollback to the primary page". Default durable commit (1PC+C): "A commit is performed with a single `fsync`." CHANGELOG 4.2.0 corroborates the fold-in semantics: "Fix `Database::check_integrity()` silently discarding transactions committed with `Durability::None` that had not yet been made durable by a later commit" and "`Durability::None` commits are about 2x faster".
- Corrected claim: openraft 0.9.25 (published 2026-07-28, not yanked) is the newest stable release on crates.io; the 0.10 line exists only as pre-releases (an alpha series whose latest is 0.10.0-alpha.37 of 2026-10-10; no 0.10.0 stable, beta or rc), and 0.10 renames the append callback type from LogFlushed to IOFlushed, so the design pins openraft 0.9. In 0.9.25, RaftLogStorage::save_vote "must be persisted on disk before returning", and RaftLogStorage::append(entries, callback: LogFlushed<C>) must invoke the callback only once "the entries must be persisted on disk" (RaftCore awaits that callback before proceeding). Heartbeats are AppendEntries RPCs with an empty entries list; on the follower an unchanged vote only "touches" the vote (SaveVote is pushed only when the incoming vote is strictly greater), empty entries produce no AppendInputEntries command, and an unchanged leader_commit produces no Commit command, so a steady-state heartbeat causes no RaftLogStorage write. Therefore a witness whose log store fsyncs on vote changes and on appended entries, and never on heartbeats, conforms to the RaftLogStorage contract. Separately, (a) save_committed is a documented "Optional feature" (default: not saved), (b) truncate/purge carry only the "no hole" invariant, and (c) the RaftStateMachine contract requires either persisting state before apply() returns or making every snapshot persistent and rebuilding from the last snapshot on startup; a heartbeat that advances leader_commit does invoke save_committed and apply, once per newly committed entry. redb 4.3.0 (crates.io 2026-09-15, not yanked; the highest stable even though 2.6.4 was published later on the 2.x line) defines a #[non_exhaustive] Durability enum with exactly None ("will not be persisted to disk unless followed by a commit with Durability::Immediate") and Immediate ("guaranteed to be persistent as soon as WriteTransaction::commit returns", the default; one fsync per durable commit by default); WriteTransaction::set_durability returns Result<(), SetDurabilityError>.
- Design impact: No change to the core premise: the fsync-on-votes-and-appends-only witness is supported by the openraft 0.9.25 contract and by the engine code, and redb's None/Immediate semantics are exactly as the design assumes. Three edits are needed. (1) Pin the dependency as openraft = "0.9" (0.9.25) and note that 0.10 is alpha-only with a renamed callback (IOFlushed); do not describe 0.10 as "only alpha.37" but as an alpha series. (2) The "one fsync per configuration change" figure must state what it covers: it is correct for the log store (one Immediate redb commit per append batch; vote changes add one fsync each, only at elections/leader changes), but the witness's RaftStateMachine must pick one of the two documented persistence modes. The cheapest conforming choice is the "persistent snapshot" mode: apply() writes the (membership-only) state with Durability::None, every snapshot is written with Durability::Immediate, and startup rebuilds from the last snapshot plus the log. If instead the design persists state before apply() returns, each committed config change costs two fsyncs (append, then apply), not one. Either way, say explicitly that save_committed is left at the default (not persisted) and that truncate/purge use Durability::None, relying on redb's documented fold-in of None commits into the next Immediate commit in the same database. (3) Record that commit-advancing heartbeats (the empty AppendEntries sent right after an entry commits) do call save_committed and apply once per committed entry, so the "never on heartbeats" statement should be phrased as "no fsync is required by any heartbeat; steady-state heartbeats perform no storage call at all". Also note for implementers that redb 4.x set_durability is fallible (SetDurabilityError when a persistent savepoint was touched) and that only None and Immediate exist (no Eventual/Paranoid as in 2.x).
- Sources: https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/openraft ; https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/redb ; https://docs.rs/openraft/0.9.25/openraft/storage/trait.RaftLogStorage.html ; https://docs.rs/openraft/0.9.25/openraft/storage/struct.LogFlushed.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/storage/v2.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/storage/callback.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/core/raft_core.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/engine/engine_impl.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/engine/handler/following_handler/mod.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/engine/handler/vote_handler/mod.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/raft_state/mod.rs ; https://docs.rs/crate/openraft/0.9.25/source/src/replication/mod.rs ; https://docs.rs/openraft/0.10.0-alpha.37/openraft/storage/trait.RaftLogStorage.html ; https://docs.rs/redb/4.3.0/redb/enum.Durability.html ; https://docs.rs/redb/4.3.0/redb/struct.WriteTransaction.html ; https://docs.rs/crate/redb/4.3.0/source/src/transactions.rs ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cberner/redb/v4.3.0/src/transactions.rs ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cberner/redb/v4.3.0/docs/design.md ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cberner/redb/v4.3.0/CHANGELOG.md

### [C33] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: Samba 4.22 idmap_rid cannot be the default (*) backend; BUILTIN and well-known SIDs (e.g. S-1-5-32-544, S-1-5-32-545) are mapped by the default allocating backend (tdb) in first-seen order per winbindd instance, so two SVMs joined to the same domain allocate different gids for the same BUILTIN SID; and net idmap set mapping can pre-seed a tdb idmap with fixed SID-to-ID pairs.
- Raised by: Opus-Storage, Opus-Protocols
- Why it matters: The rule 'one SID maps to one uid across SVMs' holds for domain RIDs only; every Windows-created ACL references BUILTIN groups, so volume rehost, host-side backup and Phase 3 multiprotocol ACLs break unless the * tdb backend is seeded from Raft.
- Summary: The core conclusion holds: with idmap_rid for the domain and an allocating '*' backend (tdb), two separately-stated SVMs will hand out different GIDs for the same BUILTIN or well-known SID, and rid is documented as unusable for '*'. But the mechanism and the remedy in the claim are wrong for Samba 4.22: BUILTIN SIDs are not resolved by the '*' tdb at all (they are routed to passdb group mappings; only Administrators/Users/Guests get auto-created, with a GID *allocated* by the '*' backend's allocator and stored in group_mapping.tdb), and `net idmap set mapping` is an unimplemented stub ("Not implemented yet"); pre-seeding is done with `net idmap restore` for winbindd_idmap.tdb and `net groupmap add`/`net sam addmem` for BUILTIN.
- Evidence: Platform version: packages.debian.org shows trixie samba "2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1"; the manpages.debian.org/trixie pages are from the same source package; source read from the upstream v4-22-stable branch.

1) rid cannot be the default backend — documented, not code-enforced. idmap_rid(8) (trixie): the backend "can NOT be used as the default backend"; "One usually needs to define a writeable default idmap range, using a backend like tdb or ldap" "in order to be able to map the BUILTIN sids and other domains." Samba wiki Idmap_config_rid: rid "cannot be set as idmap config * default ID mapping back end" because "it is unable to assign new ID, such as for BUILTIN groups"; the default domain "must use a read-write-enabled back end, such as tdb" and "must not overlap with any domain ID mapping configuration!"; "Setting the default back end is mandatory"; the example is captioned "Default ID mapping configuration for local BUILTIN accounts and groups on a domain member". smb.conf(5) 4.22 (idmapconfig.xml): '*' is "the default configuration that is used to catch all domains that do not have an explicit idmap configuration of their own"; tdb/tdb2/ldap "create mappings of their own" and "These are suitable for use in the default idmap configuration." Source: idmap_rid.c has no check for '*' or BUILTIN; idmap.c never rejects rid for '*'. rid_methods = {.init, .unixids_to_sids, .sids_to_unixids} — no allocate_id; idmap_rid_sid_to_id computes `map->xid.id = rid - ctx->base_rid + dom->low_id` ignoring the domain SID (so BUILTIN RID 544 would collide with domain RID 544), and idmap_rid_id_to_sid fails on `is_null_sid(&dom->dom_sid)`, which the '*' domain has.

2) How BUILTIN and well-known SIDs are actually mapped in 4.22. winbindd_dual_srv.c _wbint_Sids2UnixIDs calls `idmap_find_domain_with_sid(d->name.string, d->sid)` and "never tries another domain"; idmap.c: `if (sid_check_is_for_passdb(sid)) { return passdb_idmap_domain; }` else `idmap_find_domain(domname)` (unknown/empty name -> `return default_idmap_domain;`). util_sid_passdb.c: BUILTIN SIDs are "for passdb" when the passdb is responsible for BUILTIN; pdb_interface.c: `pdb_default_is_responsible_for_builtin` -> "return true;", `pdb_default_is_responsible_for_wellknown` -> "return false;". idmap_passdb.c: on `pdb_sid_to_id` failure the entry is `ID_UNMAPPED`, "It does not call any other idmap backend", and passdb_methods has no allocate_id. pdb_default_sid_to_id BUILTIN branch: `methods->getgrsid(methods, map, *sid)` (group mapping) else "Could not find map for sid" -> false. So a BUILTIN SID is mapped only if a group mapping exists. The three that exist by default are created by smbd: token_util.c finalize_local_nt_token (called from create_local_nt_token_from_info3/create_local_nt_token) checks `pdb_get_aliasinfo(&global_sid_Builtin_Administrators, info)` and on failure calls create_builtin_administrators(), warning "WARNING: Failed to create BUILTIN\\Administrators group!  Can Winbind allocate gids?"; same for BUILTIN\Users and BUILTIN\Guests. pdb_util.c pdb_create_builtin(rid): when passdb is responsible for BUILTIN it requires `lp_winbind_nested_groups()` (default "yes") and `winbind_ping()`, then `pdb_create_builtin_alias(rid, 0)`; groupdb/mapping.c: `if (gid == 0) { if (!winbind_allocate_gid(&gidformap))` ... "Could not get a gid out of winbind"; then `map->gid = gidformap; sid_copy(&map->sid, &sid); map->sid_name_use = SID_NAME_ALIAS;` and `pdb_add_group_mapping_entry(map)`. create_builtin_administrators adds DOMAIN_RID_ADMINS and "<sam>\root" as members, create_builtin_users adds DOMAIN_RID_USERS, create_builtin_guests adds local Guest/Guests and domain Guests. winbindd: _wbint_AllocateGid -> `idmap_allocate_gid` -> idmap_allocate_unixid -> `dom = idmap_find_domain(NULL)` (= default_idmap_domain, i.e. '*'), `if (dom->methods->allocate_id == NULL) return NT_STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED;` (rid has none -> BUILTIN alias creation fails). idmap_tdb.c: `.allocate_id = idmap_tdb_common_get_new_id`, db = `state_path(talloc_tos(), "winbindd_idmap.tdb")`, keys "USER HWM"/"GROUP HWM"; idmap_tdb_common.c allocator is a sequential atomic increment `dbwrap_change_uint32_atomic_bystring(db, state->hwmkey, &hwm, 1)`; get_new_id refuses any domain but "*" and does not check read_only; sids_to_unixids allocates for unmapped SIDs only when `!dom->read_only`; set_mapping stores both directions with TDB_INSERT (ID-key collision fails and the SID record is removed). idmap_tdb(8): "In contrast to read only backends like idmap_rid, it is an allocating backend" that "needs to allocate new user and group IDs in order to create new mappings." Hence: non-BUILTIN well-known SIDs (S-1-1-0, S-1-5-11, S-1-5-2, S-1-3-x ...) go to the '*' tdb and are allocated into winbindd_idmap.tdb in first-seen order; BUILTIN 544/545/546 get a GID from the same '*' HWM at the first SMB session on that instance, recorded in group_mapping.tdb; other BUILTIN aliases (551, 555, ...) stay unmapped unless an admin maps them. All state is per-instance tdb files, so two SVMs diverge.

3) net idmap set mapping. net_idmap.c (v4-22): net_idmap_set_mapping's only statement is `d_printf("%s\n", _("Not implemented yet"));` returning -1; the functable describes "mapping" as N_("Not implemented yet"). net(8) in trixie and in the samba.org 4.25.0 page list IDMAP SET SECRET/RANGE/CONFIG only; "IDMAP SET MAPPING: No. The page has no such subsection." What exists: IDMAP RESTORE "Restore the mappings from the specified file or stdin." — code accepts `GID %lu %127s`, `UID %lu %127s`, `USER HWM %lu`, `GROUP HWM %lu`, stores SID->ID and ID->SID with TDB_REPLACE inside a transaction, HWM stored unconditionally via `dbwrap_store_int32_bystring(db, "USER HWM", idval)`, default file for backend tdb `state_path(talloc_tos(), "winbindd_idmap.tdb")`, opened `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`; IDMAP DUMP prints "USER HWM %d", "GROUP HWM %d" and "%s %s" (value key) lines; IDMAP DELETE MAPPING exists. smb.conf(5) 4.22: "read only = yes|no" "can be used to turn the writing backends tdb, tdb2, and ldap into read only mode", e.g. "with a pre-filled database that shouldn't grow automatically". For BUILTIN the seeding tool is net(8) "net groupmap add {rid=int|sid=string} unixgroup=string [type={domain|local}] [ntgroup=string] [comment=string]" ("Add a new group mapping entry") plus "SAM ADDMEM <GROUP> <MEMBER>" ("Add a member to a Local group"). Not verified in this pass: that unixgroup= must resolve via getgrnam (the synopsis shows it as required).

4) autorid (alternative for '*'): idmap_autorid(8) allows `idmap config * : backend = autorid`; "A chosen list of well-known SIDs will be preallocated on first start to create deterministic mappings for those" (code list S-1-1-0, S-1-2-0/1, S-1-3-x, S-1-5-1..15, 17..20; no S-1-5-32 entries); the BUILTIN range is allocated on demand, not at startup; `.allocate_id = idmap_autorid_allocate_id` (allocation pool), so BUILTIN alias GIDs still come from a first-need pool.
- Corrected claim: Samba 4.22 (Debian trixie 2:4.22.11): idmap_rid must not be the default ('*') backend. This is a documented requirement (idmap_rid(8): it "can NOT be used as the default backend"; the Samba wiki: "must use a read-write-enabled back end, such as tdb"), not a check in the code: rid has no allocate_id method, ignores the domain SID when mapping SID->ID (BUILTIN RID 544 would collide with domain RID 544) and cannot map ID->SID for the SID-less '*' domain. Identity of domain SIDs across SVMs holds for rid-mapped domain RIDs only. Everything else is per-instance state: (a) non-BUILTIN well-known SIDs (S-1-1-0 Everyone, S-1-5-11 Authenticated Users, S-1-5-2, S-1-3-x ...) are mapped by the '*' backend; with tdb they are allocated by a sequential high-water-mark counter in state/winbindd_idmap.tdb in first-seen order; (b) BUILTIN SIDs (S-1-5-32-*) are not resolved by the '*' backend but by passdb group mappings (group_mapping.tdb). Only BUILTIN\Administrators (544), Users (545) and Guests (546) exist by default: smbd auto-creates them at the first SMB session (requires winbindd and 'winbind nested groups = yes', the default), taking the GID from the '*' backend's allocator (the same tdb HWM) and adding Domain Admins + root, Domain Users, and Guests as alias members; any other BUILTIN alias (e.g. 551 Backup Operators, 555 Remote Desktop Users) stays unmapped until an administrator creates a mapping. Consequently two SVMs joined to the same domain will in general assign different GIDs to the same BUILTIN or well-known SID. 'net idmap set mapping' cannot pre-seed anything: in 4.22 it is a stub that prints "Not implemented yet". Pre-seeding is done with 'net idmap restore [--db=<file>]' (lines 'GID <id> <SID>' / 'UID <id> <SID>' plus 'USER HWM <n>' / 'GROUP HWM <n>', written directly into winbindd_idmap.tdb) for well-known SIDs, optionally frozen with 'idmap config * : read only = yes', and with 'net groupmap add sid=S-1-5-32-544 unixgroup=<local group> type=local' plus 'net sam addmem' for BUILTIN aliases; seeding winbindd_idmap.tdb alone does not make BUILTIN GIDs consistent.
- Design impact: 1) Keep 'idmap config DOMAIN : backend = rid' with explicit ranges and a disjoint allocating '*' domain (tdb); never rid or ad for '*'. 2) Split the Raft-seeded identity table into two artifacts per SVM, both applied before winbindd/smbd first start and on every rehost: (a) a 'net idmap restore' file for winbindd_idmap.tdb containing the fixed GID/UID lines for the well-known SIDs the ACL policy will see (S-1-1-0, S-1-5-11, S-1-5-2, S-1-3-0..3, S-1-5-7, S-1-5-9, S-1-5-18 ...) with 'USER HWM'/'GROUP HWM' set above every seeded ID (the tdb allocator uses TDB_INSERT, so a later allocation that collides with a seeded ID fails), then optionally 'idmap config * : read only = yes' to stop further growth (note: read-only does not block allocate_id, which is what BUILTIN alias creation uses); (b) local Unix groups with the Raft-assigned GIDs and 'net groupmap add sid=S-1-5-32-{544,545,546,...} unixgroup=<group> type=local' for every BUILTIN alias the design references, followed by 'net sam addmem' to reproduce the memberships smbd would have added (Domain Admins and root into Administrators, Domain Users into Users, Guests into Guests), because a pre-existing alias skips smbd's auto-creation and its membership setup; without the memberships Domain Admins lose BUILTIN\Administrators (and SeDiskOperatorPrivilege by default) on that SVM. 3) Rewrite the 'one SID maps to one uid across SVMs' rule: it is a property of rid for domain RIDs only; for BUILTIN it depends on seeded group mappings, and for well-known SIDs on the seeded idmap tdb; audit rehost/backup/Phase 3 ACL projection against both files, not just winbindd_idmap.tdb. 4) Replace every mention of 'net idmap set mapping' with 'net idmap restore' (idmap tdb) and 'net groupmap add'/'net sam addmem' (BUILTIN). 5) Note that NT ACL blobs stored by vfs_acl_xattr carry SIDs, so SMB access checks survive rehost regardless; what diverges is the uid/gid projection (POSIX/NFSv4 ACLs, host-side backup, knfsd exports), which is what the seeding protects. 6) If autorid is considered for '*', document that it preallocates a fixed list of non-BUILTIN well-known SIDs at first start but BUILTIN alias GIDs still come from its allocation pool in first-need order, so it does not remove the need for (b).

### [C34] CONFIRMED
- Claim: In Samba 4.22 the durable-handle state lives in smbXsrv_open_global.tdb under 'lock directory' and is cleared when the first smbd process starts, so durable handles survive a client TCP reconnect to a running smbd but never survive an smbd restart or a move to a freshly started smbd on another node; smb.conf(5) also states that 'winbindd socket directory' is not honoured by client tools such as nss_winbind, which must be given WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR, that 'machine password timeout' defaults to 604800 seconds, and that 'kernel oplocks' and 'kernel share modes' default to no.
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Protocols
- Why it matters: Every planned SVM move and every svm stop/start restarts smbd, so the SMB column of the non-disruptive matrix must say 'open handles lost' and the 10 s LIF-blip durable-handle exit test is valid only without an smbd restart; the per-SVM private /run via a mount namespace and the secrets.tdb rotation window depend on the smb.conf defaults.
- Summary: Every factual element of C34 checks out against the Samba v4-22-stable source and its docs-xml (the source of smb.conf(5)): smbXsrv_open_global.tdb is opened via lock_path() with SMBD_VOLATILE_TDB_FLAGS, which includes TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST ("If this is the first open, wipe the db"), and the smbd parent opens it in main() before forking any client child. Durable reconnect additionally needs the disconnected share-mode entry in locking.tdb, which is opened with the same volatile flags under the same lock directory, so handles cannot outlive a full smbd restart or follow an SVM to another node. The four smb.conf(5) statements (winbindd socket directory / WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR, machine password timeout = 604800, kernel oplocks = no, kernel share modes = no) are quoted verbatim from the 4.22 parameter definitions; the only refinements are the precise wipe condition (first opener while no other process holds the file open), the durable-timeout window and the grant preconditions, which do not contradict the claim.
- Evidence: 1. Location and flags of the durable-handle state (Samba v4-22-stable):
- source3/smbd/smbXsrv_open.c, smbXsrv_open_global_init(): opens "smbXsrv_open_global.tdb" via lock_path(talloc_tos(), ...) with SMBD_VOLATILE_TDB_HASH_SIZE / SMBD_VOLATILE_TDB_FLAGS, O_RDWR|O_CREAT, 0600, DBWRAP_LOCK_ORDER_1. The function itself contains no explicit wipe call; the wipe comes from the flags. The durable cookie is stored in the global record: smbXsrv_open_close_fn keeps the record "if (global->durable)" ("Durable open -- we need to update the global part"); smb2srv_open_recreate_fn rejects a reconnect "if (!global->durable)" (logs "not durable") and then rewrites global->server_id for the new process.
- source3/lib/util_path.c: "char *lock_path(TALLOC_CTX *mem_ctx, const char *name) { return xx_path(mem_ctx, name, lp_lock_directory()); }" -- i.e. the smb.conf 'lock directory'.
- source3/include/local.h: "/* tdb flags for the databases having one entry per open file. */ #define SMBD_VOLATILE_TDB_FLAGS (TDB_DEFAULT|TDB_VOLATILE|TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST|TDB_INCOMPATIBLE_HASH)".
- lib/tdb/include/tdb.h: "#define TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST 1 /** If this is the first open, wipe the db */".
- lib/tdb/common/open.c, tdb_open_ex: "/* we need to zero database if we are the only one with it open */" -- it probes an exclusive ACTIVE_LOCK with "tdb_nest_lock(tdb, ACTIVE_LOCK, F_WRLCK, TDB_LOCK_NOWAIT|TDB_LOCK_PROBE)"; if obtained it calls tdb_new_database() which does "ftruncate(tdb->fd, 0)"; every CLEAR_IF_FIRST opener then holds a shared ACTIVE_LOCK "as we need to let all other users know we're using it". So the wipe happens on the first open by any process while no other process has the file open.
- source3/lib/dbwrap/dbwrap_open.c, db_open(): TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST is only tested ("if (tdb_flags & TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST)") to enable readonly optimisation and robust-mutex locking ("tdb_flags |= TDB_MUTEX_LOCKING"); it is never removed on the local (non-CTDB) path. Only "if (lp_clustering())" is the database handed to db_open_ctdb().
- source3/smbd/server.c, main(): "/* Setup all the TDB's - including CLEAR_IF_FIRST tdb's. */" precedes smbXsrv_version_global_init, smbXsrv_session_global_init, smbXsrv_tcon_global_init and "status = smbXsrv_open_global_init(); if (!NT_STATUS_IS_OK(status)) { exit_daemon("Samba cannot init global open", ...); }" -- all in the parent before open_sockets_smbd()/smbd_parent_loop(); client children are forked later in smbd_accept_connection(). Hence the parent is the first opener at startup and the file is wiped then.
- source3/locking/share_mode_lock.c, locking_init_internal(): "db_path = lock_path(talloc_tos(), "locking.tdb");" opened with "SMBD_VOLATILE_TDB_FLAGS | TDB_SEQNUM". source3/smbd/durable.c, vfs_default_durable_reconnect: the reconnect searches the share-mode entries for one where server_id_is_disconnected(&e->pid) and "e.share_file_id != state->op->global->open_persistent_id" is false, otherwise "NT_STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND". Both databases needed for a reconnect are therefore node-local, under lock directory, and wiped on first open.
- docs-xml/smbdotconf/misc/lockdirectory.xml (4.22): "The files placed in this directory are not required across service restarts and can be safely placed on volatile storage (e.g. tmpfs in Linux)"; default "&pathconfig.LOCKDIR;". Debian debian/rules (2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1): "--with-lockdir=/run/samba", "--with-piddir=/run/samba", "--with-sockets-dir=/run/samba", "--with-statedir=/var/lib/samba", "--with-cachedir=/var/cache/samba", "--with-privatedir=/var/lib/samba/private".

2. Durable-handle window and preconditions (conditions, not contradictions):
- source3/smbd/smb2_create.c: v1 (DHnQ): "/* Set the timeout to 16 mins. ... */ state->durable_timeout_msec = (16*60*1000);"; v2 (DH2Q): "state->durable_timeout_msec = MIN(durable_v2_timeout, 300*1000); if (state->durable_timeout_msec == 0) { /* Set the timeout to 1 min as default. This matches Windows 2012. */ state->durable_timeout_msec = (60*1000); }". Durability is granted only "if (!state->replay_operation && state->durable_requested && (fsp_lease_type(state->result) & SMB2_LEASE_HANDLE))" and the VFS cookie is non-empty, then "state->op->global->durable = true".
- source3/smbd/durable.c, vfs_default_durable_cookie returns NT_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED if "!lp_durable_handles(SNUM(conn))", if "lp_kernel_share_modes(SNUM(conn))", if "lp_kernel_oplocks(SNUM(conn))", if "(fsp->current_lock_count > 0) && lp_posix_locking(fsp->conn->params)" ("if the handle has posix locks"), for directories, alternate data streams and fake files.
- smbXsrv_open_cleanup_fn deletes disconnected records once disconnect_time + durable_timeout_msec has passed, and connected records whose owner fails serverid_exists().
- docs-xml/smbdotconf/protocol/durablehandles.xml (4.22): default yes; durable handles only take effect with kernel oplocks, kernel share modes and POSIX locking disabled (the man-page wording is stricter than the code, which only rejects handles that actually hold POSIX byte-range locks).

3. smb.conf(5) statements (Samba 4.22 docs-xml, from which the man page is generated):
- winbind/winbinddsocketdirectory.xml: "This setting controls the location of the winbind daemon's socket." "Except within automated test scripts, this should not be altered, as the client tools (nss_winbind etc) do not honour this parameter. Client tools must then be advised of the altered path with the WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR environment variable." Default "&pathconfig.WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR;"; dynconfig/wscript: WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR 'STD-PATH'/'FHS-PATH' = '${SOCKET_DIR}/winbindd', SOCKET_DIR option '--with-sockets-dir' (Debian: /run/samba).
- domain/machinepasswordtimeout.xml: "This parameter specifies how often this password will be changed, in seconds." "The default is one week (expressed in seconds), the same as a Windows NT Domain member server." "<value type="default">604800</value>".
- locking/kerneloplocks.xml: "<value type="default">no</value>" (share-level, Linux only; disabling gives Level II oplocks).
- locking/kernelsharemodes.xml: "Note that in order to use SMB2 durable file handles on a share, you have to turn kernel share modes off." Default "no".
- The samba.org 'current' smb.conf.5.html (first 100k chars) adds: "Usually, most of the TDB files are stored in the lock directory."

4. Debian version: sources.debian.org lists "2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1" under trixie and packages.debian.org/trixie/samba shows "Package: samba (2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1)"; its debian/changelog entry is "samba (2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1) trixie; urgency=medium ... -- Michael Tokarev ... Tue, 28 Jul 2026". The tracker page as fetched still showed stable = 2:4.22.10+dfsg-0+deb13u1 and stable-security = 2:4.22.10+dfsg-0+deb13u2, with news "[2026-09-04] Accepted samba 2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1 (source) into proposed-updates"; either way trixie ships 4.22.x and the code paths above are on the v4-22-stable branch.
- Corrected claim: In Samba 4.22 (Debian trixie 2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1) the SMB2 durable-handle state is the open's global record, including the VFS backend cookie, in smbXsrv_open_global.tdb, opened via lock_path() under 'lock directory' (Debian: /run/samba, tmpfs) with SMBD_VOLATILE_TDB_FLAGS = TDB_DEFAULT|TDB_VOLATILE|TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST|TDB_INCOMPATIBLE_HASH; a durable reconnect also needs the disconnected share-mode entry in locking.tdb, opened the same way. TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST wipes the file on the first open by a process while no other process holds it open, and the smbd parent opens both databases in main() before forking any client child, so a (complete) smbd restart, i.e. one where all previous smbd processes have exited, starts with empty tables. Consequently a durable handle survives a client TCP reconnect to the same running smbd only within its durable timeout (v1: 16 min; v2: client value clamped to 300 s, 60 s if the client asks for 0) and only if it was granted durability at open (durable handles = yes, a handle lease (SMB2_LEASE_HANDLE), kernel share modes = no, kernel oplocks = no, no POSIX byte-range locks held when posix locking = yes, not a directory, stream or fake file); it never survives an smbd restart or a move to a freshly started smbd on another node (non-CTDB deployment). smb.conf(5) states that 'winbindd socket directory' should not be altered except in automated tests "as the client tools (nss_winbind etc) do not honour this parameter" and "must then be advised of the altered path with the WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR environment variable" (default: build-time ${SOCKET_DIR}/winbindd, i.e. /run/samba/winbindd on Debian); 'machine password timeout' defaults to 604800 (one week); 'kernel oplocks' and 'kernel share modes' both default to no.
- Design impact: No contradiction, so the planned matrix entries stand: every planned SVM move and every svm stop/start restarts smbd, so the SMB column of the non-disruptive matrix must read "open handles lost (durable handles do not survive smbd restart)", and the only non-disruptive SMB case is a LIF blip with the same smbd processes left running. Refine the 10 s LIF-blip durable-handle exit test accordingly: (a) it is valid only when no smbd process is restarted and the blip is shorter than the negotiated durable timeout (10 s is inside the 60 s v2 default and the 300 s cap); (b) the test share must keep the defaults kernel oplocks = no, kernel share modes = no, durable handles = yes, and the test client must open with a handle lease (RWH/RH) because a handle without SMB2_LEASE_HANDLE is never durable; (c) with the default posix locking = yes a handle holding a byte-range lock is not durable, so test both a lock-free handle (must survive) and a locked handle (expected to be re-opened by the client, not a design failure), or set posix locking = no on SMB-only shares and document the loss of NFS/local lock interoperability. Make the SVM stop sequence kill the whole smbd cgroup (systemd default KillMode) so that the TDB_CLEAR_IF_FIRST wipe is deterministic; a lingering old child would keep the tables alive and make reconnect behaviour unpredictable. The per-SVM private /run via a mount namespace is consistent with the defaults: Debian compiles lock dir, pid dir and sockets dir to /run/samba, and the winbindd socket to /run/samba/winbindd, so a private /run gives each SVM its own volatile TDBs and winbind socket without touching 'winbindd socket directory'; if the design ever sets that parameter instead, nss_winbind/pam_winbind in that SVM must be started with WINBINDD_SOCKET_DIR. The secrets.tdb rotation window can be sized on the 604800 s default (secrets.tdb lives in the private dir /var/lib/samba/private, not the lock dir, so it is unaffected by the per-SVM /run). If CTDB clustering were ever adopted the volatile databases would be CTDB-managed and this analysis would have to be redone.
