### [C35] CONFIRMED
- Claim: In Linux 6.12, drivers/scsi/sd.c sd_read_block_limits parses VPD page B0 bytes 6-7 (OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH GRANULARITY) into min_xfer_blocks and bytes 12-15 (OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH) into opt_xfer_blocks, validates them (sd_validate_min_xfer_size / sd_validate_opt_xfer_size) before setting io_min and io_opt, and drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c exposes the raw page as the read-only binary attribute vpd_pgb0 beside vpd_pg83, vpd_pgb1, vpd_pgb2 and vpd_pgb7.
- Raised by: Opus-Storage
- Why it matters: Geometry discovery on hardware RAID reads io_min/io_opt from sysfs and the raw B0 page as a second opinion before falling back to the write-amplification probe or a manual override.
- Summary: Every element of the claim matches the Linux v6.12 source: sd_read_block_limits() reads VPD B0 bytes 6-7 (be16) into min_xfer_blocks and bytes 12-15 (be32) into opt_xfer_blocks, sd_revalidate_disk() gates lim.io_min/lim.io_opt on sd_validate_min_xfer_size()/sd_validate_opt_xfer_size(), and scsi_sysfs.c exposes vpd_pgb0 as a read-only (S_IRUGO, read-only handler) binary attribute next to vpd_pg0/pg80/pg83/pg89/pgb1/pgb2/pgb7. Debian trixie ships linux 6.12.107-1 and its copies of these paths are identical to v6.12. The design should note three conditions that do not contradict the claim: io_opt is seeded from the HBA's host->opt_sectors and VPD can only lower it; the block layer floors io_min at physical_block_size, so sysfs cannot distinguish "no granularity reported" from "granularity equals physical block"; and vpd_pgb0 is a cached snapshot (full page incl. 4-byte header, stat size 0) that is absent when the device does not advertise page B0.
- Evidence: 1. Parsing (drivers/scsi/sd.c, v6.12 tag, lines 3335-3382): "vpd = rcu_dereference(sdkp->device->vpd_pgb0); if (!vpd || vpd->len < 16) goto out; sdkp->min_xfer_blocks = get_unaligned_be16(&vpd->data[6]); sdkp->max_xfer_blocks = get_unaligned_be32(&vpd->data[8]); sdkp->opt_xfer_blocks = get_unaligned_be32(&vpd->data[12]);". Offsets are from byte 0 of the page including the 4-byte header (scsi.c scsi_vpd_inquiry: "result = get_unaligned_be16(&buffer[2]); ... return result + 4;" and scsi_get_vpd_buf: "vpd_buf->len = result;"), so data[6..7] and data[12..15] are page bytes 6-7 and 12-15. sd.h lines 111-113 declare "u32 min_xfer_blocks; u32 max_xfer_blocks; u32 opt_xfer_blocks;".

2. Validation before io_min/io_opt (sd.c sd_revalidate_disk, lines 3784-3798): "if (sd_validate_min_xfer_size(sdkp)) lim.io_min = logical_to_bytes(sdp, sdkp->min_xfer_blocks); else lim.io_min = 0;" then "lim.io_opt = sdp->host->opt_sectors << SECTOR_SHIFT; if (sd_validate_opt_xfer_size(sdkp, dev_max)) { lim.io_opt = min_not_zero(lim.io_opt, logical_to_bytes(sdp, sdkp->opt_xfer_blocks)); }" followed by queue_limits_commit_update(). sd_validate_min_xfer_size (3582-3603) returns false if min_xfer_blocks == 0 or "min_xfer_bytes & (sdkp->physical_block_size - 1)" (warning "Preferred minimum I/O size %u bytes not a multiple of physical block size", and it zeroes min_xfer_blocks). sd_validate_opt_xfer_size (3610-3666) returns false if opt_xfer_blocks == 0, "> dev_max", "> SD_DEF_XFER_BLOCKS", "opt_xfer_bytes < PAGE_SIZE", "opt_xfer_bytes % min_xfer_bytes" (when min nonzero), or "opt_xfer_bytes & (sdkp->physical_block_size - 1)"; each case logs once via sd_first_printk(KERN_WARNING ...). sd_read_block_limits() is called at line 3752 only inside "if (sdkp->media_present)" and "if (scsi_device_supports_vpd(sdp))".

3. Sysfs attribute (drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c, lines 898-930): macro "#define sdev_vpd_pg_attr(_page)" generates "show_vpd_##_page(...)" that does "vpd_page = rcu_dereference(sdev->vpd_##_page); if (vpd_page) ret = memory_read_from_buffer(buf, count, &off, vpd_page->data, vpd_page->len);" and "static struct bin_attribute dev_attr_vpd_##_page = { .attr = {.name = __stringify(vpd_##_page), .mode = S_IRUGO }, .size = 0, .read = show_vpd_##_page, };" (no .write). Invocations: "sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pg83); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pg80); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pg89); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pgb0); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pgb1); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pgb2); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pgb7); sdev_vpd_pg_attr(pg0);". Array scsi_sdev_bin_attrs[] (1351-1362) lists &dev_attr_vpd_pg0, _pg83, _pg80, _pg89, _pgb0, _pgb1, _pgb2, _pgb7, &dev_attr_inquiry. scsi_sdev_bin_attr_is_visible (1276-1308): "if (attr == &dev_attr_vpd_pgb0 && !sdev->vpd_pgb0) return 0; ... return S_IRUGO;". The group is attached through "static const struct device_type scsi_dev_type = { .name = "scsi_device", ... .groups = scsi_sdev_attr_groups }" on sdev_gendev named "%d:%d:%d:%llu", i.e. /sys/bus/scsi/devices/H:C:T:L/vpd_pgb0 (= /sys/block/sdX/device/vpd_pgb0).

4. Population of the cached page (drivers/scsi/scsi.c scsi_attach_vpd, 499-531): "if (!scsi_device_supports_vpd(sdev)) return;" then it walks VPD page 00h and "if (vpd_buf->data[i] == 0xb0) scsi_update_vpd_page(sdev, 0xb0, &sdev->vpd_pgb0);". include/scsi/scsi_device.h 665-680: scsi_device_supports_vpd() returns 1 if "sdev->try_vpd_pages" or "sdev->scsi_level >= SCSI_SPC_2 && !sdev->skip_vpd_pages". scsi_get_vpd_size returns SCSI_DEFAULT_VPD_LEN when "sdev->no_vpd_size".

5. Block layer and sysfs export: block/blk-settings.c blk_validate_limits (249-250): "if (lim->io_min < lim->physical_block_size) lim->io_min = lim->physical_block_size;" (no rounding of io_opt in blk_validate_limits; only blk_stack_limits zeroes a misaligned io_opt, 594-595). block/blk-sysfs.c: "QUEUE_RO_ENTRY(queue_io_min, "minimum_io_size"); QUEUE_RO_ENTRY(queue_io_opt, "optimal_io_size");". Documentation/ABI/stable/sysfs-block: minimum_io_size "[RO] ... For RAID arrays it is often the stripe chunk size"; optimal_io_size "[RO] ... For RAID arrays it is usually the stripe width or the internal track size ... If no optimal I/O size is reported this file contains 0."

6. SBC field names/positions (SBC-4 text itself not readable here; the T10 proposal 03-028r2 "SPC-3 SBC-2 Block Limits VPD page", Rob Elliott, 2003-01-20, fetched but only its metadata could be decoded). Triangulated instead by: FreeBSD sys/cam/scsi/scsi_all.h struct scsi_vpd_block_limits with "#define SVPD_BLOCK_LIMITS 0xB0": device (0), page_code (1), page_length[2] (2-3), flags (4), max_cmp_write_len (5), opt_txfer_len_grain[2] (6-7), max_txfer_len[4] (8-11), opt_txfer_len[4] (12-15), max_prefetch[4] (16-19); sg3_utils sg_vpd_common.c decoder: "u = sg_get_unaligned_be16(buff + 6);" labelled "Optimal transfer length granularity", "sg_get_unaligned_be32(buff + 8)" "Maximum transfer length", "sg_get_unaligned_be32(buff + 12)" "Optimal transfer length", and "if (len < 16)" short-page check; in-tree drivers/scsi/scsi_debug.c inquiry_vpd_b0() writes the body at &arr[4] ("arr[3] = inquiry_vpd_b0(&arr[4]);") with "/* Optimal transfer length granularity */ put_unaligned_be16(gran, arr + 2);" and "/* Optimal Transfer Length */ put_unaligned_be32(sdebug_opt_blks, &arr[8]);" = page bytes 6-7 and 12-15. Red Hat Storage Administration Guide: "The BLOCK LIMITS VPD page (0xb0) provides the I/O hints. It also uses OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH GRANULARITY and OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH to derive: /sys/block/disk/queue/minimum_io_size /sys/block/disk/queue/optimal_io_size".

7. Debian trixie: sources.debian.org API for linux/trixie reports version "6.12.107-1" with suites ["forky","sid","trixie"]; tracker.debian.org/pkg/linux shows stable "6.12.94-1" (security "6.12.111-1"). diff of the 6.12.107-1 sd.c against v6.12 shows no change in sd_read_block_limits or the two validators; sd_revalidate_disk only switched to a heap-allocated "struct queue_limits *lim" with the same io_min/io_opt logic ("lim->io_min = logical_to_bytes(sdp, sdkp->min_xfer_blocks);" ... "lim->io_opt = min_not_zero(lim->io_opt, ..."); scsi_sysfs.c differs only in two unrelated shost DEVICE_ATTR modes. sg3-utils in trixie is 1.48-3~deb13u1; sg_vpd man page lists "bl 0xb0 Block limits (SBC)" and "--raw ... output requested VPD page in binary".
- Corrected claim: In Linux 6.12 (including Debian trixie's linux 6.12.107-1, whose code on these paths is identical), drivers/scsi/sd.c sd_read_block_limits() takes the kernel's cached copy of the Block Limits VPD page (sdev->vpd_pgb0), requires vpd->len >= 16, and reads page bytes 6-7 (big-endian 16-bit OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH GRANULARITY) into sdkp->min_xfer_blocks, bytes 8-11 (MAXIMUM TRANSFER LENGTH) into max_xfer_blocks and bytes 12-15 (big-endian 32-bit OPTIMAL TRANSFER LENGTH) into opt_xfer_blocks, all in logical blocks and with offsets counted from byte 0 of the page including its 4-byte header. sd_revalidate_disk() then sets lim.io_min = min_xfer_blocks in bytes only if sd_validate_min_xfer_size() passes (non-zero and a multiple of the physical block size; otherwise io_min = 0, which the block layer's blk_validate_limits() floors to physical_block_size), and seeds lim.io_opt from the HBA's host->opt_sectors and lowers it to opt_xfer_blocks in bytes only if sd_validate_opt_xfer_size() passes (non-zero, <= dev_max, <= SD_DEF_XFER_BLOCKS, >= PAGE_SIZE, a multiple of the minimum size when one is set, and a multiple of the physical block size); rejected values are logged once as sd_first_printk warnings and optimal_io_size then reads 0 unless the HBA set opt_sectors. The results are exported read-only as /sys/block/<disk>/queue/minimum_io_size and optimal_io_size. drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c defines, via sdev_vpd_pg_attr(), read-only (S_IRUGO, read handler only, .size = 0) binary attributes vpd_pg0, vpd_pg80, vpd_pg83, vpd_pg89, vpd_pgb0, vpd_pgb1, vpd_pgb2 and vpd_pgb7 (plus inquiry) on the scsi_device, i.e. /sys/bus/scsi/devices/H:C:T:L/vpd_pgb0 = /sys/block/sdX/device/vpd_pgb0; each returns the raw cached page including its 4-byte header (length = PAGE LENGTH + 4) exactly as scsi_attach_vpd() fetched it at scan time, and the file is hidden when the device does not advertise that page in VPD page 00h or scsi_device_supports_vpd() is false (needs SPC-2+ and no skip_vpd_pages, or try_vpd_pages).
- Design impact: No change to the mechanism: reading queue/minimum_io_size and queue/optimal_io_size and the raw vpd_pgb0 page is a valid two-source geometry probe on 6.12/trixie. Tighten the discovery logic as follows. (1) Treat vpd_pgb0 as optional: it is absent (not empty) when the VD does not advertise page B0 or VPD is disabled for the device; fall through to the write-amplification probe or manual override. (2) Do not trust stat() size on vpd_pgb0 (the bin attribute declares .size = 0); read to EOF, then check data[1] == 0xB0 and total length = be16(data[2..3]) + 4 >= 16 before parsing OTLG = be16(data[6..7]), MTL = be32(data[8..11]), OTL = be32(data[12..15]); multiply by queue/logical_block_size to get bytes. (3) Interpret sysfs values with the kernel's rules in mind: minimum_io_size equal to physical_block_size can mean either a reported granularity of one physical block or no/invalid B0 granularity (block layer floor), and optimal_io_size = 0 can mean OTL = 0 or an OTL that sd rejected (below PAGE_SIZE, above dev_max or 65535 blocks, or not a multiple of the minimum size or physical block size); a non-zero optimal_io_size that differs from OTL in bytes indicates the HBA's opt_sectors won the min_not_zero, so prefer the raw OTL as the array's stripe hint and record the discrepancy. (4) Surface the once-per-device dmesg warnings ("Optimal transfer size ... not a multiple of ...", "Preferred minimum I/O size ... not a multiple of physical block size") in diagnostics, since they are the only kernel signal that B0 was rejected. (5) The sysfs page is a cached snapshot populated by scsi_attach_vpd() at scan, not a live INQUIRY; re-scan the device before re-reading after a VD is reconfigured on the controller. (6) Per the kernel ABI doc the mapping is minimum_io_size ~ stripe chunk and optimal_io_size ~ stripe width for RAID arrays; use that as the interpretation and still confirm with the write-amplification probe, because the standard only hints and controllers frequently report 0. (7) sg_vpd -p bl --raw/--hex (sg3-utils 1.48 in trixie) is an equivalent tooling cross-check that issues a fresh INQUIRY, useful when the cached page is suspect.
- Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/sd.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/sd.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/scsi.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/scsi/scsi_device.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/block/blk-settings.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/block/blk-sysfs.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/Documentation/ABI/stable/sysfs-block ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/scsi_debug.c ; https://sources.debian.org/api/src/linux/trixie/drivers/scsi/sd.c/ ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/l/linux/6.12.107-1/drivers/scsi/sd.c ; https://sources.debian.org/data/main/l/linux/6.12.107-1/drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c ; https://tracker.debian.org/pkg/linux ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hreinecke/sg3_utils/master/src/sg_vpd_common.c ; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/sg3-utils/sg_vpd.8.en.html ; https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/6/html/storage_administration_guide/iolimstandards ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/main/sys/cam/scsi/scsi_all.h ; https://www.t10.org/ftp/t10/document.03/03-028r2.pdf

### [C36] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: Per Linux 6.12 Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst and net/ipv4/devinet.c / net/ipv6/addrconf.c, arp_notify=1 and ndisc_notify=1 generate gratuitous ARP requests or unsolicited neighbour advertisements only when the device is brought up or its hardware address changes, not when an IP address is added to an already-up interface.
- Raised by: Opus-Consensus
- Why it matters: The LIF failover design has nbladed send gratuitous ARP itself (AF_PACKET sender, with iputils-arping 3:20240905-3 -U/-A as fallback); if the kernel announced address adds, that component would be unnecessary.
- Summary: The IPv4 half is confirmed from the 6.12 source: arp_notify only acts inside inetdev_event on the netdev notifier (NETDEV_UP / NETDEV_CHANGEADDR), and `ip addr add` (inet_rtm_newaddr -> __inet_insert_ifa) transmits no ARP, so the kernel never announces an IPv4 address added to an up interface. The IPv6 half is wrong: since v4.16 (commit c76fe2d98c72), with ndisc_notify=1 on the device or on `all`, addrconf_dad_completed() in net/ipv6/addrconf.c sends one unsolicited NA (to ff02::1, override=1) for every newly configured tentative, non-optimistic address when its DAD completes, which includes addresses added to an already-up interface; the ip-sysctl.rst wording is incomplete on this. Exceptions: addresses added with `nodad` (never flagged TENTATIVE) and optimistic addresses get no NA; the kernel sends the NA exactly once, after DAD (or immediately if accept_dad=0 / IFF_NOARP). Also, the ndisc_send_unsol_na callers are in net/ipv6/ndisc.c (ndisc_netdev_event), not addrconf.c.
- Evidence: Note on sources: git.kernel.org plain views returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher and the elixir.bootlin.com page was truncated by its version selector, so the v6.12 tag was read from Linus's GitHub mirror (torvalds/linux at tag v6.12, identical tree). Nothing was installed, built or run.

1) Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst (v6.12): "arp_notify - BOOLEAN / Define mode for notification of address and device changes. / 0 (default): do nothing / 1 Generate gratuitous arp requests when device is brought up or hardware address changes." and "ndisc_notify - BOOLEAN / Define mode for notification of address and device changes. / 0 - (default): do nothing / 1 - Generate unsolicited neighbour advertisements when device is brought up or hardware address changes." Also: "dad_transmits - INTEGER / The amount of Duplicate Address Detection probes to send. / Default: 1"; "accept_dad ... 0 Disable DAD / 1 Enable DAD (default)".

2) net/ipv4/devinet.c (v6.12), inetdev_event(): "case NETDEV_UP: ... ip_mc_up(in_dev); fallthrough; case NETDEV_CHANGEADDR: if (!IN_DEV_ARP_NOTIFY(in_dev)) break; fallthrough; case NETDEV_NOTIFY_PEERS: /* Send gratuitous ARP to notify of link change */ inetdev_send_gratuitous_arp(dev, in_dev); break;". inetdev_send_gratuitous_arp() loops in_dev_for_each_ifa_rtnl() and calls "arp_send(ARPOP_REQUEST, ETH_P_ARP, ifa->ifa_local, dev, ifa->ifa_local, NULL, dev->dev_addr, NULL)" (a GARP request per address). These are the only ARP-transmitting lines in the file; inet_rtm_newaddr/__inet_insert_ifa contain no arp_send/call_netdevice_notifiers. __inet_insert_ifa ends with "rtmsg_ifa(RTM_NEWADDR, ifa, nlh, portid); blocking_notifier_call_chain(&inetaddr_chain, NETDEV_UP, ifa);" which is the inetaddr chain, whereas inetdev_event is registered on the netdev chain: "static struct notifier_block ip_netdev_notifier = { .notifier_call = inetdev_event, };" ... "register_netdevice_notifier(&ip_netdev_notifier);". include/linux/inetdevice.h: "#define IN_DEV_ARP_NOTIFY(in_dev) IN_DEV_MAXCONF((in_dev), ARP_NOTIFY)" with IN_DEV_MAXCONF = max(all, per-device). => IPv4 part of the claim CONFIRMED.

3) net/ipv6/ndisc.c (v6.12), ndisc_netdev_event(): NETDEV_CHANGEADDR -> neigh_changeaddr(); fib6_run_gc(); fallthrough -> NETDEV_UP: "if (READ_ONCE(idev->cnf.ndisc_notify) || READ_ONCE(net->ipv6.devconf_all->ndisc_notify)) ndisc_send_unsol_na(dev);"; NETDEV_NOTIFY_PEERS: ndisc_send_unsol_na(dev) unconditionally. ndisc_send_unsol_na(): "/* skip tentative addresses until dad completes */ if (ifa->flags & IFA_F_TENTATIVE && !(ifa->flags & IFA_F_OPTIMISTIC)) continue;". These two call sites in ndisc.c are the only callers of ndisc_send_unsol_na; addrconf.c has none.

4) net/ipv6/addrconf.c (v6.12), addrconf_dad_completed(): "/* send unsolicited NA if enabled */ if (send_na && (READ_ONCE(ifp->idev->cnf.ndisc_notify) || READ_ONCE(dev_net(dev)->ipv6.devconf_all->ndisc_notify))) { ndisc_send_na(dev, &in6addr_linklocal_allnodes, &ifp->addr, ... /*solicited=*/ false, /*override=*/ true, ...". send_na is set in addrconf_dad_work() ("if (ifp->dad_probes == 0) { bool send_na = false; ... if (ifp->flags & IFA_F_TENTATIVE && !(ifp->flags & IFA_F_OPTIMISTIC)) send_na = true; ... addrconf_dad_completed(ifp, bump_id, send_na);") and identically in the DAD-skip branch of addrconf_dad_begin() ("if (dev->flags&(IFF_NOARP|IFF_LOOPBACK) || (accept_dad < 1 ...) || !(ifp->flags&IFA_F_TENTATIVE) || ifp->flags & IFA_F_NODAD) { ... send_na = true; ... addrconf_dad_completed(ifp, bump_id, send_na);"). The add path is inet6_addr_add(): "ifp = ipv6_add_addr(idev, cfg, true, extack); ... addrconf_dad_start(ifp);" with no IFF_UP test; ipv6_add_addr(): "/* No need to add the TENTATIVE flag for addresses with NODAD */ if (!(cfg->ifa_flags & IFA_F_NODAD)) ifa->flags |= IFA_F_TENTATIVE;" (so `nodad` addresses have send_na == false and get no NA). addrconf_dad_kick(): "ifp->dad_probes = READ_ONCE(idev->cnf.dad_transmits);" with an initial random delay bounded by rtr_solicit_delay, and addrconf_dad_work re-arms with "max(NEIGH_VAR(ifp->idev->nd_parms, RETRANS_TIME), HZ/100)" between probes, so with defaults the NA follows roughly 1-2 s after `ip -6 addr add`. => IPv6 part of the claim REFUTED: ndisc_notify=1 does announce an address added to an up interface, once DAD completes.

5) Upstream commit c76fe2d98c726224a975a0d0198c3fb50406d325, David Ahern, "net: ipv6: send unsolicited NA after DAD" (v4.16-rc1; 4.15-stable backport posted Fri Feb 09 2018): "Unsolicited IPv6 neighbor advertisements should be sent after DAD completes. Update ndisc_send_unsol_na to skip tentative, non-optimistic addresses and have those sent by addrconf_dad_completed after DAD." Fixes 4a6e3c5 ("net: ipv6: send unsolicited NA on admin up").

6) Fallback tool: packages.debian.org/trixie lists iputils-arping version "3:20240905-3". arping(8) (trixie): "-U Unsolicited ARP mode to update neighbours' ARP caches. No replies are expected."; "-A The same as -U, but ARP REPLY packets used instead of ARP REQUEST." In -U/-A mode the source address is set to the destination.

7) RFC 4861 §7.2.6: "a node MAY send up to MAX_NEIGHBOR_ADVERTISEMENT unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement messages ... These advertisements MUST be separated by at least RetransTimer seconds." and "they should only be viewed as a performance optimization"; §10: MAX_NEIGHBOR_ADVERTISEMENT = 3 transmissions. The kernel's post-DAD NA is a single transmission.
- Corrected claim: In Linux 6.12, IPv4 `arp_notify=1` (conf/{all,<dev>}/arp_notify, effective value is max() of the two) makes the kernel send gratuitous ARP requests for every address on a device only from the netdev notifier in net/ipv4/devinet.c inetdev_event(): on NETDEV_UP and NETDEV_CHANGEADDR (and unconditionally on the driver-raised NETDEV_NOTIFY_PEERS). Adding an IPv4 address to an already-up interface (RTM_NEWADDR / `ip addr add`, inet_rtm_newaddr -> __inet_insert_ifa) transmits no ARP at all, so an IPv4 LIF move must be announced by user space. For IPv6, `ndisc_notify=1` (conf/{all,<dev>}/ndisc_notify, OR-ed) triggers unsolicited NAs for all non-tentative addresses on NETDEV_UP/NETDEV_CHANGEADDR in net/ipv6/ndisc.c ndisc_netdev_event(), and additionally (not reflected in the ip-sysctl.rst text) net/ipv6/addrconf.c addrconf_dad_completed() sends exactly one unsolicited NA (dst ff02::1, override=1) for each newly configured address when its DAD completes, including addresses added to an already-up interface (since v4.16, commit c76fe2d98c72): roughly 1-2 s after `ip -6 addr add` with default dad_transmits=1, immediately if accept_dad=0 or the device is NOARP, but never for addresses added with `nodad` (not flagged TENTATIVE) or optimistic addresses. The kernel does not repeat the NA; RFC 4861 §7.2.6 allows up to MAX_NEIGHBOR_ADVERTISEMENT=3 transmissions at RetransTimer spacing.
- Design impact: Keep nbladed's own announcement component; it is still required for IPv4 and still useful for IPv6, but the rationale and the IPv6 wording must change. (1) IPv4: unchanged. arp_notify cannot announce a LIF add (only interface up / MAC change, and bouncing the interface would disturb every other LIF on it), so the AF_PACKET GARP sender with iputils-arping 3:20240905-3 `-U`/`-A` as fallback stays. (2) IPv6: set net.ipv6.conf.{all,<iface>}.ndisc_notify=1 on LIF-bearing interfaces and do NOT add LIF addresses with `nodad`, otherwise the kernel's one post-DAD NA is suppressed; alternatively, if `nodad` is chosen for faster takeover, nbladed must send the unsolicited NA itself. Either way nbladed should still send its own NAs because the kernel sends only one, only after DAD completes (~1-2 s with defaults, tunable via dad_transmits/accept_dad), and RFC 4861 treats unsolicited NAs as an unreliable optimization (up to 3 transmissions permitted). (3) Fix the source citation in the design: the ndisc_send_unsol_na callers live in net/ipv6/ndisc.c (ndisc_netdev_event), and the add-time behaviour comes from addrconf.c addrconf_dad_completed() -> ndisc_send_na(); note that ip-sysctl.rst's ndisc_notify text is incomplete. (4) Keep the suggested tcpdump acceptance test (ip addr add on an up interface with arp_notify=1 / ndisc_notify=1): expect no ARP for IPv4 and exactly one NA after DAD for IPv6; nothing was run here.
- Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/net/ipv4/devinet.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/include/linux/inetdevice.h ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/net/ipv6/ndisc.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/net/ipv6/addrconf.c ; https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/c76fe2d98c726224a975a0d0198c3fb50406d325 ; https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1802.1/01137.html ; https://packages.debian.org/trixie/iputils-arping ; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/iputils-arping/arping.8.en.html ; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4861.html

### [C37] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: open-vm-tools as packaged in Debian 13 trixie installs a udev rule that sets /sys/block/sd*/device/timeout to 180 s for VMware virtual disks, and the rule takes effect on a stock trixie guest kernel without manual steps (the default kernel SCSI disk timeout being 30 s).
- Raised by: Opus-Fabrics, Opus-Consensus
- Why it matters: The no-quorum 'stop' posture claims a 60 s hold is survived by every client class; Linux guests on ESXi survive 60 s only if their disk timeout is 180 s, and Launchpad bug 1790145 shows the rule silently failing on at least one Debian derivative.
- Summary: Trixie's open-vm-tools (2:12.5.0-2+deb13u1) does install /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/99-vmware-scsi-udev.rules, and the rule it ships is Debian's own patched form (ATTR{timeout}="180" on the scsi_device "add" event for vendor "VMware*", model "Virtual disk*"/"VMware Virtual S"), which is exactly the form Canonical verified as working in LP 1790145; the kernel default is SD_TIMEOUT = 30 s and trixie's systemd-udev-trigger.service replays "add" events at every boot, so no manual step is needed on a stock kernel at boot. Three conditions narrow the claim: it covers only SCSI-attached virtual disks (PVSCSI/LSI/BusLogic), not NVMe-controller disks (nvme_core io_timeout default 30 s) and almost certainly not SATA (libata reports vendor "ATA"); installing the package on an already-running VM does not apply it until reboot because the postinst's `udevadm trigger` uses the default "change" action while the rule matches only "add"; and LP 1790145 was an Ubuntu-only merge error (Ubuntu combined DEVTYPE=="disk" with ATTR{timeout}), fixed in 2018, that never affected Debian's rule. I verified by reading sources; no runtime observation on a trixie guest was possible here.
- Evidence: 1. Package contents (packages.debian.org, trixie/amd64 open-vm-tools file list): "/usr/lib/udev/rules.d/60-open-vm-tools.rules" and "/usr/lib/udev/rules.d/99-vmware-scsi-udev.rules". sources.debian.org lists trixie = 2:12.5.0-2+deb13u1 (bookworm 2:12.2.0-1+deb12u4, trixie-backports 2:13.0.5-1~bpo13+1). 60-open-vm-tools.rules comes from debian/open-vm-tools.udev and only does `KERNEL=="vsock", MODE="0666"`.

2. Rule text as shipped in trixie (sources.debian.org, 2:12.5.0-2+deb13u1, open-vm-tools/udev/99-vmware-scsi-udev.rules, with the quilt patch applied): `ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEMS=="scsi", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="scsi_device", ATTRS{vendor}=="VMware*" , ATTRS{model}=="Virtual disk*", ATTRS{timeout}=="?*", ATTR{timeout}="180"` and a second identical rule with `ATTRS{model}=="VMware Virtual S"`. debian/patches/series still lists `debian/scsi-udev-rule` (patch header: "Description: Fix scsi timeout setting error on debian stretch", "Author: Shota Aratono", "Last-Update: 2020-01-16"); its "-" lines are upstream's rules and its "+" lines are the two rules above. Changelog: 2:10.1.10-2 "Fix scsi timeout setting error on debian stretch"; 2:10.1.0-4449150-4 "Timeouts are set in 99-vmware-scsi-udev.rules now".

3. Upstream form for comparison (vmware/open-vm-tools tag stable-12.5.0, and master): `ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEMS=="scsi", ATTRS{vendor}=="VMware*", ATTRS{model}=="Virtual disk*", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="disk", RUN+="/bin/sh -c 'echo 180 >/sys$env{DEVPATH}/device/timeout'"` (plus the "VMware Virtual S" twin). Both forms end up writing the scsi_device's `timeout` attribute, i.e. the file reachable as /sys/block/sdX/device/timeout.

4. Why the Launchpad bug does not apply to Debian. LP 1790145 ("99-vmware-scsi-udev.rules has no effect - timeout by 30 not 180", Ubuntu 18.04/18.10, package 2:10.3.0-0ubuntu1~18.04.1): Ubuntu's merged rule was `ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEMS=="scsi", ATTRS{vendor}=="VMware*", ATTRS{model}=="Virtual disk*", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="disk", ATTR{timeout}="180"`, i.e. it assigns ATTR{timeout} on the block-device ("disk") event, whose own sysfs node has no `timeout` attribute, so the write silently fails. Christian Ehrhardt (Canonical), comment #8: "The upstream rules work." / "The Debian Rules work (and look nicer)" / "But ours don't"; comment #9: "So we exchanged Debians ENV{DEVTYPE}=="scsi_device" with upstreams ENV{DEVTYPE}=="disk" ... And this is what breaks the case here." Fix 2:10.3.0-0ubuntu1~18.04.2 (2018-09-27): "revert 'update to match changes in 10.3 (DEVTYPE checkadded upstream)'"; verification (comment #14) shows /sys/block/sd[a-d]/device/timeout going from 30 to 180 after reboot. Debian bug #908475 ("d/p/debian/scsi-udev-rule no more needed?", filed by Ehrhardt against 2:10.3.0-1) was closed by the reporter the same day after he concluded "the faulty rules came from Ubuntu's side"; the maintainer kept the Debian delta. The rule text Ehrhardt quoted as "Debian Rules" in 2018 is character-for-character what trixie ships today.

5. Takes effect at boot without manual steps. udev(7) (trixie): "The udev rules are read from the files located in the system rules directories /usr/lib/udev/rules.d and /usr/local/lib/udev/rules.d, the volatile runtime directory /run/udev/rules.d and the local administration directory /etc/udev/rules.d." systemd-udev-trigger.service (trixie systemd 257.13-1~deb13u1, "Coldplug All udev Devices"): "ExecStart=-udevadm trigger --type=all --action=add --prioritized-subsystem=module,block,tpmrm,net,tty,input" - this replays "add" for disks already found in the initramfs, which is why the ACTION=="add" rule in the root filesystem fires on every boot (the mechanism behind the LP "after reboot: 180" results).

6. Does NOT take effect at install time on a running VM. debian/open-vm-tools.postinst (trixie): `udevadm trigger --type=devices --subsystem-match=scsi || true` with no --action; udevadm(8) (trixie), trigger -c/--action: "The default value is "change"." The shipped rule matches only `ACTION=="add"`, so the postinst trigger does not apply it; a reboot (or `udevadm trigger --action=add --subsystem-match=scsi`) is needed. udev's own dpkg trigger (debian/udev.postinst, "triggered" case) only runs update_hwdb. This matters for guests that get open-vm-tools after first boot; debian-installer avoids it: hw-detect 1.171 (trixie) finish-install script 08hw-detect detects "VMware*" / "VMW*" in /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name or sys_vendor (or via systemd-detect-virt) and runs `apt-install --with-recommends open-vm-tools || true` (or open-vm-tools-desktop), so a d-i-installed trixie VM has the rule from its first boot.

7. Kernel side (Linux v6.12 source, github mirror of torvalds/linux): drivers/scsi/sd.h: "/* Time out in seconds for disks and Magneto-opticals (which are slower). */ #define SD_TIMEOUT (30 * HZ)", "#define SD_MAX_RETRIES 5", and "Flush timeout is a multiplier over the standard device timeout which is user modifiable via sysfs but initially set to SD_TIMEOUT" (SD_FLUSH_TIMEOUT_MULTIPLIER 2). drivers/scsi/sd.c sd_probe: `if (!sdp->request_queue->rq_timeout) { if (sdp->type != TYPE_MOD) blk_queue_rq_timeout(sdp->request_queue, SD_TIMEOUT); ... }` - sd never overrides an already-set timeout. drivers/scsi/scsi_sysfs.c: `static DEVICE_ATTR(timeout, S_IRUGO | S_IWUSR, sdev_show_timeout, sdev_store_timeout);` where the store sets the queue's rq_timeout to value*HZ, so the 180 written by udev is the per-command timeout. Trixie's stock kernel is linux-image-amd64 6.12.111-1 (linux-image-6.12.111+deb13-amd64) at the time of checking. For NVMe-attached virtual disks the rule cannot match (not SCSI, not sd*): drivers/nvme/host/core.c: `unsigned int nvme_io_timeout = 30; module_param_named(io_timeout, nvme_io_timeout, uint, 0644);` - i.e. 30 s unless nvme_core.io_timeout is set.

8. Not read: VMware KB 1009465 (knowledge.broadcom.com returned 404 for every URL form tried; web.archive.org is blocked). A search-engine snippet of the old kb.vmware.com copy read "VMware Tools increases the SCSI disk timeout to 60 seconds for Virtual Infrastructure 3 and 180 seconds for vSphere 4 and higher", consistent with the above, but I could not verify it on the page itself. No ESXi 8 document was found that states the default controller type for Debian guests; the Broadcom VM-administration table only states NVMe as default for Windows Server 2022+/Windows 11 on hardware version 21.
- Corrected claim: Debian 13 trixie's open-vm-tools (2:12.5.0-2+deb13u1) installs /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/99-vmware-scsi-udev.rules, carrying Debian's patched rule `ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEMS=="scsi", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="scsi_device", ATTRS{vendor}=="VMware*", ATTRS{model}=="Virtual disk*" (or "VMware Virtual S"), ATTRS{timeout}=="?*", ATTR{timeout}="180"`, which raises the per-command SCSI timeout (/sys/block/sdX/device/timeout) from the kernel default of 30 s (SD_TIMEOUT in drivers/scsi/sd.h, Linux 6.12) to 180 s for virtual disks on VMware SCSI controllers (PVSCSI, LSI Logic Parallel/SAS, BusLogic). On a stock trixie kernel it is applied automatically at every boot by systemd-udev-trigger.service's coldplug (`udevadm trigger --type=all --action=add`), with no manual step, provided open-vm-tools is installed (debian-installer installs it automatically when it detects VMware via DMI). It does not cover disks on a virtual NVMe controller (nvme_core io_timeout default 30 s) or SATA/IDE disks, and it is not applied to an already-running guest at package-install time (the postinst triggers "change" events while the rule matches only "add"), so such a guest stays at 30 s until it reboots or runs `udevadm trigger --action=add --subsystem-match=scsi`. Launchpad bug 1790145 was an Ubuntu 18.04/18.10 packaging regression (Ubuntu's merged rule mixed upstream's DEVTYPE=="disk" with ATTR{timeout}, which never matches) fixed in 2018; Debian's rule was never affected and was confirmed working by the bug's reporter (Debian #908475).
- Design impact: Keep the 180 s assumption for Linux-on-ESXi, but state its preconditions explicitly in the no-quorum 'stop' posture: (1) the guest's disks must be on a VMware SCSI controller (PVSCSI/LSI Logic SAS); guests using the virtual NVMe controller are not covered by the rule and run at nvme_core.io_timeout = 30 s unless the guest sets nvme_core.io_timeout=180 (kernel command line or modprobe.d) - the design must either exclude NVMe-controller guests from the "survives 60 s" class or require that setting, and should not assume ESXi 8 picks a SCSI controller for Debian guests (no VMware document found stating the default for Linux guests; the table only states NVMe as default for Windows 11/Server 2022 on HW 21); (2) open-vm-tools must be installed - automatic for debian-installer-built VMs, but cloud/OVA/manually built images must be checked; (3) a guest that installed open-vm-tools after first boot remains at 30 s until reboot or an explicit `udevadm trigger --action=add --subsystem-match=scsi`. Add to the client-prerequisite checklist a runtime verification, since I could only verify by source reading: `cat /sys/block/sd*/device/timeout` must read 180 and, for NVMe guests, `cat /sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/io_timeout` must read 180. Drop or reword the "silently failing on a Debian derivative" risk: it was a 2018 Ubuntu-only merge error, long fixed, and the trixie rule is exactly the form Canonical verified. Note also that 180 s is the per-command timeout (sd retries up to SD_MAX_RETRIES = 5 and the flush timeout is 2x), so a 60 s hold sits inside a single command timeout on a 180 s guest but exceeds one on a 30 s guest, which is where SCSI error handling (abort/reset) would start.

- Corrected claim: As of Debian 13.7 (released 12 September 2026) plus trixie-security on 12 October 2026, Debian 13 trixie provides mdadm 4.4-11, xfsprogs 6.13.0-2+deb13u1 (13.7), util-linux 2.41.5-0+deb13u1 (DSA-6442 / 13.7; the package installs /usr/sbin/fsfreeze and /usr/sbin/blkdiscard), sg3-utils 1.48-3~deb13u1 (13.7, "Fix missing sg_inq output fields"; 13.0-13.6 shipped 1.48-2), smartmontools 7.4-3, linux-image-amd64 6.12.111-1 depending on linux-image-6.12.111+deb13-amd64 (from trixie-security; the 13.7 point-release base kernel is 6.12.94-1, and trixie stays on the 6.12 series), samba 2:4.22.11+dfsg-0+deb13u1 (13.7), systemd 257.13-1~deb13u1 (since 13.5), nfs-common/nfs-kernel-server 1:2.8.3-1 from source nfs-utils, multipath-tools 0.11.1-2 and iputils-arping 3:20240905-3; these are floors that move with each point release and DSA. Raspberry Pi OS based on Debian 13 trixie was announced on 2 October 2025 in 32-bit and 64-bit editions; its launch images ran Raspberry Pi's 6.12 kernel (6.12.47+rpt), but since the 18 June 2026 image the Trixie images ship a Raspberry Pi 6.18 kernel (the 6 October 2026 images list kernel 6.18), so the witness host kernel is 6.18, not 6.12, while the userland remains Debian 13 arm64. aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu is a Rust Tier 1 target with host tools ("ARM64 Linux (kernel 4.1+, glibc 2.17+)"); the 32-bit Pi OS targets (arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf, armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf) are only Tier 2 with host tools. Debian 13 also ships gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu 4:14.2.0-1 on amd64 as an in-box cross linker.
- Design impact: No tool or dependency change: every in-box tool Phase C relies on exists in trixie at the stated version, so the no-vendor-RAID-CLI position holds. Three edits to the design text: (1) label the version list as a snapshot "Debian 13.7 + trixie-security, 2026-10-12" and treat the numbers as minimum versions, since four of them changed in 13.7 and the kernel changes with every DSA; (2) if the VPD/discard probing parses sg_inq output, require sg3-utils >= 1.48-3~deb13u1 (i.e. Debian 13.7) because 13.0-13.6 shipped 1.48-2 with the "missing sg_inq output fields" bug, and state that a clean 13.7 install without the security suite boots 6.12.94-1 rather than 6.12.111-1; (3) in the witness section, stop describing the Raspberry Pi host as "trixie with the 6.12 kernel": current Raspberry Pi OS Trixie images run a Raspberry Pi-built 6.18 kernel, not Debian's linux-image 6.12, so the witness binary must not depend on 6.12-specific kernel behaviour or on Debian's kernel package, and its support statement should name the 64-bit edition only (32-bit Pi OS would need a Tier 2 target). The cross-build itself is unaffected: Pi OS Trixie userland is Debian 13 arm64, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu is Tier 1 with host tools, and gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu is available in-box on the amd64 build host.

### [C40] PARTIALLY-CORRECT
- Claim: versitygw v1.8.0 (released 2026-09-04) is the latest release; its --object-lock-mode flag enables publish locking for conditional writes rather than S3 Object Lock retention; and the fix storing bucket default retention on each object at write time (PR #2479) was merged on 2026-10-08, after v1.8.0.
- Raised by: Opus-Protocols
- Why it matters: Sets the versitygw pin for the Phase C Veeam immutability test and the 'experimental' label on the S3 blade.
- Summary: Two of the three sub-claims are exactly right: v1.8.0 (published 2026-09-04T23:11:49Z) is still the latest versitygw release as of 2026-10-12, and PR #2479 ("fix: store bucket default retention on each object at write time and support Object Lock fields in browser POST") was merged into main on 2026-10-08T18:59:27Z, after v1.8.0 and in no tagged release. The middle sub-claim is right about what --object-lock-mode does (publish locking for conditional If-Match/If-None-Match writes, explicitly not S3 Object Lock retention) but wrong about which version has it: the flag does not exist in v1.8.0, whose posix command only defines the boolean --disable-object-lock-file; --object-lock-mode (flock|fcntl|local|none) was added by PR #2359, merged 2026-09-11, and exists only on unreleased main.

The releases page marks v1.8.0 "Latest" with no pre-release entries; the tags page lists v1.8.0 (Sep 4, 2026) at the top of 10 tags; the v1.8.0...main compare shows main 243 commits ahead, so nothing after v1.8.0 has been tagged.

2) The --object-lock-mode flag. v1.8.0 cmd/internal/gwcli/posix.go defines only one lock flag: Name "disable-object-lock-file", Usage "disable shared advisory lock files for conditional object publishes (unsafe with multiple gateway processes)", EnvVars VGW_DISABLE_OBJECT_LOCK_FILE, passed as PosixOpts.ForceNoObjLockFile; the fetch stated "No flag with that name [object-lock-mode] is defined in this file." v1.8.0 cmd/versitygw/main.go likewise reads only ctx.Bool("disable-object-lock-file") and prints "Warning: shared object publish locking disabled; conditional write atomicity is limited to this gateway process". On main, the same file now also reads ctx.String("object-lock-mode") == "local" / == "none" and prints "Warning: conditional writes are disabled because object-lock-mode is none". The flag was introduced by PR #2359 "fix: make conditional publish lock modes explicit" (API: created_at 2026-09-04T20:27:02Z, i.e. six minutes after the v1.8.0 release object was created; merged_at 2026-09-11T14:57:08Z; merge commit 843bed4; fixes #2351). Its file patch adds to cmd/internal/gwcli/posix.go: Name "object-lock-mode", Usage "lock mode for conditional object publishes: flock, fcntl, local, or none", EnvVars VGW_OBJECT_LOCK_MODE, DefaultText "flock", passed as PosixOpts.ObjectLockMode; and changes disable-object-lock-file's usage to "deprecated alias for --object-lock-mode=local"; scoutfs gets "object-lock-mode" with "local or none", default "none". The wiki POSIX-Backend page (revision 2fe19af, Sep 18, 2026, "...lock modes...") documents "--object-lock-mode value lock mode for conditional object publishes: flock, fcntl, local, or none (default: flock)" and states "This is publish locking for conditional writes, not S3 Object Lock retention or legal hold." It adds: "For PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload requests carrying If-Match or If-None-Match," the backend "must serialize the final condition check and publication for each key"; none "Rejects conditional object writes as NotImplemented; unconditional writes continue to work"; "--disable-object-lock-file is retained for compatibility and selects local. Do not use it in new configurations." What v1.8.0 does ship is the underlying lock-file publish locking: PR #2288 "fix(posix): make conditional PUT evaluation and publication atomic per key" (merged 2026-08-28, lock files at bucket/.sgwtmp/objlock/<shard>, flock on Unix) and PR #2321 "fix: harden posix conditional publish locking" (merged 2026-09-01); both appear in the v1.8.0 release notes.

3) PR #2479. GitHub API: title "fix: store bucket default retention on each object at write time and support Object Lock fields in browser POST", merged true, merged_at "2026-10-08T18:59:27Z", created_at 2026-10-04T19:40:49Z, base main, head sis/object-lock-default-retention-stamping, merge_commit_sha 5f063c5bbf2ffb9669531b09f6c20480daf09193, author niksis02, merged by benmcclelland; fixes #2480, no milestone. Body: bucket default retention "was never stored on objects", protection was computed at delete time from the live rule; posix and azure backends now store the rule's retention "as the object's own retention whenever a write sets no Object Lock parameters"; objects written before this change "lose bucket-derived protection" (reviewer asked about migrating legacy objects; author proposed a utility method, no evidence one shipped). Related issue #2494 (opened and closed 2026-10-08) states current behavior in "v1.8.0 and main": default retention is counted from when PutObjectLockConfiguration was called and applies to existing objects; once that window passes nothing is protected; expected AWS behavior is "each new object version gets the default retention at upload". Also relevant for the test: the wiki's POSIX metadata-storage limitation says with --nometa "retention, and legal holds therefore cannot be relied on across requests".
- Corrected claim: versitygw v1.8.0 (published 2026-09-04T23:11:49Z) is the latest tagged release as of 2026-10-12; main is 243 commits ahead of it and nothing newer is tagged. v1.8.0 ships lock-file-based publish locking for conditional writes (PRs #2288 and #2321, both in the v1.8.0 notes), controlled only by the boolean --disable-object-lock-file / VGW_DISABLE_OBJECT_LOCK_FILE ("disable shared advisory lock files for conditional object publishes"). The --object-lock-mode flag (flock | fcntl | local | none, help default flock, env VGW_OBJECT_LOCK_MODE) is NOT in v1.8.0: it was added by PR #2359, merged 2026-09-11, and exists only on unreleased main, where --disable-object-lock-file becomes a deprecated alias for --object-lock-mode=local. In both forms this is publish locking that serializes If-Match / If-None-Match PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload per key; it is not S3 Object Lock retention or legal hold. The fix that stores bucket default retention on each object at write time (PR #2479, merge commit 5f063c5) was merged into main on 2026-10-08T18:59:27Z, after v1.8.0, and is in no tagged release; v1.8.0 therefore still has the bug described in issues #2480/#2494 (default retention never stamped on objects; protection computed at delete time from the live bucket rule, so default-retention immutability does not behave like AWS).
- Design impact: Keep the S3 blade's "experimental" label. For the Phase C Veeam immutability test, do not pin v1.8.0 if the test relies on bucket default retention: pin a main build at or after merge commit 5f063c5 (2026-10-08) or wait for the next tagged release, and record in the test plan that objects written before that build lose bucket-derived protection (no migration utility was shown to exist). Any unit file, config or doc text that passes --object-lock-mode to v1.8.0 must be changed: v1.8.0 does not define that flag (use --disable-object-lock-file only if deliberately choosing per-process locking); reserve --object-lock-mode for a post-#2359 build and note the deprecation of --disable-object-lock-file there. Wherever the design mentions the flag, state that it governs conditional-write publish locking, not Object Lock retention, so it must not be presented as the immutability switch. Two further requirements for the test: Object Lock retention needs metadata storage (xattrs or --sidecar; the wiki says retention and legal holds cannot be relied on with --nometa), and for a single gateway process the default flock mode is sufficient while multi-gateway deployments must verify filesystem lock coherence (mode none rejects conditional writes as NotImplemented).

## Round 3: revised positions

### Opus-Storage

#### Opus-Storage, Session 03 round 3: responses, revised engine, Phase C plan

P = Opus-Protocols, F = Opus-Fabrics, C = Opus-Consensus, each with the S-number that persona used. The CP interval is min(timer, 4 GiB / ingest) everywhere below (C-S9).

##### 1. Responses to holes raised against me

**P-S1 / F-S1 (CP identity).** ACCEPT. A 64-bit random `cp_nonce` per cut rides in `CpBegin`, every `Chunk`, `CpEnd` and the receiver's resume record; a `CpBegin` with a known `cp_seq` and a different nonce discards the partial. `CpEnd` goes out only after the superblock completion CQE.

**P-S2 / F-S2 (hold release; apply point).** ACCEPT Fabrics' rule and Protocols' trigger: staging is released when the `WRITE_FIXED` completion and the `IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF` have both arrived; later resends read the stripe from disk by `(lseg, stripe_idx)`. The receiver gains the `ShipApply` CP trigger. `insync_lag_max` = 2 × CP timer + 5 s (25 s HDD, 15 s flash).

**P-S3 / F-S4 / C-S2 (the cut waits for a CP).** ACCEPT. Generations are index objects in a ring of 8; a cut is the epoch flip alone; each closed generation is one CP. `cut_within(deadline)` returns `Ok` only when the ring has a free slot and the last three drain rates predict a commit inside the deadline; the scheduler freezes only after `Ok`. Snapshots record `kind: Fsfreeze | Crash`; only `Fsfreeze` is mounted `norecovery`; `Crash` is exposed only as a writable clone after a replay mount.

**P-S4 (`Esxi512e` on HDD).** ACCEPT. A per-LUN alignment detector (straddling or sub-4 KiB writes per 1,000 over 10 s) switches that LUN to shadow read-modify-write with a 1 MiB prefetch (one read per 256 blocks for a sequentially local writer); throttle and alert are per LUN.

**P-S5 / C-S1 (ublk path).** ACCEPT, corrected by C03: `READ_FIXED` on `/dev/ublkcN` fails with `-EACCES`. The path is `IORING_OP_READ`/`WRITE` with a plain pointer into the arena slot, the ublkc fd `O_NONBLOCK` before `IORING_REGISTER_FILES`, never `IOSQE_ASYNC`. `pread64` is the fallback; legacy copy is measured against it in item 10.

**P-S6 (drive caches; probe; `RWF_DSYNC`).** ACCEPT the attestation (3.5), the random probe and a weekly 1 GiB re-probe. REJECT the double flush on my path: `dio_bio_write_op` sets `REQ_FUA` for a DSYNC kiocb and `blkdev_write_iter` calls `generic_write_sync` only when the write completed inline (`ret > 0`); the io_uring path returns `-EIOCBQUEUED` and io_uring adds no sync on completion [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/block/fops.c and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/io_uring/rw.c]. Synchronous `pwritev2(RWF_DSYNC)` does pay both, so the engine never issues one; ordering is my explicit flush, as C22 requires.

**P-S7 (`crossmnt`; R21).** ACCEPT. Each snapshot mount gets an explicit export with `fsid=` from `(vol_uuid, snap_uuid)`; no `crossmnt` on volume roots; Phase C mounts at `/vol/<svm>_root/.otap/snap/<vol>/@GMT-...` outside share and bucket roots; the in-junction `.snapshot` view is Phase B.

**P-S8 / C-S10 (root volume).** ACCEPT `alert` for the SVM root plus a content check: every volume carries `rollback_gen`, bumped on each rollback; `nbladed` records the root's `(cp_seq, rollback_gen)` at each successful SVM start and raises WARN "root rewound" with the machine-account and NFSv4-reclaim consequences when it differs.

**P-S9 (consistency groups).** ACCEPT. Relationship state is per consistency group, default the SVM's volumes including its root; the transport is per aggregate pair.

**F-S3 (catch-up loses snapshots).** ACCEPT. `CatchUp` becomes ordered increments: for each retained snapshot S_i in (base, T], walk S_i's pinned page index for `birth in (S_{i-1}, S_i]`, apply as one receiver CP and materialize S_i; then the live root for (S_last, T]. Cost is the per-interval churn (108 GB in Fabrics' scenario).

**F-S5 (applied lag).** ACCEPT. The receiver forces a CP on `CpEnd` when none is in flight and runs a 2 s timer while a relationship is inbound; `DeltaSink::end(commit: Immediate | NextCp)`; `applied_age_s` and `landed_age_s` are reported separately.

**F-S6 (superblock before data).** ACCEPT. A dirty boot CRC-checks every summary page of the selected CP before export (about 8 s for a 4 GiB HDD CP, under 1 s on flash), rewinding one CP on failure; `flush-opaque` backstores (C07) also get their data read (3.5 s at 1.2 GB/s) and two-CP deferred reuse, so N-2 is intact.

**F-S7 (coalescing).** ACCEPT. Random S-aligned placement over a 16 GiB span; `GeomSource::Probe { placement: Random, knee_bytes, ratio, max_hw_sectors_kb }`.

**F-S8 (learn cycle, patrol, rebuild).** ACCEPT. The attestation records `learn_mode = transparent | write_through_fallback | unknown` (C08); the CP engine publishes `drain_rate_bytes_s` and raises WARN after three CPs below 50% of the probed rate; `inflight_stripes` = measured drain × 200 ms, clamped to [4, 64].

**F-S9 (drive caches).** ACCEPT: `cache_protection = { controller: Bbu | FlashBacked | None, disk_cache: Disabled | Enabled | Unknown, learn_mode }`; `Enabled` and `Unknown` are refused for HDD VDs without a PLP attestation.

**F-S10 (second device).** ACCEPT the ordering: `flush` per device class, pool then metadata, each awaited, then the FUA superblock on its device. NVMe sets `BLK_FEAT_WRITE_CACHE | BLK_FEAT_FUA` only when Identify Controller reports VWC [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/nvme/host/core.c, `nvme_update_ns_info_block`]. REJECT the extra-flush cost (P-S6).

**F-S11 (stream fields).** ACCEPT. Records carry `cp_nonce`, `owner_epoch`, `direction_epoch`; resume is a per-CP chunk bitmap plus one byte offset per open connection, chunk-aligned by contract. `Heartbeat` gains `cp_age_at_send_ms`, `dirty_vols` (1 KiB bitset) and per-volume `acked_bytes` since the last shipped CP.

**F-S12 (TLS).** ACCEPT, strengthened by C26: kTLS refuses `SEND_ZC` with `-EOPNOTSUPP`, so TLS connections use plain `SEND` and release staging at the send CQE.

**F-S13 (intent write on VDs).** ACCEPT. The intent slot lives on the metadata class when one exists (4 KiB FUA, 0.1 to 0.5 ms), otherwise in a full stripe of its own; `nvfail_intent = conservative` is the default for HDD pools without a metadata class.

**C-S3 (relocations shipped).** ACCEPT. Summary entries carry `kind: Ingest | Relocate | Applied`; stripes are homogeneous in kind and ingest is packed per consistency group, so only ingest stripes of outbound groups ship and the receiver drops volumes that are not inbound.

**C-S4 (stale `promote_hint`).** ACCEPT. At promotion the nvfail set is every writable volume not provably idle (two consecutive `CpBegin`s with the bit clear and no later heartbeat write); `write_active` and `acked_bytes` size the alert only.

**C-S5 (intent versus superblock ring).** ACCEPT. Superblock slots are for commits only; `write_active` lives in two intent slots with a monotonic `intent_seq`; boot takes the union of the max-select superblock and any newer intent slot.

**C-S6 (RAID6 write hole), with C21.** ACCEPT by the stronger rule: every write to a parity pool is a whole stripe, data and metadata alike; metadata is log-structured in its own segments; each superblock and intent slot is one full stripe written whole; a torn write damages only uncommitted rows, so a forced dirty-degraded assembly is safe for committed data. `--write-journal` is not mandated (bitmap exclusion, no reshape).

**C-S7 (command size; scheduled write-through).** ACCEPT with C23's correction: Fusion-class PERCs cap at 256 KiB (1 MiB with large-IO firmware); only MFI-series cards sit at 128 KiB. The probe starts at 64 KiB and records `max_hw_sectors_kb`; the VD rule is strip × data disks at most the measured `max_sectors_kb`. REJECT raising the throttle threshold: R7's 2 s cap stands.

**C-S8 (md over VDs).** ACCEPT. The attestation runs on md members: a member reading "write through" whose INQUIRY vendor names a RAID controller requires `cache_protection` with `disk_cache = Disabled`; `unknown` refused.

**C-S9 (arithmetic).** ACCEPT. CP interval = min(timer, 4 GiB / ingest): 4 s at 1 GB/s, 8 s at 0.5 GB/s. Page-index entries are 16 B.

##### 2. Fact-check consequences

- **C03, C04.** Force P-S5; `dbladed` holds `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` only, `UBLK_F_UNPRIVILEGED_DEV` is excluded, `addr = 0` in every FETCH, and item 10 asserts the `io_uring_queue_async_work` tracepoint never fires.
- **C05 to C08.** Force the attestation struct, the md-member scope, the `flush-opaque` class with two-CP deferred reuse and the learn-mode field; `queue/write_cache` and `cache_type` are read-only diagnostics.
- **C09.** Mine: `UBLK_ATTR_VOLATILE_CACHE | UBLK_ATTR_FUA` in the basic params before `START_DEV`, `UBLK_IO_OP_FLUSH` served as a CP-ordering barrier, FUA writes acknowledged after the insert like any write; the reconciler asserts `queue/write_cache == "write back"` and `queue/fua == 1`.
- **C10.** NAS volumes are created at `size_max` and grown by `xfs_growfs`; client LUNs are created at their advertised size and grown only by a planned re-create.
- **C19.** Forces P-S7.
- **C21, C22.** Force C-S6; the full stripe is chunk × data disks from `md/level`, `md/chunk_size`, `md/raid_disks`; the commit is "empty flush, wait, FUA record", never a data-carrying PREFLUSH; PPL is refused because it forwards no flush.
- **C23.** Forces C-S7.
- **C24 to C26.** `WritevFixed` forbidden (6.15 only); no `SENDMSG_ZC` with fixed buffers, so the frame header is staged contiguously ahead of the stripe image; `MSG_WAITALL` per chunk; `NOTIF` is a buffer-lifetime event, never an acknowledgement; huge-page truesize inflation is measured in item 2, with 4 KiB-page staging as the fallback.
- **C35.** `vpd_pgb0` is optional, read to EOF, validated (`data[1] == 0xB0`, length at least 16) before parsing; `optimal_io_size = 0` defers to the probe.
- **C38, C39.** Version pins are a 2026-10-12 snapshot with floors; `sg3-utils` at least 1.48-3~deb13u1 if `sg_inq` is parsed; libublk's yank churn gets a re-pin procedure.
- **C01, C02, C20.** Presentation is Protocols' and Fabrics' call; my side: EIO in `NvFailed`, the export withheld until the clear (C20's server-side fence), `rollback_gen` for the fsid.
- **C11 to C18, C27 to C34, C36, C37, C40.** Not my design; no change.

##### 3. Revised design

###### 3.1 Write path

Reactors per core on `io-uring` 0.7.15 (`SINGLE_ISSUER`, `DEFER_TASKRUN`); one ublk device per LUN via `libublk` 0.4.8 with `UBLK_F_USER_COPY`. The reactor owning the LUN's queues takes the WRITE CQE, reserves a slot run in the arena, issues `IORING_OP_READ` on the `O_NONBLOCK` ublkc fd at the user-copy position into the slot, computes CRC32C per 4 KiB, takes the aggregate `seq`, inserts, and issues `COMMIT_AND_FETCH_REQ`, which is the acknowledgement. Busy-polled cost per 4 KiB: CQE 0.5 to 1.5 us; inline read (pin, copy at 10 GB/s, unpin) 1.0 to 2.0 us; CRC 0.2 to 0.3 us [believed]; `seq` and BTreeMap insert 0.5 to 1.0 us; batched commit 0.3 to 0.5 us: 2.5 to 5.3 us, 8 to 13 us with wakeups, 100 to 150 us p50 at an iSCSI initiator on 10GbE.

###### 3.2 Arena, generations, triggers, back-pressure

The arena is 8 GiB of boot-reserved 2 MiB pages, systemd-created, re-attached after `kill -9`: a ring of slots whose unflushed occupancy is the budget. The dirty index is one `BTreeMap<u64, DirtyExtent>` per volume per generation (key LBA in 4 KiB units, value `{len, slot, seq, mask}`), inserts splitting or trimming older overlaps so a generation holds the newest bytes per LBA. Generations form a ring of 8 (P-S3), each closed one becoming one CP in order. Triggers in priority: `Shutdown`/`UpsOnBattery`; `Snapshot(id)`; `ArenaHalf` (4 GiB unflushed); `Timer` (10 s HDD, 5 s flash); `BackToBack` (previous CP committed, above 1 GiB unflushed); `ShipApply` (receiver). Back-pressure above 60% occupancy: `delay = k × occ / (1 − occ)`, `k` from the last three drain rates, capped at 2 s, then Transitioning (R7): an 80%-full HDD pool drains 0.3 to 0.5 GB/s, so sustained ingest above it hits the cap within 10 to 20 s; a 4 GiB burst at 2 GB/s is absorbed in 2 s.

```rust
pub trait Allocator {
    fn reserve(&mut self, lun: LunId, nslots: u32) -> Result<RingRef, Full>;   // bump + lap; throttled
    fn insert(&mut self, vol: VolId, lba: u64, ext: DirtyExtent) -> Seq;       // split/trim; epoch-pinned
    fn cut(&mut self, reason: CutReason) -> Result<GenId, RingFull>;            // flip + grace
    fn cut_within(&self, deadline: Duration) -> Result<(), Busy>;              // promise before FIFREEZE
    fn stage(&mut self, gen: GenId, out: &mut StagingPool) -> CpProgram;       // LBA order per group
    fn release(&mut self, cp: CpSeq);                                          // staging at disk + NOTIF
}
```

###### 3.3 Stripe format, flush, commit

A generation drains volume by volume in LBA order into stripe images in the hugetlbfs staging pool: `[frame header][summary][data]`. The summary is a 64 B header `{agg, cp_seq, cp_nonce, lseg, stripe_idx, kind, group, nblocks, crc}` plus 16 B per block `{vol:20 | lba:40 | kind:2 | rsvd:2, birth: u32, crc32c: u32}`, 0.5% of a 2.5 MiB HDD stripe. Staging costs one copy (0.12 core at 1.2 GB/s) and buys one `WRITE_FIXED` per stripe, in-place patch merges and one send buffer.

Per CP: data stripes as O_DIRECT `WRITE_FIXED`, `inflight_stripes` deep; the metadata stream (CP log at 16 B per block, table deltas, map checkpoint pages when due) packed into whole stripes of metadata segments on the metadata class, else the pool; `IORING_OP_FSYNC` per device class in order, each awaited; then the superblock slot written whole with `RWF_DSYNC`, one `REQ_FUA` write on the io_uring path. A segment freed by CP N is reusable after N+1 commits (N+2 when `flush-opaque`); a dirty boot verifies the chosen CP's summaries first. Parity pools never see a sub-stripe write: the four superblock slots and two intent slots are each a full stripe written whole with FUA (15 to 25 ms on HDD, up to 250 ms behind the stripe queue; 0.1 to 0.5 ms on the metadata class).

###### 3.4 Map, stable block identity, holes, `diff`

Per-volume radix map: a page index (16 B per 4 MiB: `page_pba`, `max_birth`) and 16 KiB pages of 1024 entries `{addr: lseg:36 | off:16 | plen:12, birth: u32, crc32c: u32}`, 0.4% of volume size; every read verifies its CRC against the entry. The CP log is the map's journal; an overlay answers lookups since the last checkpoint; a checkpoint rewrites dirty pages copy-on-write at 1 GiB of log or 10 minutes. Holes are entries with a birth, the OpenZFS hole-birth lesson [verified: https://openzfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Project%20and%20Community/FAQ%20hole%20birth.html].

`addr` names a logical segment; the segment table maps `lseg → Physical(pseg) | Relocated(table)`. GC moves a victim's live blocks into new stripes (birth preserved), updates the live root through the summary backrefs, writes a relocation table `off → (lseg', off')` (8 B per moved block), frees the physical segment under deferred reuse and never touches a pinned root: snapshot and clone entries still naming `lseg` resolve through the table, one cached extra lookup. A table retires when every root predating the cleaning is gone; a weekly walk rewrites stale clone entries so tables older than 35 days retire. Tables cost about 14 GB per day at 0.4 GB/s of relocation, under 0.5% of a 100 TB pool per month of retention. Without this, one snapshot-referenced live block would pin its stripe for the life of the schedule. `diff(base)` walks pages with `max_birth > base` and emits entries with `birth > base` plus holes; `diff(base) == model(base)` now includes GC between the pair.

###### 3.5 Geometry, caches, probe

Trust order: md sysfs (`md/level`, `md/chunk_size`, `md/raid_disks`; stripe = chunk × data disks, `optimal_io_size` a cross-check, C22); block-queue sysfs and the `BLK*` ioctls [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/Documentation/ABI/stable/sysfs-block]; `vpd_pgb0` per C35; the TOML override; then the probe, mandatory for non-md backstores and a check on md: candidates 64 KiB to 8 MiB by doubling, 16 GiB of S-sized O_DIRECT writes per candidate at random S-aligned offsets over a 16 GiB reserved span, QD 8; the full stripe is the smallest S within 10% of the best; a knee at `max_sectors_kb` means no coalescing; a 1 GiB weekly re-probe raises CRIT on a knee shift.

Write-back controllers report WCE=0 (C06), the kernel strips every flush and FUA (C05) and megaraid_sas never forwards a drive-cache flush (C07): ordering rests on the attestation alone, and `controller = none` yields `flush-opaque` handling. Write-through, or a BBU fallback (C08): full-stripe writes avoid RMW only when the controller sees the stripe in one command, so strip × data disks is at most the measured `max_sectors_kb`, and `inflight_stripes` follows the measured drain. No discard: `Discard::Never`, free segments reused by whole-stripe overwrite; on flash behind such a controller `write_stop` at 90% is the only mitigation.

###### 3.6 Replication

```rust
pub enum StreamRec<'a> {
    CpBegin { agg: AggId, group: GroupId, cp: CpSeq, cp_nonce: u64, owner_epoch: u64, direction_epoch: u64,
              vols: &'a [VolDelta], snaps: &'a [SnapEvent], write_active: VolBitSet, acked_bytes: &'a [(VolId, u64)],
              mode: Mode /* Steady | Increment { from: SnapUuid, to: SnapUuid } */ },
    Chunk  { cp: CpSeq, cp_nonce: u64, idx: u32, image: &'a [u8] },
    CpEnd  { cp: CpSeq, cp_nonce: u64, nchunks: u32, bytes: u64, digest: [u8; 32], sb: SuperblockDigest },
    Heartbeat { /* fields per F-S11 */ },
}
pub trait DeltaSource {                 // sender; one per aggregate pair, state per group
    fn next(&mut self, budget: usize, out: &mut Vec<StreamRec<'_>>) -> Progress;
    fn committed(&mut self, cp: CpSeq);                                            // CpEnd may go
    fn applied(&mut self, group: GroupId, cp: CpSeq);                              // base and lag only
    fn detach(&mut self, group: GroupId);
}
pub trait DeltaSink {                   // receiver, inside dbladed
    fn begin(&mut self, b: &CpBegin) -> Result<(), Reject /* base, nonce, epochs */>;
    fn apply_chunk(&mut self, c: &Chunk) -> Result<(), Corrupt>;
    fn end(&mut self, e: &CpEnd, commit: Commit /* Immediate | NextCp */) -> Result<Applied, Corrupt>;
    fn resume_point(&self) -> Option<(CpSeq, u64 /* nonce */, ChunkBitmap)>;
}
```

Steady state: each staged ingest stripe of an outbound group goes to the flusher and the shipper at once; the shipper sends it with `SEND_ZC` plus `IORING_RECVSEND_FIXED_BUF` from the registered staging pool; the buffer is released on disk completion plus `NOTIF`. The 2 GiB hold grows only when the link is slower than staging: 2.4 s at 2 GB/s flash ingest on 10GbE, so such pairs need 25GbE. Applied lag = CP interval + CP bytes / min(link, receiver drain) + receiver commit (0.3 to 1 s): about 9 s at 1 GB/s on HDD, 14 s at 300 MB/s, 10 s on flash at 1 GB/s.

Receiver: chunks are containers of `(vol, lba, birth, data)` staged through the receiver's own CP assembler into shadow roots; at `ShipApply` every volume of the group switches roots together, so a replica is always at a sender CP boundary.

| Receiver state | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Idle | `CpBegin`, base and epochs match / mismatch | open shadow roots / Reject with my snapshots | Receiving / Idle |
| Receiving | `Chunk` | CRC, drop non-inbound volumes, stage, mark bitmap | Receiving |
| Receiving | link lost | persist `(N, nonce, bitmap)` at my next CP | Partial |
| Partial | `CpBegin{N}` same nonce / other nonce | continue from bitmap / discard partial | Receiving |
| Receiving | `CpEnd` verifies / CRC or digest failure | `ShipApply` / discard N, request resend from disk | Committing / Idle |
| Committing | my CP commits | switch roots; record `applied_*`; ack N | Idle |

Catch-up and resync: `Increment` mode walks snapshot to snapshot (F-S3) in PBA order, capped at 30% of pool read bandwidth; each increment is one receiver CP materialized as that snapshot; the round ends when the live root's increment is one CP. Sender state per group: Idle → CatchUp at creation; Steady → Lagging when the hold is exceeded or the link is down over 10 s; Lagging → CatchUp when the link returns (pin T); CatchUp → Steady once the last increment is applied (base = T); any → Resync on a base mismatch (receiver rolls back to the newest common snapshot); any → Broken when the pin crosses `break_at` or no common snapshot survives; Broken → Resync on a common scheduled snapshot. Pins and spill stand from my original: both sides pin the newest common snapshot and T; `on_space_pressure = break | hold` breaks at `gc_urgent`; a day away at 50 MB/s unique overwrite holds 4.3 TB; after a takeover the fenced old owner rolls back to the common snapshot, keeps `divergent-<ts>` for 7 days and becomes the receiver.

###### 3.7 nvfail

```rust
#[repr(C)] pub struct Superblock {    // v2; four slots, each a full stripe
    pub ver: u16, pub agg: AggId, pub epoch: u64, pub cp_seq: CpSeq, pub cp_nonce: u64, pub run_state: u8,
    pub intent_seq_seen: u64, pub write_active: VolBitSet, pub acked_bytes: [u64; MAX_VOLS],
    pub nvfail: VolBitSet, pub nvfail_cause: [NvCause; MAX_VOLS],     // DirtyBoot | TornCp | Promote
    pub rollback_gen: [u32; MAX_VOLS], pub freed_pending: [SegListPba; 2],
    pub map_roots: Pba, pub seg_table: Pba, pub reloc_index: Pba, pub cp_log_head: Pba, pub snap_table: Pba,
    pub inbound: [InboundState; MAX_GROUPS],   // applied_cp_seq, applied_owner_epoch, cp_age_at_send_ms, recv_mono, boot_id
    pub opened_stamp: u64, pub wall_ns: u64, pub crc: u32,
}
#[repr(C)] pub struct IntentSlot { pub intent_seq: u64, pub cp_seq: CpSeq, pub write_active: VolBitSet, pub crc: u32 }
```

A volume is active from its first write after idle until two consecutive CPs without a write; the idle-to-active transition writes an intent slot before the first acknowledgement; `conservative` treats every writable online volume as active. Boot with `run_state == Running`: verify the selected CP's summaries (rewind on failure, cause `TornCp`), union `write_active` with any newer intent slot, set `nvfail` for class-`on` volumes, write the superblock before any export, alert (CP sequence, window, per-volume `acked_bytes`, clear command). Promotion: every writable volume of the group not provably idle (C-S4) goes to `NvFailed` with cause `Promote`.

| State | Event | Action | Next |
|---|---|---|---|
| Online(idle) | first write | intent slot, then ack | Online(active) |
| Online(active) | two CPs without a write | clear at CP | Online(idle) |
| Offline(dirty) | boot, class `on` / `alert` | `nvfail[v]`, superblock, alert, EIO at the engine (presentation is `nbladed`'s) / alert, export | NvFailed / Online(idle) |
| NvFailed | `nvfail-clear [--restore <snap>]` | bump `rollback_gen`; optional rollback; re-export | Online(idle) |

Class defaults for owner decision D5: block LUN `on`; NAS datastore (NFSv3) `on`; NAS file `alert`; object `alert`; SVM root `alert` with the content check. `alert` still raises the CRIT with the window; `off` does not.

###### 3.8 Snapshots

`Snapshot { vol, name, uuid, cp_seq, created_wall, kind: Fsfreeze | Crash, origin: Scheduled | User | Transfer | Divergent, pins }`: a pinned root plus a deadlist merged into the next older on deletion; schedules run in `dbladed`. NAS snapshots: `cut_within(3 s)`, `FIFREEZE` inside the SVM's mount namespace, the flip, thaw at once; the window is the page-cache sync (about 2 GB at 1 GB/s) plus a sub-millisecond flip; past `freeze_timeout_ms` the snapshot is taken as `Crash`. Exposure: a read-only ublk device over the pinned root, mounted `ro,nouuid,norecovery` under `/vol/<svm>_root/.otap/snap/<vol>/@GMT-...` with an explicit `fsid=` export per mount, SMB through `vfs_shadow_copy2` with an absolute `shadow:snapdir`; clones get a replay mount and `xfs_admin -U generate`. Accounting per volume adds `snapshot_used`, `replication_hold_bytes` and `unique(snap)`.

###### 3.9 Memory model (GiB; 64 GB node, 62 usable)

| Consumer | Phase C | Phase B | Phase B survivor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arena | 8 | 8 | 8 |
| Staging, disk side | 0.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| Shipper hold / receiver staging | 0 / 0 | 2 / 2 | 2 / 2 |
| Generation ring | 1.3 | 1.3 | 1.3 |
| Map: page indexes, page cache, overlay, `lseg` index | 6 | 6 | 4 |
| DRAM read cache | 8 | 8 | 4 |
| md stripe cache | 1.5 | 1.5 | 1.5 |
| Kernel, OS, daemons | 2.5 | 2.5 | 2.5 |
| Engine total | 27.8 | 31.8 | 25.8 |
| SVM slices | 34 (`MemoryMax`) | 18 local cap, 12 headroom | 36 = both nodes' 18 |

The read and map caches shrink at takeover, which is what makes Consensus' survivor rule add up (Protocols C6, Fabrics P9). Crates, 2026-10-12 snapshot [verified: C39]: io-uring 0.7.15, libublk 0.4.8 (pinned exactly), crc-fast 1.10.0, zerocopy 0.8.62, rustix 1.1.5, memmap2 0.9.11, crossbeam 0.8.5, blake3 1.8.7, postcard 1.1.3, proptest 1.12.0, toml 1.1.8.

##### 4. Phase C work items with exit tests; Phase B and A additions

1. **`otap-format` v2 frozen**: every on-disk and on-wire structure in section 3. Exit: 1 M `proptest` round trips per structure; N/N-1 read compatibility; scanner fuzz corpus.
2. **`otap-arena`**: arena and staging from systemd units, re-attach after `kill -9`. Exit: 100 kills at 1 GB/s re-attach under 2 s p99 with zero acknowledged writes lost; the C25 truesize measurement decides huge-page versus 4 KiB-page staging.
3. **`otap-index`**: dirty index, generation ring, `cut_within`, patch masks, alignment detector. Exit: linearizability versus a model; flips under 1 M inserts/s with grace under 50 us; 64 cuts in 10 s under 1 GB/s ingest, each under 1 ms.
4. **`otap-geom`**: discovery, VPD B0, the random probe from 64 KiB, attestation including md members, weekly re-probe. Exit: on mdadm RAID6 10+2 and on a PERC VD the probe reports the configured stripe within one candidate; `unknown` refused; the write-through knee reproduced on a VD built with a 2 MiB stripe.
5. **`otap-cp`**: staging, flusher, metadata segments, commit protocol, intent slots, CP log, deferred reuse, triggers, throttle. Exit: at least 1.2 GB/s empty with zero member reads during a CP; `dm-log-writes` replay at 1,000 cut points yields a CP prefix with XFS mounting clean at every point; `dm-flakey` tearing of a superblock stripe and of a data stripe each fall back to the previous CP intact; forced dirty-degraded assembly after a torn CP loses no committed block.
6. **`otap-map`**: radix map, holes, logical segments and relocation tables, pins, deadlists, `diff`. Exit: `diff(base)` equals the model over 10 K random pairs including discards, resizes and GC between the pair; a pool with hourly snapshots and 50% random overwrite per day reclaims space at the modelled rate over 7 simulated days.
7. **nvfail**: intent slots, dirty-boot verification, `rollback_gen`, `nvfail-clear`, the alert. Exit: 1,000 simulated and 50 real power cuts engage nvfail with exactly the checker's volume set; clean shutdowns never trip; intent write p99 under 2 ms with a metadata class and under 300 ms under load without one.
8. **GC, reserves, scrub**: cost-benefit victim selection, 70/80/90, summary-driven scrub, clone fix-up walk. Exit: aged-pool drain curve at 70% and 80% published; scrub finds 100% of injected faults.
9. **Snapshots as objects**: scheduler, retention, autodelete, `Fsfreeze | Crash`, `.otap/snap` mounts with explicit fsids, clones. Exit: Windows 11 Previous Versions shows 24 hourlies through Samba 4.22; freeze window p99 under 3 s at 1 GB/s NFS ingest on an 80%-full pool; two snapshots of one volume return different bytes for the same path over NFS.
10. **The ublk front door**: `USER_COPY` as in 3.1, `VOLATILE_CACHE | FUA`, `UBLK_IO_OP_FLUSH`, `USER_RECOVERY` with `REISSUE`, both LUN classes. Exit: 50 K 4 KiB IOPS on at most 4 cores; engine p50 under 5 us and p99 under 15 us at QD1; the `io_uring_queue_async_work` tracepoint never fires; legacy copy measured; zero duplicate applies over 100 kills.
11. **Replication groundwork**: `DeltaSource` in both modes, `otapctl volume dump --since <snap>` and `restore` into a second aggregate. Exit: dump, restore and full-map digest equal for 1,000 random snapshot pairs, including pairs spanning intermediate snapshots.

**Phase B adds**: the TCP `DeltaSink`, `ShipApply`, nonce-keyed resume and per-group relationship state; lag and `applied_age_s` handed to Consensus' 1 s heartbeat; the conservative promotion set; resync in both directions with the divergent snapshot; `on_space_pressure`; the 2 GiB hold and 2 GiB receiver staging; my timer inputs (CP 10 s HDD and 5 s flash, `insync_lag_max` 25 s, lag warn 60 s, crit 600 s).

**Phase A adds**: aggregate import and export on shared disks (md assembled by the lease holder only, PR keys before `mdadm --add`), the epoch page check at CP submit and superblock completion, and the priced `ShelfSsdRing` option (two SAS SSDs as a RAID1 per-record FUA log, the only takeover path for unflushed acknowledged writes on a shelf).

##### 5. Open disagreements

- **Throttle under a controller's write-through window.** Consensus says raise the threshold and lengthen the CP timer; I say R7's 2 s cap and Transitioning stand, with the cause named. Settle by owner decision after item 5 measures a forced learn cycle.
- **`insync_lag_max`.** Consensus says 20 s; Fabrics says 3 × CP; I say 2 × timer + 5 s (25 s HDD) with the forced receiver CP. Settle by the Phase B applied-age measurement.
- **Root volume class.** Consensus says follow the strictest data volume; Protocols and I say `alert` plus the content check. Owner decision D5, presented once in 3.7.
- **`--write-journal` on RAID6.** C21 calls it the only in-md closure; I say strict full-stripe allocation makes it unnecessary and its bitmap exclusion makes it costly. Settle by item 5's forced dirty-degraded test; if a committed block is lost, the journal becomes mandatory.
- **Hold release.** Protocols wants a receiver-durable `Landed` credit; Fabrics and I release on disk plus `NOTIF`. Settle in Fabrics' credit design: if credits are free receiver staging stripes (Consensus F4), the two coincide.

##### 6. Answers to questions addressed to me

No cross-examination carried a numbered question list for me; these answer the asks embedded in their fixes.

- **Protocols (gate inputs on disk; one memory table; `size_max`; the freeze refusal).** Superblock v2 carries `applied_cp_seq`, `applied_owner_epoch`, `cp_age_at_send_ms`, `recv_mono` and `boot_id` per inbound group; a `boot_id` mismatch makes lag `Unknown` (Fabrics C1). The memory table is 3.9. `size_max` is enforced as in C10. `cut_within(deadline)` is the promise your scheduler needs: refuse a scheduled NAS snapshot when it returns `Busy`, never take a crash-consistent one silently.
- **Fabrics (hold ownership; window; `cp_nonce`; chunk header; send source).** The hold is mine, consumed only when the link is slower than staging; your 4 × 16 MiB `SO_SNDBUF` window sits well below it. `cp_nonce` is 64 random bits per cut, not derived; your frame header carries it. The staging pool is the only registered send source; the arena is never registered for sends.
- **Consensus (lag channel; nvfail truth; direction epoch; no-quorum posture; base out of Raft).** I report `applied_age_s`, `landed_age_s`, `cps_behind` and `bytes_behind` on your 1 s control heartbeat and concede 60 s for `max_auto_takeover_lag`. The aggregate's superblock is authoritative for nvfail and the clear; your `NvFail` op mirrors it with the audit. Your per-volume direction epoch is what `DeltaSink::begin` checks. Under a no-quorum freeze the engine keeps serving and keeps shipping. The base lives in both snapshot tables; Raft holds the direction epoch and the relationship label only (your C5). Your P7 `nvfail_generation` is my per-volume `rollback_gen`, bumped on every rollback and folded by `nbladed` into the export fsid.

### Opus-Protocols

#### Opus-Protocols, round 3: responses, fact-check consequences, revised SVM and protocol design

Scope note: the other personas' round-1 texts are not on disk; section 6 answers the asks identifiable from their cross-examinations. New load-bearing claims were fetched today; the rest is marked [believed].

##### 1. Responses to holes raised against me

###### Opus-Storage

**P1 (block move 8 to 15 s, mis-cited round 2). ACCEPT.** Phase B block LIFs become per-node and non-migrating, the SVM's target is instantiated on both nodes (`Presence::BlockStandby` extended to Phase B), the cutover is an ALUA flip at the CP boundary, and the ladder runs the block and NAS halves in parallel: block 1.5 to 2.5 s p50, NAS 4 to 8 s (3.9). I withdraw "a standby path would be a lie".

**P2 (one MAC on two nodes while a wedged node is on the wire). ACCEPT the gate, REJECT per-node MACs.** Per-(LIF, node) MACs make every takeover depend on clients accepting an unsolicited ARP (Windows unverified), so the persistent MAC stays.
