##### 4. Order of decisions

Before any persona's item 1 freezes a format or a wire: the nvfail enum and class table (rows 1 and 17); `Revert` versus rollback (row 3); the send source and hold-release event (row 6); ublk sizes and thick-versus-thin NAS (rows 7 and 8); the per-segment geometry field (claim 19); the Raft store's location and pool self-description (gap 5). Everything else in sections 1 and 2 can land in the timer table, the work-item lists and the documentation plan without reopening a frozen structure.


### critic:ontap-veteran

#### OpenTAP Session 03 review: the revised designs against clustered ONTAP

Reviewer: ten years of clustered ONTAP administration (SVMs, junctions, LIFs and failover groups, NPIV FC LIFs, SnapMirror and SnapRestore, nvfail, FlexClone, QoS, vsadmin, MetroCluster), now a homelab. Read in full: the revision-3 brief, the four original designs, the four revised positions and the forty fact-check verdicts.

Method note: docs.netapp.com refuses automated fetches (HTTP 403 on every page tried), so each ONTAP citation below was verified through indexed excerpts of the NetApp CLI reference, the NetApp KB, or NetApp-authored mirrors (AWS FSx, Lenovo). Where I could not reach a primary text the claim is marked [believed]. Nothing was installed, built or run.

##### 1. The frame an ONTAP administrator brings, and where the project sits in it

ONTAP has four protection products and the vocabulary of each is load-bearing:

- HA pair. NVRAM is mirrored to the partner; "on failover, the surviving partner commits the failed node's uncommitted write requests to disk" [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/concepts/high-availability-pairs-concept.html]. `storage failover takeover` and `giveback` are lossless and routine (we did them at lunchtime for upgrades).
- SnapMirror async. Scheduled snapshot deltas, a practical floor of one cron minute [believed], manual `break` and `resync`, never automatic.
- SnapMirror active sync. Synchronous, RPO 0; automatic unplanned failover exists only here and only with an ONTAP Mediator in a third failure domain; without the Mediator, I/O continues but no automatic failover is possible [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/snapmirror-active-sync/prerequisites-reference.html].
- MetroCluster. Synchronous plexes plus switchover; nvfail's documentation lives here.

The revised designs place Phase B as SVM DR over async SnapMirror with identity preserved, plus an automation ONTAP deliberately does not offer; Phase A is an HA pair whose NVRAM is not mirrored, so a shelf takeover is still a rollback unless `ShelfSsdRing` exists.

| ONTAP term | Guarantee | OpenTAP revised equivalent | Loss on the event |
|---|---|---|---|
| `storage failover takeover` | zero loss | Phase B promotion; Phase A takeover | one CP + ship + lease (B); one CP interval (A) |
| `snapmirror break` | destination writable at the exported snapshot; source untouched and unfenced | promotion at the last applied CP, lease and epoch fence | the lag |
| `snapmirror resync` (reversed) | destination data newer than the common snapshot deleted | returner rolls back to the common base, `divergent-<ts>` kept 7 d | none extra |
| SVM DR activation | `quiesce`, `abort`, `break`, `vserver stop`, `vserver start`, by hand | one Raft op, fenced | the lag |
| Automatic unplanned failover | RPO 0 with Mediator | automatic within `nvfail_force_lag` 60 s, `hold` beyond | the lag |

The mechanics are copied well. The vocabulary is not, and that is the first correction in section 12.

##### 2. SnapMirror semantics

###### 2.1 Base snapshot

ONTAP: `snapmirror resync` "finds the most recent common Snapshot copy between the source and destination volumes, removes Snapshot copies on the destination volume that are newer than the common Snapshot copy", and the reference warns it "can cause data loss on the destination volume because the command can remove the exported Snapshot copy"; `-preserve` keeps the newer destination snapshots, XDP only [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-cli/snapmirror-resync.html]. Any common snapshot is a valid base, user or scheduled, which is why a relationship broken for a week resyncs from last Sunday's weekly instead of a baseline.

OpenTAP: the newest common snapshot is pinned on both sides, scheduled snapshots are candidate bases, `Broken` recovers from the newest common scheduled snapshot, resync walks `birth > C`. Copied correctly. The divergent head pinned for `divergent_snapshot_keep = 7d` is ONTAP's `-preserve` made the default, which is better than ONTAP. One nuance to name: Storage's catch-up now materialises every retained snapshot in order (F-S3), which is the `MirrorAllSnapshots` policy; `MirrorLatest` and vault retention that differs on the destination do not exist. Fine for a homelab, but say so.

###### 2.2 Lag

ONTAP lag time is the destination's current time minus the creation time of the newest snapshot it holds; the KB is explicit that a wrong clock or time zone produces a wrong lag [verified: https://kb.netapp.com/on-prem/ontap/DP/SnapMirror/SnapMirror-KBs/How_is_SnapMirror_lag_time_calculated]. OpenTAP's `applied_age_s` from `cut_mono` with the `boot_id` guard and `Unknown` treated as unbounded is strictly better. Keep `landed_age_s` for the dashboard but show the operator one number called lag, in `h:m:s` like `snapmirror show -fields lag-time`.

###### 2.3 Cadence and throttle

ONTAP throttles the transfer, never the clients: `-throttle` caps a relationship in KB/s, minimum effective value 4 KB/s, applied at the next update [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-cli/snapmirror-modify.html]. OpenTAP ships every CP (applied age 8 to 19 s at 300 MB/s ingest on 10GbE with an HDD receiver, Fabrics' figure) and has no throttle at all. The first homelab whose DAC dies and whose stream falls back to the shared 1GbE LAN will have replication eating 110 MB/s of the family's network during the day. Add `throttle_kbps` per pipe and per endpoint (DAC unlimited, LAN capped).

###### 2.4 Break, and the writes on the old source

ONTAP break makes the destination writable: "the restart checkpoint is cleared and the clients can see the latest Snapshot copy", and later updates fail until resync [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-cli/snapmirror-break.html]. The old source is not fenced; it keeps acknowledging writes. For SVM DR the documented activation order is quiesce, abort, break, `vserver stop` on the source, `vserver start` on the destination, because two live SVMs with one identity cannot coexist [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/data-protection/make-svm-destination-volumes-writeable-task.html].

OpenTAP: promotion is at the last applied CP (the exported snapshot); the lease, the epoch page and the `arping -D` gate mean the old source cannot acknowledge after TTL plus margin; its DRAM window is gone and its committed-but-unshipped CPs become the divergent snapshot. This copies the mechanics and fixes ONTAP's split-brain-by-design. The one misunderstanding is a name: the project's `Broken` means "no common base survives"; ONTAP's `Broken-off` means "destination is writable and the relationship is intact". Every ONTAP admin will read the alert wrongly.

###### 2.5 Reverse resync direction

ONTAP reverses by running `resync` with the paths swapped: the old source becomes the destination, its data newer than the common snapshot is deleted, and a second break-plus-resync flips back. Consensus' R-a to R-f (survivor is always the source, direction reverses only through a planned migration, resync rides the ordinary stream) are the same rules with the fence added. Correct.

###### 2.6 Restore from the replica

`snapmirror restore` restores a snapshot, or a file list, from the destination back to the source, incrementally when a common snapshot exists [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/data-protection/restore-single-file-lun-task.html]. OpenTAP has no reverse restore; `dump --since` to a file is the Phase C bridge. A gap, listed in section 10.

##### 3. nvfail and the forcing switches

ONTAP: `volume modify -nvfail on` makes ONTAP detect NVRAM inconsistencies at boot, on MetroCluster switchover, or during an HA takeover if the option is set on the volume; on trigger the volume enters `in-nvfailed-state`, ONTAP "returns a stale file handle (ESTALE) error to NFS clients", CIFS clients are unaffected, and LUNs in the volume are brought offline; the clear is `volume modify -in-nvfailed-state false` at advanced privilege plus `lun online` per LUN [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-metrocluster/manage/concept_monitoring_and_protecting_database_validity_by_using_nvfail.html]. The forcing switches are `-dr-force-nvfail on` per volume (force processing on switchover without NVRAM evidence) and `metrocluster switchover -force-nvfail-all`, which sets it on every DR volume [verified: https://pubs.lenovo.com/mcc-metrocluster_ip_installation_and_configuration_guide/363B203E-2ACB-4AFC-981A-24597E8AEF4F_]. The default is off. The famous side effect is `lun online` failing with "The volume is in nvfailed state" after a routine takeover and giveback [verified: https://kb.netapp.com/on-prem/ontap/OHW/OHW-KBs/lun_online_fails_with_Error_The_volume_is_in_nvfailed_state].

Copied correctly: the persisted per-volume flag (`nvfail` bitset, `nvfail_cause`, `rollback_gen`), the explicit clear command, the NFS answer as ESTALE through a new `fsid` generation, LUN removal (PDL instead of ONTAP's offline, which C01 justifies because an offline LUN keeps ESXi in APD), and the class table with the SVM root as its own row. Also correct, and a deliberate departure: defaulting datastore classes to on. In ONTAP the trigger is suspected loss; in OpenTAP a dirty boot is certain loss of up to one CP of acknowledged writes, so ONTAP's default-off would be wrong here.

Misunderstood or missing:

1. ONTAP's two switches are per volume. Consensus has class defaults and `nvfail_force_lag` (the `-force-nvfail-all` analogue), but a database owner who wants the Oracle LUN volume held on every promotion, even at 3 s of lag, has no `dr_force_nvfail` equivalent. Add it per volume.
2. ONTAP clears per volume, then per LUN. `otapctl nvfail clear --svm X` is a convenience; the primitive must be per volume, because the admin wants the home-directory volume back while the datastore waits for the VMware host check.
3. In ONTAP clearing is rare; in Phase C every power cut on a single node is an nvfail event on every active datastore volume. The printout, the clear and the ESXi steps become the most exercised UX in the product. Measure it: one datastore with ten VMs, boot to serving 10 s, operator reads the alert and clears 10 s, ESXi rescan 30 s, VM restarts 60 s, about 2 minutes [believed; assumption: the operator is at the console].
4. Say in the class table that ONTAP's default is off. `alert` for the file class is already stricter than ONTAP; Consensus' `fence` (new fsid plus smbd restart) is ONTAP's nvfail-on behaviour. Admins choosing between them should know which one is the familiar one.

##### 4. SVM and LIF failover

ONTAP: a failover group is the set of ports a LIF may use; policies are `broadcast-domain-wide`, `system-defined` (home node plus one other node, the default for NAS data LIFs), `local-only` (home node only, the default for cluster, node-management and intercluster LIFs), `sfo-partner-only`, and `disabled` (SAN data LIFs) [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/networking/configure_failover_settings_on_a_lif.html]; `auto-revert` returns the LIF to its home node and port once the home port is healthy [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/networking/revert_a_lif_to_its_home_port.html]. NAS LIFs fail over to any node without the volumes moving, because every node serves every volume over the cluster interconnect, and `volume move` relocates a volume between aggregates or nodes non-disruptively [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-system-manager-classic/online-help-96-97/task_moving_flexvol_volumes_between_aggregates_or_nodes.html].

OpenTAP revised: NAS LIFs are macvlan with a persistent MAC; a port failure re-parents the LIF on the same node (that is `local-only`); cross-node movement happens only with the SVM (`FollowSvm`); block LIFs are per node and static with ALUA deciding the live path (that is `disabled` plus ALUA, exactly ONTAP SAN). Copied correctly as far as it goes. Missing: home node and home port as fields, `auto-revert`, a `revert` verb, and a definition of "port" under bonding. With `bond0.<vlan>` as the parent, a single cable loss is invisible and the only failure is the whole bond, so "another port of the same broadcast domain on this node" needs the broadcast domain defined as a set of `(node, port)` pairs with a reachability check, not just a VLAN. The honest statement for the UI: in OpenTAP a LIF is never on a node that does not own the data; "LIF failover" means port failover, and cross-node failover is an SVM event.

```rust
pub struct LifSpec {
    pub id: LifId, pub svm: SvmId, pub kind: LifKind,          // Nas | Block { node }
    pub transport: Transport,                                   // Ip { addr, vlan, mac } | Fc { wwpn, wwnn }
    pub home_node: NodeId, pub home_port: PortId,               // ONTAP -home-node / -home-port
    pub failover_group: BroadcastDomainId,                      // set of (node, port) in one L2 domain
    pub failover_policy: LifFailover,                           // LocalOnly | FollowSvm | Disabled (block)
    pub auto_revert: bool,                                      // revert when home_port is healthy again
    pub current: Option<(NodeId, PortId)>,                      // runtime, never in Raft
}
```

##### 5. Junction behaviour when a volume is offline

ONTAP: `volume offline` or `restrict` unmounts the junction, so the path disappears from the namespace and clients lose access to the volume and to everything junctioned below it [verified: https://kb.netapp.com/on-prem/ontap/da/NAS/NAS-KBs/Volume_offline_or_restrict_command_will_unmount_volume_junction-path]; an inactive junction is shown in parentheses, `(homevol)/childvol` [verified: https://kb.netapp.com/on-prem/ontap/da/NAS/NAS-KBs/Volume_is_unavailable_for_clients_and_has_parentheses_added_to_the_junction_path]; a volume that is merely unreachable (node or aggregate down) but still mounted makes the parent directory listing hang until the root inode can be looked up (`nblade.junctionRootLookup2`) [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-ems-9131/nblade-junctionrootlookup2-events.html]. A junction is not a directory in the parent's storage; nothing can ever be written into it.

OpenTAP: a junction is a bind mount over a directory that exists in the root volume's XFS. When the child is unmounted (nvfail, a failed mount at start, the stop ladder) the directory remains: empty, writable, and still exported, because the export carries an explicit `fsid=` from the volume table and knfsd exports whatever sits at the path. NFSv4.1 pseudo-root traversal shows `/vm` as an empty directory; ESXi runs as root and the datastore export is `no_root_squash`, so a host that reconnects during the outage creates `.lck` files and vmdks on the 1 GiB root volume and masks the outage until the root volume fills. ONTAP cannot do this. This is the most dangerous misunderstanding in the SVM design. Fix: mount-point directories owned by root with mode 000 and the immutable attribute (`chattr +i`; mounting over an immutable directory is permitted [believed], and C3's exit test should prove it), exports added only after the mount is verified and removed before the unmount, children unmounted with the parent, and the parenthesised junction state in `otapctl volume show`. Then decide hang versus error explicitly: ESTALE on nvfail, hang on a planned move so clients retry. Protocols' NAS-LIF-down-first ladder already gives the second half.

##### 6. The snapshot directory and SnapRestore

ONTAP: `.snapshot` over NFS is reachable from every directory in the volume and listed only at the root [believed, from experience; `-snapdir-access` governs it: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/data-protection/enable-disable-snapshot-dir-access-task.html]; `~snapshot` over SMB works from the share root and every junction point but not from other subdirectories, and Previous Versions depends on the same option [verified: https://kb.netapp.com/on-prem/ontap/Ontap_OS/OS-KBs/What_is_the_difference_between_the_CIFS_share_property_showsnapshot_and_volume_option_snapdir_access]. `volume snapshot restore` reverts a volume in seconds regardless of size and deletes the snapshots newer than the target; `-force` restores past the snapshot SnapMirror uses as its reference, "this will cause future SnapMirror transfers to fail", repairable with resync if a common snapshot remains [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-cli/volume-snapshot-restore.html]. Single-file SnapRestore shares blocks: no copy and no new space [believed].

OpenTAP revised: snapshots are mounted read-only outside share roots at `/vol/<svm>_root/.otap/snap/<vol>/@GMT-...`, each with its own export and deterministic `fsid` (C19), Previous Versions through `vfs_shadow_copy2` with `shadow:snapdir` set explicitly because the module's default is `.snapshots` [verified: https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/vfs_shadow_copy2.8.html]; an in-junction `.snapshot` is Phase B; automounts are capped at 8 per SVM with a 300 s idle timeout and cost one ublk device each (`ublks_max` 4096). Volume rollback exists only inside `nvfail-clear --restore` and resync; `rollback_gen` exists; there is no user-facing `volume snapshot restore` and no file-level restore primitive.

Verdict: the cheapest feature the admin uses most is absent from Phase C. `.snapshot` at the volume root under the junction is a day-one expectation; matching ONTAP's SMB root-and-junction-only behaviour is acceptable because XFS mounts cannot appear in every directory. Numbers: a 100 GB vmdk restored by copying from a snapshot mount at 1 GB/s takes 100 s and consumes 100 GB of new space; ONTAP's single-file SnapRestore is a block-map operation, seconds and no new space [believed]. Ship copy-restore now with the cost printed; a block-sharing file restore (resolve the file's extents in the snapshot with `xfs_bmap`, re-reference the same PBAs under the live root's map) is an engine feature for Phase 3, and reflink is no help because the snapshot is a different filesystem. Volume SnapRestore must be a first-class verb with the SnapMirror interaction specified: both sides hold the target snapshot (it is common), so the replica rolls back to the same snapshot instead of ONTAP's resync-and-discard, which is simpler than ONTAP; a restore past the base needs `--force` and a CRIT, exactly like ONTAP.

##### 7. FlexClone

ONTAP: a clone from any snapshot locks that snapshot (`busy,vclone`) until the clone is split or deleted; a split copies shared blocks in a low-priority background job and on non-AFF systems deletes the clone's own snapshots, which can break the clone's SnapMirror [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-system-manager-classic/online-help-96-97/task_splitting_flexclone_volume_from_its_parent_volume.html and https://kb.netapp.com/on-prem/ontap/Ontap_OS/OS-KBs/FAQ_-_FlexClone_split]; the clone lives in the parent's aggregate [believed]; cloning a SnapMirror destination is the standard DR test.

OpenTAP: a child root as a new LUN or a NAS volume with `xfs_admin -U generate`, `Clone(vol)` pins that autodelete never touches, and the logical-segment relocation tables that stop a pinned block from pinning a whole stripe. Copied correctly, including the pin. Missing: split (a re-birth of every shared block: a 2 TB clone 10 percent diverged rewrites 1.8 TB, 25 minutes at 1.2 GB/s on an empty pool, 75 minutes at 0.4 GB/s aged, so throttle it like catch-up at 30 percent of read bandwidth), clone-of-replica on the receiver while the relationship stays Steady (the DR test), and an `owners` column in `snapshot show` so the admin sees why a snapshot will not delete.

##### 8. The vsadmin role

ONTAP's predefined SVM roles: `vsadmin` manages volumes except volume moves, quotas, qtrees, snapshots, files and LUNs, configures NFS, SMB and iSCSI and the DNS, LDAP and NIS services, and only monitors network interfaces, so it cannot create LIFs; `vsadmin-volume`, `vsadmin-protocol`, `vsadmin-backup` (SnapMirror, snapshots, make a restored volume writable), `vsadmin-snaplock` and `vsadmin-readonly` scope it down [verified: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/roles-and-users.html, a mirror of https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/authentication/predefined-roles-svm-administrators-concept.html]. A vsadmin never sees another SVM.

OpenTAP defers RBAC to Phase B, which is fine; what is not fine is the Raft shape. `SvmSpec` embeds LIFs, junctions, exports, shares and QoS in one object, so tenant-scoped authorisation would need either a rewrite or a field-level policy engine. ONTAP's split maps directly: tenant objects (volumes, snapshots and their policies, LUNs, igroups, exports, shares, S3 users, DNS, QoS policy groups) carry an `svm` owner; cluster objects (aggregates, nodes, ports, broadcast domains, LIF creation, relationships) do not. Protocols asked Consensus exactly this question. Decide it before `otap-format` and the Raft schema freeze.

##### 9. QoS policy groups

ONTAP: a named policy group per SVM with `-max-throughput` in IOPS and/or MB/s (`500iops,10MB/s`), `-min-throughput` floors, and `-is-shared`, default true, which "specifies if the SLOs of the policy group are shared between the workloads or if the SLOs are applied separately to each workload" [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-cli/qos-policy-group-create.html]; assignable to SVMs, volumes, LUNs, files and qtrees; before 9.18.1 "you cannot assign a storage object to a policy group if its containing object or its child objects belong to a policy group", and from 9.18.1 nested policies apply the most restrictive one [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap/performance-admin/policy-group-assignment-restrictions.html]. It counts client protocol operations.

OpenTAP: `QosPolicy { max_iops, max_mbps, burst_ms }` attached directly to a volume, a token bucket in the ublk handler that delays and never fails, a 1 s hold cap, `REQ_META` bypass and per-bdi dirty caps for NAS, SVM buckets in Phase B, floors deferred. Three misunderstandings: there is no named policy object, so "change one policy and twenty volumes follow" and the shared-versus-per-member distinction do not exist; the IOPS counted are ublk requests behind the page cache, so a client re-reading a hot 10 GB working set from the SVM's page cache is not throttled at all and thirty-two 32 KiB NFS reads that XFS coalesces into one 1 MiB request count as one, while an ONTAP admin who sets 1,000 IOPS expects 1,000 client operations; and nesting is cheap to design now as two buckets in series. Recommend `QosPolicyGroup { svm, name, max_iops, max_mbps, min_iops: reserved, is_shared }` as a Raft object assignable to volumes and LUNs in Phase C and to SVMs in Phase B, default `is_shared = false`, and a one-line warning in the docs that OpenTAP QoS limits storage I/O rather than client operations.

##### 10. What an ONTAP administrator would miss first, in order

1. `cd .snapshot` under the junction and a file-level restore that costs seconds, not a copy.
2. The `snapmirror show` one-liner: lag, state (`Snapmirrored`, `Broken-off`), status (`Idle`, `Transferring`, `Quiesced`), healthy and unhealthy reason, last transfer size and duration; plus `update`, `quiesce`, `abort` and `-throttle`.
3. Lossless takeover for maintenance. A planned migration at 1.5 to 2.5 s of block pause, SMB handle loss and NFSv4.1 grace is acceptable, but it is not SFO, and nobody should be told it is.
4. LIF mobility independent of data, `auto-revert`, and `volume move`.
5. `volume snapshot restore` as a verb, with `-force`.
6. FlexClone split and DR-test clones on the destination.
7. QoS as named policy groups, with floors and adaptive IOPS per TB.
8. vsadmin tenant self-service.
9. Named export policies with ordered rules reused across volumes; the project writes per-export client lists like `/etc/exports`.
10. Storage efficiency (dedupe and compression, Phase 3) and the `volume show` space columns.

##### 11. What ONTAP does that this project must not copy

1. The unfenced break. After `snapmirror break` the old source keeps acknowledging writes and nothing arbitrates; the project's lease, epoch page and `arping -D` gate are the correct departure. Keep them.
2. Wall-clock lag. A wrong time zone on the destination yields a wrong lag in ONTAP; the project's monotonic `cut_mono` plus `boot_id` is right. Keep it.
3. nvfail firing on every HA takeover and giveback when a volume has it on. It generates "LUNs offline after giveback" tickets and teaches admins to leave nvfail off. OpenTAP must trigger only on evidence: a dirty boot, or a promotion with `write_active` set or lag Unknown.
4. The five-step manual SVM DR activation and the `vserver stop` prerequisite. One fenced verb.
5. `-is-shared = true` as the QoS default; it surprises everyone the first time two volumes share one ceiling. Default non-shared.
6. The pre-9.18.1 QoS nesting ban. Allow an SVM ceiling and a volume ceiling with the most restrictive winning.
7. The non-AFF FlexClone split that deletes the clone's snapshots. In a birth-stamped log-structured map a split can keep them; do.
8. Snapshot reserve (`-percent-snapshot-space`) and fractional reserve for LUNs. Twelve years of confused tickets; the project already dropped per-volume reserves in favour of aggregate accounting plus autodelete. Keep them dropped.
9. Autodelete's `destroy` commitment level, which deletes snapshots locked by clones and removes the clones [verified: https://docs.netapp.com/us-en/ontap-cli/volume-snapshot-autodelete-modify.html]. The project's "never a replication base or a clone parent" is `try`; the `on_space_pressure = break` policy is `disrupt`. Name them so, and never offer `destroy`.
10. The any-node-serves-any-volume namespace promise. Without a remote data path OpenTAP cannot honour it; the UI must never show a LIF on a node that does not own the data.
11. 7-mode `nvfail_rename` (renaming suspect files). Never.
12. `volume offline` silently unmounting the junction while clients hold handles. Pick the explicit semantics of section 5.

##### 12. Ten things to tell the lead architect before the Phase C plan is frozen

1. Fix the vocabulary now, in `otap-format` and the CLI. "Takeover" and "giveback" are reserved for lossless events and OpenTAP has none before `ShelfSsdRing`; use "failover" and "failback" with the rollback bound printed. Rename the relationship state `Broken` to `NoCommonBase`, and use ONTAP's `Broken-off` for a promoted replica with an intact relationship. Print the ONTAP equivalent in every help text.
2. Move `.snapshot` at the volume root and `otapctl volume snapshot restore` into Phase C (they are extensions of Storage's items 6 and 9), with the per-snapshot `fsid` rule from C19, the "replica rolls back to the same snapshot" rule, `--force` past the base, and copy-restore for files with its cost printed. Budget the device count: 64 volumes with ONTAP's usual 35 snapshots each are 2,240 potential mounts, so the 8-per-SVM automount cap is load-bearing and belongs in the exit test.
3. Close the junction mount-point hole: immutable mode-000 mount points, export only after a verified mount, unmount children with parents, parenthesised junction state, and the ESTALE-on-nvfail versus hang-on-move rule, all in C3's exit test with an ESXi host writing to a junction whose volume is unmounted.
4. nvfail: per-volume `nvfail` and a per-volume `dr_force_nvfail` equivalent beside Consensus' `nvfail_force_lag`; a per-volume clear primitive under the SVM-wide convenience; the "ONTAP default is off" line in the class table; and a measured boot-to-VMs-running number for the single-node power-cut case, because it will happen monthly in a homelab.
5. LIFs: add home node and home port, failover group as a set of `(node, port)`, the three policies `local-only`, `follow-svm` and `disabled`, `auto-revert` and a `revert` verb, and define what a port is under LACP before C2 measures the 2 s port-move pause.
6. Replication operator surface: a `rel show` line with lag, state, status, healthy, unhealthy reason and last transfer; `update`, `quiesce` and `abort` verbs; and a per-pipe, per-endpoint `throttle_kbps`, needed on the day the LAN fallback first carries the stream.
7. FlexClone split in Phase C+1 with the 30 percent read-share throttle and the cost model above; receiver-side clone parents in Phase B so a DR test never breaks the relationship, exactly as ONTAP admins do it.
8. QoS as named policy groups per SVM with explicit `is_shared`, nested most-restrictive, and the documented "storage I/O, not client operations" counting; reserve `min_iops` in the format now even though floors are deferred.
9. Split the Raft object model into `svm`-owned and cluster-owned objects before the schema freezes, so vsadmin in Phase B is a policy layer and not a migration; Protocols' question about LIFs and junctions as top-level objects is the same decision.
10. On automatic failover: ONTAP automates only RPO-0 replication with a Mediator and leaves async failover to a human, for the reason Consensus' gate re-derived. The revertible `hold` posture for LUNs is a sound improvement and I endorse it. `fence` for the file class is an automatic data-loss decision; make it an install-time acknowledgement that prints the bound ("up to 60 s of acknowledged NAS writes are discarded on an unplanned failover") and default to `hold` when the operator declines.


### critic:homelab-operator

(Recovered from the critic's working file review.md; see the provenance note at the top.)

#### Session 03, reviewed by the person who installs it

**Who is talking.** Three Proxmox 8.4 nodes on R730xd (a PERC H730 Mini in one, HBA330 Minis in two, 128 GB each), one ESXi 8.0 U3 host on an R740xd with a ConnectX-4, because ESXi 8 has no driver for my ConnectX-3s (section 6). QLE2562 8G cards in everything and a Brocade 300 I power on twice a year. ConnectX-3 10/40GbE in the Linux boxes. A Pi 4 running DNS and NUT. Windows 11 and Debian clients. Five years of TrueNAS CORE, one year of Ceph. I left TrueNAS because the free edition has no failover and the sync=disabled-versus-SLOG argument never ends; I left Ceph because three nodes with twelve OSDs is a science project. I read the brief, the eight design texts and the forty verdicts. This is what I think with `apt` open in the other window.

##### 1. Verdict in one paragraph

Build it, in this order, with four changes. The pivot turned OpenTAP into something I recognise: ZFS with sync=disabled and a 10 s transaction group, plus honest alerts, plus the two-node failover that free TrueNAS does not have and Ceph cannot do on two boxes. The changes: (1) the PLP-NVMe durable log comes back into v0.1 as a per-aggregate opt-in; (2) the identity bump (`strict`) is never a default on a LUN a Linux host uses; (3) there is a VM-sized evaluation profile; (4) Fibre Channel and S3 leave v0.1. Without (1) I cannot host my database VM; without (2) Phase B breaks every Proxmox cluster that upgrades; without (3) most people never reach the R730xd; without (4) v0.1 ships in 2028.

##### 2. C, then B, then A

Yes, that order, and A last because for me it does not exist: my drives are in the front bays, not in an MD1200, and that is true of nearly everyone with a used Dell. Phase A is "when someone with a shelf shows up". Phase B is the product. Phase C is the price of Phase B, and the one promise I will hold you to is the one Storage and Consensus both make: no reformat and no reinstall from v0.1 to v0.2, `otap-format` v2 and `otap-stream` v1 frozen in Phase C with property tests. If v0.2 says "recreate the aggregate", I am gone, with everyone who put 40 TB on v0.1.

What I do not want is Phase C as scoped. I count 38 work items across the four plans, each with an exit test that needs a lab: 50 real power cuts, 20 reboots of two QLogic pairs, a Brocade F_Port, ESXi 8.0 U3, Proxmox 9.1, Veeam 13, an AD forest with two domains. That is not v0.1; that is v1.0 with the ribbon still on. The v0.1 I would install: iSCSI with ALUA advertised from day one, NFSv3 datastore SVMs, NFSv4.1 and SMB file SVMs with Previous Versions, snapshots as objects, nvfail, `dump --since` to a file, mdadm and PERC backstores. FC is step 3 in the brief, fine, but as step 3 of Phase C it drags eight Fabrics items in front of the first Phase B commit; make it step 1 of Phase B. S3 on a gateway whose wiki calls versioning experimental and whose Object Lock fix is in no tagged release (C40) is not something I point Veeam at in a v0.1 either.

##### 3. Losing 15 seconds

Call it what it is. On one node a power cut loses the unflushed arena: one CP, min(10 s, 4 GiB / ingest) on HDD, 5 s on flash, and a guest `fsync` changes nothing because FLUSH is an ordering barrier, not a disk barrier (round-2 ruling, carried forward). On two nodes, Fabrics' own arithmetic gives an `applied_age` of 8 to 19 s on HDD at 300 MB/s plus the 3 s lease, and Storage's `insync_lag_max` is 25 s before anyone is warned. The honest sentence is "up to 25 s on an HDD pair under load, 60 s before the takeover is held". "15 s" is the brochure.

Acceptable? For most of what I store, yes, because I already accepted it: ZFS's `zfs_txg_timeout` is 5 s [verified: https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/man/master/4/zfs.4.html], and sync=disabled on the VM dataset is what half of r/homelab runs on TrueNAS, me included for three years. 10 to 25 s is the same family, two to five times longer, and it is the first storage product that will tell me afterwards how much it lost and on which volumes. The four-fact printout (seconds, bytes, volumes, command) is worth more to me than the 15 s.

Where it is not acceptable: the Nextcloud Postgres VM, the SMB share I edit documents on, the SVM root. Those need what ZFS calls a SLOG. Storage has it, `LocalNvmeRing`, per-record FUA to a PLP NVMe at 10 to 20 us, and deferred it to "Phase C+1" because it contradicts "acknowledge at DRAM speed". I disagree with the deferral, not the default. An iSCSI round trip on my 10GbE is 100 to 150 us at the initiator by Protocols' own ladder, so 20 us of Optane on a volume I choose is invisible to the guest and visible only in your microbenchmark. I own a 118 GB Optane P1600X; the R740xd has U.2 bays; the R730xd takes a PCIe card. Ship the ring in v0.1 as `durable = nvme` per aggregate, off by default, with the window printout reading "0 s" for those volumes. Without it the single-node product is "a NAS that lies to fsync with no way to make it stop", which is the phrase the forum will use.

One more thing: Pivot 4's "no throttling" means the window is unbounded when the partner is away. If I reboot B for a kernel update and A dies twenty minutes later, the replica is twenty minutes old. Consensus' revised answer is right: promote into `hold`, acknowledge nothing, auto-revert if A returns with its superblock intact, make `nvfail clear` the irreversible step with the number in front of me. Keep exactly that.

##### 4. nvfail on by default for a Proxmox datastore?

Yes, with three conditions, argued against the Proxmox I actually run, because the designs describe one with dm-multipath and mine has none.

A stock Proxmox iSCSI datastore is `pvesm add iscsi`, one session per portal, LVM on top, no multipath unless built by hand from the wiki. The plugin touches no timeout except `initial_login_retry_max=0` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/proxmox/pve-storage/master/src/PVE/Storage/ISCSIPlugin.pm], so open-iscsi defaults apply: NOP-out every 5 s with a 5 s timeout, then `replacement_timeout` 120 s before commands fail back [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-iscsi/open-iscsi/master/etc/iscsid.conf]. Volumes are named `<store>:<ch>.<id>.<lun>.scsi-<wwid>` and resolved as `/dev/disk/by-id/<that>` [verified: same plugin]; an LVM storage on top stores the LUN volid as `base`, resolves it only at add time, and afterwards LVM finds the VG by PV UUID [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/proxmox/pve-storage/master/src/PVE/Storage/LVMPlugin.pm].

Against that client:

- **Power cut and reboot** (an R730xd POSTs in 3 to 5 minutes): the session dies at about 10 s, I/O fails at about 130 s, qemu passes the error to the guest (Proxmox leaves qemu's `werror=enospc` default [believed]), root filesystems go read-only, and nothing resumes silently except a VM that was idle the whole time. That idle VM is the only thing nvfail protects on Proxmox, and it is real: a DNS VM that writes hourly sails through a 5-minute outage, reconnects, and keeps a page cache 10 s ahead of its disk forever. So `hold` by default, and condition one: the clear must print "reset every VM on these LUNs, including the healthy-looking ones", because `qm` cannot tell them apart. Condition two follows: no auto-clear, not even behind a UPS, because the idle VM is precisely the one auto-clear hands the rolled-back LUN to.
- **The unmap itself:** with the LUN unlinked, the next command gets 05h/25h/00h and a single-path Linux host turns ILLEGAL REQUEST into EIO on the spot, not "after about 60 s plus detection". The 60 s exists only under dm-multipath's built-in LIO-ORG entry (C17). Every "Linux hosts get EIO about 60 s after the last path fails" row in Consensus' and Protocols' tables is a multipath row; label it so and add the single-path row, because single path is what `pvesm add iscsi` builds.
- **Condition three, the one I walk away over:** `strict` is never the default for a LUN a Linux host uses. A new `vpd_unit_serial` is a new `/dev/disk/by-id/scsi-<wwid>`; every VM using the LUN directly has a dead volid in its config, the LVM storage's `base` becomes a lie, and HA cheerfully tries the VM on another node that sees the same new name. Storage wants `strict` everywhere; Protocols wants it after unplanned Phase B takeovers; Consensus wants it for Linux and mixed hosts. All three are wrong for Proxmox. On a Linux host the dead node's path is irrelevant: scsi_dh_alua fails requests in Standby or Unavailable immediately and the unmap gives EIO immediately, so there is no silent resume for an identity change to prevent. Give `host_class = linux` unmap plus remap under the same serial, and keep the bump for ESXi, where the all-paths PDL rule (C01) genuinely forces it.

An NFS Proxmox datastore: yes, hard mount, VMs hang, export withheld, fsid bump on clear, ESTALE, qemu error, reset; same ladder, no identity problem. ESXi NFSv3 costs KB 344470: power off every VM, unmount, remount. I have done that dance after a TrueNAS reboot, twenty minutes in vCenter; once a year is acceptable, and the docs should say "twenty minutes", not "remount". File-class SVMs: `fence` or `alert`, never `hold`. A home share ten seconds old is a shrug; a home share offline until I SSH in is a phone call. Protocols and Consensus have this right; Fabrics' `hold` for the root volume is wrong for the same reason.

##### 5. The install and the first hour, with every place I stop

I do it the way everyone does: in a Proxmox VM first, then the HBA330 box, then the H730 box. Nobody describes the installer, so I reconstruct it from the TOML, the "installer refuses" sentences and the platform profile.

| Step | What the designs say | What I do | Give up? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Get it | "generic amd64 image", `otap-witness_<ver>_arm64.deb` | Look for an ISO or an apt repo. Neither is described anywhere. | **#1** if it is `cargo build` with a vendored `libublk`; 90% of the audience stops here. |
| 1. VM evaluation | 64 GB budget, busy-polled reactors on isolated cores, 8 GiB hugetlbfs at boot, a 112 GiB write probe at pool creation | Boot it in a 4-vCPU, 8 GB VM on virtio disks, like every TrueNAS trial ever. | **#2**: no small profile. "A 32 GB box halves the arena" is the smallest sentence in the designs. Add `profile = lab` (1 GiB arena, no isolation, no busy-poll, manual geometry) or lose the funnel. |
| 2. Host profile | `panic=-1 hardlockup_panic=1 ...`, softdog, hugepages, isolated cores, `ublks_max=4096` | Fine if the package writes it and reboots me once. | No, but busy-poll must be opt-in: four spinning Broadwell cores are 30 to 50 W, 60 to 120 EUR a year at 0.30/kWh, on a box idling at 110 W. Storage's "8 to 13 us with wakeups" is the default I want. |
| 3. Aggregate, HBA330 box | md sysfs geometry exact, probe as a check, no attestation | `mdadm --create` RAID6 10+2, 256 KiB chunk, bitmap; `otapctl aggregate create /dev/md0` | No. This is the happy path and should be the documented default for Dell owners. |
| 4. Aggregate, H730 box | VD is a plain disk, WCE=0, attestation required, `unknown` refused, `perccli` not in Debian | Download perccli from Dell (free, 20 minutes), run `/c0/v0 show all` and `/c0/bbu show all`, type the TOML by hand | Not a stop, but print the three commands and parse pasted output; better, tell me to flip the H730 to HBA mode (section 6) and skip the whole thing. |
| 5. Networking | `nbladed` creates `bond0` (802.3ad) and `bond0.<vlan>`; macvlan LIFs; MTU 9000 "recommended for datastores" | My Mikrotik has no LACP to that server and never will for a two-port box | **#3** if LACP is the only shape: single port, then active-backup, then LACP. **#4** if 9000 is a default; half the "mounts but hangs on copy" threads on every NAS forum are MTU. |
| 6. SVM, LIF, volume, LUN, igroup | `svm create` 0.5 s, TOML as in Protocols 2.9 | SVM `hv` from the datastore template, LIF on VLAN 100, volume, LUN 1, igroup with three Proxmox IQNs | No. LUN 1 not 0, `LIO-ORG`/`OpenTAP`, TPGS on: good choices, invisible to me, which is the point. CHAP must be optional; the Windows row reads as if mutual CHAP were a default. |
| 7. Proxmox | multipath-tools, empty conf plus `find_multipaths strict`, `multipath -a` | `pvesm add iscsi`, `pvesm add lvm --base ... --shared 1`; no multipath, I have one LIF | No, but write the single-path recipe first and the multipath one second; that is the order people build them. |
| 8. ESXi | `esxcli ... satp rule add ... VMW_PSP_RR`, `Disk.PathEvalTime=30`, guest timeouts 180 s | One esxcli line, rescan, VMFS6 | No. Correct that MRU is the default and the rule is mandatory. |
| 9. Windows 11 | MPIO rows, 60 s hold time | Single path; the client edition has no MPIO feature [believed], so ALUA is irrelevant and a Standby path is an error | No, but drop MPIO from the Windows 11 matrix; it belongs to Windows Server. |
| 10. First power pull (hour one, every time) | dirty boot, `write_active` union, `nvfail` set, CRIT with CP sequence, window, bytes, clear command | Pull the cord, wait for POST, read the alert, `otapctl volume nvfail-clear`, reset VMs | No, if the printout is what Storage 3.7 describes. **#5** if `strict` fires and my `by-id` names change. |
| 11. Day two | Prometheus metrics, no UI | Grafana | No. CLI plus metrics is fine for v0.1; a web UI is not why I left TrueNAS. |

Five stops, three in the first thirty minutes, none in the engine. That is the pattern: the hard parts are designed to the bone and the easy parts (packaging, a lab profile, the default network shape) are not designed at all.

##### 6. Hardware assumptions that are wrong for my gear

**PERC H730 and H730P.** Datasheet facts: SAS3108, PCIe 3.0 x8, 1 GB NV cache on the H730 and 2 GB on the H730P, "configurable stripe size up to 1 MB" [verified: https://pcserverandparts.com/content/Spec%20Sheets/Servers/Dell/Dell%20PowerEdge%20R630/Dell%20PowerEdge%20RAID%20Controller%20H730P%20Specifications.pdf]; the smallest PERC 9 strip is 64 KiB [believed; the HII utility offers 64K to 1M]. The fact checks got the controller right (WCE=0 presentation, no flush forwarding, transparent learn on PERC 8 and later), so on my card the write-through window is a dead battery, not a monthly event. What is wrong is the "256 KiB-stripe VD rule", "8 data drives at 32 KiB strips". PERC 9 cannot make a 32 KiB strip, and with 12 bays in RAID6 the smallest full stripe is 64 KiB x 10 = 640 KiB, two and a half of the 256 KiB commands an H730 accepts by default (C23). Either the rule becomes "enable `largeIOsupport` (1 MiB, needs a reboot) and keep strip x data disks under 1 MiB", or it admits what the write-back cache is for: in WB the controller coalesces the split, the probe shows no knee, and the rule only matters in the WT fallback, where everything is slow anyway. Write it that way or people will build 4-data-disk arrays to satisfy a sentence.

The bigger miss: PERC 9 has an HBA personality. Switched to HBA mode, every drive is a non-RAID pass-through that does not use the controller write cache and gets SYNCHRONIZE CACHE relayed (C07's JBOD branch; Dell's moderator on the `jbodwritecache` thread) [verified: https://www.dell.com/community/en/conversations/poweredge-hardware-general/disable-raid-on-perc-h730p/647fa125f4ccf8a8de655b57 and https://www.dell.com/community/en/conversations/poweredge-hardware-general/when-perccli-set-jbodwritecacheon-which-of-raid-controller-cache-or-hdd-cache-is-used/647f8048f4ccf8a8deef1890; forum answers, the user's guide PDF refused the fetch]. That turns an H730 into an HBA330 with slightly worse latency and makes your commit protocol honest on it: md sees real WCE from the drives, flush and FUA go where they claim, no attestation, no `flush-opaque` two-CP rule. For a storage OS that is the recommended configuration for every PERC 9 and 10 owner, and no design mentions it. The VD path should be the fallback for people who cannot reboot into HII, not the main road. Caveat: HBA mode is controller-wide, so boot disks are md RAID1 on two SSDs or a BOSS card.

**HBA330.** SAS3008, mpt3sas, no cache: the best case, and barely named. Geometry from `/sys/block/md0/md/*` is exact; SATA drives report WCE=1 and the kernel's flush and FUA reach them through md (C22); Dell-branded SAS drives often ship with write cache off, which costs full-stripe writes nothing and makes the FUA superblock stripe free. Two requests: say "IT-mode SAS3008/3108 plus mdadm is the reference configuration" in the install guide, and run the forced dirty-degraded test (Storage item 5) before v0.1, because the alternative, `--write-journal`, is a single SSD whose death makes a 100 TB array read-only and whose presence forbids the bitmap that turns a 20-hour resync into two minutes (C21). I will take strict full-stripe allocation plus bitmap if the test proves it; I will not take a journal SSD.

**QLE2562, 8G.** Firmware: the design is right and my memory was wrong. On 6.12 the ISP25xx path tries the request_firmware blob before flash and `ql2xfwloadbin=1` reroutes it to the flash-first path [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/qla2xxx/qla_init.c; `qla25xx_isp_ops` uses `qla24xx_load_risc` per https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/qla2xxx/qla_os.c], so the installer rule stands. The target side is fine. The initiator side is not: Fabrics' exit test says "ESXi 8.0 U3 with qlnativefc 5.4.80 sees the LUN", and Marvell's ESXi 8.0 U3 and 9.0 user guide is written for the 2600, 2700 and 2800 series; whether the inbox 8.0 driver still binds an ISP2532 I could not verify from a primary source [believed; the guide PDF refused the fetch and the KB 318385 device list is an unreadable attachment]. Before that sentence becomes an exit criterion, someone checks the HCL, and the ESXi half of the FC test gets a 16G QLE2692, which is what a 2026 lab buys anyway. My Proxmox nodes drive the QLE2562 with in-tree qla2xxx on 6.14 and 6.17 and do not care. NPIV LIFs need an F_Port fabric (C28), so in a direct-attach homelab FC LIFs do not exist and one SVM owns the port; say so in the first paragraph of the FC chapter, not in a bottleneck list.

**ConnectX-3.** ESXi 8.0 has no `nmlx4_en` driver at all [verified: https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/318385/devices-deprecated-and-unsupported-in-es.html], which is why my CX3s live in Linux boxes. On Linux the mlx4 PF has no `sriov_configure`, so VFs come from `num_vfs=` and `probe_vf=` at module load, not from `sriov_numvfs` [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/net/ethernet/mellanox/mlx4/main.c]. Protocols' SR-IOV row lists ixgbe, i40e and mlx5 with a sysfs write; add "mlx4: module parameter, VF count fixed at boot" or say macvlan only. The RDMA cut costs me nothing. What the CX3 is good for here: a 40GbE QSFP DAC between two CX3s is fifteen dollars and is the replication and control link Consensus wants, and an HDD pair lands 0.3 to 0.5 GB/s whatever the link, so the throughput table can stop there.

**Pi 4 witness.** BCM2711 has no ARMv8 crypto extensions [believed], and it does not matter: 30 messages per second of 1 KiB through rustls is a rounding error on a Cortex-A72. Delete "Pi 5 or container recommended". A Pi 4 on an SD card with fsyncs only on votes and appends is the right witness, and C38's note that Pi OS now ships a 6.18 kernel only means the witness must not depend on Debian's kernel, which it does not.

**The box.** 64 GB is the floor, not the typical: used R730xds carry 128 to 256 GB of cheap RDIMM, so the budget table is conservative, fine. POST is 3 to 5 minutes, which is why every dirty boot has already errored every Proxmox VM before `dbladed` starts, and why the only VMs nvfail saves are the idle ones.

##### 7. Client claims against what I have seen

**Proxmox iSCSI.** The kernel-side timing nobody wrote down: scsi_dh_alua attaches to any TPGS device; its prep function fails every request with `BLK_STS_IOERR` in Standby, Unavailable and Offline, passes them in Transitioning, and after the RTPG transition time (your `implicit_trans_secs=10`, else 60 s) flips a still-transitioning group to Standby [verified: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/drivers/scsi/device_handler/scsi_dh_alua.c]. On a single-path Proxmox host, Transitioning is free for 10 s and at second 11 the VM gets EIO. So 10 s is the real budget for every hold in every ladder: the 5 s p50 / 9 s p99 takeover fits; the wedged 11 to 13 s and the no-quorum `stop` (Unavailable at 13 s) do not. Consensus' D7 argument is written for ESXi guests at 180 s and Linux multipath at 60 s; for a stock Proxmox cluster `stop` means "every VM errors at 13 s", and the owner should see that number beside the split-brain argument. I still vote `stop`, a split brain is worse than a reset, but with the right number.

**Proxmox NFS.** Hard mounts, qcow2 on NFSv3 means NLM, and one global lockd thread per node (C13) means a stalled volume in one SVM stalls lock calls for every SVM. Protocols' "recommend NFSv4.1 for Proxmox datastores" is right; `options vers=4.1` is a one-liner on the storage. The `rpcinfo` activity check needs port 111 on the LIF, which the nftables ruleset allows.

**ESXi.** NFSv3 matches my TrueNAS years exactly: every WRITE is stable, which is why ESXi on NFS crawls unless sync is disabled or there is a SLOG, and why OpenTAP acknowledging from DRAM will feel fast; a datastore whose server rebooted goes grey, VMs hang, and it returns by itself only if the handles still resolve, which the fsid bump prevents on purpose. iSCSI: MRU is the default PSP, the RR rule is mandatory, the PDL-on-all-paths rule (C01) is a fact of life. Consensus' idea of answering 25h/00h on the dead node's block LIF from the survivor is the only way ESXi ever reaches PDL on an unplanned takeover; it is the right lab item.

**Windows 11.** Single-path iSCSI, 60 s hold on session loss, no MPIO on the client edition [believed]. SMB durable handles survive a LIF blip and die with smbd (C34), which matches every TrueNAS service restart that ate an open spreadsheet; the matrix says "handles lost" and it should. Previous Versions through `vfs_shadow_copy2` with `@GMT-` names is the feature my family uses without knowing its name; keep it in v0.1 and keep the `shadow:snapdir = .snapshot` line, because the default is `.snapshots` (C19).

**Debian clients.** Nothing to add; open-iscsi and cifs.ko behave as the tables say.

##### 8. The one feature, the deal-breakers, the lists

**The single feature that makes me switch:** an unplanned takeover my Proxmox cluster survives inside 10 s, with the loss printed and a held promotion that reverts by itself when the old node returns. SnapMirror plus HA on two used Dells. TrueNAS sells it for money, Ceph needs three nodes and a dozen OSDs, nothing else offers it. Everything in Phase C is the road to that.

**Deal-breakers, in order:** (1) no per-aggregate durable log in v0.1; I will not host a database on storage that cannot honour fsync anywhere. (2) `strict` as a default for Linux hosts; it breaks Proxmox volids and `base`. (3) Busy-poll or isolated cores as a requirement, or no VM profile. (4) A reformat between v0.1 and v0.2. (5) FC or S3 on the v0.1 critical path. (6) LACP as the only network shape.

**v0.1, what I want:** iSCSI with ALUA, TPGS and `LIO-ORG`/`OpenTAP` from the first LUN; NFSv3 datastore and NFSv4.1 file SVMs; SMB with Previous Versions; scheduled snapshots with retention and clone LUNs; nvfail with the four-fact printout and a same-identity clear for Linux hosts; `dump --since` to a file; mdadm over IT-mode HBAs as the reference, PERC VD as the attested fallback, HBA mode documented; the PLP-NVMe log as opt-in; a NUT hook for `UpsOnBattery` (the trigger is in the CP list, its source is not); `profile = lab`; an apt repository; Prometheus metrics; `otapctl config export` that reproduces the node.

**Never:** a vendor CLI at runtime (install-time attestation is fine); targetcli or rtslib on the box; cgroup `io.max`; a web UI before the CLI is complete; a witness in Phase C (membership `{A}` is right); a mandatory DAC (recommend, do not require); `freeze` without a power fence; auto-clear of nvfail on datastore classes; FC as a replication transport (8 to 10 engineer-weeks for 1.45 GB/s that a fifteen-dollar DAC beats is the correct burial); a `secrets.tdb` that rewinds without an alert (the `rollback_gen` check is good); and the sentence "recreate the aggregate" in any release note.


### critic:implementer

#### Phase C startability audit: crates, kernel interfaces, unsafe, tests, and a 16-week plan

Prepared by the Rust and kernel lead for Fable 5.1, 2026-10-12. Scope: the four Session 03 designs, their round-3 revisions and the forty fact-check verdicts, read against `docs/04-project-brief-async-svm.md`. Design only; nothing was installed, built or run.

**Verification method.** Every crate was checked today against the crates.io API (`https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/<name>`); three APIs the data path leans on were read on docs.rs. Kernel claims were checked at the v6.12 tag. Neither elixir.bootlin.com nor git.kernel.org was usable from this session: elixir's page conversion carries only the version navigation and never reaches the file body, and git.kernel.org's cgit `plain` endpoint answered HTTP 403 or 503 to every request, single or batched. I therefore read the byte-identical tag on the GitHub mirror, `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/<path>`; every `[verified]` below names that path, and the equivalent elixir URL is `https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v6.12/source/<path>`. Debian versions come from packages.debian.org today. Anything I did not read myself is `[believed]` or cites the fact-check that read it.

##### 1. Verdict

Phase C is startable on Monday, on three conditions. First, the on-disk and on-wire formats are frozen in week 1 with reserved space for everything the personas designed but v0.1 will not build. Second, the four Phase C work lists (11 + 10 + 8 + 9 items, almost every one with an exit test that assumes an ESXi, Proxmox, Windows, Active Directory, Veeam or QLogic lab) are replaced by the plan in section 7, which ships a single-node iSCSI and NFSv3 appliance on mdadm or one NVMe, with crash-consistent snapshots, nvfail and file-based delta dump and restore. Third, the owner takes the five decisions in section 10 before the freeze. Every crate the designs name exists at the claimed version; every kernel interface the v0.1 path depends on exists in v6.12 as described, with the corrections the fact-checks already forced (ublk user copy via plain `IORING_OP_READ`/`WRITE`, no `WritevFixed`, no `UPDATE_SIZE`, one global lockd thread, namespace pins made from the host mount namespace).

##### 4. What this audit adds to the fact-checks

1. **Bindgen drift in libublk.** The crate's `sys` module advertises `UBLK_U_CMD_UPDATE_SIZE`; the 6.12 header does not define it. Any code path that compiles because a constant exists in the crate must be gated by `GET_FEATURES`, exactly as `WritevFixed` is gated by `io_uring_probe`.
2. **No user-copy helper in libublk 0.4.8.** Neither `io` nor `helpers` documents one; C03's "libublk provides ublk_user_copy_pos" is unsupported by the docs. We own the offset arithmetic and the SQE.
3. **`v4_end_grace` has two behaviours inside "6.12".** At the tag it ends grace synchronously; on Debian's 6.12.69-1 and later (trixie ships 6.12.111-1) it schedules the laundromat and returns -EBUSY in more cases. The reconciler reads the file, writes `Y`, and polls; it never trusts the write's return code alone.
4. **md's flush path races and hides errors.** `md_flush_request` lets a data-carrying PREFLUSH bio proceed while the member flushes are still in flight and completes the parent successfully after a member flush error. The commit protocol is therefore "empty `IORING_OP_FSYNC`, await, then one FUA stripe", never a data-carrying PREFLUSH, and `md: ... flush io error` in the kernel log is treated as a CRIT by the monitor because the engine cannot see it.
5. **`nfsd_svc` rewrites the scope on every call.** Confirmed at the tag. Thread-count changes after the first start are issued from inside the SVM's pinned UTS namespace (whose nodename equals the scope) and never carry a scope attribute, which would return -EBUSY.
6. **6.12 clone is whole-table only.** `struct io_uring_clone_buffers` has no offsets, so a per-connection ring clones the full staging table once into an empty ring, and the arena is never a send source (Fabrics' round-3 position stands for a second reason).
7. **`setns` accepts a pidfd.** If bind-mounted pins ever fight propagation, a holder process plus `nsenter --target` is a kernel-supported fallback; the design keeps pins as the primary mechanism.

##### 5. Unsafe code: where it is unavoidable and how it is contained

Unavoidable unsafe, by site:

- **The arena and staging mappings.** `memmap2::MmapOptions::map_mut` on a hugetlbfs file is `unsafe` because another mapping or process can mutate the bytes. Worse, the kernel writes into slot runs asynchronously (`IORING_OP_READ` on the ublkc fd lands data in the slot after submission). A `&mut [u8]` to an in-flight slot is undefined behaviour under Rust's aliasing rules, so in-flight slots are reachable only as `*mut u8` behind an `InFlight<Slot>` token that yields a slice only after its CQE is consumed.
- **io_uring submission.** `SubmissionQueue::push` is `unsafe` (the SQE references memory the kernel reads later), as are `register_buffers` and `register_files`. Every SQE is built by a typed `Op` whose buffer or fd is owned by an RAII guard dropped on completion.
- **The slot page.** The 4 KiB `MAP_SHARED` seqlock page written by `otap-ctl` and read on every I/O needs raw atomics over mapped memory.
- **Namespaces.** `unshare_unsafe` and the raw `setns` are `unsafe` in rustix because they change assumptions every thread holds; `pivot_root` and `sethostname` from nix are safe wrappers. These live in a 200-line binary (`otap-nsinit`) and in one `nbladed` module that enters a namespace on a dedicated thread after `unshare(CLONE_FS)`.
- **ioctls without a typed wrapper.** `FIFREEZE`/`FITHAW` and `BLKDISCARD` go through `rustix::ioctl` with a hand-written opcode type, which is `unsafe`; `BLKSSZGET`-class getters have safe wrappers [believed].
- **Vendored SIMD.** crc-fast, blake3 and zerocopy carry their own unsafe; we audit by version pin, not by code.

Containment rules, enforced by CI:

1. Exactly one crate, `otap-sys`, lacks `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; every other crate in the workspace carries it, and `clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks` is `deny` so each block has a `// SAFETY:` comment naming the invariant.
2. `otap-sys` exports only owning types (`Arena`, `SlotRun`, `Ring<'static>`, `Op`, `SlotPage`, `NsHandle`) whose safe methods encode the lifetime rules; engine crates never see a raw pointer.
3. The slot allocator, `SlotRun` splitting and the seqlock page run under Miri (heap-backed fake arena) and loom 0.7.2 (seqlock reader against writer) on every merge.
4. The two parsers that face untrusted bytes, `otap-format` (on-disk) and `otap-stream` (on-wire), are safe code built on zerocopy's `FromBytes`/`IntoBytes` views and fuzzed with libfuzzer-sys 0.4.13 nightly for one CPU-hour each.
5. Each reactor runs under `catch_unwind`; a panic in a reactor aborts the process (`panic = "abort"` is not set, so the arena re-attach path is exercised instead of relying on it never happening).
6. `cargo geiger` output is attached to every release as a count that must not grow without a review note.

##### 6. Test strategy

###### 6.1 Property tests that freeze the format

`otap-format` is its own crate, frozen in week 1, with `FORMAT_MAJOR = 2`. Every structure (superblock, intent slot, stripe summary header and entry, CP log record, map page and page-index entry, segment table, snapshot table, stream envelope and records) is a `repr(C)` zerocopy view with `const` assertions on `size_of` and field offsets, so a layout change fails to compile. Three test layers: proptest 1.12.0 strategies per structure with 100,000 cases per merge and 1,000,000 nightly, asserting encode, decode and re-encode are byte-identical and that every CRC covers every non-reserved byte; golden vectors (`tests/vectors/*.bin` plus a blake3 manifest) decoded and re-encoded byte-exact, so any semantic change needs a new vector and a `FORMAT_MINOR` bump in the same commit; and an N/N-1 lane that decodes the previous minor's vectors. Reserved regions are explicit zeroed fields covered by the CRC: the superblock reserves the `reloc_index`, `inbound[]`, `nvfail_cause[]` and `rollback_gen[]` space Storage designed, the summary entry carries the 2-bit `kind` and 2 reserved bits, and the stream header carries `cp_id`, `owner_epoch` and the codec byte, so Phase B and Phase 3 land without a major bump.

###### 6.2 Crash consistency with dm-log-writes and dm-flakey

Both targets exist in v6.12 (`log-writes` 1.1.0, `flakey` 1.5.0, verified above) and Debian ships them in-box (brief, Appendix A). The harness stacks `log-writes` over a loop device (or over md over loops) under the engine's `Backstore`, and the engine sends `dmsetup message <dev> 0 mark cp<N>` after every superblock completion. The workload is fio through the ublk device plus the checker's model. Replay with xfstests' `replay-log` (built from source in the CI image) to every mark and to 1,000 random bio boundaries between marks, then run the recovery path read-only: the max-select superblock must verify, the recovered image must equal a seq-prefix of the checker's acknowledged writes, and any XFS inside a NAS volume must mount clean at marks and replay without error between them. The log also proves the flusher's geometry promise: every data bio in the log must be stripe-aligned and stripe-sized, which replaces the "zero member reads" exit test that needs a real array. dm-flakey injects the torn-superblock and torn-stripe cases (`drop_writes` and `corrupt_bio_byte` during a commit window) to prove the fall-back to CP N-1 and the two-CP deferred reuse. A deterministic in-process fault injector on the `Backstore` trait (reorder, drop after a point, duplicate) covers the same invariants without a kernel, so the kernel lane runs nightly and the trait lane runs per merge.

###### 6.3 Daemon simulation: madsim where it fits, a trait simulator where it does not

madsim 0.2.34 simulates tokio-shaped `net`, `fs`, `time`, `rand` and `task` with `buggify` fault injection [verified: docs.rs/madsim/0.2.34]; it cannot stand in for io_uring, ublk, configfs or hugetlbfs. It therefore covers `otap-ctl` (state store, reconciler scheduling, lease logic that Phase B will add) and `nbladed`'s control logic with a fake `Platform` trait behind the configfs, netns and systemd writers. `dbladed` gets its own deterministic simulator, `otap-sim`: the engine core is written against `Backstore`, `FrontDoor` (the ublk queue), `Clock` and `Net` traits, and `otap-sim` provides single-threaded implementations driven by a seeded scheduler that chooses which pending completion fires next, with crash points between any two trait calls. The invariants are the same as 6.2 plus "no acknowledged write is lost across a re-attach" and "`diff(base)` equals the model". 10,000 seeds per merge, 1,000,000 nightly. turmoil 0.7.2 is used only for the stream's `TokioTcp` test transport (partition, duplicate, reorder across connections); the production `TlsTcp` transport on io_uring is exercised by the loopback test in 6.5.

###### 6.4 CI without storage hardware

Containers cannot host ublk (CAP_SYS_ADMIN plus the `ublk_drv` module) or LIO, so the CI lane is a Debian 13 cloud image under QEMU/KVM with `linux-image-amd64` 6.12.111-1, 4 vCPUs, 6 GB, 64 huge pages (a 128 MiB arena; the arena size is a profile value, never a constant), eight 2 GiB sparse qcow2 disks presented as virtio-blk, and `modprobe ublk_drv ublks_max=256`. On that VM the lane builds md RAID6 4+2 from four of the disks (real raid5.c geometry and `md_flush_request` behaviour), a single-device aggregate from a fifth, dm-log-writes and dm-flakey over the rest, a LIO iSCSI target in an SVM netns with open-iscsi in a second netns as the initiator, and knfsd in the SVM with a Debian NFSv3 client in the second netns. Performance numbers are recorded, never asserted; the only timing gates are functional (re-attach under 2 s, SVM start under 5 s). The one physical lab box runs the nightly performance lane; the development PC is not target hardware and is never used for either (brief, section 6).

###### 6.5 Loopback replication on one node

Two aggregates in one `dbladed` (two loop devices in CI, two partitions on the lab box). A `DeltaSource` on aggregate 0 feeds the real `TlsTcp` `DeltaStream` to 127.0.0.1:7430, where the receiver reactor of the same process lands into aggregate 1's `DeltaSink` through the ordinary CP assembler with shadow roots and `ShipApply`. fio writes through aggregate 0's ublk device while the harness takes a snapshot every 20 CPs. Checks: after every `Committed`, a blake3 over the pinned root at the common CP is equal on both sides; `kill -9` of the whole process at 50 random points (including between staging and the superblock write, which must yield exactly one discarded partial by `cp_id` mismatch); `ss -K` on the connection resumes from the receiver's chunk bitmap with a duplicate count equal to the resend count; a test hook that flips one byte in a chunk produces `Abort(Corrupt)` and a clean resend. The same harness drives `otapctl volume dump --since <snap>` to a file and `restore` into aggregate 1, which is the user-visible v0.1 feature; the TCP path is a test vehicle until Phase B.

Two engineers: E1 owns the engine and kernel data path, E2 owns platform, control and protocols. Each week ends with the named exit test green in CI; a red exit test stops the next week's new work.

With one engineer the two columns serialize: the engine column alone is weeks 1 to 7 and 9 to 11 (about 11 weeks), the platform column adds about 7 weeks, so v0.1 lands around week 18 with NFSv3 still in, or at week 14 if v0.1 is declared iSCSI-only and NFSv3 moves to v0.1.1. I recommend two engineers and the table as written; the single-engineer variant is a 14-week iSCSI-only appliance.

Milestones for the owner's calendar: M1 (end of week 2) the format is frozen and the arena survives `kill -9`; M2 (week 5) crash consistency proven on md; M3 (week 7) a client can log in over iSCSI and nvfail works; M4 (week 9) NFSv3 datastores and snapshots; M5 (week 12) v0.1.

##### 8. Where the personas' plans are fantasy

The four Phase C lists are good Phase C+B+3 designs with Phase C labels. Specific items that cannot be done by one or two engineers in 16 weeks, or cannot be tested without a lab the project does not have:

- **Storage items 4, 8 and 9.** The PERC write-through knee needs a PERC with large-IO firmware and a 2 MiB-stripe VD; cost-benefit GC with logical segments and relocation tables (round-3 section 3.4) is a Phase 3 allocator; snapshots as NAS objects need fsfreeze, read-only ublk devices per snapshot, per-snapshot `fsid=` exports and Samba `vfs_shadow_copy2` verified from Windows 11. Each is three to five engineer-weeks and none is on the v0.1 critical path. The "1.2 GB/s empty with zero member reads" exit needs a 12-drive RAID6; the log-writes alignment assertion is the testable form. "50 real power cuts" needs a switched PDU; five on the lab box plus 1,000 dm-flakey cuts is the honest version.
- **Protocols C4 to C10.** The client matrix (ESXi 8.0 U3, Proxmox 8.4 and 9.1, Windows 11 24H2, Debian, two AD domains, Veeam 12 or 13, QLogic HBAs) with 24-hour soaks and 100 restart cycles per client is a qualification programme for a team, not an exit test for two people. The `otap-nsexec` capability and seccomp wrapper (Fabrics P4) is a security project with a per-daemon profile to maintain; v0.1 runs tenant daemons as root inside the view and says so. The BUILTIN and well-known SID seeding (C33) is correct and belongs with AD, which is not in v0.1.
- **Fabrics items 3 to 8.** Everything FC needs QLE2562 and QLE2692 pairs, a Brocade or Cisco switch, an ESXi host with qlnativefc at or above 5.4.80 and a Proxmox 9.1 pair. The owner's "protocol step 3" survives as a sequence, but step 3 is v0.2 work: nothing in it is reachable from CI, and the kernel-side facts are now verified so no design risk is retired by building it early. Item 2's 1 GB/s intra-node stream target needs a flash box; the loopback test measures, it does not assert.
- **Consensus items 1, 7, 8 and 9.** openraft single-voter integration is one to two weeks of storage-trait and snapshot plumbing with no functional payoff in Phase C (the fsync-per-change and the slot page need redb and a seqlock, not a log); the Apalache model and the madsim harness "for 1 and 3 voters", the arm64 witness lane with a three-member CI cluster and the membership-change dry run are Phase B work. They are the right Phase B week-1 items precisely because they do not depend on Phase C code.
- **Cross-cutting.** The engine acknowledgement budget (p50 under 5 us, p99 under 15 us busy-polled) assumes isolated cores and is unmeasurable in a VM; it is a lab measurement published with the release, not a gate. The 64 GB memory table is sound but every size in it must be a profile value so the 6 GB CI VM runs the same binary. Three personas still budget time for the three-way disagreements in their section 5 (hold release, root-volume class, `no_path_retry`); none of them affects v0.1 and all of them should be parked with the Phase B timer table.

##### 9. What to cut to ship v0.1 in 12 to 16 weeks

v0.1 is: one node; aggregates on mdadm RAID1/5/6 or a single NVMe/SATA device (a hardware-RAID VD only through manual geometry plus an operator-attested write-back cache, nothing automatic); one or more SVMs with net, UTS and mount namespaces; iSCSI LUNs (`Native4k`, plus `Esxi512e` by shadow read-modify-write at ingest); NFSv3 datastore SVMs; crash-consistent snapshots with clone LUNs and a schedule; nvfail in conservative mode; `dump --since`/`restore` as backup and as the replication bridge; `otapctl`; a `.deb`. Cut or deferred, in order of how much time each saves:

1. Fibre Channel in any form (saves about 8 weeks of lab-bound work).
2. S3, versitygw, Veeam Object Lock (3 weeks).
3. AD-joined SMB, winbind, idmap seeding; SMB standalone becomes the first stretch item (3 weeks).
4. NFSv4.1 file SVM with `nfsdcld`, early grace end and the courteous-server measurements (2 weeks).
5. Snapshot exposure to NAS: `.otap/snap` mounts, per-snapshot exports, Previous Versions, fsfreeze (3 weeks).
6. Cost-benefit GC, logical segments and relocation tables, scrub; v0.1 keeps a simple cleaner and read-time CRC verification (3 weeks).
7. Precise nvfail intent slots; v0.1 ships `conservative` (1 week).
8. Per-volume QoS token bucket, bdi limits, slice tuning beyond template defaults (1 week).
9. openraft single-voter, TLA+/Apalache, three-voter madsim, arm64 witness lane, membership dry run; v0.1's control plane is redb behind `StateStore` with the same `ClusterState` types (2 to 3 weeks).
10. `otap-nsexec` hardening, seccomp profiles (1 week).
11. Automatic hardware-RAID handling: VPD B0 parsing, the full probe ladder, learn-cycle telemetry, perccli parsing (2 weeks).
12. Stream extras: compression, multiple connections, endpoint fallback, the receiver as a user feature; v0.1 ships TLS on one connection in the test harness only (2 weeks).
13. The client qualification matrix; v0.1 is tested against Debian 13 initiators and clients in CI plus one ESXi host if the owner has one.

Everything cut keeps its format reservation and its trait slot, so none of it needs a format bump when it returns in v0.1.x or v0.2.

##### 10. Decisions the owner must take before Monday

1. **Envelope plus stripe-image payload** (Fabrics item 0): the stream header is Fabrics' 64-byte frame, the chunk is Storage's stripe image with the 2-bit `kind` and the per-stripe volume bitmap in the summary. The week-1 freeze depends on it.
2. **Full-stripe allocation for every pool write** on md parity levels, with no mandatory `--write-journal`, tested by the forced dirty-degraded assembly in week 5; the journal becomes mandatory only if that test loses a committed block (Storage's round-3 position; C21 is the counter-argument).
3. **nvfail class defaults for v0.1**: LUN `on`, NFSv3 datastore `on`, everything else `alert`, all in `conservative` intent mode (D5 as it applies to a single node).
4. **Control plane for v0.1**: redb behind `StateStore` now, openraft as Phase B week 1, accepting that the Phase C binary is not byte-identical to Phase B's control plane (a departure from the standing round-2 decision, made for schedule).
5. **One or two engineers.** The table in section 7 assumes two; with one, v0.1 is iSCSI-only at week 14 and NFSv3 follows in v0.1.1.

Given those five, the first commit on Monday is `otap-format` with its golden vectors, and nothing else is written until its tests are green.
